docs.title: Fast backends in Dart
docs.text:
Everything your Dart backend needs.

Build APIs and full web apps in Dart, with batteries included. Routing, an ORM, validation, auth and a CLI work from the first command. One command adds the rest: queues, mail, GraphQL and more. Your app uses every CPU core and ships as one small native binary.

Build your first API Star on GitHub

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Fast by default

    A native HTTP server, one isolate per CPU core and streamed bodies. dox build makes one native binary. See Performance.

  • ORM and query builder

    Models, relations, migrations and transactions for Postgres, MySQL/MariaDB and SQLite. Postgres and MySQL use native drivers. See Database.

  • Typed validation

    Write a @Dto class. Dox checks the input and gives your controller a typed object. See Validation.

  • OpenAPI

    OpenAPI 3.1 docs and a Scalar docs page, made from your routes and DTOs. See dox_openapi.

  • File storage

    Local disk and S3 behind one API, with signed URLs. See dox_storage.

  • Cache

    Memory, file and Redis cache with tags and locks. See dox_cache.

  • Real time

    Socket.IO, with Redis for many servers.

  • Security

    JWT authentication, CORS, encryption and hashing.

  • CLI

    Create projects, controllers, models and migrations. Run, build and migrate. See CLI reference.

docs.title: One path for every request
docs.text:
1. Routematch the URL
  2. Middlewarego on or stop
  3. DTOcheck the input
  4. Controlleryour code
  5. Viewrender a page
  6. Responsesend the answer

Each card is a page in "The basics". See How Dox works for every step.

docs.title: What the code looks like
docs.text:
Route.post('/blogs', (BlogController c) => c.store);

@Inject() // 1
class BlogController {
  BlogController(this.blogs);
  final BlogService blogs;

  Future<Blog> store(CreateBlog input) { // 2
    return blogs.create(input);
  }
}

@Dto() // 3
class CreateBlog {
  @Length(min: 3, max: 100)
  final String title;

  @MinLength(10)
  final String body;
  ...
}
  1. Dox makes the controller and gives it the service it asks for. There is no reflection and no list of classes to keep.
  2. Ask for the DTO as a parameter. Dox reads the JSON body, checks it, and gives you a typed object. Bad input gets a 422 before your code runs.
  3. @Dto() marks an input class. The code generator writes the checks from the fields, their types and their rules.

docs.title: Run it in two minutes
docs.text:
You need Dart 3.13 or newer, and nothing else. The starter project uses SQLite, so there is no database to install.

Start the app
dart pub global activate dox   # install the CLI
dox create my_app              # download the starter project
cd my_app
dart pub get
dox s                          # start the server
In a second terminal, call the first route
curl localhost:3000/ping

pong

That is a Dox app. Next, follow the tutorial. It adds a model, a database table, validation, login and a Docker image, one short step at a time.

The CLI is not found?

dart pub global activate puts dox in $HOME/.pub-cache/bin. Add that folder to your PATH. See Installation.

docs.title: Contribute
docs.text:
This page shows how to work on Dox: set up the repo, run the tests, release packages and update the docs.

To send a change, fork the repo and open a pull request. The release parts are for maintainers.

docs.title: 1. Clone the repo
docs.text: git clone git@github.com:dartondox/dox.git

docs.title: 2. Install melos
docs.text:
The repo is a Dart pub workspace. Melos runs the commands for all packages, with its config in the root pubspec.yaml. You need Dart 3.13 or newer.

dart pub global activate melos

docs.title: 3. Run melos bootstrap
docs.text:
This gets the packages at the root and links all local packages:

melos bs

docs.title: 4. Run the tests and checks
docs.text:
Run the checks of CI before you open a pull request:

# Run all tests (not `melos test`, a built-in melos command)
melos run test

# Analyze and check format (same as CI)
melos run analyze
melos run format_check

docs.title: If the project does not run
docs.text:
If melos bs fails or the packages do not resolve, start clean:

  1. Remove pubspec.lock and .dart_tool at the root.
  2. Remove any old pubspec_overrides.yaml and pubspec.lock in packages/*.
  3. Run melos bs again.

docs.title: Release (maintainers)
docs.text: The Release workflow (.github/workflows/publish.yaml) publishes one package to pub.dev with automated publishing. Each package has its own version and its own tag, in the form <package>-v<version>.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
The full guide is RELEASING.md in the repo. In short, for each package that changed:

  1. Run bin/bump.sh <package> <version>. It sets the version of that package only. Raise the constraint of a newer sibling by hand. Then close the Unreleased section of its CHANGELOG.md.
  2. Merge the release PR, then push the tag <package>-v<version>. This publishes that package to pub.dev. Release in dependency order: dox_annotation, dox_cache, dox_builder, dox_core.
  3. Release the matching dox-sample template.

A fix in the builder needs only a dox_builder release. Many packages are in other repos. See Packages in other repos and Native packages.

For a new package, publish the first version by hand with dart pub publish. Then turn on automated publishing for it. See One-time setup.

docs.title: What the workflow does
docs.text:
1. It reads the package name and the version from the tag. It stops with an error for an unknown package or a bad version.
  2. It checks that the version in packages/<folder>/pubspec.yaml is the tag version. If not, it stops, so run bin/bump.sh <package> <version> and try again.
  3. It runs the tests, and they must pass. Then it checks that the sibling packages it needs are on pub.dev. If not, it stops with "release first".
  4. It checks that one package with a dry run, then publishes it.

    5. The workflow skips a version that is already on pub.dev. So if a run fails, fix the problem and click "Re-run jobs".

    To see the packages in publish order on your machine:

    python3 bin/publish_order.py

docs.title: Dry run
docs.text: To check a release with no publish, open Actions > Release > "Run workflow" and pick one package, or all. It runs dart pub publish --dry-run. Warnings show in yellow and do not fail the run.

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text:
Do this once for each published package, and for every new package before its first tag. python3 bin/publish_order.py lists the packages.

On pub.dev:

  1. Open https://pub.dev/packages/<name>/admin.
  2. Under "Automated publishing", click "Enable publishing from GitHub Actions".
  3. Repository: dartondox/dox.
  4. Tag pattern: <package>-v{{version}}, like dox_core-v{{version}}. Each package has its own pattern.
  5. Tick "Require GitHub Actions environment" and set the environment to pub.dev.
  6. Save.

On GitHub, in dartondox/dox > Settings > Environments, there must be an environment named pub.dev, because the publish job runs in it. Optional: add yourself as a required reviewer, and allow only the tags dox_annotation-v*, dox_builder-v*, dox_cache-v* and dox_core-v*.

docs.title: Packages in other repos
docs.text:
Package Repo dox (the CLI) dartondox/dox-cli dox_orm, dox_migration, dox_cache_database dartondox/dox-orm dox_auth dartondox/dox-auth dox_openapi dartondox/dox-openapi dox_validation dartondox/dox-validation dox_socketio dartondox/dox-socketio dox_storage dartondox/dox-storage dox_queue, dox_queue_database dartondox/dox-queue dox_scheduler dartondox/dox-scheduler dox_inertia dartondox/dox-inertia dox_view dartondox/dox-view dox_mailer dartondox/dox-mailer

The packages in this repo use them from pub.dev. dox_core uses dox_openapi and dox_validation. The database tests run in dox-orm. CI in this repo tests with their newest code: it runs ci/clone-siblings.sh, then ci/use-siblings.sh.

To work on one of them and Dox together:

  1. Clone the repos next to the Dox repo, like ../dox-orm. ci/clone-siblings.sh clones dox-orm, dox-auth, dox-openapi, dox-validation, dox-socketio, dox-storage, dox-queue, dox-scheduler and dox-cli. Clone dox-mailer, dox-view and dox-inertia by hand when you need them.

  2. Add them to the root pubspec_overrides.yaml of the Dox repo. Git ignores this file. For dox_openapi and dox_validation, ci/use-siblings.sh writes it for you.

    dependency_overrides:
  dox_openapi:
    path: ../dox-openapi
  dox_validation:
    path: ../dox-validation

  3. Run dart pub get.

The apps in examples/ use these clones, so clone them before you run an example. In the other repo, a pubspec_overrides.yaml that points to ../dox/packages/... uses your local Dox packages.

Each of these repos has its own version. To release one, push a v<version> tag in that repo.

docs.title: Native packages
docs.text:
The three native packages live in their own repos:

Package Repo dox_http_native dartondox/dox-http-native dox_postgres_native dartondox/dox-postgres-native dox_mysql_native dartondox/dox-mysql-native

Dox uses them from pub.dev. Their build hooks download ready-built libraries, so you do not need Rust to work on Dox.

To work on a native package and Dox together:

  1. Clone the package next to the Dox repo, like ../dox-http-native.

  2. Add it to the root pubspec_overrides.yaml of the Dox repo. Git ignores this file.

    dependency_overrides:
  dox_http_native:
    path: ../dox-http-native

  3. Run dart pub get.

Each native package is released from its own repo, with its own version. Push a v<version> tag in that repo. Its CI builds the libraries, uploads them, fills the hashes and publishes the package to pub.dev. Then raise the version constraint in the Dox packages that use it.

docs.title: Docs
docs.text:
The docs site is https://dartondox.dev. It is built with MkDocs Material and mike, which keeps one folder per version on the gh-pages branch.

URL What it is /<version>/... the docs of one version, built from main /latest/... a copy of the newest version / redirects to /latest/ old links like /the-basic/routing/ redirect to /latest/the-basic/routing/

docs.title: Write and preview
docs.text:
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
.venv/bin/mkdocs serve           # live preview of this branch
.venv/bin/mkdocs build --strict  # the same build as CI. Broken links fail.

The build hook hooks/docs_hooks.py writes llms.txt and llms-full.txt. Each pull request that changes the docs runs the Docs check workflow, with three checks:

  • mkdocs build --strict
  • a spell check: codespell docs --skip "*.svg,*.png,*.ico,*.css,*.js" --ignore-words .codespell-ignore
  • ci/check-no-tabs.sh: the docs must not use content tabs

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
• The docs deploy with each release. The Docs workflow (.github/workflows/docs.yaml) runs on a dox_core-v<version> tag, the same tag that publishes dox_core, and runs mike deploy. So docs for a feature that is not released yet stay off the site.
  • To deploy the docs only, push a docs-v<version> tag on main. It publishes no package and runs no tests.
  • After each deploy, the workflow writes the redirect pages, the root index.html, a 404.html and the CNAME file.
  • The workflow pushes with the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN, so gh-pages must not be a protected branch.

docs.title: Meet Doxie
docs.text: Doxie is the official mascot of Dox. Doxie is a blue dachshund.

docs.title: Why a dachshund
docs.text:
"Doxie" is a common nickname for a dachshund. It sounds like Dox, so the name came first.

A dachshund is small, fast and full of energy. Dox tries to be the same: a small native binary that serves a lot of requests.

docs.title: Logo and mascot
docs.text:
Dox has a logo and a mascot, with different jobs:

Logo Mascot What A hexagon with a "D" cut out Doxie, the blue dachshund Where The docs header, the favicon, the README, pub.dev The home page, social cards, talks, stickers Files logo.svg (white, for dark backgrounds) mascot.png (transparent background)

Use the logo in a small space, like an icon or an avatar. Doxie has too much detail for 16 or 32 pixels.

docs.title: Use Doxie
docs.text: You can use Doxie when you write or talk about Dox: blog posts, slides, videos and stickers. Do not change the colors of Doxie, and do not use Doxie for another product.

docs.title: Showcase
docs.text: This page lists real open source apps built with Dox that you can read, run and copy from.

docs.title: Monthly Expense
docs.text:
Monthly Expense is an expense tracker for you and the people you share money with. You log expenses, track wallets in many currencies and keep a shopping list. An AI assistant like Claude can add expenses and read summaries for you over MCP.

Part What it uses API Dox, with SQLite or Postgres Web app React, Vite, Tailwind and shadcn/ui Sign-in Firebase (Google), checked on every API request AI An MCP server with OAuth sign-in, 44 tools Deploy One Docker image with the web app and a native API binary

What you can learn from it:

  • ORM and migrations. Groups, members, categories, expenses, wallets and budgets as models. The app runs the migrations when it starts. See Model and Migration.
  • Token auth from another service. The API checks a Firebase ID token in middleware. It makes the user on the first sign-in. See Middleware.
  • MCP for AI clients. Each HTTP route has a matching MCP tool with the same input. See MCP.
  • Scheduled jobs. See Scheduler.
  • One container in production. The API serves the built web app and compiles to a native binary. CI runs the tests on SQLite and Postgres, then pushes the image. See Docker.

Run it on your machine:

git clone https://github.com/necessarylion/monthly-expense.git
cd monthly-expense
./dev.sh

The README lists the Firebase settings and env vars you need first.

docs.title: Coming from Laravel
docs.text:
This page shows the Laravel way and the Dox way side by side, so a Laravel developer can find the Dox name for each thing.

Most ideas have the same name in Dox. The Laravel code here is Laravel 11. For the big changes, read What is different.

docs.title: Routing
Controllers
docs.text:
Laravel Dox php artisan make:controller BlogController dox make:controller Blog php artisan make:controller BlogController --resource dox make:controller Blog -r (or --resource) php artisan make:controller BlogController --api dox make:controller Blog --api php artisan make:controller BlogController --model=Blog dox make:controller Blog --model=Blog public function show(Request $request, int $id) Future<Blog?> show(DoxRequest req, int id) public function store(StoreBlogRequest $request) Future<Blog> store(CreateBlog body) constructor injection by the service container constructor injection by the container: @Inject() above the class method injection filled by type: DoxRequest, one @Dto class, path params, models, container classes implicit route model binding the same: a User user parameter loads {user} by its key

Dox fills a parameter by its type, not by its name. Path params go by position. A controller can be a class method, a static method or a plain function.

The container is generated code, not reflection. See Dependency injection.

docs.title: Middleware
Requests and validation
Responses

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
With dox_view, templates end in .dox.html. Most Blade tags have the same name. A block ends with @end.

A Blade name that is not a Dox tag, like @foreach or @endif, is printed as text. Dox writes a warning to stderr that names the template, the line and the Dox way. See Coming from Blade.

Laravel Blade Dox {{ $user->name }}, {!! $html !!} {{ user.name }}, {{{ html }}} @if ... @endif, @foreach ($users as $user) @if ... @end, @each(user in users) ... @end @isset, @empty, @auth, @guest, @env, @production, @once, @verbatim the same names, closed with @end @class, @checked, @selected, @disabled the same @include('nav'), @include('card', ['title' => 'Hi']) @include('nav'), @include('card', { title: 'Hi' }) @includeWhen($user, 'account') @includeWhen(user, 'account') $loop->iteration, $loop->remaining, $loop->even, $loop->parent $loop.iteration, $loop.remaining, $loop.even, $loop.parent @json($data), Js::from($data) @json(data), {{ json(data) }} @error('email') {{ $message }} @enderror @error('email') {{ message }} @end <x-button>, $attributes->merge([...]), $slot @button(...) ... @end, $attributes.merge({...}), $slot @extends('layouts.app'), @section ... @endsection, @yield('content') @extends('layouts/app'), @section ... @end, @yield('content') @stack('scripts'), @push ... @endpush, @prepend ... @endprepend @stack('scripts'), @push ... @end, @prepend ... @end @csrf, @method('PUT'), old('email') @csrf, @method('PUT'), old('email') Blade::directive('datetime', ...) View.directive('datetime', DateTimeDirective())

Three things are not the same as in Blade:

  • @includeIf(condition, 'name') in Dox takes a condition first. It does not check if the template exists.
  • {{ true }} prints true, a variable that does not exist prints nothing, and the text '0' is true. Turn on the bladeOutput, strictVariables and stringZeroIsFalse options to work like Blade. See Strict options.
  • @json is safe in a <script> block and in an attribute in single quotes, not in an attribute in double quotes.

docs.title: Migrations and schema
Artisan vs the dox CLI
docs.text:
Laravel Dox laravel new blog dox create blog php artisan serve dox serve (or dox s), with hot restart and build_runner watch php artisan make:resource dox make:serializer php artisan key:generate dox key:generate php artisan route:list dox route:list (also --json) php artisan tinker not there php artisan optimize dox build (one native binary in build/bundle) php artisan queue:work dox queue:work php artisan schedule:work dox schedule:work php artisan schedule:clear-cache dox schedule:clear-cache

The make:* and migrate commands are in the tables above. Two commands have no Laravel twin: dox build_runner:build makes the generated code, and dox env:generate makes the typed env class. See Dox CLI.

docs.title: Auth
docs.text:
Laravel Dox config/auth.php guards and providers Auth.initialize(AuthConfig(guards: ...)) in a provider Auth::attempt(['email' => $e, 'password' => $p]) await Auth().attempt(<String, dynamic>{'email': e, 'password': p}) gives a token (an access token or a JWT, by the guard), or null Auth::login($user) Auth().login(user) gives a JWT. With access tokens, use Auth().createAccessToken(user) Auth::user() req.auth?.user<User>() Auth::id() req.auth?.id() Auth::guest() req.auth == null Auth::check() Auth().check() (the same as isLoggedIn()) Auth::once($credentials) await Auth().once(credentials) gives true or false, with no token and no session Auth::attempt(...) for a web page (session) await Auth().attemptSession(req, <String, dynamic>{...}) gives true or false Auth::logout() Auth().logout(req) for a session. For a token: await Auth().revokeToken(req) ->middleware('auth:sanctum') AuthMiddleware() from dox_auth ->middleware('auth:web,api') AuthMiddleware(guards: <String>['web', 'api']) ->middleware('guest') GuestMiddleware(redirectTo: '/dashboard') Crypt::encryptString($v), Crypt::decryptString($v) Crypt.encryptString(v), Crypt.decryptString(v) Hash::make($p), Hash::check($p, $hash) Hash.make(p), Hash.check(p, hash) (or Hash.verify)

For an API, use access tokens (AccessTokenAuthDriver). They work like Sanctum tokens. JWT is also available.

  • dox auth:tokens-table makes the auth_access_tokens table.
  • $user->createToken('cli', ['posts:read']) is Auth().createAccessToken(user, name: 'cli', abilities: <String>['posts:read']).
  • $request->user()->tokenCan('posts:read') is (req.auth as Auth).tokenCan('posts:read').
  • To renew a token, use rotateAccessToken.

For web pages, a guard with SessionAuthDriver keeps the login in the session cookie. See Authentication.

docs.title: Cache
docs.text:
Laravel Dox config/cache.php lib/config/cache.dart, CacheConfig(defaultStore:, stores:) Cache::put('k', $v, 600) await Cache().put('k', v, duration: Duration(minutes: 10)). The time is a named duration:, not the third value. Cache::many(['a', 'b']), Cache::putMany([...], 600) await Cache().many(<String>['a', 'b']), await Cache().putMany(<String, Object?>{...}, duration: ...) Cache::get('k', 'default') await Cache().get('k', 'default') Cache::remember('k', 600, fn) await Cache().remember('k', Duration(minutes: 10), fn) Cache::forget('k') await Cache().forget('k') Cache::store('redis') Cache().store('redis') Cache::tags(['a']) Cache().tags(<String>['a']) Cache::lock('k', 10) Cache().lock('k', Duration(seconds: 10)) drivers: file, redis, memcached, database, array drivers: file, redis, memory, database (dox_cache_database), null

A value must be a JSON type. The memory store is per isolate. See Cache.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Laravel Dox config/filesystems.php disks lib/config/storage.dart, StorageConfig(defaultDisk:, disks:), passed to a StorageProvider (dox_storage) Storage::put('a.txt', $bytes) await Storage().put('a.txt', bytes, exact: true) Storage::putFile('avatars', $file) await Storage().putFile('avatars', file) Storage::putFileAs('avatars', $file, 'u1.png') await Storage().putFileAs('avatars', file, 'u1.png') $request->file('f')->store('avatars') await file.store('avatars') $request->file('f')->storeAs('avatars', 'u1.png') await file.storeAs('avatars', 'u1.png') Storage::get($path) await Storage().get(path) Storage::exists($path) / missing($path) await Storage().exists(path) / missing(path) Storage::delete($path) await Storage().delete(path) Storage::copy($from, $to) / move($from, $to) await Storage().copy(from, to) / move(from, to) Storage::files($dir) / allFiles($dir) await Storage().files(dir) / allFiles(dir) Storage::directories($dir) / deleteDirectory($dir) await Storage().directories(dir) / deleteDirectory(dir) Storage::setVisibility($path, 'private') await Storage().setVisibility(path, Visibility.private) Storage::url($path) await Storage().url(path) Storage::temporaryUrl($path, now()->addMinutes(10)) await Storage().signedUrl(path, expiresIn: Duration(minutes: 10)) Storage::disk('s3') Storage().disk('s3') Storage::download($path, $name) return Storage().download(path, name: name); drivers: local, s3, ftp, sftp drivers: local, s3 (also R2, MinIO, Spaces), memory

Three things are different from Laravel:

  • On a local disk, setVisibility() changes the file mode only when the disk has 'permissions': true. Without it, a private file is not private on the disk.
  • Paths that Dox gives you start with /, for example from putFile, store and files.
  • put() returns nothing, and download() takes no headers. For headers, wrap it in response(...) and add .header(...).

See File Storage.

docs.title: Config and .env
docs.text:
Laravel Dox config/*.php files lib/config/*.dart files, put together in AppConfig env('APP_KEY') env.appKey (a getter in lib/config/env.dart) env('APP_PORT', 3000) env.appPort (the default is in the getter: int get appPort => 3000;) config('app.name') env.appName from the typed env class (@DoxEnv()) php artisan config:cache not needed. The typed env is read once, at start.

The typed env class gives you an int for APP_PORT, and a build error for a bad type. If a key is missing, the app stops at start and lists every missing key. See Environment Variables.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Laravel Dox php artisan test dart test $this->get('/api/ping')->assertStatus(200) (await client.get('/api/ping')).expectStatus(200) with DoxTestClient RefreshDatabase run the migrations in setUpAll, then setUp(refreshDatabase) from package:dox_orm/testing.dart Storage::fake('s3') Storage.manager.fake('s3') Mail::fake() Mail.fake(), then mail.assertSent() and mail.assertQueued() Queue::fake() Queue.fake(), then queue.assertPushed<T>() Cache::fake() Dox().cache = CacheManager(CacheConfig(...)) with a memory store $this->actingAs($user) client.withToken(token) with a token from Auth().createAccessToken(user) (access tokens) or Auth().login(user) (JWT)

Dox has no fake HTTP kernel. Instead, DoxTestClient.start(appConfig) starts the real server inside the test on a free port, and sends real requests. See Testing.

docs.title: What is different
docs.text:
• A generated container. You add @Inject() to a class, and build_runner writes the registrations in lib/generated/container.g.dart. A singleton is one instance per isolate.
  • Isolates, not PHP-FPM workers. One process runs one isolate per CPU core, and each isolate keeps its state between requests. Data that must be shared goes to the database, Redis or files. See How Dox works.
  • Code generation, not reflection. build_runner writes the model code, the DTO checks, the env class and the OpenAPI docs. Run dox build_runner:build after a change, or let dox serve watch.
  • One native binary. dox build makes an AOT binary in build/bundle, with no vendor folder on the server. The Docker image is approximately 11 MB.
  • A native HTTP server and native database drivers, written in Rust. They come ready-built, so you do not need Rust.
  • Types everywhere. A DTO has typed fields, a path param is an integer, and the compiler finds many mistakes.
  • Explicit async. Database calls return a Future, and one isolate serves many requests while it waits.
  • JSON API first. For HTML pages, add views or Inertia.

docs.title: What is missing today
docs.text:
Dox does not have these Laravel features yet:

  • events and listeners (model events are there)
  • password reset

See What Dox does not have yet for what to use today.

docs.title: Dox and the other Dart backends
docs.text:
This page compares Dox with five other ways to build a backend in Dart: Dart Frog, Serverpod, Shelf (with shelf_router), Vania and Alfred.

Each project is good at different things, so this page gives facts only. Projects change, so read their docs before you decide. For a shorter guide, read the blog post Dart backend frameworks: how to choose.

docs.title: What each one is for
docs.text:
• Dox is a full backend framework. It has routes, controllers, typed DTOs, an ORM, migrations, auth, cache, storage and a CLI.
  • Dart Frog is a small backend framework built on Shelf. Routes come from the files in the routes/ folder. It describes itself as "a fast, minimalistic backend framework for Dart".
  • Serverpod is a full-stack framework for Flutter. You write endpoint methods on the server, and Serverpod generates a typed Dart client for the Flutter app. It has an ORM, auth, streaming and a hosted service (Serverpod Cloud).
  • Shelf is the request and middleware model from the Dart team. It is a library, not a framework. shelf_router adds a router, and you pick every other part yourself.
  • Vania is a full backend framework. Its core has routes, validation, an ORM, migrations, sessions, a cache, mail and storage. Auth, OpenAPI and WebSocket rooms come as add-on packages. It works with MySQL, Postgres and MongoDB.
  • Alfred is a small server in the style of Express.js. Routes, middleware, WebSocket and static files are built in.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text: The numbers of Dox are on Performance. To compare, run the same test on your machine, with each server on the same number of cores.

docs.title: When to pick Dox
docs.text:
• You want a full framework in one place: routes, typed input, ORM, migrations, auth, cache, storage and OpenAPI docs.
  • You come from a PHP framework. See Coming from Laravel.
  • You need MySQL or MariaDB, not only Postgres.
  • You want typed DTOs with the same rules on the server and in a Dart or Flutter client. See Share code with Flutter.
  • You want an OpenAPI document made from your code, for clients that are not written in Dart.

docs.title: When to pick something else
docs.text:
• You want a framework with many years of use. Dart Frog, Serverpod and Shelf have been out for years, and Dox is new.
  • You want a hosted service. Serverpod has Serverpod Cloud. You deploy Dox yourself, as a binary or with Docker.
  • Your app is Flutter only, and you want a generated client. Serverpod makes a typed client for each endpoint. Dox makes an OpenAPI document.
  • You want a small tool with few parts. Dart Frog is simpler, and you add only what you need.
  • You want to build your own stack. Shelf gives you the base parts, and the Dart team publishes it.
  • You need a feature that Dox does not have yet, like events and listeners. See What Dox does not have yet.

docs.title: How Dox works
docs.text: This page shows the path of a request, how isolates work and what each folder of an app is for.

docs.title: The life of a request
docs.text:
Each request takes the same path. The pages in "The basics" follow this order:

  1. Routematch the URL
  2. Middlewarego on or stop
  3. DTOcheck the input
  4. Controlleryour code
  5. Viewrender a page
  6. Responsesend the answer

Dox has two parts. The native server (dox_http_native) owns the sockets and parses HTTP. Your Dart app runs the routes, middleware, DTOs, controllers and the ORM.

A request goes through these steps:

  1. The native server parses the request. A broken request gets 400, headers over 16 KB get 431, and a body over the size limit gets 413.
  2. The native server gives the requests to Dart in a batch.
  3. Dart finds the route by the method, the host and the path. No match gets 404. A CORS preflight gets 204.
  4. Dart adds the CORS headers of the route.
  5. Dart reads the body, if the request has a content type.
  6. Dart runs the middleware in this order: global, router, group, route. If a middleware returns a value that is not the request, Dart sends that value as the response.
  7. Dart fills the controller parameters. A path param that does not fit its type gets 404. Bad DTO input gets 422, a body that is not JSON gets 400, and an unknown content type gets 415.
  8. The controller runs and returns a value.
  9. The responseHandler of AppConfig runs, if you set one.
  10. Dox makes the response: a string is text, a map or model is JSON, and a file is streamed.
  11. Dart gives the answers of the batch back to the native server, which writes them to the socket.

If a step throws, Dox catches the error. An IHttpException gives its own status. Any other error gives 500 and goes to the report method of your ExceptionHandler.

ClientNative serverDart isolateMiddlewareController
  1. TCP connection, HTTP request
  2. parse request, check size limits
  3. batch of requests (one message)
  4. router: method, host, path
  5. CORS headers, read body
  6. global, router, group, route middleware
  7. request (go on) or a response
  8. path params, DTO check
  9. call with typed parameters
  10. return value
  11. response handler, build the response
  12. batch of answers (one call)
  13. bytes

Dox uses no reflection. DTOs come from a generated list, so dox build can make a native binary.

docs.title: Where things are decided
docs.text: Step Code What it decides Route match lib/routes/*.dart, Route.get(...) which controller runs Middleware AppConfig(globalMiddleware:), Router.middleware, Route.middleware(...), the route list go on, or answer early Input a @Dto class in lib/app/dtos/<name>/ what the controller gets, or 422 Output the return value, response(...), responseHandler status, headers, body Errors IHttpException, AppConfig(exceptionHandler:) the error response, logging

docs.title: Isolates
docs.text: An isolate is like a thread with its own memory. Dox starts one isolate for each CPU that the process can use, also in a container, and each isolate runs the full app.

docs.title: One port, many isolates
docs.text:
Each isolate runs its own HTTP server on the same port:

System Native server Linux one socket per isolate (SO_REUSEPORT) macOS the isolates share one socket Windows only one isolate serves HTTP

See Native server.

docs.title: What each isolate gets
docs.text:
Dox copies the AppConfig, the providers, and the routes and binders that you added before startServer() to each isolate. Then each isolate does these steps one time:

  1. It runs setup() of each provider, in list order.
  2. It registers the routes of your routers.
  3. It reads the parameter types of each controller.
  4. It starts its HTTP server.

The config and the providers are copied, so they must not hold open sockets or pools. Open them in setup(). See Providers.

docs.title: Each isolate has its own memory
docs.text:
Isolates do not share memory:

  • A static value or a singleton exists one time in each isolate.
  • The memory cache store is per isolate. Use the Redis store to share cache data.
  • To share data, use the database, Redis or files.

Dox().isolateId gives the isolate that runs the code. The first one is 1.

docs.title: When an isolate crashes
docs.text:
• An error in a request gets 500, and the isolate continues.
  • An async error outside a request goes to the ExceptionHandler, and the isolate continues.
  • If a worker isolate stops, Dox starts a new one after 1 second.
  • If the main isolate stops, the process exits with an error code. In production, use a supervisor to start it again, like Docker restart: or systemd Restart=always.

docs.title: How many isolates
docs.text: Set totalIsolate in AppConfig or APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE in .env. Dox().totalIsolate(2) before startServer() wins over the config. See Isolate.

docs.title: Where the database pools live
docs.text:
Each isolate runs setup() of the ORM provider, so each isolate asks for a pool. The native drivers give isolates with the same settings the same pool:

Driver Per isolate Per process Postgres native (dox_postgres_native) nothing one pool of maxConnectionCount connections per settings MySQL native (dox_mysql_native) nothing one pool of maxConnectionCount connections per settings SQLite one connection nothing shared

So for Postgres and MySQL, the app opens at most maxConnectionCount connections for all isolates. Set it below the max_connections of the database. See Native Postgres driver.

docs.title: The layout of a Dox app
docs.text:
dox create my_app copies the dox-sample template:

my_app/
├── bin/
│   ├── server.dart          # starts the app
│   ├── migrate.dart         # runs the migrations (dox migration:*)
│   ├── seed.dart            # runs the seeders (dox db:seed)
│   ├── queue.dart           # the queue worker (dox queue:*)
│   └── schedule.dart        # the scheduler (dox schedule:*)
├── db/
│   ├── factories/           # model factories, *.factory.dart
│   ├── migration/           # migrations (.dart with a registry, or .sql)
│   └── seeders/             # seeders, *.seeder.dart
├── lib/
│   ├── app/
│   │   ├── http/
│   │   │   └── controllers/     # *.controller.dart
│   │   ├── jobs/                # queue jobs, *.job.dart
│   │   └── models/              # one folder per model, *.model.dart
│   ├── config/
│   │   ├── app.dart             # AppConfig: port, isolates, middleware
│   │   ├── cache.dart           # cache stores
│   │   ├── cors.dart
│   │   ├── database.dart        # DatabaseConfig: connections
│   │   ├── env.dart             # typed env class (@DoxEnv)
│   │   ├── logger.dart
│   │   ├── queue.dart           # QueueConfig
│   │   ├── schedule.dart        # ScheduleConfig and your tasks
│   │   └── storage.dart         # storage disks
│   ├── routes/
│   │   ├── api.dart             # ApiRouter, prefix `api`
│   │   └── web.dart             # WebRouter
│   ├── providers/               # one DoxProvider per file
│   │   ├── orm_provider.dart        # opens the database
│   │   ├── queue_provider.dart
│   │   ├── schedule_provider.dart
│   │   └── storage_provider.dart
│   └── generated/               # made by build_runner, do not edit
│       ├── container.g.dart     # @Inject classes, routers, providers
│       ├── jobs.g.dart          # the list of queue jobs
│       └── openapi.g.dart       # the OpenAPI docs
├── test/
├── .env                         # local settings, not in git
├── .env.example
├── Dockerfile
├── docker-compose.yml
└── pubspec.yaml

The dox make:* commands add more folders when you need them, like lib/app/dtos/, lib/app/http/middleware/ and lib/app/serializers/. The app makes storage/ when it first writes files.

Folder What goes there bin/ server.dart calls Dox().initialize(appConfig), runs the migrations, then Dox().startServer(). The other files are the entry points of the dox migration:*, db:seed, queue:* and schedule:* commands. db/ Your migrations, factories and seeders. The CLI writes the list of Dart migrations in db/migration/migrations.dart. lib/app/http/ Controllers and middleware. lib/app/serializers/ Serializers. MCP and WebSocket code also use them. lib/app/dtos/ One folder per DTO: typed and checked input. lib/app/jobs/ Queue jobs. lib/app/models/ One folder per model, with its generated file. lib/config/ One file per config object. app.dart puts them together in AppConfig. lib/routes/ One Router class per file. Dox finds each router. lib/providers/ Classes that extend DoxProvider. Their setup() runs in each isolate. Dox finds each provider. lib/generated/ Generated files. Run dox build_runner:build to make them again. storage/ Files the app writes: uploads, the file cache, SQLite files.

docs.title: What Dox does not have yet
docs.text:
Some features are not built yet. This is what to do today:

Feature Status What to do today Events and listeners Not there Model events are there. See Model events. Password reset Not there Make a signed, short-lived token, send it with Mail and check it in a controller. Localization Partly Validation messages can follow the request locale (req.locale). There is no general translation helper. Keep your own message maps.

docs.title: Planned
docs.text:
These features are planned. They are not built yet:

Feature What it will do What to do today Sentry Send the errors, traces and logs of a Dox app to Sentry. Send errors from the report method of your exception handler. See Error handling. HTTPS Serve HTTPS with no reverse proxy. Put Caddy or nginx in front. See Deployment. WebSocket compression Compress WebSocket messages with permessage-deflate. Messages are sent with no compression. OpenAPI SDK generation Make a typed client from the OpenAPI document of your app. Run an OpenAPI generator on openapi.json. See OpenAPI. Localization A general translation helper. Keep your own message maps.

Changes that are done but not released are in the Unreleased section of the CHANGELOG of a package.

  • Dox and the other Dart backends: compare Dox with other frameworks.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
Connect Dox to Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB or SQLite with the dox_orm package.

Dox gives you two ways to work with the data:

  • The query builder builds SQL with methods, like QueryBuilder.table('blog').where('id', 1).get().
  • Models give you one class per table, with relations and events.

You can also run transactions, and make tables with migrations and the schema builder.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
A new app already has dox_orm. To add it to an app, run:

dox add orm --driver=sqlite

The driver is sqlite (the default), postgres or mysql. The command adds dox_orm and dox_migration, the config, the ORM provider, bin/migrate.dart, db/migration/ and the DB_* keys in .env. It never overwrites a file. See Add a package.

docs.title: Supported databases
docs.text:
Database Driver Package Pool Good for Postgres Driver.postgres dox_postgres_native yes production MySQL 8+ and MariaDB Driver.mysql dox_mysql_native yes production SQLite Driver.sqlite sqlite3 no, one connection per isolate development, tests, small apps

Postgres and MySQL use a native (Rust) driver. If the native library can not load, the app stops with an error. See Postgres and MySQL.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Put your connections in lib/config/database.dart. connection is the name of the default connection:

lib/config/database.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: env.dbConnection,
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.postgres,
      host: env.dbHost,
      port: env.dbPort ?? 5432,
      user: env.dbUsername,
      password: env.dbPassword,
      database: env.dbName,
      extra: <String, dynamic>{'maxConnectionCount': 10},
      debug: appConfig.isDevelopment,
    ),
    'mysql': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.mysql, // also for MariaDB
      host: env.dbHost,
      port: env.dbPort ?? 3306,
      user: env.dbUsername,
      password: env.dbPassword,
      database: env.dbName,
      extra: <String, dynamic>{'maxConnectionCount': 10},
      debug: appConfig.isDevelopment,
    ),
    'sqlite': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.sqlite,
      database: env.dbName, // file path, like db/dox.sqlite, or ':memory:'
      debug: appConfig.isDevelopment,
    ),
  },
);

Change my_app to the name of your app. With debug on, each query prints with its values put in:

▌ [db:default] SELECT * FROM "users" WHERE "email" = 'a@b.com' LIMIT 1;

docs.title: Connection options
docs.text:
Option What it does driver Driver.postgres, Driver.mysql or Driver.sqlite. host, port, user, password The server. SQLite does not use them. database The database name. For SQLite, the file path or :memory:. useSSL Turn on TLS. See Postgres TLS and MySQL. debug Print each query. printer The query printer: PrettyQueryPrinter (default), ConsoleQueryPrinter, FileQueryPrinter or your own QueryPrinter. logRedact Names of values to show as *** in the log, like ['password', 'token']. A key that ends with a name matches. slowQueryMs Log queries slower than this. See Slow query log. extra Driver options. See All extra options. read, write, sticky Read replicas. See Read replicas. driverFactory A function that makes your own DBDriver from the config.

DatabaseConfig also takes url (DATABASE_URL), flags (ORM flags) and strict. For strict, see Strict mode in the ORM.

docs.title: Environment values
docs.text:
The app config and the migration commands read these keys from .env:

.env
DB_CONNECTION=postgres # postgres, mysql or sqlite
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432           # 3306 for mysql
DB_NAME=dox            # for sqlite: the file path, like db/dox.sqlite
DB_USERNAME=postgres
DB_PASSWORD=postgres

docs.title: Starting the ORM
docs.text:
The ORM starts in a provider. The app template already has this file:

lib/providers/orm_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

class ORMProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig);
  }

  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await SqlQueryBuilder.close();
  }
}

After you add a provider, run dart run build_runner build. Isolates with the same settings share one pool, so maxConnectionCount is for the whole process.

docs.title: DATABASE_URL
docs.text:
Many hosts give you one database url. Dox reads it from the DATABASE_URL key, in .env or in the shell. The shell wins:

DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:s%40cret@db.example.com:5432/blog?sslmode=require
Form Database postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db or postgresql://... Postgres mysql://user:pass@host:3306/db or mariadb://... MySQL, MariaDB sqlite:///abs/path.db, sqlite://db/dox.sqlite, sqlite::memory:, file:db/dox.sqlite SQLite

The url replaces the config of the default connection. That config still gives debug, printer, logRedact, slowQueryMs, extra and the read hosts. Pass the url through the env class, so the app and dox migrate read the same url:

lib/config/database.dart
DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  url: env.databaseUrl, // String? get databaseUrl; in env.dart
  connection: env.dbConnection,
  connections: {...},
);

Without the url line, Dox reads DATABASE_URL only from the shell. An empty url turns it off.

  • The user, password and database name are url-decoded. Write @ in a password as %40.
  • For Postgres, sslmode works like libpq. require does not check the certificate, so use verify-full when you can. See Postgres TLS.
  • For MySQL, ssl=true turns on TLS and checks the certificate. verifyCertificate=false skips the check, for development only.
  • Other options go to extra, like ?maxConnectionCount=20.

To make one ConnectionConfig from a url, use ConnectionConfig.fromUrl(url).

docs.title: Unix socket
docs.text:
A host that starts with / is a Unix socket:

DB_HOST=/cloudsql/my-project:europe-west1:blog
# or
DATABASE_URL=postgres://blog:secret@/blog?host=/cloudsql/my-project:europe-west1:blog

For Postgres, the host is the socket folder, like in libpq. For MySQL and MariaDB, the host is the socket file, like /var/run/mysqld/mysqld.sock. In the url, ?socket= and ?host= do the same.

docs.title: Pool settings
docs.text:
Set the pool of Postgres and MySQL in the extra map. A time is a Duration or a number of seconds:

extra: <String, dynamic>{
  'maxConnectionCount': 10,
  'requestTimeout': const Duration(seconds: 30),
  'maxConnectionAge': const Duration(minutes: 30),
  'idleTimeout': const Duration(minutes: 5),
  'serverKill': false, // MySQL only
},

A request is a wait for a connection, the connect and the query. A transaction with no request for the requestTimeout is rolled back. Set serverKill to false behind a proxy like ProxySQL, because the kill can reach another server.

docs.title: All extra options
docs.text:
Key Database Default What it does maxConnectionCount Postgres, MySQL 10 Most connections in the pool. requestTimeout Postgres, MySQL 300 s The longest time for one request. maxConnectionAge Postgres, MySQL no limit on Postgres, 12 hours on MySQL Close a connection older than this, when it has no query. idleTimeout Postgres, MySQL no limit on Postgres, 12 hours on MySQL Close a connection not used for this long. serverKill MySQL true Stop a cancelled or timed out query on the server with KILL QUERY. preparedStatementCacheSize MySQL, SQLite 100 Prepared statements kept per connection. sslMode Postgres disable TLS mode: disable, prefer, require, verify-ca or verify-full. sslRootCert Postgres none PEM file with the CA certificates for verify-ca and verify-full. verifyCertificate MySQL true false skips the TLS certificate check. Development only. timeZone Postgres UTC Time zone of the session. applicationName Postgres none Name of the app in pg_stat_activity. busyTimeout SQLite 5000 Milliseconds a query waits for a lock. background SQLite false Run the queries in a helper isolate.

To stop one query, see Cancelling a query.

docs.title: Skip unused drivers
docs.text:
dox_orm brings all three drivers, and the build downloads a native library for each. To skip the ones you do not use, add a hooks: user_defines: block to the root pubspec.yaml. A new app uses SQLite and already has this block:

pubspec.yaml
hooks:
  user_defines:
    dox_postgres_native:
      skip: true
    dox_mysql_native:
      skip: true

For a Postgres app:

pubspec.yaml
hooks:
  user_defines:
    dox_mysql_native:
      skip: true
    sqlite3:
      source: system

For a MySQL app:

pubspec.yaml
hooks:
  user_defines:
    dox_postgres_native:
      skip: true
    sqlite3:
      source: system

Only the bool true skips. With sqlite3: source: system, the app loads the libsqlite3 of the system. If your app opens SQLite, remove these lines, because an image without libsqlite3 fails.

When you change the database, remove the skip line of the new driver and run dart pub get.

docs.title: Running raw queries
docs.text:
QueryBuilder.query() runs your own SQL. Use @name for values, so they are bound:

List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.query(
  'select * from blog where id = @id',
  substitutionValues: <String, dynamic>{'id': 1},
);

await QueryBuilder.query('select 1', connection: 'mysql');

docs.title: Using other connections
docs.text:
withConnection() runs a query on another connection from the config:

List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('blog')
    .withConnection('mysql')
    .get();

A model keeps its connection, so save() and delete() use it:

Blog blog = Blog()..withConnection('mysql');
blog.title = 'Hello';
await blog.save(); // saved on 'mysql'

docs.title: Listen to queries
docs.text:
SqlQueryBuilder().listen() runs your function after each query, on every connection:

void onQuery(QueryEvent e) {
  print('${e.connection} ${e.time.inMilliseconds} ms: ${e.sql}');
}

SqlQueryBuilder().listen(onQuery);

A QueryEvent has sql, bindings (with logRedact values as ***), time and connection. A failed query is not sent. SqlQueryBuilder().removeListener(onQuery) stops it.

docs.title: Slow query log
docs.text:
Set slowQueryMs on a connection to log each query slower than that many milliseconds. It works with debug off:

'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
  driver: Driver.postgres,
  // ...
  debug: appConfig.isDevelopment,
  slowQueryMs: 500,
),

The line goes to the query printer:

▌ [db:postgres SLOW 812ms] SELECT * FROM "orders" WHERE "user_id" = 42;

Set it to 0 to log every query.

docs.title: ORM flags
docs.text:
OrmFlags turns on opt-in ORM behaviors. Each flag is off by default. Pass them as flags in DatabaseConfig:

lib/config/database.dart
DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: env.dbConnection,
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{ /* ... */ },
  flags: OrmFlags.all(), // every flag on
);

To turn on only some flags, name them:

flags: const OrmFlags(pluralTableNames: true, sumReturnsZero: true),
Flag Off (default) On skipCleanUpdateEvents save() with no changes fires saving, updating, updated and saved. It fires only saving and saved. A model with a Map or List field always counts as changed. belongsToKeyFromRelation The belongsTo foreign key comes from the class name: @BelongsTo(User) User? author uses user_id. It comes from the relation name: author_id. pluralTableNames The table name is singular: User uses user. It is plural: users, blog_posts, categories. A name in @DoxModel(table: ...) does not change. createWritesNull create() does not send a null key, so the column default is used. It writes NULL for a null key. sumReturnsZero sum() gives null when no row matches. It gives 0. selectRawAdds selectRaw() replaces the select list. It adds to it. groupByAdds A second groupBy() replaces the first. It adds to the first. groupByRaw() too. lastPageAtLeastOne paginate() gives lastPage 0 when there are no rows. It gives 1. updateSetsUpdatedAt A model query update() does not set updated_at. It sets updated_at, unless the data has it. incrementFiresEvents increment() and decrement() on a model fire no events and do not set updated_at. They fire saving, updating, updated and saved, and set updated_at. preloadUnknownThrows preload('typo') loads nothing, with no error. It throws an ArgumentError. toJsonLoadedRelations toJson() has only the relations named in preload(). It also has the relations loaded with $getRelation(). laravelPostgresTypes On Postgres, timestamps() and softDeletes() make TIMESTAMPTZ, and json() makes JSONB. A new table gets TIMESTAMP and JSON.

bin/migrate.dart does not start the ORM, so give the flags to the migrator too: Migrator(migrations: migrations, flags: databaseConfig.flags). See Migration.

docs.title: SQLite
docs.text:
SQLite is good for development, tests and small apps. The sqlite3 package brings SQLite with a build hook, so you do not install it.

For the AOT binary, use dox build. It puts the library in build/bundle/lib/, so keep it next to build/bundle/bin/. See Deployment.

SQLite has no bool, JSON or date type, so Dox converts them:

  • boolean() is saved as 0 or 1 and read back as a bool.
  • json() is saved as text and read back as a map or a list.
  • Dates are saved as ISO text in UTC and read back as a DateTime.

This works for columns with these type names: BOOLEAN, JSON, TIMESTAMP, DATE and DATETIME. Schema limits are in SQLite notes.

docs.title: Run queries in a helper isolate
docs.text:
A SQLite query blocks its isolate. Set background to true to run the queries in a helper isolate, so your isolate keeps serving requests:

'sqlite': ConnectionConfig(
  driver: Driver.sqlite,
  database: 'db/dox.sqlite',
  debug: false,
  extra: {'background': true},
),

With DATABASE_URL, add ?background=true. Each query costs two messages, so turn it on for slow queries and leave it off for many tiny queries.

docs.title: MySQL and MariaDB
docs.text: The driver is dox_mysql_native. On MySQL and MariaDB, a transaction can not undo CREATE, ALTER and DROP.

docs.title: Without Dox
docs.text:
dox_orm also works on its own:

dart pub add dox_orm

Start it with a DatabaseConfig, or with your own database object: a PgNativePool, a MysqlNativePool or a SQLite Database:

import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig);
// or
SqlQueryBuilder.initialize(database: db, driver: Driver.sqlite);

initialize also takes debug, printer, flags and strict. Call await SqlQueryBuilder.close() to close the connections.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Query Builder: write queries.
  • Model: work with rows as objects.
  • Migration: create and change tables.

docs.title: Factories
docs.text: A factory makes models with sample data, so you can fill the database quickly in tests and seeders.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
make:factory makes a factory:

dox make:factory User

This makes db/factories/user.factory.dart. Set the default values in definition:

db/factories/user.factory.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/factory.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class UserFactory extends Factory<User> {
  @override
  User definition() {
    User user = User();
    user.name = 'Jane';
    user.email = 'jane@example.com';
    return user;
  }
}

definition runs once for each model. Import factories from package:dox_orm/factory.dart, because the main import does not have them.

docs.title: Fake data
docs.text:
The faker package gives random values:

dart pub add faker
db/factories/user.factory.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/factory.dart';
import 'package:faker/faker.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class UserFactory extends Factory<User> {
  @override
  User definition() {
    return User()
      ..name = faker.person.name()
      ..email = faker.internet.email();
  }
}

docs.title: Saving models
docs.text:
create makes models and saves them. count sets how many, 1 by default:

List<User> users = await UserFactory().count(10).create();

createOne makes and saves one model:

User user = await UserFactory().createOne();

Each model is saved with save(), so model events run.

docs.title: Making models without saving
docs.text:
make gives a list, and makeOne gives one model. They save nothing:

User user = UserFactory().makeOne();
List<User> users = UserFactory().count(3).make();

docs.title: States
docs.text:
A state changes each model after definition:

User admin = await UserFactory()
    .state((User u) => u..isAdmin = true)
    .createOne();

States run in the order you add them. Put a state you use often in a method of the factory:

class UserFactory extends Factory<User> {
  @override
  User definition() => User()..name = 'Jane';

  UserFactory admin() {
    state((User u) => u..isAdmin = true);
    return this;
  }
}

List<User> admins = await UserFactory().admin().count(3).create();

Call your own methods first, because count() and state() return a Factory<User>.

docs.title: Sequences
docs.text:
sequence is a state that also gets the index of the model, from 0:

List<User> users = await UserFactory()
    .count(3)
    .sequence((User u, int i) => u..email = 'user$i@example.com')
    .create();
// user0@example.com, user1@example.com, user2@example.com

docs.title: Belongs to relationships
docs.text:
Set the parent key with a state:

User user = await UserFactory().createOne();

await PostFactory()
    .count(3)
    .state((Post p) => p..userId = user.id)
    .create();

docs.title: Has many relationships
docs.text:
has creates children for each saved model. The function sets the parent on each child:

List<User> users = await UserFactory()
    .count(2)
    .has(PostFactory().count(3), (Post p, User u) => p..userId = u.id)
    .create();
// 2 users, each with 3 posts

has works only with create and createOne.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Set up the ORM first, like in your app. Then create the data the test needs:

import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/factories/user.factory.dart';

void main() {
  test('lists users', () async {
    await UserFactory().count(3).create();
    // call your route and check the result
  });
}

Each call like count() changes the factory, so make a new factory for each set of models. See Testing with a database.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Seeders: fill the database with factories.
  • Model: the models a factory makes.
  • Testing with a database: data for each test.

docs.title: Migration
docs.text:
A migration changes your database schema step by step, with an up method that makes the change and a down method that undoes it.

You write migrations in Dart with the schema builder, so one migration works on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. Plain .sql migrations work too.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
The migration commands read the database from .env and the environment variables. An environment variable wins over .env:

.env
DB_CONNECTION=postgres # or mysql (also MariaDB), or sqlite
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
DB_NAME=postgres
DB_USERNAME=admin
DB_PASSWORD=password

For SQLite, you need only two keys:

.env
DB_CONNECTION=sqlite
DB_NAME=db/dox.sqlite # file path, made if missing

docs.title: Database settings
docs.text:
Without DB_CONNECTION, the migrations use SQLite. DB_DATABASE works in place of DB_NAME. DATABASE_URL wins over all DB_* keys, see DATABASE_URL. Migrations use TLS only with a DATABASE_URL that has sslmode (Postgres) or ssl (MySQL).

bin/migrate.dart does not start the ORM. To give the ORM flags to the schema of each migration, pass them to the migrator:

bin/migrate.dart
Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await Migrator(
    migrations: migrations,
    flags: databaseConfig.flags,
  ).run(args);
}

docs.title: Generating migrations
docs.text:
make:migration makes a new migration file:

dox make:migration create_users_table

This makes db/migration/2026_10_21_120000_create_users_table.dart. The numbers are the date and time, so the migrations run in the right order. The name decides what the file has:

Name The file has create_users_table schema.create('users', ...) in up, and dropIfExists('users') in down add_avatar_to_users_table (also _from_, _in_, _on_) schema.table('users', ...) in up and down any other name empty up and down

dox make:model Blog -m makes a model and its create_blogs_table migration.

docs.title: Migration structure
docs.text:
up adds tables, columns or indexes. down undoes what up did:

db/migration/2026_10_21_120000_create_users_table.dart
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

class CreateUsersTable extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.create('users', (Table table) {
      table.id();
      table.string('email').unique();
      table.timestamps();
    });
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.dropIfExists('users');
  }
}

See Schema for all column types.

docs.title: Running raw SQL
docs.text:
schema.driver runs SQL on the connection and transaction of the migration:

await schema.driver.execute("UPDATE users SET role = 'admin' WHERE id = 1");

Do not use models or QueryBuilder in a migration, because they use another connection.

docs.title: Running migrations
docs.text:
migration:run runs the migrations that did not run yet. dox migrate is the short name:

dox migration:run
dox migrate --seed # also run the seeders

If a migration fails, the command shows its name and exits with code 1. The later migrations do not run.

docs.title: Checking the status
docs.text:
migration:status shows each migration, its batch, and if it ran:

dox migration:status

docs.title: Rolling back migrations
docs.text:
migration:rollback undoes the last batch: the migrations of one run. --step undoes a number of migrations, and --batch undoes one batch:

dox migration:rollback
dox migration:rollback --step=2
dox migration:rollback --batch=3

migration:reset undoes all migrations:

dox migration:reset

docs.title: Refreshing the database
docs.text:
migration:refresh undoes all migrations and runs them again. migration:fresh drops all tables and runs all migrations:

dox migration:refresh
dox migration:fresh --seed

Warning

migration:fresh also drops tables that no migration made. Do not run it on a database that you share with other apps.

docs.title: Running in production
docs.text:
With APP_ENV=production, the commands that drop tables ask first. --force skips the question:

dox migration:fresh --force

With no terminal, like in CI, they print a warning and run.

docs.title: Run on server start
docs.text:
The AOT server binary can run the migrations itself. The app template already does this:

bin/server.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() async {
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);
  await Migrator(
    migrations: migrations,
    config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
  ).migrate();
  await Dox().startServer();
}

It uses the config of the app, so it works without .env. If you have .sql migrations, keep the db/migration folder next to the binary.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
Each migration runs in one transaction. On Postgres and SQLite, a failed migration undoes all its changes.

MySQL

On MySQL and MariaDB, CREATE, ALTER and DROP save right away. If a migration fails half way, these changes stay. Keep each MySQL migration to one table change.

For SQL that can not run in a transaction, like CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, set withinTransaction to false:

class AddSearchIndex extends Migration {
  @override
  bool get withinTransaction => false;

  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.driver.execute(
      'CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY posts_title_index ON posts (title)',
    );
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.driver
        .execute('DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY posts_title_index');
  }
}

On SQLite, foreign key checks are off while a migration runs. At the end, the migration fails if a foreign key is broken.

docs.title: SQL migrations
docs.text:
Use a .sql migration for SQL that only one database knows:

dox make:migration create_blog_table --sql

Put the up SQL under a -- up line and the down SQL under a -- down line:

-- up
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS blog (
    id serial PRIMARY KEY,
    title VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL
);

-- down
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS blog

Dart and .sql migrations run together in file name order. A Dart and a .sql migration with the same name is an error.

SQLite ids

On SQLite, id serial PRIMARY KEY does not make an auto increment id. Use id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT. table.id() in Dart does this for you.

docs.title: The migration list
docs.text:
An AOT build can not load a file at run time, so Dox keeps a list of the Dart migrations in db/migration/migrations.dart. dox make:migration and every dox migration:* command write it again, so do not edit it:

import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import '2026_10_21_120000_create_users_table.dart' as m1;

final List<MigrationEntry> migrations = <MigrationEntry>[
  MigrationEntry(
    '2026_10_21_120000_create_users_table',
    m1.CreateUsersTable(),
  ),
];

The migrations that ran are in the dox_db_migration table.

docs.title: The Migrator class
docs.text:
The dox migration:* commands run bin/migrate.dart, which calls Migrator.run:

bin/migrate.dart
Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await Migrator(migrations: migrations).run(args);
}

run takes run, rollback --step=2, reset, refresh, fresh or status, so dart run bin/migrate.dart status works too.

docs.title: Where it runs
docs.text:
With config, the migrator opens that database and closes it at the end. With connection, it uses a driver that is open, and does not close it:

Migrator(migrations: migrations,
    config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig());
Migrator(migrations: migrations, connection: SqlQueryBuilder().dbDriver);

With neither, it reads .env. directory sets the folder of the .sql migrations, db/migration by default.

docs.title: Running from code
docs.text:
Each command is also a method:

Migrator migrator = Migrator(migrations: migrations);
await migrator.migrate();
await migrator.rollback(step: 2); // or batch: 3
await migrator.reset();
await migrator.refresh();
await migrator.fresh();

List<MigrationStatus> list = await migrator.status();
Migrator.printStatus(list);

A MigrationStatus has name, batch (null when it did not run), ran and exists (false when its file is gone). A failed migration throws a MigrationException with the migration name and the error.

docs.title: Native MySQL driver
docs.text:
dox_mysql_native is the MySQL and MariaDB driver of the Dox ORM, written in Rust.

You use it through your models and queries. Rust (mysql_async) owns the connections and the pool, and each connection keeps its prepared statements. It works with MySQL 8.4 and MariaDB 11.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
dox_orm already depends on dox_mysql_native. Add it yourself only to use MysqlNativePool without the ORM:

dart pub add dox_mysql_native

The build hook downloads a ready library for your system, so you do not need Rust. The package has its own repo: dartondox/dox-mysql-native.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
The driver reads host, port, user, password, database and useSSL of the ConnectionConfig, and these keys from extra:

Key Default What it does maxConnectionCount 10 Most connections in the pool, for the whole process. requestTimeout 300 s The longest time for one request. maxConnectionAge 12 hours Close a connection older than this, when it has no query. idleTimeout 12 hours Close a connection with no traffic for this long. serverKill true Stop a cancelled or timed out query on the server with KILL QUERY. preparedStatementCacheSize 100 Prepared statements kept per connection. verifyCertificate true With useSSL, check the server certificate. Set false only for a self-signed certificate in development.

See Pool settings. The connection uses utf8mb4. A login with sha256_password does not work. The default caching_sha2_password and mysql_native_password work.

docs.title: Behind a proxy
docs.text:
A cancelled query gets a KILL QUERY on a new connection. Behind a proxy with its own connection ids, like ProxySQL, that connection can reach another server. Turn it off there:

extra: <String, dynamic>{'serverKill': false},

Then a cancelled query fails in Dart at once, but it runs to its end on the server. In DATABASE_URL, use ?serverKill=false.

docs.title: When the library does not load
docs.text:
If the native library does not load, SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig throws an UnsupportedError:

dox_mysql_native did not load: <reason>.
Dox needs it to talk to MySQL. Fix: run the app with `dart run` or `dart build cli`. ...

To fix it:

  • Run the app with dart run, dart test or dart build cli, because they run the build hook. dart compile exe does not.
  • Or install Rust. The build hook then builds the library from source.
  • If you set lib_path in pubspec.yaml, check that the file is there and fits your system.

MysqlNativePool.isAvailable tells you if the library loaded, and MysqlNativePool.loadError gives the reason.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Rows come back with these Dart types:

MySQL, MariaDB Dart TINYINT(1) (boolean()) bool TINYINT, SMALLINT, INT, BIGINT, YEAR int FLOAT, DOUBLE, DECIMAL double CHAR, VARCHAR, TEXT, ENUM String DATE, DATETIME, TIMESTAMP DateTime in UTC TIME String, like 12:34:56 JSON the decoded JSON value BLOB, BINARY, VARBINARY Uint8List NULL null

MariaDB keeps JSON columns as LONGTEXT. So on MariaDB, TEXT that holds a JSON object or array comes back decoded.

docs.title: Handling errors
docs.text:
Every error throws a MysqlException. For a server error, code is the MySQL error number, like 1062 for a duplicate key:

try {
  await QueryBuilder.table('users')
      .insert(<String, dynamic>{'email': email});
} on MysqlException catch (error) {
  if (error.code == 1062) print('taken');
}

sqlState is the 5 letter SQLSTATE. For other errors, like a down server, both are null. A cancelled query throws a MysqlQueryCancelledException. They come from package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart.

docs.title: Opening a pool
docs.text:
MysqlNativePool.open opens a pool. query returns a MysqlNativeResult with columns and rows:

MysqlNativePool pool = MysqlNativePool.open(
  host: 'localhost',
  user: 'root',
  password: 'password',
  database: 'app',
);

MysqlNativeResult result = await pool.query(
  'SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id = ?',
  parameters: <Object?>[1],
);
print(result.rows); // [{id: 1, name: Ada}]

parameters is a list for ?, or a map for @name. A write also gives the new id and the changed row count:

MysqlNativeResult insert = await pool.query(
  'INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (@name)',
  parameters: <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Bob'},
);
print(insert.insertId);     // the new AUTO_INCREMENT id
print(insert.affectedRows); // 1

docs.title: Pool settings
docs.text:
open also takes port (3306), maxConnections (10), secure (TLS), verifyCertificate, sslRootCert, statementCacheSize (32), requestTimeout, maxConnectionAge, idleTimeout and serverKill:

MysqlNativePool pool = MysqlNativePool.open(
  host: 'localhost',
  user: 'root',
  password: 'password',
  database: 'app',
  secure: true,
  sslRootCert: '/etc/ssl/certs/db-ca.pem',
  requestTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 30),
);

A host that starts with / is a Unix socket file. Here maxConnectionAge has no limit by default.

docs.title: Pool from a url
docs.text:
MysqlNativePool.fromUrl takes a url with the mysql_async options, like ?pool_max=20. The kill option there is server_kill:

MysqlNativePool pool =
    MysqlNativePool.fromUrl('mysql://root:password@localhost:3306/app');

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
begin gives a transaction id. execute is like query, but it sends no rows back:

int tx = await pool.begin();
await pool.execute('UPDATE users SET name = ?',
    parameters: <Object?>['Cy'], transaction: tx);
await pool.commit(tx); // or pool.rollback(tx)

docs.title: Cancelling a query
docs.text:
Pass a MysqlCancelToken to query, execute or stream, and call cancel(). isCancelled is true after it:

MysqlCancelToken token = MysqlCancelToken();
Future<MysqlNativeResult> slow =
    pool.query('SELECT SLEEP(10)', cancelToken: token);
token.cancel(); // slow fails with MysqlQueryCancelledException

In the ORM, use cancelWith().

docs.title: Streaming rows
docs.text:
stream gives the rows in chunks of up to chunkSize rows. Rust reads at most 2 chunks ahead:

await for (MysqlNativeResult chunk
    in pool.stream('SELECT * FROM logs', chunkSize: 1000)) {
  print(chunk.rows.length);
}

Stop the loop with break to stop the query. Do not pause a stream for longer than the net_write_timeout of the server (60 s by default). In the ORM, use cursor().

docs.title: Sharing and closing a pool
docs.text:
pool.handle works in every isolate of the process. Open the same pool there with MysqlNativePool.fromHandle(handle). close() gives back one open, and the last close closes the pool:

MysqlNativePool other = MysqlNativePool.fromHandle(pool.handle);
pool.close();

docs.title: Native Postgres driver
docs.text:
dox_postgres_native is the Postgres driver of the Dox ORM, written in Rust.

You use it through your models and queries. Rust (tokio-postgres) owns the connections and the pool, and each connection keeps its prepared statements.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
dox_orm already depends on dox_postgres_native. Add it yourself only to use PgNativePool without the ORM:

dart pub add dox_postgres_native

The build hook downloads a ready library for your system, so you do not need Rust. The package has its own repo: dartondox/dox-postgres-native.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
The driver reads these keys from extra of the ConnectionConfig:

Key Default What it does maxConnectionCount 10 Most connections in the pool, for the whole process. requestTimeout 300 s The longest time for one request. maxConnectionAge no limit Close a connection older than this, when it has no query. idleTimeout no limit Close a free connection not used for this long. sslMode disable TLS mode, see TLS. sslRootCert none PEM file with the CA certificates for verify-ca and verify-full. sslWarning true false hides the warning for mode require. timeZone UTC Time zone of the session. applicationName none Name of the app in pg_stat_activity.

See Pool settings. Isolates with the same settings share one pool.

docs.title: When the library does not load
docs.text:
If the native library does not load, SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig throws an UnsupportedError:

dox_postgres_native did not load: <reason>.
Dox needs it to talk to Postgres. Fix: run the app with `dart run` or `dart build cli`. ...

To fix it:

  • Run the app with dart run, dart test or dart build cli, because they run the build hook. dart compile exe does not.
  • Or install Rust. The build hook then builds the library from source.
  • If you set lib_path in pubspec.yaml, check that the file is there and fits your system.

docs.title: TLS
docs.text:
Use TLS when the database is on another machine. Set the mode with extra['sslMode'], useSSL, or sslmode in DATABASE_URL:

ConnectionConfig(
  driver: Driver.postgres,
  // ... host, user, password, database
  extra: <String, dynamic>{'sslMode': 'verify-full'},
  debug: false,
),
Mode What it does disable No TLS. The default. prefer TLS when the server has it. No certificate check. require TLS. No certificate check, like libpq. useSSL: true gives this mode. verify-ca TLS. The certificate is checked, the host name is not. verify-full TLS. The certificate and the host name are checked.

Warning

Mode require does not check the server certificate. Use verify-full when your host supports it. Dox prints one warning per isolate for require.

docs.title: Trusting your own CA
docs.text:
verify-ca and verify-full trust the Mozilla roots and the roots of the system. For another CA, give a PEM file in extra['sslRootCert']:

extra: <String, dynamic>{
  'sslMode': 'verify-full',
  'sslRootCert': '/etc/ssl/certs/db-ca.pem',
},

In the url, use sslrootcert:

DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:secret@db.example.com/blog?sslmode=verify-full&sslrootcert=/etc/ssl/certs/db-ca.pem

Then only the certificates in that file are trusted. A missing or bad file throws a PgException when the pool opens.

docs.title: Values and types
docs.text:
Send plain Dart values: null, a bool, an int, a double, a String, a DateTime, a Duration (interval), a Uint8List (bytea), a Map (json) or a List (an array). If the server can not pick the type, add a cast, like @id::int8.

The ORM sends a List as json text on insert and update. With the pool alone, send jsonEncode(list) for a json column.

Postgres Dart int2, int4, int8 int float4, float8 double numeric String text, varchar, char String bool bool timestamp, timestamptz, date DateTime in UTC infinity dates the text 'infinity' or '-infinity' time String, like '13:45:01.5' interval Duration (a month is 30 days) json, jsonb the decoded JSON value uuid String bytea Uint8List arrays of most types above List NULL null

Other types come back as a Uint8List.

docs.title: Handling errors
docs.text:
A server error throws a PgServerException. Its code is the SQLSTATE, like 23505 for a unique violation:

try {
  await QueryBuilder.table('users')
      .insert(<String, dynamic>{'email': email});
} on PgServerException catch (error) {
  if (error.code == '23505') print('taken: ${error.constraint}');
}

It also has severity and message, and detail, hint, schema, table, column and constraint when the server sends them.

Other errors, like a down server, TLS or a timeout, throw a PgException. A cancelled query throws a PgQueryCancelledException, which is a PgException. All of them come from package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart.

docs.title: Opening a pool
docs.text:
PgNativePool.open opens a pool. query runs SQL and returns a PgNativeResult with columns and rows:

PgNativePool pool = PgNativePool.open(
  host: 'localhost',
  user: 'postgres',
  password: 'postgres',
  database: 'postgres',
);

PgNativeResult result = await pool.query(
  'SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id = @id',
  parameters: <String, dynamic>{'id': 1},
);
print(result.rows); // [{id: 1, name: Ada}]

parameters is a map for @name, or a list for $1, $2. A host that starts with / is a Unix socket folder.

docs.title: Pool settings
docs.text:
open also takes port (5432), maxConnections (10), timeZone, applicationName, sslMode, sslRootCert, requestTimeout, maxConnectionAge and idleTimeout:

PgNativePool pool = PgNativePool.open(
  host: 'localhost',
  user: 'postgres',
  password: 'postgres',
  database: 'postgres',
  maxConnections: 20,
  requestTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 30),
  idleTimeout: const Duration(minutes: 5),
);

A request over requestTimeout fails with a timeout PgException.

docs.title: Pool from a url
docs.text:
PgNativePool.fromUrl reads sslmode, sslrootcert and application_name from the url:

PgNativePool pool = PgNativePool.fromUrl(
    'postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db?sslmode=require');

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
begin gives a transaction id. Pass it as transaction to each query:

int tx = await pool.begin();
await pool.query('UPDATE users SET name = @n',
    parameters: <String, dynamic>{'n': 'Bob'}, transaction: tx);
await pool.commit(tx); // or pool.rollback(tx)

docs.title: Cancelling a query
docs.text:
Pass a PgCancelToken and call cancel(). isCancelled is true after it:

PgCancelToken token = PgCancelToken();
Future<PgNativeResult> slow =
    pool.query('SELECT pg_sleep(60)', cancelToken: token);
token.cancel();
try {
  await slow;
} on PgQueryCancelledException {
  print('stopped');
}

In a transaction, a cancelled query aborts the transaction, so roll it back. In the ORM, use cancelWith().

docs.title: Streaming rows
docs.text:
stream gives the rows in chunks of up to chunkSize rows, 1000 by default. About two chunks are in memory at a time:

await for (PgNativeResult chunk in pool.stream(
  'SELECT * FROM events WHERE day = @day',
  parameters: <String, dynamic>{'day': '2026-01-01'},
  chunkSize: 500,
)) {
  for (Map<String, dynamic> row in chunk.rows) {
    // ...
  }
}

Stop the loop with break to stop the query. In the ORM, use cursor().

docs.title: Sharing and closing a pool
docs.text:
pool.handle is an int that works in every isolate of the process. Open the same pool there with PgNativePool.fromHandle(handle). close() gives back one open, and the last close closes the pool:

PgNativePool other = PgNativePool.fromHandle(pool.handle);
pool.close();

docs.title: Query Builder
docs.text:
The query builder makes SQL from chained methods and runs it with bound values on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite.
