Every value goes to the database as a bound parameter, so you do not escape values yourself. Set up the database first, see Database.

docs.title: Starting a query
docs.text:
Start a query from a model to get models, or from a table name to get one map per row:

List<Actor> actors = await Actor().where('age', '>=', 23).get();

List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('actor')
    .where('age', '>=', 23)
    .get();

A query object keeps its parts, so start each new query with a new object. The examples use an Actor model on the table actor. The SQL in the comments is for Postgres.

docs.title: Another primary key
docs.text:
A table query uses id as the primary key. Set another one with setPrimaryKey:

await QueryBuilder.table('device').setPrimaryKey('uid').find('a1');

docs.title: Another connection
docs.text:
Run the query on another connection from the config:

await QueryBuilder.table('blog').withConnection('mysql').get();

See Using other connections. To read from the write database of a connection with replicas, use onWriteConnection(), see Read replicas.

docs.title: All rows
docs.text:
get runs the query and returns the rows that match:

List<Actor> actors = await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').get();
// SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "name" = @name_p0

all returns the rows that match the where part, but it ignores joins, order and limit:

List<Actor> actors = await Actor().all();

docs.title: One row
docs.text:
find gets one row by its primary key, or by a column and a value. It returns null when no row matches:

Actor? actor = await Actor().find(1);
Actor? byName = await Actor().find('name', 'John Wick');

first returns the first row, or null. getFirst does the same:

Actor? actor = await Actor().where('age', '>', 60).orderBy('age').first();
// SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "age" > @age_p0 ORDER BY "age" LIMIT 1

docs.title: Throwing when no row is found
docs.text:
firstOrFail and findOrFail throw a ModelNotFoundException when no row matches. A route that does not catch it answers 404:

Actor actor = await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').firstOrFail();
Actor byId = await Actor().findOrFail(1);
Actor byName = await Actor().findOrFail('name', 'John Wick');

sole expects exactly one row. It throws a ModelNotFoundException for no row, and a MultipleRecordsFoundException for more than one:

Actor actor = await Actor().where('email', 'john@example.com').sole();

docs.title: One value
docs.text:
valueOf returns one column of the first row, or null:

dynamic age = await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').valueOf('age');

docs.title: A list of column values
docs.text:
pluck returns the values of one column:

List<dynamic> names = await Actor().orderBy('name').pluck('name');
// ['John Doe', 'John Wick']

pluckMap returns a map. The second column gives the keys:

Map<dynamic, dynamic> names = await Actor().pluckMap('name', 'id');
// {1: 'John Wick', 2: 'John Doe'}

docs.title: Checking if rows exist
docs.text:
hasRows returns true when a row matches. hasNoRows and doesntExist return the opposite. They read one row at most:

bool taken = await User().where('email', email).hasRows();
bool free = await User().where('email', email).hasNoRows();

docs.title: Aggregates
docs.text:
count returns the number of rows:

int adults = await Actor().where('age', '>=', 18).count();
// SELECT count(*) as total FROM "actor" WHERE "age" >= @age_p0

sum, avg, min and max return one value, or null when no row matches:

num? total = await Actor().sum('age');
double? average = await Actor().avg('age');
dynamic youngest = await Actor().min('age');
dynamic newest = await Actor().max('created_at');

They ignore limit, offset and order. With groupBy, use selectRaw and get in place of them. To make sum give 0 for no rows, see ORM flags.

docs.title: Basic where clauses
docs.text:
where adds a condition. With two arguments it checks for equal. With three, the middle one is the operator:

await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').get();
// WHERE "name" = @name_p0

await Actor().where('age', '>=', 23).get();
await Actor().where('name', 'like', 'John%').get();

Many calls join with AND. The operator is one of =, !=, <>, <, >, <=, >=, like, not like or ilike. Another operator throws an ArgumentError.

docs.title: Or where clauses
docs.text:
orWhere joins a condition with OR:

await Actor().where('age', '<', 18).orWhere('age', '>', 60).get();
// WHERE "age" < @age_p0 OR "age" > @age_p1

docs.title: Checking for null
docs.text:
whereNull and whereNotNull check for NULL. A null value in where does the same:

await Actor().whereNull('deleted_at').get();
await Actor().whereNotNull('deleted_at').get();
await Actor().where('deleted_at', null).get(); // IS NULL
await Actor().where('deleted_at', '!=', null).get(); // IS NOT NULL

Each one has an or form: orWhereNull and orWhereNotNull.

docs.title: Grouping conditions
docs.text:
whereGroup puts conditions in brackets. orWhereGroup joins the brackets with OR:

await Actor()
    .where('status', 'active')
    .whereGroup((QueryBuilder<Actor> q) {
      q.where('age', '<', 18).orWhere('age', '>', 60);
    })
    .get();
// WHERE "status" = @status_p0 AND ("age" < @age_p1 OR "age" > @age_p2)

Give the function its type, like QueryBuilder<Actor> q, or q is dynamic.

docs.title: Where not clauses
docs.text:
whereNot keeps the rows where the conditions are not true. orWhereNot joins it with OR:

await Actor()
    .whereNot((QueryBuilder<Actor> q) {
      q.where('status', 'draft').orWhere('age', '<', 18);
    })
    .get();
// WHERE NOT ("status" = @status_p0 OR "age" < @age_p1)

await Actor().whereNot('age', '<', 18).get();

docs.title: Matching any or all columns
docs.text:
whereAny matches when one of the columns matches. whereAll matches when all of them match:

await Actor().whereAny(<String>['name', 'email'], 'like', '%john%').get();
// WHERE ("name" like @name_p0 OR "email" like @email_p1)

await Actor()
    .whereAll(<String>['first_name', 'last_name'], 'like', 'J%')
    .get();

Each one has an or form: orWhereAny and orWhereAll.

docs.title: Matching a list of values
docs.text:
whereIn keeps the rows where the column is in the list. whereNotIn keeps the others:

await Actor().whereIn('id', <int>[1, 2]).get();
// WHERE "id" IN (@id_p0,@id_p1)

await Actor().whereNotIn('id', <int>[1, 2]).get();

An empty list matches no rows for whereIn and all rows for whereNotIn. The value can also be a query that selects one column:

await Actor()
    .whereIn('id',
        QueryBuilder.table('award').select('actor_id').where('year', 2024))
    .get();

Each one has an or form: orWhereIn and orWhereNotIn. MySQL and MariaDB do not allow a limit in the inner query.

docs.title: Matching a range
docs.text:
whereBetween keeps the rows where the column is between two values, both included:

await Actor().whereBetween('age', <int>[18, 60]).get();
// WHERE "age" BETWEEN @age_p0 AND @age_p1

await Actor().whereNotBetween('age', <int>[18, 60]).get();

Each one has an or form: orWhereBetween and orWhereNotBetween.

docs.title: Comparing two columns
docs.text:
whereColumn compares two columns:

await Actor().whereColumn('updated_at', '>', 'created_at').get();
// WHERE "updated_at" > "created_at"

The or form is orWhereColumn.

docs.title: Matching a pattern
docs.text:
whereLike matches a pattern. % is any text and _ is one character. The match ignores case by default:

await Actor().whereLike('name', '%wick%').get();
await Actor().whereNotLike('name', '%doe%').get();
await Actor().whereLike('name', 'John%', caseSensitive: true).get();

Each one has an or form: orWhereLike and orWhereNotLike. On MySQL and MariaDB, the column collation decides the case match.

docs.title: Where exists clauses
docs.text:
whereExists keeps the rows where a subquery on another table finds a row:

List<User> users = await User()
    .whereExists('post', (QueryBuilder<Map<String, dynamic>> q) {
      q.whereColumn('post.user_id', 'user.id');
    })
    .get();
// WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM "post" WHERE "post"."user_id" = "user"."id")

The other forms are whereNotExists, orWhereExists and orWhereNotExists. The subquery skips global scopes and soft deletes. For a model relation, whereHas is shorter.

docs.title: Comparing dates
docs.text:
These methods compare one part of a date column. They take an operator, like where:

await Actor().whereDate('created_at', '2024-05-01').get();
await Actor().whereDate('created_at', '>=', DateTime(2024, 5, 1)).get();
await Actor().whereTime('created_at', '>', '18:00:00').get();
await Actor().whereYear('created_at', 2024).get();
await Actor().whereMonth('created_at', 5).get();
await Actor().whereDay('created_at', 15).get();

Each one has an or form, like orWhereDate. On SQLite, a date or time string must have zero padding, like 2024-05-01.

docs.title: JSON columns
docs.text:
Use -> in a column name to read a key inside a JSON column:

await Actor().where('options->lang', 'en').get();
await Actor().where('options->address->city', 'Paris').get();
await Actor().whereIn('options->lang', <String>['en', 'de']).get();

It works in the where methods, select, orderBy, groupBy and joins. In a select, give the value a name with as, like 'options->lang as lang'.

docs.title: Checking JSON arrays
docs.text:
whereJsonContains keeps the rows where a JSON array has the value. A list value needs all its items:

await Actor().whereJsonContains('tags', 'action').get();
await Actor().whereJsonContains('tags', <String>['action', 'drama']).get();
await Actor().whereJsonDoesntContain('tags', 'horror').get();

Each one has an or form, like orWhereJsonContains.

docs.title: Raw where clauses
docs.text:
whereRaw adds your own SQL. Put the values in a map and use @key in the SQL:

await Actor()
    .whereRaw('lower(name) = @name', <String, dynamic>{'name': 'john wick'})
    .get();

The or form is orWhereRaw.

Warning

Never put user input into the SQL text. Always send it in the map.

docs.title: Filtering by a relation
docs.text:
whereHas, whereDoesntHave and has filter by related rows. See Query by relations:

List<User> users = await User().whereHas('posts').get();

docs.title: Conditional clauses
docs.text:
when runs the function only when the condition is true. A third function runs when it is false:

await Actor()
    .when(status != null, (QueryBuilder<Actor> q) {
      q.where('status', status);
    })
    .get();

unless runs the function when the condition is false:

await Actor()
    .unless(showDrafts, (QueryBuilder<Actor> q) {
      q.where('status', 'published');
    })
    .get();

whenValue runs the function when the value is not null, and gives it the value:

await Actor()
    .whenValue(req.query['status'], (QueryBuilder<Actor> q, status) {
      q.where('status', status);
    })
    .get();

docs.title: Selecting columns
docs.text:
select sets the columns, as a list or a comma separated string:

await Actor().select(<String>['id', 'name']).get();
// SELECT "id","name" FROM "actor"

await Actor().select('id, name as actor_name').get();

Each part is a plain name, like name, table.* or name as alias. Each call replaces the columns of the call before.

docs.title: Raw select expressions
docs.text:
selectRaw takes an expression. Values go in the map:

await QueryBuilder.table('actor')
    .selectRaw('age * @rate as score', <String, dynamic>{'rate': 2})
    .get();

selectRaw replaces the select list. To make it add to the list, see ORM flags.

docs.title: Distinct rows
docs.text:
distinct returns each row only once:

await QueryBuilder.table('actor').select('age').distinct().get();
// SELECT DISTINCT "age" FROM "actor"

docs.title: Counting relations
docs.text:
withCount, withSum, withAvg, withMin, withMax and withExists add a value from a relation to each model. See Counting relations:

List<User> users = await User().withCount('posts').get();

docs.title: Ordering rows
docs.text:
orderBy sorts the rows, asc by default. orderByDesc sorts in desc order:

await Actor().orderBy('name', 'asc').orderBy('id', 'desc').get();
// ORDER BY "name" asc,"id" desc

await Actor().orderByDesc('age').get();

For an expression, use orderByRaw('count(*) desc'). Never put user input in it.

docs.title: Latest and oldest rows
docs.text:
latest and oldest sort by a date column, created_at by default:

Actor? newest = await Actor().latest().first();
await Actor().oldest('updated_at').get();

docs.title: Random order
docs.text:
inRandomOrder sorts at random. It is slow on a big table:

Actor? random = await Actor().inRandomOrder().first();

docs.title: Removing the order
docs.text:
reorder removes the order. It can also set a new one:

await Actor().latest().reorder().get();
await Actor().latest().reorder('name', 'desc').get();

docs.title: Limit and offset
docs.text:
limit sets the most rows, and offset skips rows. take and skip are the same:

await Actor().limit(10).offset(20).get();
await Actor().skip(20).take(10).get();

forPage gets one page. The first page is 1, and the page size is 15 by default:

await Actor().forPage(2, 50).get(); // rows 51 to 100

docs.title: Grouping rows
docs.text:
groupBy takes a column or a list of columns. For an expression, use groupByRaw:

await QueryBuilder.table('actor')
    .selectRaw('count(*) as total, age')
    .groupBy('age')
    .get();

Use a table query for groups, because a group row is a map. On a model, get with groupBy throws a StateError.

docs.title: Filtering groups
docs.text:
having filters the groups, with the same arguments as where. The or form is orHaving:

await QueryBuilder.table('actor')
    .selectRaw('status, count(*) as total')
    .groupBy('status')
    .having('status', '!=', 'draft')
    .get();

For an aggregate, use havingRaw or orHavingRaw. Postgres does not allow a select alias there:

await QueryBuilder.table('actor')
    .selectRaw('status, count(*) as total')
    .groupBy('status')
    .havingRaw('count(*) > @min', <String, dynamic>{'min': 5})
    .get();

docs.title: Basic joins
docs.text:
join adds the matching rows of another table. leftJoin and rightJoin work the same:

await Actor().join('actor_info', 'actor_info.actor_id', 'actor.id').get();
// JOIN "actor_info" on "actor_info"."actor_id" = "actor"."id"

await Actor()
    .leftJoin('actor_info', 'actor_info.actor_id', '=', 'actor.id')
    .get();

docs.title: Joins with more conditions
docs.text:
Pass a function in place of the columns. on and orOn compare columns, and where and orWhere compare with a value:

await Actor()
    .join('contact', (JoinClause j) {
      j
          .on('contact.actor_id', 'actor.id')
          .orOn('contact.agent_id', 'actor.id')
          .where('contact.active', true);
    })
    .get();

docs.title: Cross joins
docs.text:
crossJoin joins each row with each row of the other table:

await QueryBuilder.table('size').crossJoin('color').get();

docs.title: Raw joins
docs.text:
joinRaw, leftJoinRaw and rightJoinRaw take your own SQL. Values go in the map:

await Actor().rightJoinRaw(
  'actor_info on actor_info.actor_id = actor.id '
      'and actor_info.type = @type',
  <String, dynamic>{'type': 'main'},
).get();

docs.title: Subquery joins
docs.text:
joinSub and leftJoinSub join the rows of another query. The second argument names those rows:

QueryBuilder<Map<String, dynamic>> latest = QueryBuilder.table('post')
    .selectRaw('actor_id, MAX(created_at) as last_post')
    .groupBy('actor_id');

await Actor()
    .joinSub(latest, 'latest', 'latest.actor_id', 'actor.id')
    .get();

docs.title: Selecting from a subquery
docs.text:
fromSub reads from the rows of another query in place of a table:

QueryBuilder<Map<String, dynamic>> totals = QueryBuilder.table('order')
    .selectRaw('actor_id, SUM(amount) as total')
    .groupBy('actor_id');

await QueryBuilder.table('totals')
    .fromSub(totals, 'totals')
    .where('total', '>', 100)
    .get();

docs.title: Unions
docs.text:
union adds the rows of another query and drops the same rows. unionAll keeps them:

List<Actor> actors = await Actor()
    .where('age', '<', 18)
    .union(Actor().where('age', '>', 60))
    .orderBy('name')
    .get();

Both queries select the same number of columns. The order and limit of the first query apply to the whole result. A union is for reads only: the write methods throw a StateError.

docs.title: Raw queries
docs.text:
rawQuery sets the full SQL of a table query. Values go in the map:

List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('blog')
    .rawQuery('select * from blog where id = @id',
        <String, dynamic>{'id': 1})
    .get();

To run SQL with no query builder, use QueryBuilder.query(), see Running raw queries.

docs.title: Page numbers
docs.text:
paginate returns one page and the page info. It runs a count query and a select query:

Pagination<Actor> page = await Actor()
    .where('age', '>=', 18)
    .paginate(currentPage: 2, perPage: 10);

print(page.total);    // rows that match
print(page.lastPage); // number of pages

toJson() gives total, per_page, last_page, current_page and data, so a controller can return the page.

docs.title: Simple pagination
docs.text:
simplePaginate skips the count, so it runs one query:

SimplePagination<Actor> page = await Actor()
    .orderBy('id')
    .simplePaginate(currentPage: 2, perPage: 10);

print(page.hasMorePages);

toJson() gives per_page, current_page, from, to, has_more_pages and data.

docs.title: Cursor pagination
docs.text:
cursorPaginate reads the rows after a cursor, so it stays fast on a big table:

CursorPagination<Actor> page = await Actor()
    .orderBy('age', 'desc')
    .cursorPaginate(perPage: 10, cursor: req.input('cursor'));

print(page.nextCursor); // send it back as cursor for the next page

toJson() gives per_page, next_cursor, prev_cursor and data. The order columns must be in the select and must have no null values. With no orderBy, it orders by the primary key. A cursor that is not valid gives the first page.

docs.title: Chunking results
docs.text:
chunk reads a few rows at a time. Return false from the function to stop:

await Actor().where('age', '>=', 18).chunk(100, (List<Actor> actors) {
  for (Actor actor in actors) {
    print(actor.name);
  }
  return true;
});

chunk pages with an offset. If the function changes or deletes rows, use chunkById. It reads the rows after the last id:

await Actor().chunkById(100, (List<Actor> actors) async {
  for (Actor actor in actors) {
    await actor.delete();
  }
  return true;
});

chunkById throws a StateError with an orderBy. For another unique column, add column: 'uuid'.

docs.title: Streaming results
docs.text:
lazy, lazyById and cursor give the rows as a stream, for await for:

await for (Actor actor in Actor().where('age', '>=', 18).lazy()) {
  print(actor.name);
}
Method Queries How it reads lazy({chunkSize}) many By id, like chunkById. With an offset when the query has an order, a limit or an offset. lazyById({chunkSize, column}) many By id, or by the unique column. cursor({chunkSize}) one The database sends the rows when you are ready for more.

The default chunk size is 1000. Stop the loop with break to stop the queries.

Warning

In a transaction on Postgres or MySQL, do not run another query of the transaction inside a cursor() loop. It waits forever. Use lazy() there.

docs.title: Inserting one row
docs.text:
create inserts one row and returns it as it is in the table. insert does the same:

Actor actor = await Actor().create(<String, dynamic>{
  'name': 'John Wick',
  'age': 60,
});

Map<String, dynamic> row = await QueryBuilder.table('actor')
    .insert(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'John Doe'});

On a model with events, create calls save(). Without events, it does not set created_at and updated_at.

docs.title: Getting the new id
docs.text:
insertGetId inserts one row and returns its id:

dynamic id = await QueryBuilder.table('actor')
    .insertGetId(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'John Wick'});

docs.title: Inserting many rows
docs.text:
insertMultiple inserts many rows in one query and returns the new ids:

await Actor().insertMultiple(<Map<String, dynamic>>[
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'John Wick', 'age': 60},
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'John Doe', 'age': 25},
]);

On MySQL and MariaDB, the result has only the first id.

insertMany reads nothing back and returns true, so it works on a table with no id column:

await QueryBuilder.table('actor_movie').insertMany(<Map<String, dynamic>>[
  <String, dynamic>{'actor_id': 1, 'movie_id': 2},
  <String, dynamic>{'actor_id': 1, 'movie_id': 3},
]);

These methods fire no model events and set no timestamps.

docs.title: Upserts
docs.text:
upsert inserts rows, or updates the row that is there. It returns the number of changed rows:

int count = await Flight().upsert(
  <Map<String, dynamic>>[
    <String, dynamic>{'from': 'Oakland', 'to': 'San Diego', 'price': 99},
    <String, dynamic>{'from': 'Chicago', 'to': 'New York', 'price': 150},
  ],
  <String>['from', 'to'], // the unique columns
  <String>['price'], // the columns to update
);

The unique columns must be the primary key or a unique index. Leave out the third list to update every other column. Every row must have the same keys.

docs.title: Ignoring duplicate rows
docs.text:
insertOrIgnore skips the rows that clash with a unique key. It returns the number of new rows:

int added = await QueryBuilder.table('tag')
    .insertOrIgnore(<Map<String, dynamic>>[
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'action'},
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'drama'},
]);

docs.title: Finding or creating a row
docs.text:
The first map finds the row, and the second map has the other values:

User user = await User().firstOrCreate(
  <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com'},
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann'},
);

User other = await User()
    .firstOrNew(<String, dynamic>{'email': 'bob@example.com'});

User updated = await User().updateOrCreate(
  <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com'},
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann Lee'},
);
Method Row found No row found firstOrCreate returns it creates a row from both maps firstOrNew returns it returns a new model, not saved updateOrCreate updates it with the second map creates a row from both maps

Warning

Two requests at the same time can both create a row. Add a unique index, and use upsert when this matters.

docs.title: Updating or inserting rows
docs.text:
updateOrInsert updates every row that matches the first map. When none matches, it inserts one row. It does not read the row back:

await QueryBuilder.table('setting').updateOrInsert(
  <String, dynamic>{'key': 'theme'},
  <String, dynamic>{'value': 'dark'},
);

docs.title: Updating many rows
docs.text:
update changes the rows that match and returns their number:

int count = await Actor()
    .where('id', 3)
    .update(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'Updated AJ', 'age': 120});

On a model, the keys that fillable does not allow are dropped. To set every key, use forceUpdate, see skip the fillable check. A query update fires no model events and does not set updated_at.

Warning

On a model, update with no where throws a StateError. To change every row on purpose, see Writing every row.

docs.title: Incrementing and decrementing
docs.text:
increment and decrement change a number column in one query. The amount is 1 by default, and a map sets other columns too:

await Actor().where('id', 1).increment('views');
await Actor().where('id', 1).decrement('views', 2);
await Actor().where('id', 1)
    .increment('views', 1, <String, dynamic>{'status': 'hot'});

On a model from the table, they change only its row and its field.

docs.title: Touching timestamps
docs.text:
touch sets updated_at to now, or another column:

await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').touch();
await Actor().where('id', 1).touch('seen_at');

docs.title: Deleting rows
docs.text:
delete removes the rows that match and returns their number. On a model with softDelete: true, it sets deleted_at:

int count = await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').delete();
// DELETE FROM "actor" WHERE "name" = @name_p0

Warning

On a model, delete with no where throws a StateError. To delete every row on purpose, see Writing every row.

docs.title: Deleting soft deleted rows for good
docs.text:
forceDelete really deletes the rows, also the soft deleted ones:

await Actor().where('name', 'John Wick').forceDelete();

docs.title: Including soft deleted rows
docs.text:
withTrash also gives the soft deleted rows. onlyTrashed gives only them:

await Actor().withTrash().where('name', 'John Wick').get();
await Actor().onlyTrashed().get();

docs.title: Restoring soft deleted rows
docs.text:
restore sets deleted_at back to NULL. It returns true when it changed a row:

bool restored = await Blog().where('status', 'old').restore();

docs.title: Writing every row
docs.text:
To update or delete every row of a model on purpose, add whereRaw('1 = 1'):

await Actor().whereRaw('1 = 1').update(<String, dynamic>{'status': 'old'});
await Actor().whereRaw('1 = 1').delete();

Warning

QueryBuilder.table('actor').delete() and truncate skip soft deletes, so they really delete the rows.

docs.title: Truncating a table
docs.text:
truncate deletes all rows and resets the id counter:

await Actor().truncate();
await Actor().truncate(resetId: false);

On Postgres, truncate also empties every table with a foreign key to this table.

docs.title: Locking rows
docs.text:
lockForUpdate and sharedLock lock the rows that a select reads. Use them in a transaction, see Row locks:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  Actor actor = await Actor().lockForUpdate().findOrFail(1);
  actor.age = actor.age! + 1;
  await actor.save();
});

docs.title: Cancelling a query
docs.text:
cancelWith gives the query a QueryCancelToken. Then token.cancel() stops it on Postgres and MySQL:

QueryCancelToken token = QueryCancelToken();
Future<List<Actor>> actors =
    Actor().where('age', '>', 18).cancelWith(token).get();

token.cancel();
try {
  await actors;
} on PgQueryCancelledException {
  // Postgres
} on MysqlQueryCancelledException {
  // MySQL
}

On SQLite the query runs to its end.

docs.title: Global scopes
docs.text:
withoutGlobalScope and withoutGlobalScopes leave out the global scopes of a model. See Scopes:

await User().withoutGlobalScope('active').get();

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text: QueryBuilder.transaction, beginTransaction and afterCommit are on the Transactions page.

docs.title: Showing the SQL
docs.text:
toSql returns the SQL with the values put in, not quoted. toRawSql quotes each value:

Actor().where('name', "it's").toSql();    // ... WHERE "name" = it's
Actor().where('name', "it's").toRawSql(); // ... WHERE "name" = 'it''s'

Use them to read a query. Do not run this text.

docs.title: Printing queries
docs.text:
debug prints the SQL of the query when it runs:

await Actor().debug(true).where('age', 60).get();
// ▌ [db:default] SELECT * FROM "actor" WHERE "age" = 60;

To print all queries, set debug: true in the ConnectionConfig. See Configuration.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Transactions: run many queries as one unit.
  • Model: work with rows as objects.
  • Pagination: a list route with pages.

docs.title: Read replicas
docs.text:
A read replica is a copy of your database that only answers reads, and Dox can send reads to replicas and writes to the main database.

Postgres and MySQL support replicas. SQLite does not.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Add read to the ConnectionConfig. The host of the config is the write host:

lib/config/database.dart
'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
  driver: Driver.postgres,
  host: env.dbHost, // the write host
  user: env.dbUsername,
  password: env.dbPassword,
  database: env.dbName,
  debug: _debug,
  read: <Map<String, dynamic>>[
    <String, dynamic>{'host': 'replica-1.db'},
    <String, dynamic>{'host': 'replica-2.db', 'user': 'reader'},
  ],
  sticky: true,
),

Each read map can change host, port, user, password, database and extra. The other settings come from the config.

docs.title: Another write host
docs.text:
write sets the write host, with the same keys as one read map:

write: <String, dynamic>{'host': 'primary.db', 'port': 6432},

When DATABASE_URL is set, the url is the write host and write is not used.

docs.title: Where queries go
docs.text:
A plain SELECT goes to a read host. The read hosts take turns. These go to the write host:

  • INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE
  • a raw query that is not a SELECT
  • schema changes and migrations
  • a SELECT with a lock or with INTO
  • every query in a transaction

ReplicaDriver.isReadQuery(sql) tells you if a query can go to a replica.

docs.title: Reading from the write host
docs.text:
onWriteConnection() sends the queries of a query to the write host, also its preload() queries:

User? user = await User().onWriteConnection().find(id);

insert(), create() and updateOrCreate() always read the new row from the write host.

docs.title: Sticky reads
docs.text:
A replica can be a little behind. With sticky: true, the reads that follow a write in the same request go to the write host. So a request always reads what it wrote.

In a Dox app this works by itself, because dox_orm adds the stickyReads global middleware. Outside a request, like in a job, wrap the work in stickyScope():

await ReplicaDriver.stickyScope(() async {
  await Post().create(<String, dynamic>{'title': 'Hello'});
  List<Post> posts = await Post().get(); // read from the write host
});

When a replica read follows a write outside a scope, Dox prints one warning.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Database: connections and settings.
  • Transactions: all queries of a transaction go to the write host.

docs.title: Schema builder
docs.text: The schema builder creates, changes and drops tables with Dart code that works on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
In a migration, up and down get a Schema on the migration connection:

await schema.create('posts', (Table table) {
  table.id();
  table.foreignId('user_id').constrained().cascadeOnDelete();
  table.string('title');
  table.text('body').nullable();
  table.timestamps();
});

Outside a migration, Schema() uses the query builder connection and flags. Schema(driver, flags) takes your own:

Schema schema = Schema();
await schema.dropIfExists('posts');

docs.title: Creating tables
docs.text:
create makes a new table. The function adds the columns:

await schema.create('users', (Table table) {
  table.id();
  table.string('email');
});

docs.title: Updating tables
docs.text:
table changes a table that exists:

await schema.table('users', (Table table) {
  table.string('avatar').nullable();
});

docs.title: Renaming and dropping tables
docs.text:
rename renames a table. drop drops it, and dropIfExists does not fail when it is missing:

await schema.rename('posts', 'articles');
await schema.drop('users');
await schema.dropIfExists('users');

docs.title: Checking tables and columns
docs.text:
hasTable, hasColumn and hasColumns return true when the table or columns exist:

if (await schema.hasTable('users')) {
  // ...
}

await schema.hasColumn('users', 'email');
await schema.hasColumns('users', <String>['name', 'email']);

getColumnListing returns the column names of a table, in order:

List<String> columns = await schema.getColumnListing('users');

docs.title: Available column types
docs.text:
Each column type is a method on Table:

Method Postgres MySQL, MariaDB SQLite id(), bigIncrements('id') BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT increments('id') SERIAL PRIMARY KEY INT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT string('c', [255]) VARCHAR(n) VARCHAR(n) VARCHAR(n) char('c', [255]) CHAR(n) CHAR(n) CHAR(n) text('c') TEXT TEXT TEXT mediumText('c') TEXT MEDIUMTEXT TEXT longText('c') TEXT LONGTEXT TEXT integer('c') INTEGER INT INTEGER bigInteger('c') BIGINT BIGINT INTEGER smallInteger('c') SMALLINT SMALLINT INTEGER tinyInteger('c') SMALLINT TINYINT INTEGER unsignedInteger('c'), unsignedBigInteger, unsignedSmallInteger, unsignedTinyInteger signed type ... UNSIGNED INTEGER float('c') REAL FLOAT FLOAT double('c') DOUBLE PRECISION DOUBLE DOUBLE decimal('c', [8], [2]) DECIMAL(p, s) DECIMAL(p, s) DECIMAL(p, s) boolean('c') BOOLEAN TINYINT(1) BOOLEAN date('c') DATE DATE DATE dateTime('c') TIMESTAMP DATETIME DATETIME dateTimeTz('c') TIMESTAMPTZ DATETIME DATETIME time('c') TIME TIME TIME timestamp('c') TIMESTAMP TIMESTAMP TIMESTAMP timestampTz('c') TIMESTAMPTZ TIMESTAMP TIMESTAMP json('c'), jsonb('c') JSONB JSON JSON uuid(['uuid']) UUID CHAR(36) TEXT binary('c') BYTEA BLOB BLOB enumeration('c', ['a', 'b']) VARCHAR(255) + CHECK ENUM('a', 'b') VARCHAR(255) + CHECK foreignId('user_id') BIGINT BIGINT UNSIGNED INTEGER foreignUuid('user_id') UUID CHAR(36) TEXT foreignIdFor(User()) BIGINT BIGINT UNSIGNED INTEGER ulid(['ulid']), foreignUlid('user_id') CHAR(26) CHAR(26) CHAR(26) year('c') INTEGER YEAR INTEGER ipAddress(['ip_address']) VARCHAR(45) VARCHAR(45) VARCHAR(45)

With the laravelPostgresTypes flag, a new Postgres table gets TIMESTAMP and JSON in place of TIMESTAMPTZ and JSONB.

docs.title: Column helpers
docs.text:
timestamps adds nullable created_at and updated_at columns:

table.timestamps();

softDeletes adds a nullable deleted_at column, for models with softDelete: true. softDeletesTz is the same:

table.softDeletes();

morphs adds the columns of a polymorphic relation: owner_id, owner_type and one index on both. nullableMorphs allows NULL, and uuidMorphs makes owner_id a uuid:

table.morphs('owner');

rememberToken adds a nullable remember_token column:

table.rememberToken();

docs.title: Column modifiers
docs.text:
Modifiers come after the column type:

table.string('email').nullable().unique();
Modifier What it does nullable() Allow NULL. Columns are NOT NULL by default. nullable(false) makes it NOT NULL again. defaultTo(value) Set a default value. Strings are escaped. A bool, a number, null, a map or list (as JSON) and a DateTime work too. withDefault is the same. defaultRaw('sql') Set the default as raw SQL, not escaped. Put an expression in brackets, like defaultRaw('(1 + 1)'). useCurrent() Default to the current time. useCurrentOnUpdate() Set the current time on each update. MySQL only. unique() Add a unique index {table}_{column}_unique. index() Add an index {table}_{column}_index. primary() Make the column the primary key. unsigned() UNSIGNED. MySQL only. comment('text') Add a column comment. Postgres and MySQL only. collation('utf8mb4_bin') Set the collation of a text column. MySQL and MariaDB only. after('column') Put the new column after another one. MySQL only, in schema.table. change() Change a column that exists. See Modifying columns.

Other databases ignore the MySQL only modifiers.

docs.title: Modifying columns
docs.text:
In schema.table, a column is added. To change a column that exists, add .change():

await schema.table('posts', (Table table) {
  table.string('title', 500).nullable().defaultTo('x').change();
});

change() sets the full new column, so give every modifier you want to keep. A default you leave out is gone.

docs.title: Renaming columns
docs.text:
renameColumn renames a column:

await schema.table('users', (Table table) {
  table.renameColumn('bio', 'about');
});

docs.title: Dropping columns
docs.text:
dropColumn drops one column, and dropColumns drops many. dropTimestamps and dropSoftDeletes drop the helper columns:

await schema.table('users', (Table table) {
  table.dropColumn('age');
  table.dropColumns(<String>['a', 'b']);
  table.dropTimestamps();
  table.dropSoftDeletes();
});

docs.title: Creating indexes
docs.text:
index, unique and primary on the table take a column or a list of columns:

// posts_state_created_at_index
table.index(<String>['state', 'created_at']);
table.unique('slug'); // posts_slug_unique
table.primary(<String>['post_id', 'tag_id']); // composite primary key

The last argument sets your own name, like table.unique('slug', 'my_name'). indexName gives the default name: table.indexName('unique', ['slug']).

docs.title: Full text indexes
docs.text:
fullText makes a FULLTEXT index on MySQL, and a gin index on to_tsvector('english', ...) on Postgres:

table.fullText('body'); // posts_body_fulltext

docs.title: Renaming indexes
docs.text:
renameIndex takes the old and the new name:

table.renameIndex('posts_slug_unique', 'posts_url_unique');

docs.title: Dropping indexes
docs.text:
dropIndex and dropUnique take the columns or the index name:

table.dropIndex(<String>['state', 'created_at']);
table.dropUnique('posts_slug_unique');

dropPrimary drops the primary key. On Postgres it takes the name, {table}_pkey by default:

table.dropPrimary();

docs.title: Checking an index
docs.text:
hasIndex takes an index name, or all its columns in order:

await schema.hasIndex('posts', 'posts_slug_unique');
await schema.hasIndex('posts', <String>['state', 'created_at']);

On MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite, the primary key is named primary.

docs.title: Creating foreign keys
docs.text:
foreignId with constrained makes the column and the key:

table.foreignId('user_id').constrained().cascadeOnDelete();

It is the same as this long form:

table.foreignId('user_id');
table.foreign('user_id').references('id').on('users').onDelete('cascade');

constrained guesses the table from the column: user_id gives users. Dox models use singular table names by default, so give the name if your table is singular:

table.foreignId('user_id').constrained('user');
table.foreignId('editor_id').nullable().constrained('users');

Put nullable() before constrained(). The second argument of constrained is the parent column, id by default. foreignId('user_id').references('id').on('users') also works.

docs.title: Foreign keys for a model
docs.text:
foreignIdFor makes the foreign key column of a model, like user_id. Then constrained uses the table and key of that model:

table.foreignIdFor(User()).constrained().cascadeOnDelete();

A second argument sets the column name. foreignIdFor is always a big integer, so for a text key use foreignUuid or foreignUlid.

Same type on both sides

id() and foreignId() are both big integers. If the parent uses increments(), use unsignedInteger() for the child on MySQL.

docs.title: Foreign key actions
docs.text:
onDelete and onUpdate take cascade, set null, restrict or no action:

table.foreign('user_id').references('id').on('users').onDelete('set null');

The short forms are cascadeOnDelete(), nullOnDelete(), restrictOnDelete(), cascadeOnUpdate(), nullOnUpdate() and restrictOnUpdate().

docs.title: Dropping foreign keys
docs.text:
dropForeign takes the columns or the key name. dropConstrainedForeignId drops the key and then the column:

table.dropForeign(<String>['user_id']);
table.dropForeign('posts_user_id_foreign');
table.dropConstrainedForeignId('user_id');

docs.title: Turning foreign key checks off
docs.text:
withoutForeignKeyConstraints turns the checks off for the function, and on again after it:

await schema.withoutForeignKeyConstraints(() async {
  await QueryBuilder.table('posts')
      .insert(<String, dynamic>{'user_id': 1, 'title': 'Hi'});
  await QueryBuilder.table('users')
      .insert(<String, dynamic>{'id': 1, 'name': 'Ann'});
});

On SQLite, run it outside a transaction. On Postgres, only DEFERRABLE keys wait, and Dox keys are not DEFERRABLE.

disableForeignKeyConstraints and enableForeignKeyConstraints do the same in two steps. On MySQL, MariaDB and Postgres, run them in a transaction, or they throw a StateError:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await schema.disableForeignKeyConstraints();
  // ...
  await schema.enableForeignKeyConstraints();
});

docs.title: SQLite notes
docs.text:
SQLite ALTER TABLE can only add, rename and drop columns. For change(), foreign(...) on a table that exists and dropForeign(...), Dox makes the table again in one transaction. This fails on a table with other CHECK rules or with generated columns.

  • primary(...) on a table that exists does not work.
  • fullText and dropPrimary throw an UnsupportedError.
  • A new NOT NULL column needs a default, and a new column can not default to CURRENT_TIMESTAMP.
  • dropColumn fails when the column is in an index or a foreign key. Drop those first.

docs.title: See the SQL
docs.text:
A Table is a blueprint. toSql turns it into SQL with a grammar: PostgresGrammar, MysqlGrammar or SqliteGrammar:

Table table = Table('users', creating: true)
  ..id()
  ..string('email').unique();
print(table.toSql(PostgresGrammar()));
// [CREATE TABLE "users" (...),
//  CREATE UNIQUE INDEX "users_email_unique" ...]

schema.build(table) runs the SQL of a blueprint.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Migration: write and run migrations.
  • Model: the class for each table.

docs.title: Seeders
docs.text: A seeder puts data in your database, like sample data for development or a list of countries your app needs.

docs.title: Writing seeders
docs.text:
make:seeder makes a seeder:

dox make:seeder UserSeeder

This makes db/seeders/user.seeder.dart. It also writes db/seeders/seeders.dart, the list of all seeders, and bin/seed.dart. Do not edit the list, because Dox writes it again.

Put your code in run. You can use factories, models or the query builder:

db/seeders/user.seeder.dart
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import '../factories/user.factory.dart';

class UserSeeder extends Seeder {
  @override
  Future<void> run() async {
    await UserFactory().count(10).create();
  }
}

docs.title: Calling other seeders
docs.text:
dox db:seed runs DatabaseSeeder. Use its call method to run your other seeders, one after another:

db/seeders/database.seeder.dart
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import 'post.seeder.dart';
import 'user.seeder.dart';

class DatabaseSeeder extends Seeder {
  @override
  Future<void> run() async {
    await call(<Seeder>[UserSeeder(), PostSeeder()]);
  }
}

docs.title: Running seeders
docs.text:
db:seed runs DatabaseSeeder. --class runs one seeder:

dox db:seed
dox db:seed --class=UserSeeder

--class finds the seeder by its name, which is the class name. To seed after the migrations, add --seed to migration:run, migration:refresh or migration:fresh:

dox migration:fresh --seed

The seeders use the same database as the migrations. See Database settings.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
A seed runs in one transaction. If a seeder throws, nothing is saved, and the command exits with code 1. For a very large seed, turn the transaction off:

class BigSeeder extends Seeder {
  @override
  bool get withinTransaction => false;

  @override
  Future<void> run() async {
    // ...
  }
}

Only the seeder you run decides this. For dox db:seed, it is DatabaseSeeder.

docs.title: The seed script
docs.text:
dox db:seed runs bin/seed.dart. SeederRunner sets up the ORM, runs the seeder and closes the ORM. Pass config to use the database config of the app in place of .env:

bin/seed.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

import '../db/seeders/seeders.dart';

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SeederRunner(
    seeders: seeders,
    config: databaseConfig,
  ).run(args);
}

You can run it yourself, like dart run bin/seed.dart --class=UserSeeder. From code, seed runs one seeder by name:

await SeederRunner(seeders: seeders).seed('UserSeeder');

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
In a test, set up the ORM, then call run:

await DatabaseSeeder().run();

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Factories: make many rows fast.
  • Migration: make the tables first.
  • Testing with a database: use the database in tests.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text: A transaction runs many queries as one unit, so either all of them are saved or none of them.

docs.title: Running a transaction
docs.text:
QueryBuilder.transaction() commits when the function ends. When the function throws, it rolls back and throws the error again:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  Actor actor = Actor();
  actor.name = 'John Wick';
  await actor.save();
  await QueryBuilder.table('actor_info').insert(<String, dynamic>{
    'actor_id': actor.id,
  });
});

All queries and models inside the function use the transaction. The function can return a value:

int? id = await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  Actor actor = Actor();
  actor.name = 'John Wick';
  await actor.save();
  return actor.id;
});

docs.title: Another connection
docs.text:
Pass connection to use a named connection:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  // ...
}, connection: 'mysql');

On MySQL and MariaDB, a rollback can not undo CREATE, ALTER and DROP TABLE.

docs.title: Nested transactions
docs.text:
A transaction inside another one uses a savepoint. If the inner function throws, only its work is undone:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await Actor().create(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'John Wick'});
  try {
    await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
      await Actor().create(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'Bad row'});
      throw StateError('stop');
    });
  } on StateError {
    // only 'Bad row' is undone
  }
});

If you do not catch the error, the outer transaction rolls back too. Run nested transactions one after another, not in Future.wait, because they share one connection.

docs.title: Handling deadlocks
docs.text:
attempts runs the whole function again after a deadlock or a lock failure, up to that many runs in all:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  // ...
}, attempts: 3);

Other errors throw at once. The function runs again from the start, so put a mail or a call to another service in afterCommit().

DatabaseTransaction.isConcurrencyError(error) tells you if an error counts:

Database Errors Postgres SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization failure), 40P01 (deadlock) MySQL, MariaDB error 1213 (deadlock), 1205 (lock wait timeout), 1020 (record changed), SQLSTATE 40001 SQLite SQLITE_BUSY and SQLITE_LOCKED

docs.title: Begin and commit by hand
docs.text:
If the work can not fit in one function, use QueryBuilder.beginTransaction(). Only code inside run() uses the transaction:

DatabaseTransaction tx = await QueryBuilder.beginTransaction();
try {
  await tx.run(() async {
    User user = await User().create(<String, dynamic>{'email': email});
    await QueryBuilder.afterCommit(() => sendWelcomeMail(user));
  });
  await tx.run(() => QueryBuilder.table('audit')
      .insert(<String, dynamic>{'event': 'signup'}));
  await tx.commit();
} finally {
  await tx.rollBack(); // does nothing after commit
}
  • Await each run() before commit().
  • commit() saves the work, then runs the afterCommit() functions.
  • rollBack() undoes the work. It does nothing on a closed transaction.
  • tx.isOpen is true until commit(), rollBack() or the timeout.

docs.title: Timeout
docs.text:
A transaction that is still open after the timeout (1 minute by default) is rolled back, and its work is lost. Set your own timeout:

QueryBuilder.beginTransaction(timeout: const Duration(seconds: 10))

On Postgres, after a database error inside run(), call rollBack(). A commit() then saves nothing and gives no error.

docs.title: Run code after the commit
docs.text:
QueryBuilder.afterCommit() runs a function after the outermost transaction commits. A rollback drops it:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  User user = await User().create(<String, dynamic>{'email': email});
  await QueryBuilder.afterCommit(() => sendWelcomeMail(user));
});

Outside a transaction, the function runs at once. If a function throws, the data stays saved and the transaction() call throws the error. For a named connection, pass the same connection:

await QueryBuilder.afterCommit(() => notify(order), connection: 'mysql');

Queue jobs use this with dispatch(afterCommit: true).

docs.title: Row locks
docs.text:
A row lock stops two requests from changing the same row at the same time. Lock the row in a transaction, then change it:

Future<void> buy(int productId, int quantity) async {
  await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
    Product product = await Product().lockForUpdate().findOrFail(productId);

    if (product.stock! < quantity) {
      throw BadRequestException(message: 'Not enough stock');
    }

    product.stock = product.stock! - quantity;
    await product.save();
  });
}

The lock lasts until the transaction ends. Outside a transaction, it ends at once. Aggregates like count() do not lock.

Database lockForUpdate() sharedLock() Postgres FOR UPDATE FOR SHARE MySQL, MariaDB FOR UPDATE LOCK IN SHARE MODE SQLite nothing nothing

With sharedLock(), other transactions can read the rows, but they wait to change them. SQLite has no row locks, but a Dox transaction there takes the write lock of the whole database. So the same code is safe.

For one number column, increment() needs no lock.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Query Builder: the queries you run in a transaction.
  • Read replicas: where a query goes when you have replicas.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
A model is a Dart class for one database table, used to read, create, change and delete its rows.

Each object of the model is one row. A model also has all the query builder methods, so you can query the table through it.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Use make:model to make a new model. The -m option also makes a migration for the table:

dox make:model Blog      # only the model
dox make:model Blog -m   # the model and a migration for the table blogs
dox make:model Blog -a   # also a migration, factory, seeder, controller

This makes lib/app/models/blog/blog.model.dart. For the other options, see the CLI reference.

A model uses a generated class, so run the generator after you make or change a model. Use watch in place of build to run it on each save:

dart run build_runner build

docs.title: Model options
docs.text:
All options go in @DoxModel(...):

Option Default What it does table class name in snake_case The table name. primaryKey 'id' The primary key column. primaryKeyType int The Dart type of the primary key, like String for a UUID. createdAt 'created_at' The column that keeps the create time. null turns it off. updatedAt 'updated_at' The column that keeps the last update time. null turns it off. timestamps true false turns off createdAt and updatedAt. softDelete false delete() sets deleted_at and keeps the row.

docs.title: Defining models
docs.text:
A model is a class with @DoxModel(). Each @Column() field is one column of the table:

lib/app/models/blog/blog.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'blog.model.g.dart'; // (1)!

@DoxModel() // (2)!
class Blog extends BlogGenerator { // (3)!
  @Column() // (4)!
  String? title;

  @Column(name: 'body') // (5)!
  String? description;

  @Column(name: 'user_id')
  int? userId;
}
  1. build_runner writes this file. It holds the generated BlogGenerator class.
  2. Marks the class as a model. See Model options.
  3. The generated class gives the model id, createdAt and updatedAt, and the query builder methods.
  4. The column name is the field name in snake_case.
  5. Use name when the column name is not the snake_case of the field.

Make every column field nullable, because a new model has no values yet.

docs.title: Table names
docs.text:
The default table name is the class name in snake_case: BlogPost uses blog_post. Set table for another name:

@DoxModel(table: 'blogs')
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}

dox make:model Blog sets table: 'blogs' for you. With the pluralTableNames flag, the default name is plural.

docs.title: Primary keys
docs.text:
Set primaryKey for a key with another name, and primaryKeyType for a key that is not an integer:

@DoxModel(primaryKey: 'uuid', primaryKeyType: String)
class Device extends DeviceGenerator {}

The field name is the key in camelCase. save() inserts a new model, also when you set the key yourself.

docs.title: Timestamps
docs.text:
save() sets created_at and updated_at to the current UTC time. Set other column names, or turn them off:

@DoxModel(createdAt: 'created', updatedAt: 'modified')
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}

@DoxModel(timestamps: false)
class Setting extends SettingGenerator {}

docs.title: Column types
docs.text:
The field type tells Dox how to read the value:

Field type Column String? text, varchar int? integer types double? float, double. MySQL also gives decimal as a double. Postgres gives numeric as a string. bool? boolean, or a number like tinyint (0 is false) DateTime? date, datetime, timestamp Map<String, dynamic>? or List<dynamic>? JSON an enum, like Status? text with the enum name

For other types, use a cast.

docs.title: Changing values on save and read
docs.text:
beforeSave and beforeGet take a static function of the model. The function gets a map of the values and returns the new value:

@Column(beforeSave: makeSlug)
String? slug;

@Column(beforeGet: readStatus)
String? status;

static String? makeSlug(Map<String, dynamic> map) {
  return map['title']?.toString().toLowerCase().replaceAll(' ', '-');
}

static String? readStatus(Map<String, dynamic> map) {
  return map['status'] as String? ?? 'draft';
}

beforeSave gets the model values by column name. beforeGet gets the row from the database.

docs.title: Using another connection
docs.text:
Use a named connection for the query, and for the save and delete of its models:

Blog blog = Blog()..withConnection('mysql');
await blog.save();

docs.title: Retrieving models
docs.text:
Use the query builder methods to read rows:

Blog? found = await Blog().find(1);
List<Blog> drafts = await Blog().where('status', 'draft').get();

docs.title: Starting a new query
docs.text:
A model object keeps the parts of its query. query() gives a new, empty model to start another query:

Blog blog = Blog();
List<Blog> active = await blog.where('status', 'active').get();
List<Blog> deleted = await blog.query().where('status', 'deleted').get();

docs.title: Refreshing models
docs.text:
refresh() reads the row again into this model, with its relations. fresh() gives a new model and keeps this one as it is:

await blog.refresh();
Blog? now = await blog.fresh(); // null when the row is gone

Both read the row by its primary key. They also find a soft deleted row.

docs.title: Reloading relations
docs.text:
reload() loads the relations of the model again, for example after a save:

await blog.save();
await blog.reload();

docs.title: Inserts
docs.text:
Make a new model, set its fields and call save():

Blog blog = Blog();
blog.title = 'My first blog';
await blog.save();
print(blog.id); // the new id

Null fields are not sent, so the database default is used.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
save() on a model from the table updates it. It sends only the fields that changed:

Blog? found = await Blog().find(1);
found?.title = 'New title';
await found?.save();

To clear a column, set the field to null and save. A map or list field is always sent, because it can change in place.

save() returns false when a model event cancels it. saveQuietly() saves with no events.

docs.title: Checking if a row exists
docs.text:
exists is true when the model is in the table. wasRecentlyCreated is true after a save inserted the row:

User user = await User().firstOrCreate(<String, dynamic>{'email': email});
if (user.wasRecentlyCreated) await sendWelcomeMail(user);

docs.title: Creating from a map
docs.text:
create() makes a new row from a map and returns the model. The model needs fillable, see Mass assignment:

Blog created = await Blog().create(<String, dynamic>{
  'title': 'My first blog',
  'status': 'draft',
});

It works like save() on a new model, with the events. A null key is not sent, unless the createWritesNull flag is on. insert() on a model does the same as create().

docs.title: Updating from a map
docs.text:
update() on a model from the table changes only that row and sets updated_at. It fires no model events:

await blog.update(<String, dynamic>{'status': 'live'});

docs.title: Mass assignment
docs.text:
create(), insert(), update(), upsert() and the find or create methods take their keys from a map. So a model is guarded by default. List the keys that may come from a map:

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  // only these keys are taken from a map
  @override
  List<String> get fillable => <String>['name', 'email'];

  // or: every key but these is taken from a map
  @override
  List<String> get guarded => <String>['is_admin'];
}

With fillable, other keys are dropped. A model with no fillable and the default guarded throws a MassAssignmentException for a map with keys. Fields you set in code are always saved.

To take every key, set guarded to an empty list. This is not safe with user input:

@override
List<String> get guarded => const <String>[];

docs.title: Skip the fillable check
docs.text:
These methods ignore fillable and guarded. Never pass user input, like req.body, to them:

await User().forceCreate(
    <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann', 'is_admin': true});
await User().where('id', 1)
    .forceUpdate(<String, dynamic>{'is_admin': true});
await user.forceFill(<String, dynamic>{'is_admin': true}).save();

forceFill() sets the fields and does not save. Model events that fire inside forceCreate() and forceUpdate() also skip the check.

Model.unguarded() turns the check off for everything inside the callback. Await all work inside it, because work that ends later also runs with the check off:

await Model.unguarded(() async {
  await User().create(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'Bob', 'is_admin': true});
});

Model.isUnguarded is true inside the callback.

docs.title: Find or create
docs.text:
These methods find a row by the first map. When there is no row, they use both maps:

User user = await User().firstOrCreate(
  <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com'},
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann'},
);

User other = await User().firstOrNew(
    <String, dynamic>{'email': 'bob@example.com'});

User updated = await User().updateOrCreate(
  <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com'},
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann Lee'},
);

firstOrNew() does not save the new model. See the query builder.

docs.title: Incrementing and decrementing
docs.text:
Add to or take from a number column in one query. The field gets the new value too:

await blog.increment('views');      // views + 1
await blog.increment('views', 5);   // views + 5
await blog.decrement('views');      // views - 1
await blog.increment('views', 1, <String, dynamic>{'status': 'hot'});

The third argument sets other columns. They fire no model events and do not set updated_at, unless the incrementFiresEvents flag is on.

docs.title: Touch and replicate
docs.text:
touch() sets updated_at, or the column you give, to now. It fires the save events. touchQuietly() fires none:

await blog.touch();               // updated_at = now
await blog.touch('published_at'); // published_at = now

replicate() makes an unsaved copy with no primary key and no timestamps. List the columns to leave out:

Blog copy = blog.replicate(<String>['slug'])..title = 'Copy';
await copy.save();

Relations are not copied. The copy of a soft deleted model is soft deleted too.

docs.title: Checking changed columns
docs.text:
These methods tell you what changed before or after a save. The names are column names, like user_id:

blog.title = 'New title';

blog.isDirty();             // true
blog.isDirty('title');      // true
blog.isClean('body');       // true
blog.getDirty();            // {title: New title}
blog.getOriginal('title');  // the old title

await blog.save();
blog.wasChanged('title');   // true
blog.getChanges();          // {title: New title, updated_at: ...}

isDirty(), isClean() and wasChanged() also take a list of names.

docs.title: Deleting models
docs.text:
delete() deletes the row of the model. It returns 1, or 0 when the row was not there or a model event cancelled it:

int count = await blog.delete();

A model with no primary key value throws a StateError, so Blog().delete() can not delete every row. To delete the rows of a query, add a where. A global scope counts as a where. See writing every row.

docs.title: Soft deleting
docs.text:
A soft delete keeps the row and sets its deleted_at. Turn it on with softDelete:

@DoxModel(softDelete: true)
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}

The table needs a nullable deleted_at column. In a migration, add table.softDeletes();. Queries then leave out soft deleted rows.

docs.title: Reading soft deleted rows
docs.text:
withTrash() also gets the soft deleted rows. onlyTrashed() gets only them:

List<Blog> all = await Blog().withTrash().get();
List<Blog> trashed = await Blog().onlyTrashed().get();

docs.title: Restoring soft deleted models
docs.text:
trashed() tells you if a model is soft deleted. restore() brings it back:

Blog? blog = await Blog().withTrash().find(1);
if (blog!.trashed()) await blog.restore();

docs.title: Deleting for good
docs.text:
forceDelete() deletes the row, also on a soft delete model:

await blog.forceDelete();

docs.title: Converting to a map or JSON
docs.text:
toMap() gives all columns and computed values. toJson() gives the same without hidden fields:

Map<String, dynamic> map = blog.toMap();
Map<String, dynamic> json = blog.toJson();
Map<String, dynamic> row = blog.toMap(original: true); // the raw row

jsonEncode(blog) uses toJson(), so a controller can return a model or a list of models.

docs.title: Hide fields
docs.text:
Put fields like a password in hidden, and toJson() leaves them out. Use the column names:

@override
List<String> get hidden => <String>['password', 'remember_token'];

To keep only some fields, list them in visibleFields:

@override
List<String> get visibleFields => const <String>['id', 'name'];

For one model or a list of models, use makeHidden() and makeVisible():

return user.makeVisible(<String>['email']).toJson();
return users.makeHidden(<String>['phone']);

docs.title: Computed values
docs.text:
A computed value is a getter in the JSON that is not a column. Add @Computed(), then run the generator:

@Computed() // json key: full_name
String get fullName => '$firstName $lastName';

@Computed(name: 'initials') // custom json key
String get shortName => '${firstName?[0]}${lastName?[0]}';

The getter runs each time toJson() or toMap() runs, so keep it fast. hidden hides it by its json key.

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text: A model can load related models. See HasOne, HasMany, BelongsTo, ManyToMany, HasManyThrough and Polymorphic.

docs.title: Preloading relations
docs.text:
preload() loads a relation for all rows of a query. A dot path also loads the relations of the loaded rows:

Blog? blog = await Blog().preload('comments').find(1);
List<User> users = await User().preload('posts.comments').get();

docs.title: Filtering a preload
docs.text:
Give a callback to load only some related rows. With a dot path, it is for the last relation:

await User().preload('posts', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('published', true);
}).get();

docs.title: Loading a relation on a model
docs.text:
$getRelation() loads a relation into its field. related() gives a query for the related rows:

await blog.$getRelation('comments');
List<Comment> recent = await blog
        .related<Comment>('comments')
        ?.orderBy('id', 'desc')
        .get() ??
    <Comment>[];

docs.title: Saving through a relation
docs.text:
These methods save a related model and set the foreign key. They work with @HasMany, @HasOne, @MorphMany and @MorphOne:

Comment c = await blog.createRelated<Comment>('comments',
    <String, dynamic>{'body': 'hi'});
await blog.saveRelated('comments', Comment()..body = 'hi');
await blog.saveManyRelated('comments', <Comment>[c1, c2]);

createRelated() uses create(), but the foreign key does not need to be in fillable. For a @BelongsTo, use associate() and dissociate(). See BelongsTo.

docs.title: Debugging queries
docs.text:
debug(true) prints the SQL of the model in the terminal:

Blog blog = Blog()..debug(true);
blog.title = 'John Wick';
await blog.save();

docs.title: Methods on other pages
docs.text: Methods Page Model.observe(), Model.forgetObservers(), Model.withoutEvents() Model events withCount(), withSum(), withAvg(), withMin(), withMax(), withExists(), countOf(), aggregate() Counting relations whereHas(), orWhereHas(), whereDoesntHave(), orWhereDoesntHave(), has() Query by relations withoutGlobalScope(), withoutGlobalScopes() Query scopes associate(), dissociate() BelongsTo attach(), detach(), sync(), syncWithoutDetaching(), toggle(), updateExistingPivot(), pivot ManyToMany Model.morphMap(), Model.morphTypeOf(), Model.morphModel() Polymorphic

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• HasMany: connect one model to many.
  • Query scopes: keep a query you use often in the model.
  • Model events: run code when a model is saved or deleted.
  • Factories: make test rows.

docs.title: Attribute casts
docs.text:
A cast changes a column value between the database and Dart, for example to read JSON text as a map or to save an enum by its name.

A cast runs when a row is read, when the model is saved, and in toJson(). Casts work the same on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite.

docs.title: Defining casts
docs.text:
Set a cast with cast on @Column(), then run dart run build_runner build:

@DoxModel()
class Item extends ItemGenerator {
  @Column(cast: JsonCast())
  Map<String, dynamic>? meta;

  @Column(cast: ListCast<String>())
  List<String>? tags;

  @Column(cast: EnumCast<Level>(Level.values, byIndex: true))
  Level? level;
}

A bool field gets BoolCast() and an enum field gets EnumCast(values) by itself. A column with beforeGet does not use its cast.

A cast does not change a where() value, so use the database value there:

where('status', Status.live.name)

docs.title: Built-in casts
docs.text: Cast Dart value Database value JsonCast() a map or a list JSON, or JSON in a text column ListCast<E>() a typed list, like List<String> JSON, or JSON in a text column BoolCast() a bool boolean, a number (0 is false), or the text 1, 0, true, false, t, f EnumCast<E>(E.values) an enum text with the enum name EnumCast<E>(E.values, byIndex: true) an enum a number, the enum index

docs.title: Unknown enum values
docs.text:
A stored value that the enum does not have reads as null, with one warning in the log. Give unknown to read it as a value of your own:

@Column(cast: EnumCast(Status.values, unknown: Status.draft))
Status status = Status.draft;

A field that can not be null and has no unknown throws a StateError. A save does not overwrite the stored value, unless you set a real enum value.

docs.title: Custom casts
docs.text:
Extend Cast<T>. get() changes the database value to the Dart value, and set() changes it back. The class needs a const constructor:

class MoneyCast extends Cast<Money> {
  const MoneyCast();

  @override
  Money? get(dynamic value) => value == null ? null : Money(value as int);

  @override
  dynamic set(Money? value) => value?.cents;
}

@DoxModel()
class Product extends ProductGenerator {
  @Column(cast: MoneyCast())
  Money? price;
}

The generator copies the cast code into the generated file, so import the names it uses in the model file.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Model: the column types of a model.
  • Serializer: set the JSON shape of a model.

docs.title: Counting relations
docs.text:
withCount() adds the number of related rows to each model, without loading the rows.

It adds a subquery to the select, so you get the counts with the same query. Use the relation name, which is the field name.

docs.title: Counting related rows
docs.text:
Read the count with countOf(). In JSON, the key is the relation name in snake_case with _count:

List<User> users = await User().withCount('posts').get();

users.first.countOf('posts'); // 3
users.first.toJson();         // {..., "posts_count": 3}

It works with every relation but @BelongsTo and @MorphTo, which throw an UnsupportedError. The global scopes and soft deletes of the related model apply.

docs.title: Counting only some rows
docs.text:
Give a function with conditions, and use as to give the count its own key. Read a custom key with aggregate():

List<User> users = await User()
    .withCount('posts as published_count', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
      q.where('published', true);
    })
    .get();

users.first.aggregate('published_count');

docs.title: Counting and loading together
docs.text:
withCount() works with the other query methods and with preload():

User? user = await User().preload('posts').withCount('posts').find(1);

docs.title: Sum, average, min and max
docs.text:
withSum(), withAvg(), withMin() and withMax() work like withCount() on one column. The value is null when there is no related row:

User? user = await User()
    .withSum('posts', 'views')
    .withAvg('posts', 'views')
    .withMin('posts', 'views')
    .withMax('posts', 'views')
    .find(1);

user?.aggregate('posts_sum_views');

The keys are posts_sum_views, posts_avg_views, posts_min_views and posts_max_views.

docs.title: Checking if related rows exist
docs.text:
withExists() adds <relation>_exists, which is true when there is a related row. It takes a function and as, like withCount():

User? user = await User().withExists('posts').find(1);
user?.aggregate('posts_exists'); // true or false

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Query by relations: keep only the rows that have related rows.
  • HasMany: define a relation.

docs.title: Model events
docs.text:
A model fires events when you save, delete or restore it, so you can run your own code at these moments.

There are two ways to listen. A hook is a method in the model class. An observer is a separate class, for code that needs other services, like a mailer.

Events fire only on one model object. A query write, like Post().where('draft', true).update({...}), runs one query and fires no events.

docs.title: Defining hooks
docs.text:
Override an on... method in the model class, then run dart run build_runner build:

lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
@DoxModel()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  @Column()
  String? slug;

  @override
  Future<void> onSaving() async {
    slug = title?.trim().toLowerCase().replaceAll(' ', '-');
  }
}

A before hook runs before the query, so it can change values or cancel the operation. An after hook runs when the row is written:

Before hook After hook Runs on onSaving onSaved every save() onCreating onCreated save() or create() on a new model onUpdating onUpdated save() on a model from the table onDeleting onDeleted delete() onForceDeleting onForceDeleted forceDelete() onRestoring onRestored restore()

onTrashed runs after onDeleted when a soft delete changed the row. touch(), firstOrCreate() and updateOrCreate() fire the save events too.

docs.title: Order of events
docs.text:
The model hook runs first. Then the observers run, in the order you added them:

Call Events, in order save() on a new model saving, creating, INSERT, created, saved save() on a model from the table saving, updating, UPDATE, updated, saved delete() deleting, DELETE, deleted, then trashed after a soft delete forceDelete() forceDeleting, deleting, DELETE, deleted, forceDeleted restore() restoring, UPDATE, restored

A save with no changes runs no UPDATE, but it fires the same events. With the skipCleanUpdateEvents flag, it fires only saving and saved.

docs.title: Setting a value only on create
docs.text:
Use onCreating for a value that you set one time, on a new row:

@override
Future<void> onCreating() async {
  status ??= 'draft';
}

docs.title: Doing something after a change
docs.text:
Use an after hook for side effects, because the row is already in the database:

@override
Future<void> onSaved() async {
  await Cache().forget('post:$id');
}

docs.title: Cancelling an operation
docs.text:
Throw CancelModelEvent in a before hook, and the query does not run:

lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
@override
Future<void> onDeleting() async {
  if (status == 'published') {
    throw CancelModelEvent('unpublish the post first');
  }
}

save() and restore() then return false, and delete() and forceDelete() return 0. create() returns the unsaved model, with a null id.

docs.title: Observers
docs.text:
Extend ModelObserver<T> and override only the methods you need. They have the names of the hooks, and each one gets the model:

lib/app/observers/user.observer.dart
class UserObserver extends ModelObserver<User> {
  final Mailer mailer;

  UserObserver(this.mailer);

  @override
  Future<void> onCreated(User model) async {
    await mailer.sendWelcome(model.email!);
  }
}

A before method can also throw CancelModelEvent.

docs.title: Registering observers
docs.text:
Add the observer with Model.observe() in the setup() of a provider. The provider runs it in every isolate:

lib/providers/observer_provider.dart
class ObserverProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Model.observe<User>(UserObserver(Mailer()));
  }
}

A model can have more than one observer.

docs.title: Removing observers
docs.text:
Model.forgetObservers() removes the observers of one model, or of all models:

Model.forgetObservers<User>();
Model.forgetObservers();

docs.title: Listening to soft deletes
docs.text:
Add the TrashedObserver mixin and override onTrashed:

class PostObserver extends ModelObserver<Post> with TrashedObserver<Post> {
  @override
  void onTrashed(Post post) => print('trashed ${post.id}');
}

docs.title: Saving without events
docs.text:
saveQuietly() saves one model with no events, and touchQuietly() touches it with no events:

await user.saveQuietly();

Model.withoutEvents() turns off events for everything inside the callback:

await Model.withoutEvents(() async {
  await user.save();
  await post.delete();
});

docs.title: Events and transactions
docs.text:
save() does not start a transaction, so the row stays written when an after hook throws. To undo it, use a transaction:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await user.save(); // if onCreated() throws, the INSERT is rolled back
});

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Model: save and delete models.
  • Providers: register observers.
  • Transactions: undo a write when a hook fails.

docs.title: Query by relations
docs.text:
whereHas(), whereDoesntHave() and has() keep the rows of a query by their related rows.

They add a subquery to the where part and do not load the related rows. To load them, use preload(). Use the relation name (the field name), and start the query with a model, like User().

docs.title: Rows that have a relation
docs.text:
whereHas() keeps the rows that have a related row. A function adds conditions to the related rows:

List<User> users = await User().whereHas('posts').get();

List<User> writers = await User().whereHas('posts',
    (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('published', true);
}).get();

Soft deleted related rows do not count. The global scopes and the onQuery function of the relation apply.

docs.title: Rows that do not have a relation
docs.text:
whereDoesntHave() keeps the rows that have no related row. It also takes a function:

List<User> users = await User().whereDoesntHave('posts').get();

docs.title: Joining with or
docs.text:
orWhereHas() and orWhereDoesntHave() join the condition with OR:

List<User> users = await User()
    .where('name', 'Ann')
    .orWhereHas('posts')
    .get();

await User().where('name', 'Ann').orWhereDoesntHave('posts').get();

docs.title: Counting related rows
docs.text:
has() takes an operator and a number. The default is at least one related row:

await User().has('posts', '>=', 3).get();
await User().has('posts', '=', 0).get();

await User().has('posts', '>', 1, (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('published', true);
}).get();

The operator is one of =, !=, <>, <, >, <= or >=.

docs.title: Relations of relations
docs.text:
Use a dot path. The function is for the last relation:

await User().whereHas('posts.comments', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('user_id', 1);
}).get();

With has(), the count is for the last relation of one row. So has('posts.comments', '>=', 2) keeps the users that have a post with two comments or more.

docs.title: A relation to the same table
docs.text:
It works for a relation to the same table, like a category and its parent:

List<Category> books = await Category()
    .whereHas('parent', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
      q.where('name', 'Books');
    })
    .get();

In the function, write the column without the table name: name, not categories.name.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Counting relations: count the related rows.
  • HasMany: define a relation.

docs.title: Query scopes
docs.text: A scope is a query part that you use again and again, like "only active users", written once in the model and called like a query method.

docs.title: Local scopes
docs.text:
Add a static method with @Scope() to the model. It takes the query first and returns the query. Then run dart run build_runner build:

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Scope()
  static QueryBuilder<User> isActive(QueryBuilder<User> q) {
    return q.where('active', true);
  }

  @Scope()
  static QueryBuilder<User> olderThan(QueryBuilder<User> q, int age) {
    return q.where('age', '>', age);
  }
}

Call each scope as a method on the query, without the query argument:

List<User> adults = await User().isActive().olderThan(18).get();

The scope name must not be the name of a field, a method of the model or a query method. So name a scope isActive, not active, next to an active field.

docs.title: Global scopes
docs.text:
A global scope adds a condition to every query of the model. Use @Scope(global: true):

@DoxModel()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Scope(global: true)
  static QueryBuilder<Post> notArchived(QueryBuilder<Post> q) {
    return q.where('archived', false);
  }
}

await Post().get(); // ... WHERE ("archived" = false)

It applies to reads, counts, query updates and deletes, and relation queries. So Post().delete() deletes only the rows in the scope.

docs.title: Removing global scopes
docs.text:
Remove one scope by its method name, or remove all of them:

await Post().withoutGlobalScope('notArchived').get();
await Post().withoutGlobalScopes().find(1);

A query write with withoutGlobalScopes() and no where throws a StateError.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Query Builder: the methods you can use in a scope.
  • Model: the model basics.

docs.title: BelongsTo
docs.text:
Use BelongsTo when this table keeps the foreign key to another table.

For example, a comment belongs to a user, so the comment table has the column user_id. It is the other side of HasOne and HasMany.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Add a nullable field with @BelongsTo() to the model that has the foreign key column:

lib/app/models/comment/comment.model.dart
@DoxModel()
class Comment extends CommentGenerator {
  @Column()
  int? userId; // column user_id

  @Column()
  String? content;

  @BelongsTo(User)
  User? user;
}

Run dart run build_runner build after you add a relation.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
The default foreign key comes from the class name of the related model, not from the field name. So a field author still uses user_id. Set the key for another name:

@BelongsTo(User, foreignKey: 'author_id', localKey: 'id')
User? author;
Option Default What it is foreignKey {related model}_id, like user_id The column in this table that points to the related model. localKey the primary key of the related model The column in the related table that foreignKey points to. onQuery none A static function that changes the query. eager false Load the relation on every query.
