size gives the size in bytes, and lastModified gives the time of the last change. Both throw FileNotFoundException when the file is missing:

int size = await Storage().size(path);
DateTime changed = await Storage().lastModified(path);

docs.title: Downloading files
docs.text:
stream shows a file in the browser, and download makes the browser save it. Both stream the file, and a missing file answers 404:

Route.get('/photo', (DoxRequest req) {
  return Storage().stream(req.input('path'));
});

Route.get('/report', (DoxRequest req) {
  return Storage().disk('s3').download('reports/2024.pdf');
});

download uses the last part of the path as the file name. Give name: to use another name:

Route.get('/invoice', (DoxRequest req) {
  return Storage().download('invoices/42.pdf', name: 'Invoice 42.pdf');
});

To add headers, put the download in a response():

Route.get('/invoice', (DoxRequest req) async {
  DownloadableFile file = await Storage().download('invoices/42.pdf');
  return response(file).header('Cache-Control', 'no-store');
});

docs.title: File URLs
docs.text:
url gives the URL of a file. On a local disk with no url option, it gives /storage/<path>:

String url = await Storage().url(path);

Dox serves that URL only with Storage.route('storage', signed: false). See Serving local files.

docs.title: Signed URLs
docs.text:
A signed URL opens a file for a short time, like a private invoice. temporaryUrl is the same as signedUrl:

String signed =
    await Storage().signedUrl(path, expiresIn: Duration(minutes: 10));
String same = await Storage().temporaryUrl(path);

On a local disk, signedUrl needs the disk url option: the full URL of the route, like https://app.test/files.

docs.title: Serving local files
docs.text:
Storage.route adds a route that serves the files of a disk:

lib/routes/web.dart
Storage.route('files');                  // GET /files/{key*}, signed only
Storage.route('public', signed: false);  // any file of the disk
Storage.route('docs', disk: 'memory', signed: false); // another disk
Storage.route('uploads', download: true); // every file is a download

A signed URL of the files route looks like this:

String url = await Storage().signedUrl('invoices/1.pdf');
// https://app.test/files/invoices/1.pdf?expires=...&signature=...

A missing, wrong or expired signature answers 403. Signed routes work only on a local disk. An html, svg, xml or javascript file is always sent as a download in a sandbox, so its script cannot run on your site.

docs.title: Copying and moving files
docs.text:
copy and move replace an old file at the new path:

await Storage().copy('notes/a.txt', 'backup/a.txt');
await Storage().move('backup/a.txt', 'old/a.txt');

On S3, the copy runs inside S3. A missing source file answers 404.

docs.title: Deleting files
docs.text: await Storage().delete(path);

docs.title: Directories
docs.text:
files gives the files in a folder, allFiles also gives the files in sub-folders, and directories gives the sub-folders. Each path starts with /:

List<String> files = await Storage().files('images');
List<String> all = await Storage().allFiles('images');
List<String> folders = await Storage().directories('images');

directoryExists checks for a folder. On S3 and memory disks, a folder exists when a file is in it:

bool folder = await Storage().directoryExists('images');

makeDirectory makes a folder. It works only on a local disk:

await Storage().makeDirectory('reports');

deleteDirectory deletes a folder and all files in it:

await Storage().deleteDirectory('old');

The root ('' or /) throws InvalidKeyException. To empty a full disk, use Storage().use().deleteAll().

docs.title: File visibility
docs.text:
A file is public or private. Use setVisibility and getVisibility:

await Storage().setVisibility(path, Visibility.private);
Visibility visibility = await Storage().getVisibility(path);

On S3, setVisibility sets the ACL. With 'acl': false (R2 and similar), it does nothing, and getVisibility gives the disk visibility. On a local disk it is the same, unless you turn on permissions.

docs.title: Visibility on a local disk
docs.text:
Add 'permissions': true to use file modes. Then setVisibility runs chmod, and getVisibility reads the mode:

'local': <String, dynamic>{
  'driver': 'local',
  'root': 'storage',
  'permissions': true,
},

The modes are: public file 0644, private file 0600, public folder 0755, private folder 0700. On Windows, permissions does nothing.

docs.title: Custom file modes
docs.text:
Give permissions a map with a file and a dir key. Dart has no octal numbers, so write the modes in hex: 0x1a0 is 0640:

'private': <String, dynamic>{
  'driver': 'local',
  'root': 'storage-private',
  'visibility': 'private',
  'permissions': <String, dynamic>{
    'file': <String, int>{'public': 0x1a4, 'private': 0x1a0},
    'dir': <String, int>{'public': 0x1ed, 'private': 0x1e8},
  },
},

A mode you leave out keeps its default. A mode that is not an int from 0 to 0x1ff throws an ArgumentError.

docs.title: The disk API
docs.text:
Storage() has short methods for common work. For more control, get a Disk with use. With no name, you get the default disk:

Disk disk = Storage().use('s3');

A Disk also has get, exists, missing, delete, copy, move, size, lastModified, append, prepend, files, allFiles, directories, directoryExists, makeDirectory, deleteDirectory, getVisibility and setVisibility. Its get throws FileNotFoundException when the file is missing.

docs.title: Write options
docs.text:
put on a Disk writes to the exact key. WriteOptions sets the content type and the visibility. copy and move also take options::

await disk.put('a.json', '{}',
    options: WriteOptions(
        contentType: 'application/json', visibility: Visibility.public));

docs.title: Storing big files
docs.text:
putStream writes a stream, so the file is not loaded into memory:

await disk.putStream('videos/big.mp4', File('big.mp4').openRead());

On S3, put has a limit of 5 GiB. putStream uses a multipart upload with parts of multipartPartSize (8 MiB, a field of S3DriverConfig), up to about 78 GiB.

docs.title: Reading text and streams
docs.text:
getString reads a file as text. For a big file, use getStream. Both throw FileNotFoundException when the file is missing:

String text = await disk.getString('notes/a.txt');

Stream<List<int>> stream = await disk.getStream('videos/big.mp4');

getStreamWithMetaData gives the stream and the metadata together. On S3 it is one request:

ObjectStream file = await disk.getStreamWithMetaData('videos/big.mp4');
// file.stream, file.metaData

docs.title: All metadata in one call
docs.text:
getMetaData gives the size, content type, last change time and etag:

ObjectMetaData meta = await disk.getMetaData('avatars/1.png');

docs.title: Public URLs
docs.text:
getUrl gives the public URL of a file:

String url = await disk.getUrl('avatars/1.png');

docs.title: Deleting many files
docs.text:
deleteAll removes all files under a prefix. With '' or no argument, it empties the disk:

await disk.deleteAll('avatars');

docs.title: Listing page by page
docs.text:
For a big folder, read one page at a time with listAll:

ListResult page = await disk.listAll('avatars',
    ListOptions(recursive: true, limit: 100));
// next page: ListOptions(paginationToken: page.paginationToken)

docs.title: Signed URL options
docs.text:
getSignedUrl takes SignedUrlOptions. expiresIn is 30 minutes by default, and on S3 the maximum is 7 days. contentDisposition sets the header of the download:

String signed = await disk.getSignedUrl('avatars/1.png',
    options: SignedUrlOptions(expiresIn: Duration(minutes: 10)));

docs.title: Signed upload URLs
docs.text:
On S3, the browser can upload a file directly to the bucket with a signed upload URL:

String upload = await disk.getSignedUploadUrl('avatars/2.png',
    options: SignedUrlOptions(contentType: 'image/png'));

docs.title: S3-compatible services
docs.text: These examples use S3DriverConfig, the class behind an s3 disk. In a Dox config, the same settings are the disk keys endpoint, path_style, acl and batch_delete. See Configuration.

docs.title: Cloudflare R2
docs.text:
R2 does not take ACL headers, so set supportsAcl: false:

S3DriverConfig(
  bucket: 'my-bucket',
  region: 'auto',
  endpoint: 'https://<account-id>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com',
  accessKeyId: '...',
  secretAccessKey: '...',
  supportsAcl: false,
);

docs.title: MinIO
docs.text:
MinIO needs path style URLs:

S3DriverConfig(
  bucket: 'my-bucket',
  region: 'us-east-1',
  endpoint: 'http://localhost:9000',
  forcePathStyle: true,
  accessKeyId: 'minioadmin',
  secretAccessKey: 'minioadmin',
);

docs.title: DigitalOcean Spaces
docs.text:
Put the region of your space in region and in the endpoint:

S3DriverConfig(
  bucket: 'my-space',
  region: 'nyc3',
  endpoint: 'https://nyc3.digitaloceanspaces.com',
  accessKeyId: '...',
  secretAccessKey: '...',
);

docs.title: Google Cloud Storage
docs.text:
GCS does not take ACL headers or the S3 batch delete call:

S3DriverConfig(
  bucket: 'my-bucket',
  region: 'auto',
  endpoint: 'https://storage.googleapis.com',
  accessKeyId: 'GOOG...',
  secretAccessKey: '...',
  supportsAcl: false,
  supportsBatchDelete: false,
);

docs.title: Custom drivers
docs.text:
Implement DriverContract, and register it in a provider so every isolate has it:

Storage.manager.register('dropbox', DropboxDriver());
await Storage().disk('dropbox').put('notes/a.txt', 'hello', exact: true);

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
All errors extend StorageException and have the key:

Error When FileNotFoundException the file does not exist PermissionDeniedException a file system permission error, or S3 403 InvalidKeyException an unsafe key UnsupportedOperationException the driver cannot do this DriverException any other error. The first error is in cause

A key with .., an absolute path like /etc/passwd, or a null byte throws InvalidKeyException. So a user cannot get files outside the disk.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
To replace a disk with a memory disk in tests, see Testing. A disk also has assertExists and assertMissing. They throw a StateError when the check fails:

Disk fake = Storage.manager.fake('s3');
await fake.assertExists('avatars/1.png');
await fake.assertMissing('avatars/old.png');

Storage.manager.restore('s3') removes one fake, and Storage.manager.restoreAll() removes all fakes.

docs.title: Without Dox
docs.text:
dox_storage also works on its own:

dart pub add dox_storage

Make a DriveManager with your disks:

import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';

Map<String, String> env = Platform.environment;

DriveManager drive = DriveManager(
  defaultDisk: 'local',
  disks: <String, DriverContract>{
    'local': LocalDriver(LocalDriverConfig(
      root: 'storage',
      urlBase: 'https://app.test/uploads',
      atomicWrites: true, // off by default
      appKey: env['APP_KEY'], // signs local URLs
    )),
    's3': S3Driver(S3DriverConfig(
      bucket: 'my-bucket',
      region: 'us-east-1',
      accessKeyId: env['AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID']!,
      secretAccessKey: env['AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY']!,
    )),
  },
);

Disk disk = drive.use('s3'); // or drive.use() for the default disk

To add your own driver, call drive.register('dropbox', DropboxDriver()). For file modes, give LocalDriverConfig(permissions: LocalPermissions()).

docs.title: Checking a local signed URL
docs.text:
Check a local signed URL in the route that serves the file:

LocalDriver local = LocalDriver(localConfig);
bool ok = local.verifySignedUrl(keyFromPath, req.uri.queryParameters);
if (!ok) {
  return response('Forbidden').statusCode(403);
}

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• File upload: a full upload route, from the DTO to the URL.
  • Request: read an uploaded file.
  • Static files and SPA: serve a folder.

docs.title: gRPC
docs.text:
gRPC lets your services call each other with typed messages, on the same port as your HTTP routes.

You write the calls one time in a .proto file, and each side gets typed code from it. A client in any language can call your app.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Run the setup command in your app:

dox add grpc

It adds the packages, a sample protos/greeter.proto file, lib/routes/grpc.dart and APP_HTTP2=true in .env. To add the packages yourself, run dart pub add dox_grpc protobuf grpc.

gRPC works only over HTTP/2. A new app turns it on from the APP_HTTP2 key:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  http2: env.appHttp2 ?? false,
  // ...
);

If your AppEnv has no appHttp2 getter, add bool? get appHttp2; and run dart run build_runner build. Or set http2: true.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Give a GrpcOptions to Grpc.register to change the limits of one service:

Option Default What it does maxReceiveMessageSize 4 MiB The largest request message, also after unzip. maxSendMessageSize 4 MiB The largest reply message. gzipResponses false Gzip the replies for clients that accept gzip. idleTimeout 5 minutes Stop a call with no message in or out for this time. null means no limit.

A bigger message stops the call with RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED. An idle call stops with DEADLINE_EXCEEDED. See Changing the options.

docs.title: Write the .proto file
docs.text:
A .proto file gives the calls of a service and their messages. The setup command wrote this sample:

protos/greeter.proto
syntax = "proto3";

package greeter;

service Greeter {
  rpc SayHello (HelloRequest) returns (HelloReply);
}

message HelloRequest {
  string name = 1;
}

message HelloReply {
  string message = 1;
}

docs.title: Generate the Dart code
docs.text:
Install protoc and its Dart plugin one time. ~/.pub-cache/bin must be on your PATH:

brew install protobuf
dart pub global activate protoc_plugin

Generate the code. Do this again after each change to the .proto file:

mkdir -p lib/generated
protoc --dart_out=grpc:lib/generated -Iprotos protos/greeter.proto

It writes the message classes and a GreeterServiceBase class to lib/generated.

docs.title: Write the service
docs.text:
Extend the generated base class. Each rpc of the .proto file is one method:

lib/app/grpc/greeter_service.dart
import 'package:dox_grpc/dox_grpc.dart';

import '../../generated/greeter.pbgrpc.dart';

class GreeterService extends GreeterServiceBase {
  @override
  Future<HelloReply> sayHello(
      ServiceCall call, HelloRequest request) async {
    return HelloReply(message: 'Hello ${request.name}');
  }
}

docs.title: Register the service
docs.text:
Call Grpc.register in the router that the setup command wrote. Keep the health check as the first call:

lib/routes/grpc.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_grpc/dox_grpc.dart';

import '../app/grpc/greeter_service.dart';

class GrpcRouter extends Router {
  @override
  void register() {
    Grpc.register(HealthService());
    Grpc.register(GreeterService());
  }
}

Run dart run build_runner build and start the app again.

The router must have no prefix, because a gRPC client always calls /<package.Service>/<Method>. So do not use the api router or a Route.group. A changed path throws a StateError at start.

docs.title: Call the service
docs.text:
Test a call with grpcurl. Give it the .proto file, because Dox has no server reflection:

grpcurl -plaintext -import-path protos -proto greeter.proto \
  -d '{"name": "Ann"}' localhost:3000 greeter.Greeter/SayHello

The reply is { "message": "Hello Ann" }.

docs.title: Add auth
docs.text:
Your Dox middleware runs before each call. Put the services that need a login in Route.middleware, and keep the health check out of it:

lib/routes/grpc.dart
class GrpcRouter extends Router {
  @override
  void register() {
    Grpc.register(HealthService());

    Route.middleware(<dynamic>[AuthMiddleware()], () {
      Grpc.register(GreeterService());
    });
  }
}

A client sends its token as metadata. The middleware reads it as a header:

lib/app/http/middleware/auth.middleware.dart
class AuthMiddleware implements IDoxMiddleware {
  @override
  dynamic handle(IDoxRequest req) {
    String token = Env.get<String>('API_TOKEN');
    String sent = req.header('authorization') ?? '';
    if (!Hash.equals(sent, 'Bearer $token')) {
      throw HttpStatusException(401, message: 'Bad token');
    }
    return req;
  }
}

The client gets the gRPC status of the HTTP error, so 401 becomes UNAUTHENTICATED. See HTTP errors and gRPC statuses.

docs.title: Middleware for a full router
docs.text:
Set the middleware of the router when all its services need it:

lib/routes/grpc.dart
class GrpcRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware()];

  @override
  void register() {
    Grpc.register(GreeterService());
  }
}

Then register the health check in a router with no middleware, and put it first in routers of the app config. See Routers and providers. The first Grpc.register of the app in Route.middleware throws a StateError at start.

docs.title: Call types
docs.text:
gRPC has four types of calls. The place of stream in the .proto file sets the type:

protos/greeter.proto
service Greeter {
  rpc SayHello (HelloRequest) returns (HelloReply);
  rpc SayHelloMany (HelloRequest) returns (stream HelloReply);
  rpc CollectNames (stream HelloRequest) returns (HelloReply);
  rpc Chat (stream HelloRequest) returns (stream HelloReply);
}

docs.title: Unary calls
docs.text:
One request and one reply. The method returns a Future:

@override
Future<HelloReply> sayHello(ServiceCall call, HelloRequest request) async {
  return HelloReply(message: 'Hello ${request.name}');
}

docs.title: Server streaming
docs.text:
One request and many replies. The method returns a Stream:

@override
Stream<HelloReply> sayHelloMany(
    ServiceCall call, HelloRequest request) async* {
  for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
    if (call.isCanceled) return;
    yield HelloReply(message: 'Hello ${request.name} $i');
  }
}

docs.title: Client streaming
docs.text:
Many requests and one reply. The method gets a Stream of requests:

@override
Future<HelloReply> collectNames(
  ServiceCall call,
  Stream<HelloRequest> request,
) async {
  List<String> names = <String>[];
  await for (HelloRequest item in request) {
    names.add(item.name);
  }
  return HelloReply(message: 'Hello ${names.join(', ')}');
}

docs.title: Bidirectional streaming
docs.text:
Many requests and many replies. The method gets a Stream and returns a Stream:

@override
Stream<HelloReply> chat(
    ServiceCall call, Stream<HelloRequest> request) async* {
  await for (HelloRequest item in request) {
    yield HelloReply(message: 'Hello ${item.name}');
  }
}

docs.title: Return errors
docs.text:
Throw a GrpcException with a GrpcStatus and a message for the client:

throw GrpcException(GrpcStatus.notFound, 'No user 5');

The third argument is a list of protobuf messages. The client gets them as error details. A GrpcError from package:grpc also works.

Any other error stops the call with INTERNAL and goes to your exception handler. The client sees its text only when APP_ENV is development or local. A call to an unknown service or method gets UNIMPLEMENTED.

docs.title: Status codes
docs.text:
GrpcStatus has the 17 gRPC status codes. code is the number, fromCode gives the status of a number, and fromHttp gives the status of an HTTP error:

int code = GrpcStatus.notFound.code; // 5
GrpcStatus status = GrpcStatus.fromHttp(401); // unauthenticated

docs.title: HTTP errors and gRPC statuses
docs.text:
Dox changes an HTTP error of a middleware to a gRPC status:

HTTP error gRPC status 400, 422 INVALID_ARGUMENT 401 UNAUTHENTICATED 403 PERMISSION_DENIED 404 NOT_FOUND 408, 504 DEADLINE_EXCEEDED 409 ABORTED 413, 429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED 501 UNIMPLEMENTED 502, 503 UNAVAILABLE other 4xx FAILED_PRECONDITION other 5xx INTERNAL

The client also gets the message of the error. The message of a 5xx error shows only when APP_ENV is development or local.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
Metadata is the gRPC name for headers. call.clientMetadata has the headers of the client, with no grpc-* headers. Set call.headers before the first reply, and call.trailers for the end of the call:

@override
Future<HelloReply> sayHello(ServiceCall call, HelloRequest request) async {
  String? language = call.clientMetadata!['accept-language'];
  call.headers!['x-served-by'] = 'greeter';
  call.trailers!['x-done'] = 'yes';
  return HelloReply(message: 'Hello ${request.name} ($language)');
}

The maps are nullable in the ServiceCall type, so use !.

docs.title: Binary metadata
docs.text:
A value with a name that ends in -bin is base64 text. GrpcWire.decodeBinary gives its bytes, and GrpcWire.encodeBinary makes a value from bytes:

Uint8List bytes = GrpcWire.decodeBinary(call.clientMetadata!['trace-bin']!);
call.trailers!['trace-bin'] = GrpcWire.encodeBinary(bytes);

docs.title: Deadlines and cancelled calls
docs.text:
When the deadline of the client passes, Dox stops the call with DEADLINE_EXCEEDED. Your method can still run, so a long method must check call.isCanceled and call.isTimedOut:

@override
Stream<HelloReply> sayHelloMany(
    ServiceCall call, HelloRequest request) async* {
  while (!call.isCanceled && !call.isTimedOut) {
    yield HelloReply(message: 'Hello ${request.name}');
    await Future<void>.delayed(Duration(seconds: 1));
  }
}

call.deadline is the time of the deadline, or null. gRPC routes skip the RequestTimeout middleware, so a long stream does not stop.

docs.title: Changing the options
docs.text:
Give a GrpcOptions to Grpc.register. All options are in Options:

Grpc.register(
  GreeterService(),
  options: GrpcOptions(
    maxReceiveMessageSize: 16 * 1024 * 1024,
    maxSendMessageSize: 16 * 1024 * 1024,
    gzipResponses: true,
    idleTimeout: Duration(minutes: 30),
  ),
);

Set idleTimeout longer than your slowest method, because the time also counts while your method sends no message. A quiet Watch stream also stops, so send a message from time to time. Dox always reads gzip requests.

docs.title: Health check
docs.text: HealthService is the standard grpc.health.v1.Health service, with Check and Watch. Load balancers and Kubernetes use it. Do not put it behind auth middleware, because a load balancer has no token.

docs.title: Set the status of a service
docs.text:
The full server has the empty name '', and it starts as SERVING. Keep the HealthService object to set the status of one service in all isolates:

HealthService health = HealthService();
Grpc.register(health);

health.setStatus('greeter.Greeter', ServingStatus.SERVING);
health.setStatus('greeter.Greeter', ServingStatus.NOT_SERVING);

statusOf(name) gives the status, or null. clearStatus(name) removes it, and a Check for that name then gets NOT_FOUND.

docs.title: Services and isolates
docs.text:
Each isolate gets its own copy of your service. A database connection or a socket can not be copied, so make it on the first call:

class GreeterService extends GreeterServiceBase {
  HttpClient? _client;

  // made on the first call, in the isolate that runs the call
  HttpClient get client => _client ??= HttpClient();
}

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
Build your app with dox build. See Deployment.

Dox has no TLS, so put a proxy in front of the app. The proxy does the TLS and sends h2c to Dox. With nginx, use grpc_pass. With Caddy, use h2c:// in reverse_proxy. See Deployment: HTTP/2 and gRPC.

docs.title: Benchmark
docs.text:
On one core, dox_grpc does the most small calls. Small calls are the most usual type of gRPC call.

One core: the most small calls

Unary calls with a small message. Every server has one core: Dox one isolate, grpc-go GOMAXPROCS=1.

calls/s Doxdox_grpc 48,700fastest Gogrpc-go 44,0001.1× slower dart:iopackage:grpc 35,3001.4× slower

Linux · 16 connections · 128 calls in flight · ghz · median of 3 runs

With large messages and with streaming, grpc-go is faster on one core. dox_grpc is faster than package:grpc in all three tests.

Calls a second on one core:

Test dox_grpc package:grpc grpc-go Unary, small message 48,700 35,300 44,000 Unary, 100 KB reply 14,600 11,400 17,200 Server streaming, 100 messages of 1 KB 4,390 2,010 6,240

On four cores, Dox runs four isolates. Then the two servers are almost equal:

Test dox_grpc grpc-go Unary, small message 56,500 56,800 Unary, 100 KB reply 19,300 21,000 Server streaming, 100 messages of 1 KB 7,550 7,650

For small calls, both servers stop at approximately 57,000 calls a second. This number is near the limit of the client on 4 cores.

docs.title: Test setup
docs.text:
• All servers run the same service: the gRPC interop TestService.
  • The Dart servers are AOT builds. The build command is dart build cli.
  • package:grpc runs on dart:io and has one isolate. For this reason, it is only in the one-core table.
  • All tests ran in Linux containers on one machine with 8 cores. The server used 4 cores. The client, ghz, used the other 4 cores.
  • The client used 16 connections. For small calls, it kept 128 calls open at the same time. For the other two tests, it kept 32 calls open.
  • Each number is the median of 3 runs. Each run took 10 seconds, after a warm up of 3 seconds.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• HTTP/2: gRPC runs on HTTP/2.
  • Deployment: put a proxy in front.

docs.title: Health check
docs.text: A health route tells a load balancer, Docker or Kubernetes if the app can serve requests.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Add Route.health in a router. Use a router with no auth middleware, or the check gets 401:

lib/routes/web.dart
@override
void register() {
  Route.health('/health');
}

A GET request to /health gets 200 with {"status": "ok"}.

docs.title: Checking the database and the cache
docs.text:
Give named checks. A check fails when it throws, returns false or takes longer than the timeout:

lib/routes/web.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

Route.health(
  '/health',
  checks: <String, HealthCheckFunction>{
    'database': () => QueryBuilder.query('select 1'),
    'cache': HealthCheck.cache(),
  },
);

When all checks pass, the answer is 200:

{"status": "ok", "checks": {"database": "ok", "cache": "ok"}}

When one check fails, the answer is 503:

{"status": "fail", "checks": {"database": "fail", "cache": "ok"}}

HealthCheck.cache() writes a key to the default cache store and reads it back. HealthCheck.cache('redis') checks the store with that name.

docs.title: Changing the timeout
docs.text:
A check fails after 5 seconds by default. Set timeout to change it:

Route.health(
  '/health',
  timeout: Duration(seconds: 2),
  checks: <String, HealthCheckFunction>{
    'database': () => QueryBuilder.query('select 1'),
  },
);

docs.title: Seeing why a check failed
docs.text: The error of a failed check goes to exceptionHandler.report(), so it is in your logs. The answer shows the error text in errors only when APP_ENV is development or local.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Docker: a health check in the image.
  • Deployment: run the app on a server.

docs.title: HTTP/2
docs.text:
Dox serves HTTP/2 on the same port as HTTP/1.1, so one connection can send many requests at the same time.

Turn it on to serve gRPC, or when your proxy sends HTTP/2 to the app. HTTP/2 is off by default.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Set http2 to true in the app config. The port then accepts HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, and your routes stay the same:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  http2: true,
  // ...
);

docs.title: Read the protocol of a request
docs.text:
req.protocolVersion is 2.0 for an HTTP/2 request, and 1.0 or 1.1 for HTTP/1.x:

Route.get('/protocol', (DoxRequest req) {
  return req.protocolVersion; // '2.0'
});

Test it with curl:

curl --http2-prior-knowledge http://localhost:3000/protocol

docs.title: Limit the open requests on one connection
docs.text:
maxConcurrentStreams is the most open requests on one connection. The default is 250:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  http2: true,
  maxConcurrentStreams: 100,
  // ...
);

docs.title: Use a proxy
docs.text:
Dox speaks h2c: HTTP/2 over plain TCP, with no TLS. Browsers use HTTP/2 only with TLS, so your proxy does the TLS:

browser  --HTTP/2 + TLS-->  proxy  --h2c or HTTP/1.1-->  Dox

For the Caddy and nginx config, see Deployment: HTTP/2 and gRPC.

docs.title: Protection
docs.text:
Dox has protection against the known HTTP/2 attacks by default:

  • A cancelled request stays in the maxConcurrentStreams count until your handler stops. This stops the Rapid Reset attack.
  • Too many resets, SETTINGS frames, PING frames or empty frames close the connection with GOAWAY ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM.
  • A request body has the same limits as on HTTP/1.1. See Size limits.
  • A connection with no open request closes after idleTimeout.

docs.title: Benchmark
docs.text:
On one isolate, HTTP/2 does approximately 1.6 times the requests of HTTP/1.1, when a client sends many requests on one connection.

One isolate: HTTP/2 is 1.6× faster

GET / answers Hello, World!. The server has 4 cores and runs one isolate.

req/s HTTP/216 conn × 16 requests 587,000fastest HTTP/24 conn × 64 requests 465,0001.3× slower HTTP/1.1256 conn, http2 on 373,0001.6× slower HTTP/1.1256 conn, http2 off 364,0001.6× slower

Dox · one isolate · Linux · oha · median of 3 runs

The two HTTP/1.1 rows are almost the same, so http2: true does not make HTTP/1.1 clients slower.

Load Requests a second HTTP/1.1, 256 connections, http2 off 364,000 HTTP/1.1, 256 connections, http2 on 373,000 HTTP/2, 16 connections × 16 requests each 587,000 HTTP/2, 4 connections × 64 requests each 465,000

With 4 isolates, HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 both do approximately 630,000 requests a second. This number is the limit of the load tool on 4 cores, not the limit of Dox. HTTP/2 gives the largest increase when the app has few isolates.

docs.title: Test setup
docs.text:
• The app has one route, GET /. This route sends Hello, World!.
  • The app is an AOT build. The build command is dart build cli.
  • All tests ran in Linux containers on one machine with 8 cores. The server used 4 cores. The load tool, oha, used the other 4 cores.
  • Each number is the median of 3 runs. Each run took 10 seconds, after a warm up of 3 seconds.

docs.title: Without Dox
docs.text:
With the native server on its own, give the same options to NativeHttpServer.bind. http2ResetBurst and http2ResetRate limit the resets of one connection. Raise them behind a proxy that sends many cancels:

NativeHttpServer server = await NativeHttpServer.bind(
  3000,
  http2: true,
  maxConcurrentStreams: 100,
  http2ResetBurst: 1000,
  http2ResetRate: 100, // a second
);

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• gRPC: gRPC services on the same server.
  • Native server: the server below Dox.
  • Deployment: put a proxy in front.

docs.title: Isolate
docs.text:
Dox runs your app on many isolates (threads) at once, so it can use every CPU core.

Each isolate runs its own native server on the same port, and the operating system spreads the connections between them:

Port 3000the OS spreads the connections
  1. Rust acceptor
  2. Isolate 1, mainown memory cache
  3. Supervisorrestarts the process: Docker, systemd
  1. Rust acceptor
  2. Isolate 2own memory cachecrash: started again after 1 second
  1. Rust acceptor
  2. Isolate Nown memory cachecrash: started again after 1 second

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Dox starts one isolate per CPU the process may use. In a container, it uses the CPU limit, and a quota rounds up: 1.5 CPUs gives 2 isolates. On Windows only one isolate serves HTTP.

To change the number, set totalIsolate in the app config. A new app reads it from APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  totalIsolate: env.appTotalIsolate,
);

docs.title: Setting the number in code
docs.text:
Call Dox().totalIsolate() before startServer(). It wins over the config:

bin/server.dart
Dox().initialize(appConfig);
Dox().totalIsolate(2);
await Dox().startServer();

docs.title: Each isolate has its own memory
docs.text: A static value, a singleton and the memory cache store exist one time per isolate. To share data between isolates or servers, use a database, Redis or files.

docs.title: Finding the current isolate
docs.text:
Dox().isolateId is the id of the isolate that runs your code. The first isolate is 1. Dox().isolateCount is the number of running isolates:

int id = Dox().isolateId;
int count = Dox().isolateCount;

docs.title: Sending a message to the other isolates
docs.text:
IsolateBus sends a message from one isolate to all the other isolates in the same process. Listen in the setup() of a provider, and publish from anywhere:

IsolateBus.instance.on('users').listen(onMessage);
IsolateBus.instance.publish('users', <Object>['changed', 42]);

An isolate never gets its own message, and a listener gets only the messages sent after it started to listen. A message must be a value a SendPort can send, or publish throws an ArgumentError.

IsolateBus.instance.size is the number of isolates that listen, this one included. For many servers, use Redis. Socket.IO uses the bus to share broadcasts.

docs.title: What each isolate does at start
docs.text:
Dox copies the AppConfig, the providers and the routes to each new isolate. Then every isolate:

  1. runs setup() of each provider,
  2. registers the routes of your routers,
  3. reads the parameter types of each controller one time,
  4. runs boot() of each provider,
  5. starts its HTTP server.

So the config and the providers must not hold open sockets or database pools. Open them in setup(). See Providers.

docs.title: Heavy CPU work
docs.text:
Heavy CPU work in a request blocks every other request on the same isolate. Run it on a worker isolate with Dox().compute:

Future<List<int>> renderPdf(Map<String, dynamic> data) {
  return Dox().compute(() => buildPdf(data));
}

The task can use only values that can go between isolates: numbers, strings, lists, maps and plain objects. It can not use the container, a database connection or a cache store, so read the data first and pass it in. Make the task in a small top-level or static function.

The tasks run on a pool of 4 workers, and more tasks wait in line. Set computeWorkers to change the number:

AppConfig(
  // ...
  computeWorkers: 8,
);

An error of the task is thrown at the await. compute also works with no server, like in a command, a test or a queue job.

docs.title: When an isolate crashes
docs.text:
An error in a request gives a 500, and an async error outside a request goes to the exception handler. If a worker isolate dies, Dox starts a new one after 1 second.

If the first isolate dies, the process exits with a non-zero code. Let a supervisor start it again, like Docker restart: or systemd Restart=always. See Deployment.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Providers: code that runs in each isolate at start.
  • Native server: the HTTP server in each isolate.
  • Deployment: run the app on a server.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
The dox_mailer package sends email from your app with SMTP, Amazon SES, Azure, Resend, Mailgun, Postmark or sendmail.

You make a Message and call Mail.send(), and a transport sends it. The config picks the transport, so you can change providers with no code change.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Add the package. Add --transport=smtp (or resend, mailgun, postmark, ses) to pick a transport. The default is log:

dox add mailer

It writes the mail config and the provider, and adds MAIL_MAILER, MAIL_FROM and the transport keys to .env. It never overwrites a file.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
A mailer is a name and a transport. Mail.send() uses the defaultMailer:

lib/config/mail.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

MailConfig mailConfig = MailConfig(
  /// the mailer of Mail.send()
  defaultMailer: Env.get('MAIL_MAILER', 'log'),

  /// for messages with no from address
  from: Address(Env.get('MAIL_FROM', 'hello@example.com'), 'My app'),

  mailers: <String, Transport>{
    'smtp': SmtpTransport(
      host: Env.get('MAIL_HOST', 'localhost'),
      port: Env.get<int>('MAIL_PORT', 587),
      username: Env.get<String?>('MAIL_USERNAME'),
      password: Env.get<String?>('MAIL_PASSWORD'),
    ),

    /// prints emails, sends nothing
    'log': LogTransport(),
  },
);
.env
MAIL_MAILER=smtp
MAIL_FROM=hello@example.com
MAIL_HOST=smtp.example.com
MAIL_PORT=587
MAIL_USERNAME=me
MAIL_PASSWORD=secret
Option Default What it does defaultMailer log the mailer of Mail.send() mailers a log mailer each mailer name and its transport from none the from address of a message that has none replyTo none the reply-to addresses of a message that has none

Mail.config gives this config in your code.

docs.title: The mail provider
docs.text:
The provider sets up the mailers in every isolate. Put it in lib/providers/:

lib/providers/mail_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

import '../config/mail.dart';

class AppMailProvider extends MailProvider {
  AppMailProvider() : super(mailConfig);
}

When the server stops, the provider closes the SMTP connections and HTTP clients.

docs.title: Sending mail
docs.text:
Make a Message and give it to Mail.send():

import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

await Mail.send(
  Message(
    to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com', 'Ann Lee')],
    subject: 'Welcome',
    text: 'Hello Ann, welcome!',
    html: '<p>Hello Ann, <b>welcome</b>!</p>',
  ),
);

A message needs a from address, a recipient, and a text or HTML body. When the send fails, send() throws a MailException with the statusCode and the body of the server answer. It gives a SentMessage with the messageId.

docs.title: Using another mailer
docs.text:
Send with a mailer that is not the default:

await Mail.mailer('ses').send(message);

docs.title: Short ways to send
docs.text:
For a short plain text email, use Mail.raw():

await Mail.raw('Your code is 1234',
    to: 'ann@example.com', subject: 'Your code');

Mail.to() starts an email for a mailable. to(), cc() and bcc() take an Address, an email text, or a list of these:

await Mail.to('ann@example.com')
    .cc('Bob Lee <bob@example.com>')
    .bcc(<String>['audit@example.com'])
    .send(WelcomeMail(user));

queue() and later() also work here, like Mail.to(email).queue(WelcomeMail(user)).

docs.title: The message
Attachments
docs.text:
Add files with attachments. The content type comes from the file extension, or from contentType:

Message(
  to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com')],
  subject: 'Your invoice',
  text: 'The invoice is attached.',
  attachments: <Attachment>[
    Attachment(pdfBytes, 'invoice.pdf'),
    Attachment.fromFile('storage/terms.pdf'),
  ],
);

To attach a file from a storage disk, read its bytes first:

Uint8List? pdf = await Storage().disk('s3').get('invoices/42.pdf');
Attachment(pdf!, 'invoice.pdf');

docs.title: Inline images
docs.text:
Give the file a cid, and use it in the HTML with cid::

Message(
  to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com')],
  subject: 'Hello',
  html: '<img src="cid:logo.png"> Hello!',
  attachments: <Attachment>[
    Attachment.fromFile('assets/logo.png', cid: 'logo.png'),
  ],
);

Mailgun uses the file name as the cid, so use a cid with the extension, like logo.png.

docs.title: HTML from a view
docs.text:
Render a view template to HTML:

String html =
    View.render('emails/welcome', <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann'});
await Mail.send(Message(to: to, subject: 'Welcome', html: html));

docs.title: Mailables
docs.text:
A mailable is one kind of email in its own class, like the welcome email. Make one with the CLI. Add --no-view for a plain text body. See dox make:mail:

dox make:mail Welcome

It writes lib/app/mail/welcome_mail.dart and resources/views/emails/welcome.dox.html. Override the getters you need:

class WelcomeMail extends Mailable {
  WelcomeMail(this.user);

  final User user;

  @override
  List<Address> get to => <Address>[Address(user.email, user.name)];

  @override
  String get subject => 'Welcome';

  @override
  String? get view => 'emails/welcome';

  @override
  Map<String, Object?> get data => <String, Object?>{'name': user.name};
}
Getter What it is to, cc, bcc, replyTo the addresses from the sender. Null: the from of the mail config subject the subject html, text the body as text, when there is no template view a dox_view template for the HTML body textView a dox_view template for the plain text body markdown a dox_view template with Markdown. See Markdown mail data the variables of the templates attachments the files mailer the mailer name, like ses. Null: the default mailer

docs.title: Sending a mailable
docs.text:
Call send(), or put the mailable on the queue with queue() or later():

await WelcomeMail(user).send();
await WelcomeMail(user).queue();
await WelcomeMail(user).later(Duration(minutes: 10));

queue() and later() render the templates at once. They take the options of Mail.queue().

docs.title: Changing the message
docs.text:
toMessage() gives the email as a Message. Override it to set more, like headers or tags:

@override
Message toMessage() {
  return super.toMessage().copyWith(tags: <String>['welcome']);
}

docs.title: Markdown mail
docs.text:
Write the email in Markdown. One template gives an HTML email with a layout and a plain text part:

resources/views/emails/welcome.dox.html
# Hi {{ name }}

Thanks for joining. Here is what you can do next:

- Fill in your profile
- Invite your team

[Open your profile]({{ profileUrl }})

<a href="https://example.com/dashboard" class="button">Open the app</a>

Then set the markdown getter:

@override
String? get markdown => 'emails/welcome';

<a class="button"> shows as a button. Do not indent the Markdown in @if or @each, because 4 spaces make a code block.

{{ }} escapes HTML and Markdown, and a link with an unsafe URL, like javascript:, loses its URL. Raw HTML in the template, like <a href="{{ url }}">, is not checked, so write links as [text]({{ url }}). To put Markdown from a value in the email, give a SafeString.

docs.title: Custom layout
docs.text:
Override layout() to use your own look. It gets the HTML of the Markdown and gives the full page:

import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';
import 'package:dox_view/dox_view.dart'; // View, SafeString

abstract class AppMail extends Mailable {
  @override
  String layout(String body) {
    return View.render('emails/layout',
        <String, Object?>{'body': SafeString(body)});
  }
}

docs.title: A simple email with no template
docs.text:
MailMessage is a mailable for a few lines and a button. It uses the Markdown layout:

await (MailMessage(
        subject: 'Invoice paid',
        to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com')])
      ..line('We got your payment.')
      ..action('View invoice', 'https://example.com/invoices/1')
      ..line('Thank you!'))
    .send();
  • cc: in the constructor adds cc addresses.
  • attach(Attachment(...)) adds a file.
  • error() makes the buttons red.
  • greeting (default Hello!) starts the email, and salutation (default none) ends it.

Lines can use Markdown, like **bold**. action() throws an ArgumentError for an unsafe URL. To send one email on more channels, see Notifications.

docs.title: Queue an email
docs.text:
A queue worker sends the email later, so the request does not wait:

await Mail.queue(message);

To send it after a time, use Mail.later(). Both give the job id:

await Mail.later(Duration(minutes: 10), message);

To pick another mailer and another queue:

await Mail.mailer('ses').queue(message, queue: 'emails');

This uses dox_queue, so you need its QueueProvider and a worker. The worker must also run your MailProvider, or the job fails with "Mail is not set up". The message is checked at once, so a bad message fails in the request.

Option Default What it does queue default the queue name encrypt false encrypt the job data with the app key. The worker needs the same key

The full email, with its attachments, is saved in Redis or in the jobs table. So keep attachments small. An email has personal data, so use encrypt: true if other people can read the queue.

With encrypt: true, the send error of a failed job is encrypted too. Read it with RedactedMailError.decrypt(job.error). To use a queue other than dox_queue, call Mail.useQueue(queue).

docs.title: SMTP
docs.text:
'smtp': SmtpTransport(
  host: 'smtp.example.com',
  port: 587,
  username: Env.get('MAIL_USERNAME'),
  password: Env.get('MAIL_PASSWORD'),
  encryption: SmtpEncryption.starttls,
),
Option Default What it does host required the server port 465 for tls, 587 for starttls, 25 for none the port username, password none the login. No username: no login encryption starttls none, starttls (TLS after connect) or tls (TLS from the start) allowInsecure false accept a self-signed TLS certificate. Only for test servers auth PLAIN, or LOGIN when the server has no PLAIN SmtpAuth.plain, SmtpAuth.login or SmtpAuth.xoauth2 localDomain localhost the name of this machine, for EHLO timeout 30 seconds the time to connect, and to wait for each reply keepAlive false keep the connection open for the next message

With starttls, the send fails when the server has no STARTTLS, so your password never goes in plain text. For Gmail or Outlook with OAuth 2, use SmtpAuth.xoauth2 with the access token as the password.

For local work, Mailpit catches all emails:

'mailpit': SmtpTransport(
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 1025,
  encryption: SmtpEncryption.none,
),

docs.title: Amazon SES
docs.text:
SesTransport uses SES API v1, and SesV2Transport uses SES API v2. Both send attachments and inline images:

'ses': SesV2Transport(
  key: Env.get('AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID'),
  secret: Env.get('AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY'),
  region: Env.get('AWS_REGION', 'us-east-1'),
),
Option Default What it does key required the AWS access key id secret required the AWS secret access key sessionToken none for temporary keys, like from a role region us-east-1 the AWS region of SES configurationSet none the SES configuration set, to track events endpoint https://email.<region>.amazonaws.com/ another API address

docs.title: Azure Communication Services
docs.text:
'azure': AzureTransport(
  endpoint: 'https://my-app.europe.communication.azure.com',
  accessKey: Env.get('AZURE_EMAIL_KEY'),
),

Or use the connection string from the Azure portal:

'azure': AzureTransport.fromConnectionString(
  Env.get('AZURE_EMAIL_CONNECTION_STRING'),
),
Option Default What it does endpoint required the address of your resource accessKey required the access key of the resource apiVersion 2023-03-31 the API version. Inline images need a newer version disableTracking false turn off open and click tracking

docs.title: Resend
docs.text: 'resend': ResendTransport(apiKey: Env.get('RESEND_API_KEY')),

docs.title: Mailgun
docs.text:
Use the region of your Mailgun domain: MailgunRegion.us (the default) or MailgunRegion.eu:

'mailgun': MailgunTransport(
  apiKey: Env.get('MAILGUN_API_KEY'),
  domain: 'mg.example.com',
  region: MailgunRegion.eu,
),

docs.title: Postmark
docs.text:
messageStream is optional. Without it, Postmark uses the default stream:

'postmark': PostmarkTransport(
  serverToken: Env.get('POSTMARK_TOKEN'),
  messageStream: 'outbound',
),

docs.title: sendmail
docs.text:
Send with the sendmail program of the server (Postfix, Exim, msmtp and others):

'sendmail': SendmailTransport(
  path: '/usr/sbin/sendmail',
  mode: SendmailMode.smtp,
),
Mode Command How it works SendmailMode.smtp (default) sendmail -bs speaks SMTP on stdin and stdout SendmailMode.pipe sendmail -t -i sends the message in. sendmail reads the recipients from the headers

docs.title: Log
docs.text:
Print each email and send nothing. output sets where it prints, and bothBodies: true also shows the HTML body:

'log': LogTransport(bothBodies: true, output: stderr.writeln),

docs.title: Array
docs.text:
Keep each email in a list and send nothing. See Testing:

'array': ArrayTransport(),

docs.title: Failover
docs.text:
FailoverTransport tries each transport in order, until one sends the email. If all fail, it throws the error of the last one:

SesV2Transport ses = SesV2Transport(key: '...', secret: '...');
SmtpTransport smtp = SmtpTransport(host: 'smtp.example.com');

MailConfig mailConfig = MailConfig(
  defaultMailer: 'main',
  mailers: <String, Transport>{
    'main': FailoverTransport(<Transport>[ses, smtp]),
  },
);

Give onError to get the error of each transport that fails.

docs.title: Tags and metadata
docs.text:
Each transport uses tags and metadata in its own way:

Transport tags metadata SES not used message tags Resend tags with the value true tags Mailgun o:tag variables (v:name) Postmark the first tag metadata Azure, SMTP, sendmail not used not used

For SMTP and sendmail, use headers.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
Run code before or after each email, for example to log it. Each isolate has its own hooks, so add them in setup() of your mail provider:

class AppMailProvider extends MailProvider {
  AppMailProvider() : super(mailConfig);

  @override
  void setup() {
    super.setup();
    Mail.clearHooks(); // a second setup() does not add each hook twice
    Mail.onSending((Message message) {
      print('sending "${message.subject}" to ${message.to}');
    });
    Mail.onSent((SentMessage sent) {
      print('sent ${sent.messageId}');
    });
  }
}

Hooks run for every mailer, for queued emails and with Mail.fake(). When an onSending hook throws, the email is not sent. When an onSent hook throws, the error is only logged.

docs.title: Sending all mail to one address
docs.text:
On a staging server, send every email to your own inbox with Mail.alwaysTo(). Call it in setup() of your mail provider:

class AppMailProvider extends MailProvider {
  AppMailProvider() : super(mailConfig);

  @override
  void setup() {
    super.setup();
    if (Env.get<String>('APP_ENV') == 'staging') {
      Mail.alwaysTo('qa@example.com');
    }
  }
}

The to of each email becomes that address, and cc and bcc are removed. Mail.alwaysTo(null) turns it off.

docs.title: Custom transports
docs.text:
Extend Transport and add it to mailers:

class MyApiTransport extends Transport {
  @override
  Future<SentMessage> send(Message message) async {
    // call your API here
    return SentMessage(message, messageId: 'id from the API');
  }
}

The message already has a from address. For a provider that takes raw MIME, MimeBuilder().build(message) gives the MIME text.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Mail.fake() sends all mailers to one ArrayTransport, so nothing goes out:

import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  late ArrayTransport mail;

  setUp(() {
    mail = Mail.fake();
  });

  tearDown(() {
    Mail.restore();
  });

  test('sign up sends a welcome email', () async {
    await signUp('ann@example.com');

    expect(mail.messages, hasLength(1));
    Message message = mail.messages.single;
    expect(message.to.single.email, 'ann@example.com');
    expect(message.subject, 'Welcome');
  });
}

docs.title: Testing queued mail
docs.text:
Queued emails go to mail.queued, not to the job queue, so you need no queue setup:

await Mail.queue(message);

mail.assertQueued((Message m) => m.subject == 'Welcome');
mail.assertNothingSent();

Each item in mail.queued is a QueuedMessage with mailer, message, id, delay, queue and encrypt.

docs.title: Assertions
docs.text:
Method Checks assertSent([test]) an email was sent. With test, one of them passes it assertSentCount(count, [test]) count emails were sent. With test, count emails pass it assertNotSent(test) no sent email passes test assertNothingSent() no email was sent assertQueued([test]) an email was queued. With test, one of them passes it assertNotQueued(test) no queued email passes test assertNothingQueued() no email was queued

test is a bool Function(Message). A failed check throws a StateError. mail.clear() removes the sent and the queued emails.

docs.title: Without Dox
docs.text:
dox_mailer also works on its own. Call Mail.configure() at the start, and Mail.close() at the end:

import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  Map<String, String> env = Platform.environment;

  Mail.configure(MailConfig(
    defaultMailer: 'smtp',
    from: Address('hello@example.com', 'My app'),
    mailers: <String, Transport>{
      'smtp': SmtpTransport(
        host: env['MAIL_HOST'] ?? 'localhost',
        username: env['MAIL_USERNAME'],
        password: env['MAIL_PASSWORD'],
      ),
    },
  ));

  await Mail.send(Message(
    to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com')],
    subject: 'Hello',
    text: 'Hello Ann!',
  ));

  // closes open SMTP connections and HTTP clients
  await Mail.close();
}

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Notifications: send one message on many channels.
  • Queue: send mail in the background.
  • Views: write the mail templates.

docs.title: Native server
docs.text: Dox runs on a native HTTP server from the package dox_http_native: Rust owns the sockets and parses HTTP, and all your code stays in Dart.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Every Dox app uses the native server, and you do not need Rust. The package gets a ready-built library for your system when you build the app. See Performance for the numbers.

Build with dox build or dart build cli. dart compile exe does not run build hooks, so the app has no library. See Deployment.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Limit Value Answer Request line and headers 16 KB 431 Body maxBodySize (10 MB) 413 Multipart form maxMultipartSize (100 MB) 413 No body bytes for bodyTimeout (120 seconds) 408 Request head arrives in idleTimeout (30 seconds) connection closed Keep-alive connection with no request idleTimeout (30 seconds) connection closed Both Content-Length and chunked - 400 Transfer encoding other than chunked - 501

These are the defaults of AppConfig, where you can change them. See App config.

docs.title: Writing handlers
docs.text: The server has the same API as the dart:io HttpServer, so code for dart:io keeps working. Each isolate runs the server on its own thread, so a slow synchronous handler blocks all the sockets of its isolate. An await gives the isolate back.

docs.title: When the library does not load
docs.text:
Dox stops at start and the error says why and how to fix it:

Unsupported operation: dox_http_native did not load: <reason>.
Fix: install Rust (cargo, see https://rustup.rs), then run the app again ...

A reason like native library ABI 8, expected 9 means the library on disk is from another version of the package. See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: HTTP/2
docs.text: The native server also speaks HTTP/2 (h2c) on the same port, with http2: true. See HTTP/2.

docs.title: WebSocket
docs.text:
NativeWebSocket.upgrade(request) gives a dart:io WebSocket. Your route, middleware and the Origin check run first, and a normal answer (like 403) refuses the upgrade:

if (NativeWebSocket.isUpgradeRequest(request)) {
  WebSocket socket = await NativeWebSocket.upgrade(request,
      protocol: 'chat', maxMessageSize: 64 * 1024);
}

A message over maxMessageSize (16 MB by default) closes the socket with code 1009. On a graceful stop, every open socket gets code 1001.

docs.title: Finding lost clients
docs.text:
Set pingInterval to find clients that vanished with no close, like a phone that lost its network. When the client stays quiet for two intervals, the socket closes with 1001:

socket.pingInterval = Duration(seconds: 30);

docs.title: Streaming a response
docs.text:
Write with add() and call flush(). The first flush() sends the status, the headers and the bytes so far:

import 'dart:convert';
import 'dart:io';

server.listen((HttpRequest req) async {
  req.response.headers.contentType = ContentType('text', 'event-stream');
  req.response.add(utf8.encode('data: hello\n\n'));
  await req.response.flush();
});

A streamed response with a contentLength must send exactly that many bytes, or add() or close() fails.

docs.title: Checking the response state
docs.text:
Cast req.response to NativeResponse to read its state. headSent is true when the status and headers went out, so no error page can go out after it. isGone is true when the client left, and gone completes when it leaves:

NativeResponse res = req.response as NativeResponse;
bool sent = res.headSent;
bool left = res.isGone;
await Future.any(<Future<void>>[res.gone, res.done]);

gone never completes for a response that ends normally, so always race it against done or a timeout.

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
• On the internet, run the app behind a reverse proxy like Caddy or nginx. The proxy does HTTPS and buffers slow clients.
  • Set maxConnections when the app port is open to the internet.
  • Another process of the same OS user can bind the same port. Do not run untrusted code as the user of the app.
  • req.uri resolves .. in the path. Never build a file path from the raw path. Use the storage helpers.

docs.title: Where the library comes from
docs.text:
The build hook of dox_http_native uses the first one that works:

  1. A path in the root pubspec.yaml of your app:

    hooks:
  user_defines:
    dox_http_native:
      lib_path: /path/to/libdox_http_native.so

  2. A local build in native/target/release of the package.

  3. The ready-built library from the GitHub release, checked with sha256. There are builds for macOS (arm64, x64), Linux (x64, arm64) and Windows (x64).
  4. A build from source with cargo, when Rust is installed.

For a git or path dependency, step 4 comes before step 3. When none works, the app stops at start with the error above.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The server runs on the thread of the isolate, in a loop:

  1. Dart calls Rust (one FFI call).
  2. Rust writes the answers of the last batch, reads the sockets and parses the new requests. It gives them back to Dart as one batch.
  3. Dart runs your handlers and calls Rust again with their answers.

When the isolate has nothing to do, a small helper thread watches the sockets and wakes it. The OS spreads connections, not requests, between the isolates. So a few busy connections (like from one proxy) can keep some isolates idle. Use more connections than isolates.

docs.title: Without Dox
docs.text:
dox_http_native also works on its own, in any Dart app:

dart pub add dox_http_native

Bind a server and listen for requests, like with the dart:io HttpServer:

import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_http_native/dox_http_native.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  NativeHttpServer server = await NativeHttpServer.bind(3000);
  server.listen((HttpRequest req) async {
    req.response.write('Hello World');
    await req.response.close();
  });
}

With no address, the server listens on all interfaces. These are the options of bind:

NativeHttpServer.bind(
  3000,
  address: '127.0.0.1',
  maxConnections: 10000, // no limit by default
  maxBodySize: 10 * 1024 * 1024,
  maxMultipartSize: 50 * 1024 * 1024,
  bodyTimeout: Duration(seconds: 120),
  idleTimeout: Duration(seconds: 30),
  http2: true, // see HTTP/2
);

At maxConnections, the server stops accepting until a connection closes. Behind a load balancer, set idleTimeout longer than the idle timeout of the balancer, or clients can get 502.

docs.title: Checking the library
docs.text:
NativeHttpServer.isAvailable is true when the native library loads. loadError says why it did not, and ensureAvailable() throws that error:

if (!NativeHttpServer.isAvailable) print(NativeHttpServer.loadError);

docs.title: Stopping the server
docs.text:
close() waits for open requests. close(force: true) closes every connection at once. isOpen is false after the close:

await server.close();

docs.title: Encrypting with AES-GCM
docs.text:
AesGcm does AES-256-GCM in Rust. Dox uses it for encrypted cookies. The key is 32 bytes, and open gives null when the data or the aad is wrong:

Uint8List sealed = AesGcm.seal(key, plain, aad);
Uint8List? plain2 = AesGcm.open(key, sealed, aad);

docs.title: Working on the native code
docs.text:
dox_http_native lives in its own repo: dartondox/dox-http-native. The Rust code is in its native folder:

cd dox-http-native/native
cargo build --release   # the hook uses this build from now on
cargo test
cd .. && dart test --concurrency=1

To use your local copy in the Dox repo, see Contribute.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• HTTP/2: turn on HTTP/2.
  • Performance: the benchmark numbers.
  • Isolate: one server per CPU core.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
A notification tells a user about something, like "your invoice is paid", by email or by a channel you write.

Each notification is a class that holds the text and the channels. Notifications are in the dox_mailer package, so set up mail first.

docs.title: Creating notifications
docs.text:
A notification extends Notification. The via method gives the channels, and toMail makes the email:

class InvoicePaid extends Notification {
  InvoicePaid(this.invoiceId);

  final int invoiceId;

  @override
  List<NotificationChannel> via(Object notifiable) {
    return <NotificationChannel>[const MailChannel()];
  }

  @override
  Mailable toMail(Object notifiable) {
    return MailMessage(subject: 'Invoice paid')
      ..line('We got your payment.')
      ..action('View invoice', 'https://example.com/invoices/$invoiceId');
  }
}

toMail() can return any mailable, like a WelcomeMail with a template.

docs.title: Making a model notifiable
docs.text:
Add the Notifiable mixin to the class that gets notifications. Its routeNotificationFor method gives each channel the destination:

class User extends Model<User> with Notifiable {
  @override
  Object? routeNotificationFor(String channel) {
    return channel == 'mail' ? Address(email!, name) : null;
  }
}

The mail route can be an Address, an email text like Ann <ann@example.com>, or a list of these. A to address on the mailable wins over the route.

docs.title: Sending to one user
docs.text:
Call notify on the model:

await user.notify(InvoicePaid(1));

docs.title: Sending to many users
docs.text:
Use Notification.send with a list:

await Notification.send(users, InvoicePaid(1));

docs.title: Sending to an address with no user
docs.text:
For a guest with no user row, give an Address:

await Notification.send(<Object>[Address('ann@example.com')],
    InvoicePaid(1));

docs.title: Handling errors
docs.text:
When one channel throws, the other channels and notifiables still get the notification. At the end, Notification.send() throws a NotificationException. Its errors list gives the notifiable, the channel and the error of each failure:

try {
  await Notification.send(users, InvoicePaid(1));
} on NotificationException catch (e) {
  for (NotificationError error in e.errors) {
    print('${error.channel}: ${error.error}'); // null channel: via()
  }
}

The error text has no email addresses, so it is safe for logs. With one notifiable and one error, like in user.notify(), you get the initial error, like a MailException.

docs.title: Queueing notifications
docs.text:
Override shouldQueue to send the email in the background. The mail channel then puts the email on the queue, like Mail.queue():

@override
bool get shouldQueue => true;

The email is rendered at once, and the worker sends it. These getters set the queue options:

Getter Default What it does queue null (default) the queue name delay null the worker sends the email after this wait encrypt false encrypt the job data with the app key

These options change only the mail channel. To queue your own channel, dispatch a job in it.

docs.title: Custom channels
docs.text:
To send a notification another way, like to a database table, write a channel. A channel implements NotificationChannel and gets the data from toArray():

import 'dart:convert';

class DatabaseChannel implements NotificationChannel {
  @override
  Future<void> send(Object notifiable, Notification notification) async {
    // only a user has a row. An Address or an email text has none.
    if (notifiable is! User) return;
    AppNotification row = AppNotification()
      ..userId = notifiable.id
      ..data = jsonEncode(notification.toArray(notifiable));
    await row.save();
  }
}

Then add the channel to via(), and give the data in toArray():

class InvoicePaid extends Notification {
  @override
  List<NotificationChannel> via(Object notifiable) {
    return <NotificationChannel>[const MailChannel(), DatabaseChannel()];
  }

  @override
  Map<String, Object?> toArray(Object notifiable) {
    return <String, Object?>{
      'type': 'invoice_paid',
      'invoice_id': invoiceId,
    };
  }

  // ...
}

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Mail.fake() also catches the emails of the mail channel:

ArrayTransport mail = Mail.fake();
await user.notify(InvoicePaid(1));
expect(mail.messages.single.subject, 'Invoice paid');

With shouldQueue, the email goes to mail.queued. Check it with mail.assertQueued(). See Mail.

docs.text:
• Mail: mailables, templates and transports.
  • Queue: run the workers that send queued email.

docs.title: Package commands
docs.text: A package or an app can add its own dox commands, and the dox CLI finds them by itself.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Add the package and run its command. For example, dox queue:table comes from the dox_queue_database package:

dart pub add dox_queue_database
dox queue:table

dox help lists the commands of each package, under the package name.

docs.title: Add a command to your package
docs.text: A package command needs three things: the command class, a list of commands and a key in pubspec.yaml.

docs.title: 1. Write the command
docs.text:
A command extends Command from package:dox_core/command.dart. The run method gets the words after the command name:

lib/src/commands/hello_command.dart
import 'package:dox_core/command.dart';

class HelloCommand extends Command {
  @override
  String get name => 'hello:say';

  @override
  String get description => 'Say hello';

  /// optional, shown by `dox help`. The default is the name.
  @override
  String get usage => 'hello:say <name>';

  @override
  Future<void> run(List<String> args) async {
    print('Hello ${args.join(' ')}');
  }
}

So dox hello:say Ann calls run(['Ann']). A package with no dox_core dependency imports package:dox_annotation/command.dart.

docs.title: 2. List the commands
docs.text:
Make one library with a top-level commands list:

lib/commands.dart
import 'package:dox_core/command.dart';

import 'src/commands/hello_command.dart';

final List<Command> commands = <Command>[HelloCommand()];

docs.title: 3. Name the library in pubspec.yaml
docs.text:
Add the dox: commands: key. Its value must be a library of the package itself:

pubspec.yaml
dox:
  commands: package:my_package/commands.dart

An app that depends on your package now has dox hello:say.

docs.title: Add a command to your app
docs.text:
dox make:command writes the command, adds it to lib/app/commands/commands.dart and sets the dox: commands: key:

dox make:command send_report

The command name is app:send-report. See dox make:command.

docs.title: Name clashes
docs.text: A built-in command always wins over a package command with the same name. When two packages have a command with the same name, dox <name> prints an error with both package names.

docs.title: Failing a command
docs.text:
Set exitCode from dart:io, or throw. The exit code of the command is the exit code of dox:

exitCode = 1;

A thrown error prints its stack trace and gives exit code 1.

docs.title: Writing a migration
docs.text:
MigrationFile().create writes a migration with the same file name format as dox make:migration. It returns null and writes nothing when a migration with this name is already there:

String? path = MigrationFile().create('create_queue_tables', source);
if (path == null) {
  print('A create_queue_tables migration is already in db/migration.');
  exitCode = 1;
}

MigrationFile().exists(name) only tells you if the migration is there. The next dox migrate runs the new file.

docs.title: Ship an install command
docs.text:
dox add <x> adds the package dox_x, then runs its <x>:install command. If your package needs config files, env keys or a provider, ship an <x>:install command.

Installer from package:dox_annotation/install.dart does the steps. A step never overwrites a file and never adds a key twice, so it is safe to run twice:

lib/src/commands/hello_install_command.dart
import 'package:dox_annotation/command.dart';
import 'package:dox_annotation/install.dart';

class HelloInstallCommand extends Command {
  @override
  String get name => 'hello:install';

  @override
  String get description => 'Set up dox_hello in this app';

  @override
  Future<void> run(List<String> args) async {
    Installer installer = Installer();
    String app = installer.appName;
    installer.writeFile(
      'lib/config/hello.dart',
      "import 'package:$app/config/env.dart';\n",
    );
    installer.addEnvGetter("String get helloName => 'world';");
    installer.addEnv('HELLO_NAME', 'world');
    await installer.buildRunner();
    installer.printSummary(<String>['Restart the server.']);
  }
}
Member What it does Installer(root: dir) Works in the folder dir. The default is the current folder. appName The name of the app pubspec.yaml, for package:<app>/... imports. writeFile(path, content) Writes the file only when it is not there. Returns true when it wrote it. makeFolder(path) Makes the folder when it is not there. addEnv(key, value) Adds KEY=value to .env.example and .env when the key is missing. addEnvGetter(getter) Adds a getter to AppEnv in lib/config/env.dart when the class has no member with that name. hasDependency(package) True when the app pubspec.yaml has the package. addDependency(package, dev: false) Runs dart pub add when the app does not have the package. buildRunner() Runs dart run build_runner build. note(line) Adds your own line to the summary, like added hooks to pubspec.yaml. lines The lines of the summary. ok False when a step failed. printSummary(nextSteps) Prints what was done and the next steps. Sets exit code 1 when a step failed.

Read the options from args, like --driver=postgres, and give a good default, so dox add <x> works with no options. dox_orm has an example: orm:install.

docs.title: Performance mistakes
docs.text:
These are the mistakes that make a Dox app slow, with the fix for each one, and a strict mode that warns you about the worst of them.

Dart runs one thing at a time in each isolate. When one request does slow work with no await, every other request on that isolate waits. For server settings, see Performance.

docs.title: Heavy CPU work in a request
docs.text:
A PDF, an image or a huge JSON file keeps the CPU busy. Run the work on a worker isolate with Dox().compute:

Wrong
Future<List<int>> invoice(DoxRequest req) async {
  Order order = await Order().findOrFail(req.param['id']);
  return buildPdf(order.toJson()); // blocks the isolate
}
Right
Future<List<int>> invoice(DoxRequest req) async {
  Order order = await Order().findOrFail(req.param['id']);
  return renderPdf(order.toJson());
}

Future<List<int>> renderPdf(Map<String, dynamic> data) {
  return Dox().compute(() => buildPdf(data));
}

Pass only plain values to the task, like numbers, strings, lists and maps. See Heavy CPU work.

docs.title: Sync password hashing
docs.text:
Hash.make and Hash.verify run bcrypt on the isolate, and bcrypt is slow on purpose. In a handler, use the async methods:

Wrong
bool ok = Hash.verify(password, user.password);
Right
bool ok = await Hash.verifyAsync(password, user.password);
String hashed = await Hash.makeAsync(password);

docs.title: Sync file calls
docs.text:
A sync file call stops the isolate until the disk answers. Use the async call:

Wrong
String text = File('data/terms.txt').readAsStringSync();
Right
String text = await File('data/terms.txt').readAsString();

docs.title: Loading a whole table
docs.text:
all() and get() read every row into memory. On a big table, read one page:

Wrong
List<Order> orders = await Order().all();
Right
Pagination<Order> page =
    await Order().orderBy('id').paginate(currentPage: 1, perPage: 50);

To work on all rows, use chunk(), lazy() or cursor():

await for (Order order in Order().orderBy('id').cursor(chunkSize: 500)) {
  // one row at a time
}

See Paginating results, Chunking results and Streaming results.

docs.title: A query inside a loop
docs.text:
This is the N+1 problem: 100 posts make 101 queries. preload() loads the relation for all rows in one extra query:

Wrong
List<Post> posts = await Post().all();
for (Post post in posts) {
  await post.$getRelation('author'); // one query per post
  User? author = post.author;
}
Right
List<Post> posts = await Post().preload('author').get();
for (Post post in posts) {
  User? author = post.author; // already loaded
}

docs.title: Awaiting independent work one by one
docs.text:
Start two calls that do not need each other at the same time. The total time is then the slowest call:

Wrong
int users = await User().count();
int orders = await Order().count();
Right
(int, int) counts = await (User().count(), Order().count()).wait;

For a list of futures, use Future.wait(futures).

docs.title: A static Map as a cache
docs.text:
A static map that you never clean grows until the memory is full, and each isolate has its own copy. Use the cache with a time to live:

Wrong
static final Map<String, Object> _settings = <String, Object>{};
Right
Map<String, dynamic> settings = await Cache().remember(
  'settings',
  Duration(minutes: 10),
  loadSettings,
);

With the redis or database store, all isolates and servers share the same values.

docs.title: Forgetting await
docs.text:
An async call with no await loses its error, and it can end after the response is sent:

Wrong
mailer.sendWelcome(user);
Right
await mailer.sendWelcome(user);

The unawaited_futures lint in analysis_options.yaml finds these. To answer the client first, use a queue job with dispatchAfterResponse.

docs.title: A new client for every request
docs.text:
A new HTTP or Redis client in each request opens and closes a connection every time. Make one client and share it:

Wrong
Future<String> rate(DoxRequest req) async {
  HttpClient client = HttpClient();
  // ...
}
Right
class RateService {
  RateService(this._client);

  final HttpClient _client;

  Future<String> rate() async {
    // use _client
  }
}

Register the client one time in the container and inject it.

docs.title: A long transaction
docs.text:
A transaction holds one database connection until it ends, so a slow API call inside it can empty the pool. Do the slow call before or after the transaction:

Wrong
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await order.save();
  await paymentApi.charge(order); // the connection waits here
});
Right
await paymentApi.charge(order);
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await order.save();
});

docs.title: Reading a big file into memory
docs.text:
bytes loads the whole upload into memory. Stream it. See Request and Files and big responses:

Wrong
List<int> data = await file.bytes;
Right
Stream<List<int>> data = file.stream();

docs.title: Timers and listeners that never stop
docs.text:
On a long connection, like a WebSocket, a Timer.periodic or a stream listener keeps running after the client leaves. Cancel it when the connection closes:

StreamSubscription<Event> subscription = events.listen(send);
// when the client disconnects
await subscription.cancel();

docs.title: Let Dox warn you
docs.text: Strict mode writes a warning for the worst mistakes while you develop. It is off by default.

docs.title: Strict mode in Dox
docs.text:
Set strict in AppConfig, only in development:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  strict: StrictConfig(enabled: Env.appEnv == 'development'),
  // ...
);

Warnings go to stderr with a [strict] tag. blockLimit is how long code may block the isolate, 50 ms by default:

StrictConfig(enabled: true, blockLimit: Duration(milliseconds: 100))

A route that blocks the isolate for too long warns one time:

[strict] GET /invoices/{id} blocked the isolate for 180 ms (limit 50 ms). Other requests on this isolate had to wait. Move heavy CPU work (like bcrypt, PDF or image work) to await Dox().compute(...), and use Hash.makeAsync or Hash.verifyAsync for passwords.

Code that blocks the event loop after an await warns at most one time in 10 seconds, with no name of the code:

[strict] The event loop of isolate 1 was blocked for about 120 ms (limit 50 ms). Some code ran that long without an await, so other requests had to wait. Move heavy CPU work to await Dox().compute(...).

Hash.make, Hash.verify and Hash.check in the web server warn one time for each place in your code:

[strict] Hash.make ran in the web server at AuthController.register (package:my_app/app/http/controllers/auth_controller.dart:21:18). It blocks the isolate while bcrypt runs, so other requests wait. Use await Hash.makeAsync(...) instead.

docs.title: Strict mode in the ORM
docs.text:
Set strict in DatabaseConfig:

lib/config/database.dart
DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  // ...
  strict: OrmStrict(enabled: appConfig.isDevelopment),
);

nPlusOneCount (default 5) is how many row by row loads of one relation in about one second give a warning. maxRows (default 1000) is how many rows get() or all() may read. The warnings have a [db] tag:

[db] Strict mode: possible N+1 query. The relation "author" of Post was loaded row by row 5 times in a short time. Load it for all rows in one query with preload('author').

[db] Strict mode: table "orders" read 25000 rows into memory (the limit is 1000). Use paginate(), chunk(), lazy() or cursor() for big results.
