docs.title: Performance
docs.text: This page shows how fast Dox is, and how to keep your app fast in production.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Dox is fast by default. In production, follow these rules:

  1. Build with dox build and run the AOT binary. See Deployment.
  2. Put Caddy or nginx in front, for HTTPS and gzip.
  3. Keep the default isolates, one per CPU core.
  4. Keep the body limits on.

For the code mistakes that slow an app down, see Performance mistakes.

docs.title: Bodies, uploads and big responses
docs.text:
Dox keeps big requests and responses out of the memory by default:

  • A body over maxBodySize or maxMultipartSize gets 413 before Dart reads it. Set the same limit in the proxy. See Size limits.
  • An upload over 1 MB streams to a temp file. See Request.
  • A File or Stream response streams. See Files and big responses.

docs.title: gzip
docs.text:
A proxy does gzip better than Dart, so gzip in Dart is off by default. With no proxy, turn it on:

AppConfig(compress: true);

Dox gzips only a body over 256 bytes, for a client that accepts gzip. A streamed response is not compressed.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
LogMiddleware logs one line per request. A new project turns it off when APP_ENV is production or not set, because the proxy writes access logs.

Logger writes its lines every 20 ms in one write. If the process is killed hard, the last 20 ms of logs can be lost.

docs.title: Response handler
docs.text: Leave responseHandler unset if you do not need it. With no handler, Dox sends a plain value (text, map, list) with no DoxResponse.

docs.title: Benchmark
docs.text:
This benchmark uses the rules of the-benchmarker/web-frameworks. Each server answers GET / (empty body), GET /user/:id (the id) and POST /user (empty body). "Dox server only" is dox_http_native with no framework.

It measures only the HTTP stack. A real app spends most of its time on the database and your own code. See App benchmark.

docs.title: 2 cores
docs.text:
2 cores: ahead of Rust hyper and Bun

GET /, 256 connections. Every server has one worker per core: Dox and Relic one isolate, Bun and Node one process, Go and Rust one thread.

req/s p99 RAM Doxfull app 652,400fastest 0.7 ms 21 MB Rusthyper 572,1321.14× slower 0.8 ms 14 MB BunBun.serve 504,6721.29× slower 1.0 ms 40 MB Relic 2relic_native 471,0051.39× slower 0.7 ms 40 MB Nodenode:http 282,1302.3× slower 1.7 ms 199 MB Gonet/http 237,1462.8× slower 3.3 ms 36 MB dart:ioHttpServer 124,9965.2× slower 4.8 ms 56 MB

Dox · Rust 1.99 · Bun 1.4 · Relic 2.0 · Node 26 · Go 1.26 · Dart 3.13 · 2 cores · 256 connections · wrk

All the servers are from the same run on 2026-11-22. Each number is the median of 3 rounds. See How it was run.

Requests per second on GET / at 64, 256 and 512 connections:

Server 64 256 512 p99 at 256 peak MB Dox 541,489 652,400 669,691 0.74 ms 21 Dox server only 576,078 685,300 701,441 0.70 ms 20 Rusthyper 499,992 572,132 559,617 0.77 ms 14 BunBun.serve 496,865 504,672 521,648 1.02 ms 40 Relic 2relic_native 461,710 471,005 494,225 0.71 ms 40 Nodenode:http 263,438 282,130 278,923 1.73 ms 199 Gonet/http 245,400 237,146 230,919 3.32 ms 36 dart:io 115,790 124,996 132,746 4.82 ms 56

Server GET /user/:id POST /user Dox 582,861 576,435 Dox server only 666,149 676,363 Rusthyper 553,689 563,347 Bun 488,315 496,905 Relic 2 432,465 376,030 Node 268,959 291,521 Go 229,640 232,201 dart:io 94,084 124,623

docs.title: Why it is fast
docs.text:
The server runs on the thread of the isolate, so a request never waits for another thread to wake up. See Native server. A profile with perf (4 server cores, 64 connections):

Dox Bun CPU time per request 4.85 µs 5.5 µs Context switches per request 0.08 0.035

docs.title: How it was run
docs.text:
• Docker on an Apple M2 (8 CPUs in the Docker VM), linux/arm64.
  • One server at a time. The server and wrk run in two containers on different CPUs: the server on 2 CPUs, wrk on the other 6. Host network, keep-alive.
  • wrk 4.1, 64, 256 and 512 connections, 5 seconds warm-up, then 15 seconds per route.
  • 3 rounds on 2026-11-22. In each round, every server runs one time. The tables show the median of the 3 rounds.
  • Every server has as many workers as server CPUs.
  • Peak memory is the peak of the container (all workers).
  • Dart 3.13.7, AOT build with dart build cli (this is what dox build does). dox_core and dox_http_native are the releases of 2026-11-22. Node 26.13, Bun 1.4.5, Go 1.26, Rust 1.99 with hyper 1.
  • Relic is relic 2.0.0 with relic_native 2.0.0, started with serveNative().

docs.title: App benchmark
docs.text:
A small real app, the same in each language: GET /json returns a map, GET /db reads one row by id from Postgres, and GET /queries?n=20 reads 20 rows one after another. The table has 10,000 rows, and each app uses its database driver with no ORM.

2 cores: one row from Postgres

GET /db, 256 connections. Requests per second, higher is better.

req/s p99 RAM Doxdox_postgres_native 297,000fastest 2.6 ms 93 MB BunBun.sql 198,2961.5× slower 2.1 ms 64 MB Rusttokio-postgres 128,0652.3× slower 2.6 ms 11 MB Nodepg 75,4473.9× slower 4.1 ms 232 MB Gopgx 55,9035.3× slower 6.3 ms 31 MB dart:iopackage:postgres 28,59810.4× slower 14.2 ms 47 MB

Dox · Bun 1.4 · Rust 1.99 · Node 26 · Go 1.26 · Dart 3.13 · Postgres 18 · 2 cores · 256 connections · wrk

The Dox numbers are from 2026-11-16. The other servers are from the run before, on the same Mac.

All three routes at 256 connections, requests per second:

Server /json /db /queries?n=20 peak MB Doxdox_postgres_native 592,900 297,000 18,015 93 BunBun.sql 564,362 198,296 18,994 64 Rusthyper + tokio-postgres 667,718 128,065 9,312 11 Nodenode:http + pg 205,774 75,447 7,458 232 Gonet/http + pgx 206,398 55,903 6,635 31 dart:iopackage:postgres 89,480 28,598 2,269 47
  • On one query per request, Dox is the fastest: 1.5 times Bun.
  • On 20 queries per request, Dox and Bun are about the same. Postgres is the limit here. Both are about twice as fast as Rust.

The same app on MySQL 8.4 (dox_mysql_native). The dart:io app has no MySQL version.

How it was run: the same rig as the benchmark above. The server gets 2 CPUs, the database gets 2 CPUs and wrk gets the other 4. Each server has 4 database connections per core, 8 in total. One run of 15 seconds per route. The Postgres Dox row was measured again on 2026-11-16 (same Mac, a new Docker VM). The other servers and the MySQL table are from the run before.

docs.title: Database drivers
docs.text:
One find-by-id query, AOT build (dart build cli), database on the same machine (Apple M-series), one isolate:

Database One query at a time Many queries in flight App CPU time per query Postgres 144 connections 60 µs 12.5 µs each64 in flight MySQL 8.410 connections 67 µs 11 µs each32 in flight 13.5 µs MariaDB 1110 connections 63 µs 9.7 µs each32 in flight 12.4 µs

The CPU time counts the Dart thread and the Rust thread. For MySQL, it is about 75,000 queries per second on one core. Many requests at the same time, like in a web server, get the most out of the driver.

docs.title: Dart VM flags
docs.text: A bigger young generation (DART_VM_OPTIONS=--new_gen_semi_max_size=64 or 128) did not give a better p99 in 5 runs, so Dox sets no VM flags. The AOT binary of dox build reads DART_VM_OPTIONS, so you can try your own.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
A provider is a class that sets up one part of your app in every isolate when it starts, like the database, auth or a Redis connection.

Dox runs your app on many isolates, and they do not share memory. So code in bin/server.dart sets up only the first isolate. Each isolate runs every provider itself.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Make a provider with the CLI. It writes lib/providers/cache_provider.dart:

dox make:provider Cache

Dox finds every class that extends DoxProvider after dart run build_runner build. You do not register it. Its constructor can ask for other classes of the container. See Dependency injection.

docs.title: Setting up a part of the app
docs.text:
Put the code in setup(). It runs in each isolate before the routes are registered, and Dox waits for it:

lib/providers/orm_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

class ORMProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig);
  }
}

Open connections in setup(), not in the constructor. Dox copies a provider to each isolate, and an open socket can not be copied.

A package with no dox_core dependency imports DoxProvider from package:dox_annotation/provider.dart.

docs.title: Running code after all providers
docs.text:
boot() runs after setup() of every provider is done. Use it for work that needs the other providers, like a background worker:

class ReportProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {}

  @override
  Future<void> boot() async {
    // every provider has run setup() here
  }
}

The web server and the queue worker (bin/queue.dart) run boot(). The scheduler (bin/schedule.dart) and dox openapi:generate run only setup().

docs.title: Clean up on shutdown
docs.text:
shutdown() runs in every isolate when the server stops, after the open requests are done. See Graceful shutdown:

lib/providers/redis_provider.dart
class RedisProvider extends DoxProvider {
  late RedisConnection redis;

  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    redis = await RedisConnection.open();
  }

  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await redis.close();
  }
}

Dox closes the cache stores by itself. An error in shutdown() goes to the exception handler, and the other providers still run.

docs.title: Choosing the order
docs.text:
Providers run in the order of their file path. List a provider in AppConfig to run it first:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  container: registerContainer,
  providers: <DoxProvider>[ORMProvider()], // runs before the others
);

No provider runs twice.

docs.title: Adding a provider in code
docs.text:
Call Dox().addProvider() or Dox().addProviders() before startServer():

bin/server.dart
Dox().initialize(appConfig);
Dox().addProvider(MyProvider());
Dox().addProviders(<DoxProvider>[OtherProvider()]);
await Dox().startServer();

docs.title: Adding global middleware
docs.text:
A provider can add a global middleware in setup(). It runs before the middleware of the app. See Middleware:

@override
void setup() {
  Dox().addGlobalMiddleware(AuditMiddleware());
}

docs.title: Work only in the web server
docs.text:
Dox().isWebServer is true only in the web server process. It is false in the queue worker, the scheduler and tests:

@override
void boot() {
  if (Dox().isWebServer) startMetrics();
}

docs.title: Example: auth
docs.text:
This provider sets up authentication. Its name is AppAuthProvider, because dox_auth already has an AuthProvider class:

lib/providers/auth_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

class AppAuthProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Auth.initialize(AuthConfig(
      defaultGuard: 'web',
      guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
        'web': AuthGuard(
          driver: JwtAuthDriver(secret: SecretKey(env.appKey)),
          provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
        ),
      },
    ));
  }
}

docs.title: Queue
docs.text:
A queue runs slow work in the background, so the request can answer at once.

You put a slow task, like an email or a report, on a queue as a job. A worker process then takes each job and runs it. The dox_queue package has a redis driver and a sync driver. The database driver is in the dox_queue_database package.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
A new app already has the queue. In an older app, run this command:

dox add queue

The default driver is database. Add --driver=redis or --driver=sync to pick another one. The command writes the config, the provider, bin/queue.dart and a sample job. It never overwrites a file.

With database, it also adds dox_queue_database and the migration of the jobs tables, so run dox add orm first. With redis, it adds the REDIS_* keys.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The queue config picks the driver and lists your jobs:

lib/config/queue.dart
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';

import '../generated/jobs.g.dart';

QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  /// sync, database or redis
  driver: 'database',

  /// every @Job class, from lib/generated/jobs.g.dart
  jobs: jobRegistry,
);

dart run build_runner build writes jobRegistry. Queue.config gives this config in your code.

  • sync: dispatch() runs the job at once. There is no worker, no retry and no delay. Use it for tests and local work.
  • database: jobs are rows in the jobs table. It needs dox_queue_database, and Postgres, MySQL 8+, MariaDB 10.6+ or SQLite.
  • redis: jobs are in Redis.

Keep retryAfter bigger than your longest job

A job that runs longer than retryAfter (default 90 seconds) looks crashed, so a second worker runs it again.

docs.title: All options
docs.text: Option Default What it does driver sync sync, database (needs dox_queue_database) or redis jobs empty jobRegistry from lib/generated/jobs.g.dart redis 127.0.0.1:6379 RedisOptions for the redis driver. See Redis driver prefix dox_queue: the start of every Redis key connection default the dox_orm connection name, for dox_queue_database retryAfter 90 seconds when a worker does not finish a job in this time, another worker can take it inProcess false run a worker in the web server. See Running jobs in the web server workerQueues ['default'] the queues of the in-process worker workerConcurrency 1 jobs at once in the in-process worker workerTimeoutGrace none the --timeout-grace wait of the in-process worker serializeSync false the sync driver saves the job and reads it back before it runs connections none more queue connections by name. See Queue connections afterCommit false push jobs from a transaction only after the commit. See Dispatching after the commit failedAtTimestamp false the failed_at column is a timestamp. See The failed_at column

docs.title: The provider
docs.text:
The provider sets up the queue in every isolate. Put it in lib/providers/:

lib/providers/queue_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';

import '../config/queue.dart';

class AppQueueProvider extends QueueProvider {
  AppQueueProvider() : super(queueConfig);
}

docs.title: The worker file
docs.text:
The worker runs from bin/queue.dart. It starts the providers of your app, but not the HTTP server:

bin/queue.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';

/// run queued jobs: `dart run bin/queue.dart [work] [flags]`.
Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await QueueWorker(app: appConfig).run(args);
}

docs.title: Database driver
docs.text:
The database driver, job batches and dispatching after the commit need the dox_queue_database package:

dart pub add dox_queue_database

Then make your queue provider extend DatabaseQueueProvider:

lib/providers/queue_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_queue_database/dox_queue_database.dart';

import '../config/queue.dart';

class AppQueueProvider extends DatabaseQueueProvider {
  AppQueueProvider() : super(queueConfig);
}

Make the jobs, failed_jobs and job_batches tables. Batches need the job_batches table with every driver:

dox queue:table
dox migrate

The migration looks like this:

db/migration/2026_10_25_000000_create_queue_tables.dart
// ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue_database/dox_queue_database.dart';

class CreateQueueTables extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await QueueTables.up(schema);
    await QueueTables.upBatches(schema);
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await QueueTables.downBatches(schema);
    await QueueTables.down(schema);
  }
}

To keep the jobs in another database connection, use QueueConfig(connection: 'postgres').

docs.title: Adding the pop indexes to an old table
docs.text:
A jobs table from an earlier migration can be slow to poll. Add the missing indexes with a new migration:

db/migration/2026_11_20_000000_add_queue_pop_index.dart
// ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue_database/dox_queue_database.dart';

class AddQueuePopIndex extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await QueueTables.popIndex(schema);
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {}
}

docs.title: The connection column
docs.text:
failed_jobs.connection keeps the name of the queue connection. An older table without it still works, but failed --connection=X then lists all failed jobs. Add the column, then restart the workers:

await schema.table('failed_jobs', (Table table) {
  table.string('connection').nullable();
});

docs.title: The failed_at column
docs.text:
failed_jobs.failed_at is an integer with unix time in milliseconds. For a UTC timestamp, set failedAtTimestamp: true in the migration and in the queue config:

await QueueTables.up(schema, failedAtTimestamp: true);

QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'database',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  failedAtTimestamp: true,
);

The setting and the column must match

If they do not match, the failed job commands throw a StateError, and a job that fails all its tries stays in jobs and runs again after retryAfter.

On MySQL and MariaDB, a TIMESTAMP cannot hold a time after 2038-01-19. To change an existing integer column, stop all workers, run the SQL for your database, set failedAtTimestamp: true, then start the workers.

SQLite (3.35 or newer):

ALTER TABLE failed_jobs ADD COLUMN failed_at_utc TIMESTAMP;
UPDATE failed_jobs SET failed_at_utc =
  strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%fZ', failed_at / 1000.0, 'unixepoch');
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs DROP COLUMN failed_at;
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs RENAME COLUMN failed_at_utc TO failed_at;

Postgres:

ALTER TABLE failed_jobs ALTER COLUMN failed_at TYPE TIMESTAMP
  USING to_timestamp(failed_at / 1000.0) AT TIME ZONE 'UTC';

MySQL and MariaDB:

ALTER TABLE failed_jobs ADD COLUMN failed_at_utc TIMESTAMP NULL;
UPDATE failed_jobs SET failed_at_utc = FROM_UNIXTIME(failed_at DIV 1000);
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs DROP COLUMN failed_at;
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs CHANGE failed_at_utc failed_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL;

docs.title: Redis driver
docs.text:
Set the driver to redis and give the Redis server:

QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'redis',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  redis: RedisOptions(
    host: env.redisHost,
    port: 6379,
    commandTimeout: Duration(seconds: 5),
    maxQueuedCommands: 1000,
  ),
);

commandTimeout (default 10 seconds) fails a command that gets no reply, and null turns it off. maxQueuedCommands limits the commands that wait for a connection. It is off by default.

To read the Redis server from the env, use QueueConfig.redisFromEnv():

QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'redis',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  redis: QueueConfig.redisFromEnv(),
);

It reads REDIS_URL, like rediss://user:password@host:6380/0, where rediss turns on TLS. Without REDIS_URL, it reads REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_USERNAME, REDIS_PASSWORD and REDIS_TLS.

docs.title: Generating job classes
docs.text:
Make a new job file in lib/app/jobs/:

dox make:job SendWelcomeEmail

docs.title: Class structure
docs.text:
A job is a class with @Job() that extends DoxJob. The worker calls its handle() method:

lib/app/jobs/send_welcome_email.job.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';

@Job()
class SendWelcomeEmail extends DoxJob {
  SendWelcomeEmail({required this.userId});

  final int userId;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    MailService mail = Dox().ioc.get<MailService>();
    await mail.sendWelcome(userId);
  }
}

Run dart run build_runner build after you add or change a job.

docs.title: Job data
docs.text:
The parameters of the unnamed constructor are saved with the job. Each parameter needs a field or getter with the same name. These types work:

  • int, double, num, String, bool
  • DateTime
  • enums (saved by name)
  • List and Map<String, ...> of these, also nested
  • dynamic and Object (the value must be JSON)
  • the nullable types of all of them

Save an id, not an object. Load the user in handle(), so you get the newest data.

docs.title: Using services in a job
docs.text:
A job is made again from its saved data, so get services in handle() from the container:

UserService users = Dox().ioc.get<UserService>();

docs.title: Setting the number of tries
docs.text:
A job runs one time by default. Set tries to try again when handle() throws, and backoff to wait between the tries:

/// run up to 3 times
@override
int get tries => 3;

/// wait 10 seconds before the 2nd try, 60 seconds before the 3rd
@override
List<Duration> get backoff => const <Duration>[
  Duration(seconds: 10),
  Duration(seconds: 60),
];

The last backoff entry is used for all later tries. Three more settings change the retries:

  • retryUntil retries until a time, in place of a number of tries.
  • maxExceptions fails the job after this many tries that threw an error.
  • failOnTimeout fails the job at once when a try times out.

docs.title: Setting a timeout
docs.text:
timeout is the maximum run time of one try. The default is the worker --timeout, 60 seconds:

@override
Duration? get timeout => const Duration(seconds: 30);

docs.title: Choosing the queue
docs.text:
Jobs go on the default queue. Give a job its own queue, so a worker can run it first or apart:

@override
String get queue => 'emails';

docs.title: Handling failed jobs
docs.text:
failed() runs one time, after the last try failed:

@override
Future<void> failed(Object error, StackTrace stack) async {
  // tell someone, or clean up
}

docs.title: Encrypting job data
docs.text:
Add the ShouldBeEncrypted mixin to encrypt the data of the job with the app key. The worker needs the same key, or one of AppConfig.previousKeys:

@Job()
class ChargeCard extends DoxJob with ShouldBeEncrypted {
  // ...
}

The job name, the queue and the id stay plain text.

docs.title: Renaming a job class
docs.text:
The class name is saved with each job. When you rename a class, keep the old name with name:

@Job(name: 'SendWelcomeEmail')

docs.title: Dispatching jobs
docs.text:
Call dispatch() to put a job on the queue. It gives the job id. Queue.dispatch() does the same:

await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: user.id).dispatch();
await Queue.dispatch(SendWelcomeEmail(userId: user.id));

docs.title: Delayed dispatching
docs.text:
Use delay to wait before the job runs. You can also pick another queue:

await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatch(
  delay: Duration(minutes: 10),
  queue: 'emails',
);

To wait until a time, use delayUntil. Give delay or delayUntil, not both:

await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatch(
  delayUntil: DateTime.utc(2030, 1, 1, 9),
);

docs.title: Conditional dispatching
docs.text:
dispatchIf dispatches only when the condition is true, and dispatchUnless only when it is false. They give null when the job was not dispatched:

await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatchIf(user.wantsEmail);
await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatchUnless(user.isBlocked);

docs.title: Synchronous dispatching
docs.text:
Run the job now, in this process, with no queue. Queue.dispatchSync(job) does the same:

await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatchSync();

docs.title: Dispatching after the response
docs.text:
Run the job in this process after the response is sent. Queue.dispatchAfterResponse(job) does the same:

SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatchAfterResponse();

It gives nothing, so do not await it. The job has no retry, and it is lost if the server stops first.

docs.title: Dispatching after the commit
docs.text:
A job dispatched in a transaction can run before the commit, or after a rollback. Use afterCommit: true to push it after the commit. This needs dox_queue_database:

await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  User user = await User().create(<String, dynamic>{'email': email});
  await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: user.id).dispatch(afterCommit: true);
});

A rollback drops the job, and outside a transaction it is pushed at once. It waits only for a transaction on the default dox_orm connection. To do this for every dispatch, set QueueConfig(afterCommit: true). Chains and batches also take afterCommit.

docs.title: Queueing an email
docs.text:
To send an email later, you do not need a job class. With dox_mailer, call Mail.queue():

await Mail.queue(message);
await Mail.later(Duration(minutes: 10), message, queue: 'emails');

docs.title: Running the worker
docs.text:
Start a worker to run the jobs:

dart run bin/queue.dart

--queue picks the queues, and the first one goes first. --concurrency runs more jobs at once on one thread:

dart run bin/queue.dart work --queue=emails,default --concurrency=4

For CPU heavy jobs, run more worker processes. The dox CLI runs the same file: dox queue:work, dox queue:failed, dox queue:retry <id|all>, dox queue:forget <id>, dox queue:flush, dox queue:clear [queue], dox queue:restart and dox queue:prune-failed.

docs.title: Worker flags
docs.text:
Flag Default What it does --queue=high,default default the queues to work. The first one goes first --concurrency=4 1 jobs at once in this process --once off run one job, then stop --tries=3 1 tries of a job that does not set tries --timeout=60 60 maximum run time in seconds of a job that does not set timeout --sleep=3 3 seconds to wait when the queues are empty --max-sleep=30 off double the sleep on each empty poll, up to this many seconds --stop-when-empty off stop when the queues are empty --timeout-grace=10 none after a timeout, wait up to this many seconds for the old run to end --backoff=1,5,10 none seconds to wait before each retry of a job that does not set backoff --max-jobs=1000 off stop after this many jobs --max-time=3600 off stop after this many seconds --memory=256 off stop when the process uses more than this many MB --connection=name main the queue connection to use

After --max-jobs, --max-time and --memory, let your process manager start the worker again.

docs.title: Stopping the worker
docs.text: Press Ctrl+C, or send SIGTERM. The worker waits for the running jobs, then stops. A second signal stops it at once.

docs.title: Restarting after a deploy
docs.text:
The worker keeps your code in memory, so restart it after each deploy:

dart run bin/queue.dart restart

Each worker stops after its current jobs, and your process manager starts it again. The workers and the command must share a cache store, like file on one machine, or redis.

docs.title: Running the worker in production
docs.text:
Run the binary that dox build makes in build/bundle/bin/queue. It takes the same commands and flags:

cd build/bundle
./bin/queue work --concurrency=4

Run it as its own process, next to the web server. For example, with Docker Compose:

services:
  web:
    build: .
    command: /app/bin/server
  worker:
    build: .
    command: /app/bin/queue work --concurrency=4

Set your process manager to restart it when it stops.

docs.title: Running jobs in the web server
docs.text:
A small app can skip the worker process. With inProcess: true, the first isolate of the web server also runs jobs:

QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'database',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  inProcess: true,
);

The jobs share the isolate with web requests, so heavy jobs make those requests slow.

docs.title: Dealing with failed jobs
docs.text:
When handle() throws or times out, the worker waits the backoff time and tries again, up to tries times. After the last try, the job goes to the failed jobs, and failed() runs.

A timeout does not stop the code

Dart cannot stop a running Future, so handle() continues after a timeout. Write jobs that are safe to run two times.

To wait for the old run, start the worker with --timeout-grace=SECONDS. Keep timeout plus the grace time below retryAfter.

docs.title: Retrying failed jobs
docs.text:
List the failed jobs, and put one or all of them back on their queue:

dart run bin/queue.dart failed
dart run bin/queue.dart retry 6f1c0e...
dart run bin/queue.dart retry all

docs.title: Deleting failed jobs
docs.text:
forget deletes one failed job, and flush deletes all of them. prune-failed deletes failed jobs older than --hours=N (default 24):

dart run bin/queue.dart forget 6f1c0e...
dart run bin/queue.dart flush
dart run bin/queue.dart prune-failed --hours=48

docs.title: Controlling the job from handle()
docs.text:
Add the InteractsWithQueue mixin, then call one of these in handle():

Call What it does attempts() how many times a worker took the job. The first run gives 1 release(delay) put the job back on its queue. It runs again after delay fail(error) fail the job now, with no retry. failed() runs delete() delete the job, with no retry and no failed() 
@Job()
class SendReport extends DoxJob with InteractsWithQueue {
  SendReport({required this.reportId});

  final int reportId;

  @override
  int get tries => 5;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    ReportApi api = Dox().ioc.get<ReportApi>();
    if (await api.isBusy()) {
      release(Duration(seconds: 30));
      return;
    }
    if (!await api.hasReport(reportId)) {
      delete();
      return;
    }
    await api.send(reportId);
  }
}

release() counts as a try, so set tries above 1. In a test file, write this.fail(...), because package:test also has a fail().

docs.title: Clearing jobs from a queue
docs.text:
Delete all jobs of a queue, also the running ones. The default queue is default:

dart run bin/queue.dart clear emails

docs.title: Job middleware
docs.text:
Job middleware wraps handle() of a job, for rules that many jobs share. Add the HasMiddleware mixin and list the middleware. The first one runs first:

@Job()
class SendReport extends DoxJob with HasMiddleware {
  SendReport({required this.reportId});

  final int reportId;

  @override
  int get tries => 5;

  @override
  List<JobMiddleware> get middleware => <JobMiddleware>[
    RateLimited('report-api', 10, Duration(minutes: 1)),
  ];

  // ...
}

The built-in middleware keeps its counts and locks in the default cache store. All workers must share it, so do not use the memory store. A middleware that puts the job back counts as a try.

docs.title: Rate limiting
docs.text:
RateLimited(key, max, per) runs max jobs of key in each per window at most. The other jobs go back on the queue:

RateLimited('report-api', 10, Duration(minutes: 1)),

docs.title: Preventing job overlaps
docs.text:
WithoutOverlapping(key) runs one job of key at a time:

WithoutOverlapping(
  'report-$reportId',
  releaseAfter: Duration(seconds: 30),
  expireAfter: Duration(minutes: 10), // longer than the longest run
),

releaseAfter (default zero) puts the other jobs back after this time. With null, they are dropped. expireAfter frees the lock after this time, so a crash cannot keep it forever.

docs.title: Throttling exceptions
docs.text:
ThrottlesExceptions(key, maxAttempts:, decay:, retryAfter:) is for jobs that call a service that is down. After maxAttempts errors (default 10), jobs of key wait until decay is over (default 10 minutes):

ThrottlesExceptions('report-api',
    maxAttempts: 5, decay: Duration(minutes: 5)),

docs.title: Writing your own middleware
docs.text:
Extend JobMiddleware. Call next() to continue, or release(job, delay) to put the job back:

class SkipAtNight extends JobMiddleware {
  @override
  Future<void> handle(DoxJob job, JobNext next) async {
    if (DateTime.now().hour < 6) {
      release(job, Duration(hours: 1));
      return;
    }
    await next();
  }
}

If you do not call next(), the job is skipped and counts as done.

docs.title: Unique jobs
docs.text:
Add the ShouldBeUnique mixin to keep one job of a class and uniqueId on the queue. While one waits or runs, dispatch() pushes nothing and gives '':

@Job()
class UpdateSearchIndex extends DoxJob with ShouldBeUnique {
  UpdateSearchIndex({required this.productId});

  final int productId;

  @override
  String get uniqueId => '$productId';

  @override
  Duration? get uniqueFor => Duration(hours: 1);

  // ...
}

Set uniqueFor, or the lock of a crashed worker never ends. The lock is in the default cache store, so the web app and the workers must share it.

To free the lock when a worker starts the job, use ShouldBeUniqueUntilProcessing.

docs.title: Job chaining
docs.text:
A chain runs jobs one after the other. When a job fails for good, the rest of the chain is dropped and the catch job runs:

await Queue.chain(<DoxJob>[
  ResizeImage(imageId: 1),
  UploadImage(imageId: 1),
  TellUser(imageId: 1),
]).catchError(TellAdmin(imageId: 1)).dispatch(queue: 'images');

dispatch() gives the id of the first job. delay counts for the first job only. Each job carries the data of the jobs after it, so keep chains short.

docs.title: Handling chain failures
docs.text:
The catch handler is a job too. Add the CatchesError mixin to read the error:

@Job()
class TellAdmin extends DoxJob with CatchesError {
  TellAdmin({required this.imageId});

  final int imageId;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    await alertAdmin('image $imageId failed: $caughtError');
  }
}

The catch job runs one time, in the worker, with no retry. queue:retry of the failed job continues the chain.

docs.title: Job batching
docs.text:
A batch runs many jobs and does something when they are all done. Batches need dox_queue_database and the job_batches table, with every driver:

Batch batch = await Queue.batch(<DoxJob>[
  ImportRows(from: 0),
  ImportRows(from: 1000),
  ImportRows(from: 2000),
])
    .name('import')
    .then(ImportDone())
    .catchError(ImportFailed())
    .whenComplete(CleanUpImport())
    .dispatch(queue: 'imports');

print(batch.id);

docs.title: Batch callbacks
Defining batchable jobs
docs.text:
Add the Batchable mixin to read the batch of a job. batchId is the id, and batch() reads the batch:

@Job()
class ImportRows extends DoxJob with Batchable {
  ImportRows({required this.from});

  final int from;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    Batch? batch = await this.batch();
    if (batch?.cancelled ?? false) return;
    await importRows(from);
  }
}

docs.title: Inspecting batches
docs.text:
Queue.findBatch(id) reads a batch, or gives null. A Batch has these fields:

Field What it holds id, name the id and the name totalJobs how many jobs the batch has pendingJobs how many jobs are not done. Failed jobs are counted, because you can retry them failedJobs how many jobs failed processedJobs how many jobs are done progress the percent of done jobs, from 0 to 100 finished true when every job ran, or the batch was cancelled cancelled true after cancel(), or after a first failure createdAt, cancelledAt, finishedAt the times of these steps 
Batch? batch = await Queue.findBatch(id);

docs.title: Cancelling batches
docs.text:
The first job that fails for good cancels the batch. Add allowFailures() to continue. You can also call cancel(). The jobs still run, so a Batchable job reads cancelled to skip its work:

await batch.cancel();

docs.title: Adding jobs to a batch
docs.text:
add(jobs) adds jobs to a batch, for example from a job of the batch. It throws a StateError when the batch is finished or cancelled:

await batch.add(<DoxJob>[ImportRows(from: 3000)]);

docs.title: Chains in a batch
docs.text:
Use chain(jobs) to put a chain in a batch. The batch counts the chain as one job:

await Queue.batch(<DoxJob>[ImportUsers()])
    .chain(<DoxJob>[ImportOrders(), SumOrders()])
    .dispatch();

docs.title: Pruning batches
docs.text:
Delete batches that finished or were cancelled more than --hours ago (default 24). --unfinished also deletes old batches that never finished:

dart run bin/queue.dart prune-batches --hours=48
dart run bin/queue.dart prune-batches --hours=48 --unfinished=168

In code, use Queue.pruneBatches(before, unfinishedBefore:).

docs.title: Queue events
docs.text:
Listen to the steps of a job, for example to log or count jobs:

Queue.before(
    (QueueEvent event) => print('start ${event.name} ${event.id}'));
Queue.after((QueueEvent event) => print('done ${event.name}'));
Queue.failing((QueueEvent event) => alert(event.name, event.error));
Hook When Queue.queued dispatch() pushed a job Queue.before a worker starts a job Queue.after a worker finished a job and deleted it Queue.released a worker put a job back (release() or a retry) Queue.exceptionOccurred handle() threw and the job will be tried again Queue.failing a job failed for good Queue.looping a worker is about to take the next job Queue.stopping a worker stops

Each isolate has its own listeners, so register them in a provider. Queue.forgetListeners() removes all listeners. A listener gets a QueueEvent:

Field What it holds type the kind of event job the job. Null for looping and stopping name the job name of the registry id the job id queue the queue name attempts the try number. 0 for queued, looping and stopping error, stack the error and its stack trace, for exceptionOccurred and failing delay the wait, for queued and released batch the Batch, for the batch events

The sync driver, dispatchSync() and dispatchAfterResponse() fire no job events.

docs.title: Batch events
docs.text:
In a batch event, event.batch is the batch after the step:

Queue.batchProgress((QueueEvent event) {
  Batch batch = event.batch!;
  print('${batch.name}: ${batch.progress}%');
});
Queue.batchFailed(
    (QueueEvent event) => alert(event.batch!.id, event.error));
Hook When Queue.batchDispatched the batch was saved, before its jobs are pushed Queue.batchProgress a job (or a chain) of the batch is done. With allowFailures(), also when one failed Queue.batchFailed the first job failed for good Queue.batchCancelled the batch was cancelled Queue.batchFinished every job ran, done or failed

Each event fires one time for each step, also with many workers.

docs.title: Queue connections
docs.text:
The config is the main connection. Add more queue stores in connections:

QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'redis',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  connections: <String, QueueConfig>{
    'database': QueueConfig(driver: 'database'),
  },
);

Pick a connection when you dispatch:

await SendReport(reportId: 1).dispatch(connection: 'database');

Run a worker for each connection. Every command of bin/queue.dart takes --connection:

dart run bin/queue.dart work
dart run bin/queue.dart work --connection=database
dart run bin/queue.dart failed --connection=database

An entry uses only driver, redis, prefix, connection, retryAfter, serializeSync and failedAtTimestamp. The in-process worker runs only the main connection. Queue.driverOf(name) gives the job store of a connection.

docs.title: Custom drivers
docs.text:
Write a QueueDriverFactory that makes your QueueDriver, and add it with Queue.extend before the first use of the queue:

class MyDriverFactory implements QueueDriverFactory {
  @override
  QueueDriver create(QueueConfig config, {String? name}) {
    return MyQueueDriver(config);
  }
}

Queue.extend('mine', MyDriverFactory()); // QueueConfig(driver: 'mine')

Call it in setup() of your queue provider, before super.setup().

docs.title: Running jobs in tests
docs.text:
Use the sync driver. dispatch() then runs the job at once:

import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/jobs/send_welcome_email.job.dart';
import 'package:my_app/generated/jobs.g.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  setUp(() {
    Queue.configure(QueueConfig(driver: 'sync', jobs: jobRegistry));
  });

  test('sends the welcome email', () async {
    await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatch();
    // check the email was sent
  });
}

A job that uses Dox() needs Dox().initialize(appConfig) in setUpAll. Set serializeSync: true to save the job and read it back before it runs, like a worker. Then a job that is not in jobRegistry throws:

Queue.configure(
  QueueConfig(driver: 'sync', jobs: jobRegistry, serializeSync: true),
);

To test a job alone, call handle():

await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).handle();

docs.title: Faking the queue
docs.text:
Queue.fake() keeps every dispatch() in a list and runs nothing:

late QueueFake queue;

setUp(() {
  queue = Queue.fake();
});

tearDown(Queue.restore);

test('signing up queues the welcome email', () async {
  await signUp(userId: 1);

  queue.assertPushed<SendWelcomeEmail>();
  queue.assertPushed<SendWelcomeEmail>(
    (SendWelcomeEmail job) => job.userId == 1,
  );
  queue.assertPushedTimes<SendWelcomeEmail>(1);
  queue.assertNotPushed<SendInvoice>();
});
Method Checks assertPushed<T>([test]) a T job was pushed. With test, one of them passes it assertPushedTimes<T>(n) n T jobs were pushed assertNotPushed<T>() no T job was pushed assertNothingPushed() no job was pushed assertChained(<Type>[A, B]) a chain of these job classes, in this order, was dispatched assertBatched([test]) a batch was dispatched. test gets a PendingBatch assertBatchedChain(<Type>[A, B]) a batch has a chain of these job classes, in this order assertBatchCount(n) n batches were dispatched

queue.pushed gives the jobs, with the job, the queue, the delay and the connection. queue.jobsOf<T>() gives the T jobs, and queue.clear() removes them. dispatchSync() and dispatchAfterResponse() still run, and their jobs are in queue.dispatchedSync and queue.dispatchedAfterResponse.

The fake does not encode the job. So a job that is not in QueueConfig.jobs passes a faked test, but fails in a worker.

docs.title: Testing the queue itself
docs.text:
Use the database driver with SQLite :memory:, and run a worker that stops when the queue is empty:

await Worker(
  driver: Queue.driver,
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  options: WorkerOptions(stopWhenEmpty: true),
).run();

docs.title: Without Dox
docs.text:
dox_queue also works in a plain Dart app. Add build_runner and dox_builder, so it writes lib/generated/jobs.g.dart:

dart pub add dox_queue dox_core
dart pub add dev:build_runner dev:dox_builder

Write your jobs as in Creating jobs, and run dart run build_runner build. Then set up the queue and run a worker:

import 'dart:async';
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';
import 'package:my_app/generated/jobs.g.dart';
import 'package:my_app/jobs/resize_image.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  // the worker logs with the Dox logger, so it needs an AppConfig
  Dox().initialize(AppConfig(appKey: 'not-used'));

  Queue.configure(QueueConfig(
    driver: 'redis',
    jobs: jobRegistry,
    redis: RedisOptions(host: '127.0.0.1', port: 6379),
  ));

  await ResizeImage(path: 'photo.png').dispatch();

  Worker worker = Worker(
    driver: Queue.driver,
    jobs: jobRegistry,
    options: WorkerOptions(queues: <String>['default'], concurrency: 4),
  );

  // Ctrl+C: finish the running jobs, then stop
  StreamSubscription<ProcessSignal> signal =
      ProcessSignal.sigint.watch().listen((_) => worker.stop());
  await worker.run();
  await signal.cancel();
  await Queue.close();
}

WorkerOptions takes the settings of the work flags, like queues, concurrency, once, tries, timeout, sleep and stopWhenEmpty. For the database driver, call QueueDatabase.register() before Queue.configure(), after you set up the default dox_orm connection.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Background work: pick the right tool for work after the response.
  • Scheduler: run work on a timer.
  • Mail: queue an email.

docs.title: Scheduler
docs.text:
dox_scheduler runs your tasks on a schedule, so you do not need a cron line for each task.

You write the full schedule in Dart, in one file, and each task is a plain function. A task runs one time for each tick, also when many isolates or servers run the schedule.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
A new app already has the scheduler. In an older app, run this command:

dox add scheduler

It adds the package and writes these files. It never overwrites a file:

  • lib/config/schedule.dart: your tasks and the ScheduleConfig. See Defining tasks.
  • bin/schedule.dart: the program that runs the schedule. See Running the scheduler.
  • lib/providers/schedule_provider.dart: runs the schedule inside the server. See Run inside the server.

docs.title: Defining tasks
docs.text:
Add a task with s.call(name, function) in lib/config/schedule.dart, then add a frequency:

lib/config/schedule.dart
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';

ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig();

void schedule(Schedule s) {
  s.call('cleanup', cleanup).dailyAt('02:00');
  s.call('report', sendReport).hourly();
  s.call('ping', ping).cron('*/5 * * * *').timezone('Asia/Yangon');
}

Future<void> cleanup() async {
  // delete old rows, files, ...
}

The name must be unique, because the logs and the locks use it. A task with no frequency runs every minute. s.find(name) gives the task with that name, or null.

docs.title: Scheduling queued jobs
docs.text:
For a slow task, put a queue job on the queue. A queue worker then runs it:

s.call('report', () => SendReport().dispatch()).hourly();
s.call('prune', () => PruneFiles().dispatch(connection: 'redis')).hourly();

docs.title: Scheduling shell commands
docs.text:
Use exec to run a program. An exit code that is not 0 fails the task:

s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['-f', 'backup.sql', 'mydb']).daily();

No shell is used, so |, > and * are plain text. To use a shell, run it yourself:

s.exec('sh', args: <String>['-c', 'pg_dump mydb | gzip > backup.sql.gz'])
    .daily();

docs.title: Scheduling dox commands
docs.text:
Use command to run dox <command> <args>:

s.command('queue:prune', args: <String>['--hours=48']).hourly();

The task name is the command line, and the logs show it. If args has a secret, give your own name:

s.command('sync', args: <String>['--token=$token'], name: 'sync');

If dox is not on the PATH, set Schedule.doxExecutable = '/usr/local/bin/dox';.

docs.title: Frequency options
docs.text:
Add one of these methods to set how often a task runs:

Method Runs everySecond() every second. Also everyTwoSeconds, everyFiveSeconds, everyTenSeconds, everyFifteenSeconds, everyTwentySeconds, everyThirtySeconds everyMinute() every minute (the default) everyTwoMinutes() every 2 minutes. Also everyThreeMinutes, everyFourMinutes, everyFiveMinutes, everyTenMinutes, everyFifteenMinutes everyThirtyMinutes() at minute 0 and 30 hourly() at minute 0 of every hour hourlyAt(17) at minute 17 of every hour everyTwoHours() every 2 hours at minute 0. Also everyThreeHours, everyFourHours, everySixHours. Give a minute: everyTwoHours(15) everyOddHour() at 01:00, 03:00 ... 23:00. Give a minute: everyOddHour(30) daily() every day at 00:00 dailyAt('13:00') every day at 13:00. at('13:00') is the same twiceDaily(1, 13) every day at 01:00 and 13:00 twiceDailyAt(1, 13, 15) every day at 01:15 and 13:15 weekly() every Sunday at 00:00 weeklyOn(DateTime.monday, '08:00') every Monday at 08:00 monthly() the 1st of every month at 00:00 monthlyOn(15, '12:00') the 15th of every month at 12:00 twiceMonthly(1, 16, '13:00') the 1st and 16th of every month at 13:00 lastDayOfMonth('15:00') the last day of every month at 15:00 quarterly() January, April, July and October 1st at 00:00 quarterlyOn(4, '14:00') January, April, July and October 4th at 14:00 yearly() January 1st at 00:00 yearlyOn(6, 1, '17:00') June 1st at 17:00 cron('*/5 9-17 * * 1-5') any 5 field cron expression

The last method that sets a field wins. So .dailyAt('09:00').weekly() runs at 00:00, but .weekly().dailyAt('09:00') runs at 09:00.

docs.title: Day constraints
docs.text:
Add a day method to run a task only on some days:

Method Runs weekdays() Monday to Friday weekends() Saturday and Sunday mondays() ... sundays() only on that day of the week days(<int>[DateTime.monday, DateTime.friday]) only on these days 
s.call('standup', remind).weekdays().dailyAt('09:00');

A day of the month and a day of the week join with OR, like in cron. So monthlyOn(15).fridays() runs on the 15th and on every Friday.

docs.title: Sub-minute tasks
docs.text:
A seconds method, like everyFiveSeconds(), repeats the task in each due minute. Call it first, because it also sets the task to every minute:

s.call('poll', poll).everyFiveSeconds().between('09:00', '17:00');

docs.title: Cron expressions
docs.text:
cron() takes the 5 standard fields: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week.

Field Values minute 0-59 hour 0-23 day of month 1-31 month 1-12 or JAN-DEC day of week 0-7 or SUN-SAT (0 and 7 are Sunday)

Each field takes *, a number 5, a range 1-5, a list 1,15, and a step */15 or 0-30/10.

docs.title: Time zones
docs.text:
The schedule uses UTC by default. Use timezone() to read the time of a task in another zone:

s.call('report', sendReport).dailyAt('08:00').timezone('Asia/Yangon');

The name is an IANA name, like Europe/London. To use one zone for all tasks, set it in the config:

ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig =
    const ScheduleConfig(timezone: 'Asia/Yangon');

On a summer time change, a time that does not exist that day does not run. A time that occurs two times runs one time.

docs.title: Between times
docs.text:
Use between to run a task only in a time of day, and unlessBetween to skip a time of day. A range can cross midnight:

s.call('sync', sync).everyFiveMinutes().between('09:00', '17:00');
s.call('night', night).hourly().between('22:00', '06:00');
s.call('quiet', quiet).hourly().unlessBetween('23:00', '04:00');

docs.title: Truth tests
docs.text:
when runs the task when the function gives true. skip skips the task when the function gives true:

s.call('promo', promo).daily().when(isPromoOn);
s.call('backup', backup).daily().skip(isHoliday);

docs.title: Environments
docs.text:
Run a task only when APP_ENV is one of the names:

s.call('emails', sendEmails).daily()
    .environments(<String>['production']);

When APP_ENV is not set, the task does not run.

docs.title: Preventing task overlaps
docs.text:
Skip a run while the last run of the task still runs:

s.call('report', sendReport).everyFiveMinutes().withoutOverlapping();

The lock expires after 24 hours. Give another time with withoutOverlapping(Duration(hours: 1)). After a crash, remove the lock with clear-cache.

docs.title: Running tasks on one server
docs.text:
A task runs one time for each tick on all isolates and servers. This is onOneServer(), the default. The locks are in a cache store, so use a shared store like Redis for many servers:

ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig(store: 'redis');

To run a task on every process, use onEveryServer():

s.call('clear-tmp', clearTmp).hourly().onEveryServer();

docs.title: Background tasks
docs.text:
Tasks of the same minute run one after the other. Use runInBackground so a long task does not stop the next one:

s.call('export', export).daily().runInBackground();

docs.title: Timeouts
docs.text:
Count a run as failed when it takes too long. The failure hooks then run:

s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['mydb']).daily()
    .timeout(Duration(minutes: 5));

An exec() or command() process gets SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after Schedule.processGrace (5 seconds). A Dart function cannot be stopped, so its work can continue.

docs.title: Running the scheduler
docs.text:
bin/schedule.dart runs your schedule. With app, it starts your app providers first, like the database:

bin/schedule.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/schedule.dart';
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SchedulerRunner(
    schedule: schedule,
    app: appConfig,
    config: scheduleConfig,
  ).run(args);
}

The dox CLI runs the same file: dox schedule:work is dart run bin/schedule.dart work.

docs.title: Running the worker
docs.text:
Start a process that runs the due tasks at each full minute. Run it next to your server:

dox schedule:work

On Ctrl+C or SIGTERM, it waits for the running tasks. A second signal stops it at once.

docs.title: Running from cron
docs.text:
run runs the tasks of this minute one time, then exits. Add one line to the crontab:

* * * * * cd /path/to/app/build/bundle && ./bin/schedule run

./bin/schedule is the binary that dox build makes. The exit code is 1 when a task failed.

docs.title: Listing tasks
docs.text:
Show each task, its schedule and its next run:

dox schedule:list

Task     Schedule                   Next run
cleanup  0 2 * * *                  2026-10-26 02:00 UTC
report   0 * * * *                  2026-10-25 14:00 UTC
ping     */5 * * * * Asia/Yangon    2026-10-25 20:35 Asia/Yangon

The next run does not check when(), skip() and environments().

docs.title: Running one task now
docs.text:
Run one task now, with its hooks. The schedule, the filters and the locks are not checked:

dox schedule:test cleanup

docs.title: Clearing overlap locks
docs.text:
Remove the withoutOverlapping() locks that a crash left in the store:

dox schedule:clear-cache

Run it only when the task does not run on another process. If it does, the task can start a second time.

docs.title: Run inside the server
docs.text:
For a small app, run the schedule inside the Dox server. Add a provider that extends SchedulerProvider:

lib/providers/schedule_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/schedule.dart';

class ScheduleProvider extends SchedulerProvider {
  ScheduleProvider() : super(schedule: schedule, config: scheduleConfig);
}

Then turn it on, and run dart run build_runner build:

lib/config/schedule.dart
ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig(inProcess: true);

Only the first isolate of the web server runs the tasks, so heavy tasks can slow its requests. Use work for heavy tasks. In a test of the in-process schedule, set Dox().isWebServer = true; first.

docs.title: Logging the schedule
docs.text:
Send the [schedule] lines through the app Logger:

lib/config/schedule.dart
ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig(
  flags: SchedulerFlags(loggerLines: true),
);

The lines then get the tag [scheduler], like [scheduler] ran cleanup in 12ms. SchedulerFlags.all() turns on every flag.

docs.title: Task output
docs.text:
These hooks keep the output of an exec() or command() task. Without them, the output is lost.

Write the output to a file. Each run replaces the file:

s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['mydb']).daily()
    .sendOutputTo('storage/logs/backup.log');

Add the output to the end of the file:

s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['mydb']).daily()
    .appendOutputTo('storage/logs/backup.log');

Get the output in code after the process ends:

s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['mydb']).daily()
    .onOutput((String output) {...});

onOutput keeps the full output in memory, so do not use it for very large output.

docs.title: Task hooks
docs.text:
Run code around a task, for example to tell your team when it fails:

s
    .call('report', sendReport)
    .daily()
    .before(logStart)
    .onSuccess(logDone)
    .onFailure(alertTeam)
    .after(cleanUp);

Future<void> alertTeam(Object error, StackTrace stack) async {
  await notifyTeam('report failed: $error');
}
Hook Runs before before the task. If it throws, the task does not run and fails onSuccess after the task worked onFailure after the task threw or timed out. It gets the error and the stack trace after after the task, always

An error in a task is logged, and the next task still runs.

docs.title: Pinging URLs
docs.text:
Send a GET request to a URL around a task, for example to a health check service:

s
    .call('backup', backup)
    .daily()
    .pingBefore('https://health.example.com/backup/start')
    .pingOnSuccess('https://health.example.com/backup')
    .pingOnFailure('https://health.example.com/backup/fail');

thenPing(url) pings after the task, always. Each ping method has an If form, like pingOnFailureIf(isProduction, url). A failed ping is logged, and the task does not fail. A ping stops after ScheduledTask.pingTimeout (10 seconds).

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Give Scheduler a fake clock to test a schedule with no wait:

import 'package:dox_cache/dox_cache.dart';
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/schedule.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

class FakeClock extends ScheduleClock {
  FakeClock(this.time);

  DateTime time;

  @override
  DateTime now() {
    return time;
  }
}

test('cleanup runs at 02:00', () async {
  Schedule s = Schedule(timezone: scheduleConfig.timezone);
  schedule(s);
  Scheduler scheduler = Scheduler(
    tasks: s.tasks,
    store: CacheStore(MemoryDriver()),
    clock: FakeClock(DateTime.utc(2026, 10, 25, 2)),
  );
  Map<String, TaskOutcome> outcomes = await scheduler.runDue();
  expect(outcomes['cleanup'], TaskOutcome.ran);
});

To run one task, use scheduler.runTask(task, time). To check a schedule with no run, use task.isDue(time) and task.nextRun(time). To replace the ping request, set ScheduledTask.sendPing = (Uri url) async {...};.

docs.title: Without Dox
docs.text:
dox_scheduler also works in a plain Dart app. Leave out app:

import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';

void schedule(Schedule s) {
  s.call('cleanup', cleanup).dailyAt('02:00');
}

Future<void> cleanup() async {
  // delete old files, ...
}

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SchedulerRunner(schedule: schedule).run(args);
}

With no app, the locks use a memory store. For many servers, give a shared CacheStore from dox_cache: SchedulerRunner(schedule: schedule, store: myRedisStore).

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Queue: jobs that must not get lost.
  • Background work: pick the right tool for work after the response.
  • CLI: the schedule:* commands.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: This page shows how to test a Dox app with the test package: HTTP routes, cache, storage, env and the database.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
A new app from dox create already has the test package. In another app, add it as a dev dependency:

dart pub add dev:test

Put your tests in the test/ folder and run them:

dart test

docs.title: Creating a test
docs.text:
dox make:test writes test/ping_test.dart, which starts the app with a DoxTestClient. Add --unit for a plain test with no app:

dox make:test Ping

See dox make:test.

docs.title: Test HTTP routes
docs.text:
DoxTestClient from package:dox_core/testing.dart starts your app inside the test and sends requests to it. Start it in setUpAll and close it in tearDownAll:

test/http_test.dart
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('GET /api/ping', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.get('/api/ping');
    res.expectStatus(200).expectBody('pong');
  });
}

start runs your providers and adds your routes, like a real start. It uses one isolate on 127.0.0.1 and a free port. close stops the server and runs shutdown() of every provider.

docs.title: Making requests
docs.text:
The client has get, post, put, patch and delete. Use send for any other method:

await client.get('/api/users?page=2');
await client.post('/api/posts',
    body: <String, dynamic>{'title': 'Hello'});
await client.send('OPTIONS', '/api/users');

A map or list body goes as JSON. A string or byte list body goes as it is. The client does not follow redirects, so you can check a 302 and its Location header.

docs.title: Sending headers
docs.text:
Pass headers for one request. withHeaders gives a copy of the client that sends the headers with each request:

await client.get('/api/me',
    headers: <String, String>{'Accept-Language': 'de'});

DoxTestClient german =
    client.withHeaders(<String, String>{'Accept-Language': 'de'});

docs.title: Log in as a user
docs.text:
withToken gives a copy of the client that sends Authorization: Bearer <token>:

TestResponse login = await client.post(
  '/api/auth/login',
  body: <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com', 'password': 'secret'},
);
DoxTestClient ann = client.withToken(login.json['token'] as String);
(await ann.get('/api/auth/me')).expectStatus(200);

docs.title: Keep a session (cookies and CSRF)
docs.text:
withSession gives a client that works like a browser. It keeps the cookies of each response and sends the CSRF token on POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE:

test('log in with a form', () async {
  DoxTestClient browser = client.withSession();

  // the first page gives the session and XSRF-TOKEN cookies
  (await browser.get('/login')).expectStatus(200);

  (await browser.post(
    '/login',
    body: <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com', 'password': 's3'},
  )).expectStatus(303).expectHeader('location', '/dashboard');

  (await browser.get('/dashboard')).expectStatus(200);
});

browser.cookies has the kept cookies, and you can change them. The normal client keeps no cookies. To send the cookies of one response, use withCookies(res.cookies).

docs.title: Testing a server that runs
docs.text:
Give the URL of a running server to the constructor. baseUri and headers show the URL and the headers of a client:

DoxTestClient client = DoxTestClient(Uri.parse('http://127.0.0.1:3000'));

docs.title: Checking the response
docs.text:
A TestResponse has the status, the body, the headers and the cookies:

int status = res.status;
String body = res.body;
List<int> bytes = res.bodyBytes;
dynamic json = res.json; // the body read as JSON
String? type = res.header('content-type'); // any case
Map<String, String> cookies = res.cookies;

res.headers has all headers, with lower case names.

docs.title: Expect methods
docs.text:
Each expect method fails the test when the response is not right. It returns the response, so you can chain them:

res
    .expectStatus(422)
    .expectHeader('content-type', contains('application/json'))
    .expectJson(<String, dynamic>{'title': 'The title is required'});
  • expectStatus(code): the failure message shows the body.
  • expectJson(value): a value or a matcher, like containsPair('id', 1).
  • expectBody(value): the body as text.
  • expectHeader(name, value): use isNull for a header that must be missing.

docs.title: Test the cache
docs.text:
Replace Dox().cache with a memory store in setUp. Cache() then uses it, and each test starts with an empty cache:

setUp(() {
  Dox().cache = CacheManager(CacheConfig(
    defaultStore: 'memory',
    stores: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
      'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory'},
    },
  ));
});

test('caches the posts', () async {
  await Cache().put('posts', <String>['a', 'b']);
  expect(await Cache().get('posts'), <dynamic>['a', 'b']);
});

See Cache.

docs.title: Test file storage
docs.text:
Storage.manager.fake(name) from dox_storage puts an empty memory disk in place of one disk. restore(name) puts the real disk back:

setUpAll(() {
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);
});

test('saves the report', () async {
  Disk fake = Storage.manager.fake('s3');

  String path = await Storage()
      .disk('s3')
      .putFile('reports', <int>[1, 2, 3], extension: 'pdf');

  expect(await fake.exists(path.substring(1)), isTrue);
  Storage.manager.restore('s3');
});

Call Dox().initialize() first, or Storage.manager has only the local disk. A Storage() path starts with / and a Disk key does not, so remove the first /.

assertExists(key) and assertMissing(key) of a disk throw a StateError when the check fails:

await fake.assertExists('reports/a.pdf');

See File Storage.

docs.title: Use a test database with .env.testing
docs.text:
Put the values for tests in a .env.testing file, next to .env:

.env.testing
DB_NAME=my_app_test
CACHE_STORE=memory

In tests (dart test, or APP_ENV=testing), Dox reads .env and then .env.testing. A key in .env.testing wins, and a real environment variable wins over both files.

docs.title: Test the database
docs.text:
Run the migrations one time in setUpAll. refreshDatabase() from package:dox_orm/testing.dart empties the tables before each test:

test/user_test.dart
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    await Migrator(
      migrations: migrations,
      config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
    ).migrate();
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig); // runs the ORM provider
  });

  // every test starts with empty tables
  setUp(refreshDatabase);

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('register makes a user', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.post(
      '/api/auth/register',
      body: <String, dynamic>{
        'name': 'Ann',
        'email': 'ann@example.com',
        'password': 'secret123',
      },
    );
    res.expectStatus(201);
  });
}

refreshDatabase() empties every table and starts the ids at 1 again. It keeps the tables and the rows of the dox_db_migration table.

Warning

refreshDatabase() deletes all rows. Use a separate test database, set in .env.testing.

docs.title: Keeping some tables
docs.text:
Pass the tables that every test needs in keep:

refreshDatabase(keep: <String>['dox_db_migration', 'countries']);

See Testing with a database for a full example with SQLite.

docs.title: Running test files one by one
docs.text:
dart test runs test files at the same time. When two files use the same tables, run them one by one:

dart test --concurrency=1

docs.title: Test the env
docs.text:
Give your own values to AppEnv.load(). Then it reads nothing from the shell or the .env file:

AppEnv env = AppEnv.load(
  EnvReader(
    environment: <String, String>{'APP_KEY': 'test'},
    dotEnv: <String, String>{'DB_PORT': '5433'},
  ),
);
expect(env.dbPort, 5433);

A missing or bad key throws an EnvException. A getter default that calls Env.get() reads the real env, so use other getters in a default. See Environment Variables.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Testing with a database: a full example with SQLite.
  • Cache: the cache stores.
  • File Storage: the disks.

docs.title: Add a package
docs.text: dox add adds a Dox package to your app and sets it up.

docs.title: Adding a package
docs.text:
Give the short name of the package. The full name, like dox_orm, also works:

dox add orm

It runs dart pub add dox_orm, then dart pub get, then the setup command of the package (here dox orm:install). The setup command writes the config files, adds the keys to .env and .env.example, and runs build_runner if necessary. At the end it shows what it did and the next steps.

A package with no setup command is only added.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Words after the name go to the setup command, for example to pick a driver:

dox add orm --driver=postgres

Add --dev to add the package as a dev dependency.

docs.title: Running it again
docs.text: The setup command never overwrites a file or a .env key. So you can run dox add again, and it adds only what is missing.

docs.title: Packages with a setup command
docs.text:
Command What it sets up dox add orm [--driver=sqlite\|postgres\|mysql] The ORM and migrations. See Database. dox add queue [--driver=database\|redis\|sync] Queued jobs and bin/queue.dart. database is the default and needs dox add orm first. See Queue. dox add scheduler Scheduled tasks and bin/schedule.dart. See Scheduler. dox add mailer [--transport=log\|smtp\|resend\|mailgun\|postmark\|ses] Mail. log is the default. See Mail. dox add cache [--store=file\|redis\|memory\|database] Cache stores. database needs dox add orm first. See Cache. dox add auth Access token auth. Needs dox add orm and a User model first. See Authentication. dox add storage [--disk=local\|s3] File storage. See File storage. dox add socketio [--broadcasting] Socket.IO, and broadcasting with the flag. See Socket.IO. dox add view Views and resources/views/. See Views. dox add inertia The server side of Inertia. It prints the Vite steps. See Inertia. dox add mcp An MCP server with a sample tool. See MCP. dox add grpc gRPC: a sample .proto file, a router with the health service and APP_HTTP2 in .env. See gRPC.

The first dox add orm can download or build the Postgres and MySQL drivers one time. After that, pubspec.yaml skips the drivers that you do not use.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Package commands: add a setup command to your own package.
  • CLI: all commands of the CLI.

docs.title: AI agents
docs.text:
Give your AI coding agent the real Dox API with skills, AGENTS.md and the llms files.

Without the real API, an agent guesses class and method names, and the code does not compile. Dox gives two sources:

  • Skills: short guides that each package ships. The agent reads them while it writes code in your app.
  • llms files: these docs as plain text, for a chat or a tool with no skills.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
A skill is a SKILL.md file with the real API of one package and the steps for the usual tasks. The agent reads a skill only when your task matches it. A skill comes with the package, so it always agrees with the package version of your app.

These packages ship a skill:

Package Skill Use it for dox_core dox-core-guide routes, controllers, DTOs, serializers, middleware, providers, env config, CLI commands, HTTP tests dox_orm dox-orm-guide models, queries, relations, pagination, transactions, factories, the switch to Postgres or MySQL dox_migration dox-migration-guide migrations, table changes, seeders dox_validation dox-validation-guide DTO rules, custom rules and messages, fluent schemas, database rules dox_auth dox-auth-guide login and logout, JWT, session and access token guards, gates and policies dox_openapi dox-openapi-guide the API docs at /docs, annotations for the OpenAPI document dox_cache dox-cache-guide cache stores, remember, tags, cache locks, the cache in tests dox_queue dox-queue-guide queue jobs, the worker, the Redis and database drivers, failed jobs, chains and batches dox_scheduler dox-scheduler-guide scheduled tasks, cron frequencies, no double runs on many servers dox_storage dox-storage-guide files and uploads, local, S3 and memory disks, signed URLs dox_mailer dox-mailer-guide mail config, mailables, Markdown mail, queued mail, transports, mail in tests dox_socketio dox-socketio-guide realtime events, rooms, socket login, the Redis adapter, broadcasts dox_view dox-view-guide HTML pages with .dox.html templates, layouts, components, forms with CSRF dox_inertia dox-inertia-guide Inertia.js pages with React, Vue or Svelte, shared props, Vite and SSR dox_mcp dox-mcp-guide an MCP server: tools, a route with auth, sessions, OAuth sign-in dox_grpc dox-grpc-guide gRPC services: the .proto file, the service class, status codes, deadlines dox_graphql dox-graphql-guide a GraphQL API from annotations and ORM models, auth and limits ioredis ioredis-guide Redis connections, commands, pipelines, transactions, pub/sub

docs.title: Install the skills
docs.text:
The skills tool copies the skills from your packages into the skills folder of your agent. Run it in the root folder of your app, after dart pub get:

dart run skills@ get

It asks which skills to install. Add --all to install all of them:

dart run skills@ get --all

docs.title: Select your agent
docs.text:
The tool finds your agent from the folders in your project, like .claude/. If it finds none, it asks you. To set the agent, use --agent:

dart run skills@ get --all --agent claude
Agent --agent Skills folder Claude Code claude .claude/skills/ Codex codex .agents/skills/ Cursor cursor .cursor/skills/ GitHub Copilot copilot .github/skills/ Cline cline .cline/skills/ OpenCode opencode .opencode/skills/ Antigravity antigravity .agents/skills/ Other agents generic .agents/skills/

The tool does not find GitHub Copilot, so for Copilot always add --agent copilot.

docs.title: Run it again after a package change
docs.text:
The installed skills are copies. Run the tool again after you add or update a package:

dart run skills@ get

With --all, it also removes the skills of packages that you do not use now.

docs.title: Packages that come in through another package
docs.text:
The tool reads only the packages in your pubspec.yaml. For example, the cache uses ioredis. To get its skill, add it to your app:

dart pub add ioredis
dart run skills@ get

docs.title: Make sure that it worked
docs.text:
List the installed skills:

dart run skills@ list

For Claude Code, the core skill is .claude/skills/dox-core-guide/SKILL.md. If your tool has no skills, give the SKILL.md file to the agent.

docs.title: AGENTS.md
docs.text:
The AGENTS.md file in the root folder of your app tells the agent how your project is organized. Most coding agents read it before they change code.

The starter project has one. It holds:

  • what the project is, and the links to the llms files
  • the command that installs the skills, and the list of skills
  • the folder layout and the file names
  • the dox commands that make files
  • when to run the code generator, and which files are generated
  • the conventions for routes, input, models, migrations, jobs, config and errors
  • how to switch the database
  • the checks to run before a change is done: dart format ., dart analyze and dart test
  • a list of things that the agent must not do

The file is yours. Edit it when your app gets its own rules.

docs.title: llms.txt and llms-full.txt
docs.text:
For a chat or a tool with no skills, the docs site has two plain text files in the llms.txt format:

File What it holds llms.txt A short description of Dox, then one line for each page with its title and its link. llms-full.txt All the docs as one Markdown file, in the order of the menu.

The docs build makes them again at each change, so they agree with this site.

docs.title: Use them
docs.text:
Give the files to an agent in one of these ways:

  1. Paste the link https://dartondox.dev/llms-full.txt in a chat agent that can open links.
  2. Add the link as a docs source in your editor.

  3. Download the file, then attach it to the chat:

    curl -o dox-docs.md https://dartondox.dev/llms-full.txt

If your agent cannot hold the large file, give it llms.txt. The agent then opens only the pages that it needs.

docs.title: Skills or llms-full.txt
docs.text: Skills llms-full.txt Use it for code changes in your app questions in a chat, or a tool with no skills Size small, one skill for each package large, all the docs Version the package version of your app the latest Dox version How the agent gets it automatically, when the task matches you give it the link or the file

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Installation: create a project.
  • MCP server: give AI clients tools from your own app.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
This page shows how to install the Dox CLI, make a new project and start the server.

Dox needs Dart 3.13 or newer.

docs.title: Install the CLI
docs.text:
The dox CLI makes projects, runs the server and makes files. Install it with pub:

dart pub global activate dox

Check that it works:

dox version

If the shell shows "dox: command not found", the pub bin folder is not in your path. Add this line to ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc, then open a new terminal:

export PATH="$PATH":"$HOME/.pub-cache/bin"

docs.title: Create a new project
docs.text:
Give dox create the name of your app, then get the packages:

dox create new_blog
cd new_blog
dart pub get

It downloads the newest release of the starter project, dox-sample. Add --version with a release tag to get one release. It also makes your .env file with a new random app key.

The starter project uses SQLite, so you do not install a database. To use Postgres or MySQL, change DB_CONNECTION and the other database keys in .env. See Database.

docs.title: Add Dox to a Dart project
docs.text:
In a Dart project that you have, add the packages with dart pub add:

dart pub add dox_core dox_orm dox_migration
dart pub add dev:dox_builder dev:build_runner

docs.title: Start the server
docs.text:
Start the server in dev mode:

dox s

It runs bin/server.dart and build_runner watch. It hot reloads a change in lib/app/, and it restarts the server for a change to routes, providers or config. At each start the server runs the new migrations, on the port in APP_PORT (default 3000):

curl localhost:3000/ping

pong

Add --ignore-build-runner to skip the builder, or --no-reload to stop hot reload. To start the server with no CLI, run dart run bin/server.dart.

For production, build a native binary with dox build. See Deployment.

docs.title: Start the server with Docker
docs.text:
The starter project has a Docker setup. This starts the app, a queue worker and a Postgres database:

docker compose up -d --build

The app and the worker always use the Postgres service. The database port is open on this machine only.

To run only the database in Docker and the app with dox s, run docker compose up -d postgres. Then set DB_CONNECTION=postgres and DB_NAME=dox in .env.

docs.title: Run the code generator
docs.text:
Dox makes code for models and DTOs with build_runner. dox s runs it. To run it alone:

dox build_runner:watch   # runs again on each file change
dox build_runner:build   # runs one time

docs.title: AI agents
docs.text: To give an AI coding agent the real API of each package, run dart run skills@ get after dart pub get. See AI agents.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
Dox has many packages, so you add only what you need:

Package What it does dox the CLI dox_core HTTP server, routing, requests, responses, validation dox_orm query builder and models dox_migration database migrations dox_auth Login with access tokens, JWT or sessions dox_builder, dox_annotation code generation for models, DTOs and the container dox_validation typed validation schemas dox_openapi OpenAPI docs dox_storage file storage: local, S3 dox_cache cache: memory, file, Redis dox_cache_database cache in a database table dox_socketio Socket.IO server dox_queue background jobs dox_queue_database queue in a database table dox_scheduler scheduled tasks dox_mailer send email dox_view HTML views dox_inertia Inertia.js pages dox_http_native native HTTP server (Rust) dox_postgres_native, dox_mysql_native native drivers for Postgres and MySQL/MariaDB

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Build a blog API: a full app, step by step.
  • Add a package: add a feature with one command.
  • CLI: all commands of the CLI.

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
Each guide solves one job from start to end: you copy the files, run the commands and check the result.

To know more about one part, follow the links to the reference pages.

Guide What you get File upload Accept an image, check its size and type, save it, return its URL. Pagination A list route with page and per_page, and the JSON shape it returns.
