JWT authentication Register, log in, protect routes, read the user, log out. Custom errors Your own exception classes, one JSON shape for every error, logging. Background work Run work after the response, on another thread, in a queue job, or on a schedule. Static files and SPA Serve a folder or a single page app, with cache headers. CORS for a browser front-end The CORS setup that works with a React, Vue or Flutter web app. Environments Dev, staging and production config, .env files, secrets and APP_KEY. Testing with a database Tests on SQLite or a test Postgres, with migrations and cleanup. Share code with Flutter One DTO package that the server and the Flutter app both use to check input. API docs with OpenAPI A docs page for your API, made from your routes, DTOs and models. Docker A small production image, Postgres in Docker Compose, env and a health check. Deploy to a Linux server Your own server with systemd, and Caddy in front for HTTPS. Deploy to Fly.io Fly.io from your Dockerfile, with SQLite on a volume or with Postgres. Deploy to Google Cloud Run Cloud Run from your Dockerfile, with Cloud SQL and Secret Manager.

docs.title: The example apps
docs.text:
Most guides use the app that dox create my_app makes, so the package name is my_app. Change it to your own package name in the imports.

The OpenAPI guide and the deploy guides use the blog API of the tutorial. Its package name is blog.

All the code is on GitHub:

  • the app guides: examples/guides
  • the blog API: examples/blog-api

CI builds both apps and runs their tests on every push, so the code on these pages keeps working.

docs.title: API docs with OpenAPI
docs.text:
Turn on OpenAPI docs for the blog API, open the docs page, and make the docs better with annotations.

Dox makes the docs from your code, so they stay up to date.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• The blog API from the tutorial, or any Dox app.
  • build_runner and dox_builder. A new app has both, and dox_core has dox_openapi.

docs.title: 1. Write the config
docs.text:
build_runner writes openApiRegistry to lib/generated/openapi.g.dart, with your routes, DTOs and models. Pass it to an OpenApiConfig:

lib/config/openapi.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:blog/generated/openapi.g.dart';

OpenApiConfig openApi = OpenApiConfig(
  info: Info(title: 'Blog API', version: '1.0.0'),
  registry: openApiRegistry,
);

Add it to AppConfig:

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:blog/config/openapi.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  /// OpenAPI docs (config/openapi.dart)
  openApi: openApi,
);

docs.title: 2. Build and start
docs.text:
Build the code and start the server:

dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dox serve

The docs routes are on, because .env has APP_ENV=development.

docs.title: 3. Open the docs page
docs.text:
Open http://localhost:3000/docs. It is a Scalar page with every route and "Try it" buttons. The app now has three new routes:

Route What it gives GET /docs the Scalar docs page (HTML) GET /openapi.json the OpenAPI 3.1 document as JSON GET /openapi.yaml the same document as YAML

docs.title: 4. Read the JSON
docs.text:
Get the document:

curl http://localhost:3000/openapi.json

This is the top level for the blog API, made shorter:

{
  "openapi": "3.1.0",
  "info": {"title": "Blog API", "version": "1.0.0"},
  "paths": {
    "/api/ping": {},
    "/api/posts": {},
    "/api/posts/{id}": {},
    "/api/auth/register": {},
    "/api/auth/login": {},
    "/api/auth/user": {},
    "/ping": {}
  },
  "components": {
    "schemas": {
      "Post": {},
      "SavePost": {},
      "RegisterUser": {},
      "LoginUser": {},
      "User": {},
      "ValidationError": {}
    },
    "securitySchemes": {
      "bearerAuth": {"type": "http", "scheme": "bearer"}
    }
  }
}

This is POST /api/posts. You wrote no docs code for it:

{
  "tags": ["Post"],
  "summary": "POST /api/posts",
  "operationId": "PostController.store",
  "requestBody": {
    "required": true,
    "content": {
      "application/json": {
        "schema": {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/SavePost"}
      }
    }
  },
  "responses": {
    "200": {"description": "Successful response"},
    "401": {
      "description": "Not logged in",
      "content": {
        "application/json": {
          "schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
              "code": {"type": "string"},
              "message": {"type": "string"}
            }
          }
        }
      }
    },
    "422": {
      "description": "Validation failed",
      "content": {
        "application/json": {
          "schema": {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/ValidationError"}
        }
      }
    },
    "500": {"description": "Server error"}
  },
  "security": [{"bearerAuth": []}]
}

Each part comes from your code:

Part Comes from tags: ["Post"] the class name PostController, without Controller summary no @Summary here, so the first line of the /// comment: /// POST /api/posts requestBody the argument SavePost body of store 401 and bearerAuth AuthMiddleware on the route 422 the route has a request class 200 with no body store returns DoxResponse, so the builder can not see the body. Step 6 fixes this

The Can middleware or a req.authorize(...) call gives 401 and 403. GuestMiddleware and ValidateSignature give 403. A req.validateSchema(...) call gives 422.

docs.title: 5. See how a DTO becomes a schema
docs.text:
Dox turns each DTO into a schema with the rules of every field. This is the SavePost DTO of the tutorial:

lib/app/dtos/save_post/save_post.dto.dart
@Dto()
class SavePost {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 3, max: 100)
  final String title;

  @Trim()
  @MinLength(10)
  final String body;

  const SavePost({required this.title, required this.body});

  static const DtoSchema<SavePost> schema = $SavePostDto;
}

And this is its schema in /openapi.json:

"SavePost": {
  "type": "object",
  "title": "SavePost",
  "properties": {
    "title": {"type": "string", "minLength": 3, "maxLength": 100},
    "body": {"type": "string", "minLength": 10}
  },
  "required": ["title", "body"]
}

Each rule becomes a schema key:

In the DTO In the schema String title (not nullable) "type": "string" and title in required @Length(min: 3, max: 100) "minLength": 3, "maxLength": 100 @MinLength(10) "minLength": 10 @Email() (in RegisterUser) "format": "email" @Describe('...') or /// A comment "description". @Describe wins over the comment @Trim(), @Lowercase(), @Unique(...) nothing. They change or check the value on the server only

A model becomes a schema too. Keys in hidden are left out, so User has no password. When you change a rule, run build_runner again.

docs.title: 6. Make the docs better
docs.text:
Add @Summary, @Description, @Tags and @Response to a controller method. They fill the gaps that the builder can not see, like the body of a DoxResponse:

lib/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart
@Inject()
class PostController {
  @Summary('List all posts')
  @Description('Newest posts are not first. There is no paging yet.')
  Future<List<Post>> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Post().all();
  }

  @Summary('Create a post')
  @Tags(<String>['Posts'])
  @Response(201, Post, description: 'The new post')
  Future<DoxResponse> store(SavePost body) async {
    Post post = Post()
      ..title = body.title
      ..body = body.body;
    await post.save();
    return response(post).statusCode(201);
  }

  // ...
}

Run dart run build_runner build again and restart the app. The result:

"get": {
  "tags": ["Post"],
  "summary": "List all posts",
  "description": "Newest posts are not first. There is no paging yet.",
  "operationId": "PostController.index",
  "responses": {
    "200": {
      "description": "Successful response",
      "content": {
        "application/json": {
          "schema": {
            "type": "array",
            "items": {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/Post"}
          }
        }
      }
    },
    "500": {}
  }
},
"post": {
  "tags": ["Posts"],
  "summary": "Create a post",
  "operationId": "PostController.store",
  "responses": {
    "201": {
      "description": "The new post",
      "content": {
        "application/json": {
          "schema": {"$ref": "#/components/schemas/Post"}
        }
      }
    },
    "401": {},
    "422": {},
    "500": {}
  }
}
  • @Response(201, Post) replaces the empty 200.
  • @Tags(['Posts']) moves the route to the group "Posts" in the docs page.
  • @Summary('...') and @Description('...') set the text. A /// comment gives the same result, but the annotation wins.
  • @ApiIgnore() leaves a method, or a whole controller, out of the docs.

See OpenAPI: describe a route for all annotations.

docs.title: 7. Turn it off in production
docs.text:
The docs routes are on only when APP_ENV is development or local. With APP_ENV=production all three routes give 404:

# 404
curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:3000/docs
# 404
curl -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:3000/openapi.json

To turn the docs on in production, set enabled: true. See OpenAPI: turn the docs on in production. To serve files made at build time, see OpenAPI: production setup.

To show the docs on staging, but never in production, set enabled yourself:

lib/config/openapi.dart
import 'package:blog/config/env.dart';

OpenApiConfig openApi = OpenApiConfig(
  enabled: env.appEnv != 'production',
  info: Info(title: 'Blog API', version: '1.0.0'),
  registry: openApiRegistry,
);

Warning

enabled: true in production shows every route of your API to anyone. Do it only for a public API.

To write the document to files, run dox openapi:generate. See OpenAPI: write the files.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Read the start of the document:

curl -s http://localhost:3000/openapi.json | head -n 5

{
  "openapi": "3.1.0",
  "info": {
    "title": "Blog API",
    "version": "1.0.0"

Open http://localhost:3000/docs, find "Create a post" under "Posts", and send a request with "Try it".

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• OpenAPI: all the options, Swagger UI and login schemes.
  • Validation rules: the rules and their JSON Schema keys.
  • Environments: set APP_ENV.

docs.title: Background work
docs.text: Answer the request now and do the slow work later: after the response, on another thread, in a queue, or on a timer.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A Dox app (dox create my_app). A new app has the queue (dox_queue) and the scheduler (dox_scheduler).

docs.title: Pick the right tool
docs.text:
Pick a tool by the type of work, and by whether the work may get lost:

You want Use Runs where Lost when the process stops small I/O work after the response (a log line, a cache update) a Future you do not await the same isolate, between requests yes CPU work (resize an image, parse a big file, compute) Isolate.run() a new thread yes work that must not get lost (an email, a payment call), with retries a queue job the queue worker process no work every N minutes (cleanup, sync) a scheduled task the schedule process it runs again at the next tick

docs.title: 1. Work after the response
docs.text:
For small I/O work, start the future with unawaited and return. An error of the future goes to report of the exception handler. This file has the code of steps 1, 2 and 3:

lib/app/http/controllers/report.controller.dart
import 'dart:async';
import 'dart:isolate';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/jobs/build_report.job.dart';

@Inject()
class ReportController {
  /// POST /api/reports
  /// Answers at once. The work runs after the response, in this isolate.
  Map<String, String> store(DoxRequest req) {
    String id = DateTime.now().microsecondsSinceEpoch.toString();
    unawaited(_build(id));
    return <String, String>{'id': id, 'status': 'queued'};
  }

  /// POST /api/reports/queued
  /// Saves a job in the jobs table and answers at once.
  /// The queue worker (`dox queue:work`) runs it, and tries again when
  /// it fails. The job is not lost when the server stops.
  Future<Map<String, String>> queue(DoxRequest req) async {
    String id = DateTime.now().microsecondsSinceEpoch.toString();
    String jobId = await BuildReport(reportId: id).dispatch();
    return <String, String>{'id': id, 'job': jobId, 'status': 'queued'};
  }

  /// I/O work (database, HTTP calls, email) is fine here. It shares the
  /// event loop with the requests, so it must not block the CPU.
  Future<void> _build(String id) async {
    await Future<void>.delayed(const Duration(seconds: 2));
    print('report $id is ready');
  }

  /// GET /api/primes/{limit}
  /// CPU work runs on another thread with `Isolate.run`.
  /// The request waits for the result, but other requests are not blocked.
  Future<Map<String, int>> primes(int limit) async {
    int count = await Isolate.run(() => countPrimes(limit));
    return <String, int>{'limit': limit, 'primes': count};
  }
}

/// Must be a top level or static function with plain arguments.
/// The new isolate has no Dox, no database and no providers.
int countPrimes(int limit) {
  List<bool> sieve = List<bool>.filled(limit + 1, true);
  int count = 0;
  for (int i = 2; i <= limit; i++) {
    if (!sieve[i]) continue;
    count++;
    for (int j = i * i; j <= limit; j += i) {
      sieve[j] = false;
    }
  }
  return count;
}

Do not block the event loop

_build shares the thread with the requests of this isolate, so a long loop makes them all wait. Put a long loop in Isolate.run.

docs.title: 2. CPU work on another thread
docs.text:
Isolate.run runs a function on a new isolate and sends the result back. Pass plain data in, like an integer, a string or bytes, and get plain data out.

If many requests do CPU work, use Dox().compute. It uses a pool of workers. See Heavy CPU work.

primes above waits for the result. To not wait, combine both patterns:

unawaited(Isolate.run(() => countPrimes(limit)).then(saveResult));

docs.title: 3. A job that must not get lost
docs.text:
For work that must happen, use a queue job. dispatch() saves the job in the database. A worker runs handle(), and tries again if it fails.

Make the job:

dox make:job BuildReport

Write the work in handle():

lib/app/jobs/build_report.job.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';

/// Builds a report in the queue worker.
/// Dispatch it: `await BuildReport(reportId: id).dispatch();`
@Job()
class BuildReport extends DoxJob {
  BuildReport({required this.reportId});

  final String reportId;

  /// try 3 times, wait 10 seconds between tries
  @override
  int get tries => 3;

  @override
  List<Duration> get backoff => const <Duration>[Duration(seconds: 10)];

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    Logger.info('report $reportId is ready');
  }
}

Dox saves the fields of the job with it, so use plain values, like strings, numbers, dates, lists and maps. Save an id, not a model, and load the model in handle().

Run dart run build_runner build after you add or change a job. The queue method of the controller dispatches the job.

Start the worker in a second terminal:

dox queue:work

dox queue:failed lists the jobs that failed every try. dox queue:retry all puts them back on the queue.

docs.title: 4. Work on a timer
docs.text:
Put a task that runs again and again in lib/config/schedule.dart:

lib/config/schedule.dart
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

/// `inProcess: false`: run `dox schedule:work` next to the server.
ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig();

/// The tasks. `dox schedule:list` shows them.
void schedule(Schedule s) {
  s.call('cleanup', cleanupUsers).hourly();
}

/// Removes the users that were soft deleted more than 30 days ago.
Future<void> cleanupUsers() async {
  DateTime limit = DateTime.now().subtract(const Duration(days: 30));
  List<User> old = await User()
      .withTrash()
      .where('deleted_at', '<', limit)
      .get();
  int removed = 0;
  for (User user in old) {
    removed += await user.forceDelete();
  }
  print('cleanup: removed $removed users');
}

Start the scheduler in a third terminal:

dox schedule:work

dox schedule:list shows each task and its next run. dox schedule:test cleanup runs the task now.

With many servers, set ScheduleConfig(store: 'redis'), so each task runs one time per tick. For a small app, you can run the schedule inside the server.

docs.title: 5. Add the routes
docs.text:
Add the three routes to the API router:

lib/routes/api.dart
Route.post('/reports', (ReportController c) => c.store);
Route.post('/reports/queued', (ReportController c) => c.queue);
Route.get('/primes/{limit}', (ReportController c) => c.primes);

Run dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs and dox serve.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Start a report:

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/reports

The response comes at once:

{"id":"1792677668393002","status":"queued"}

Two seconds later, the server prints report 1792677668393002 is ready.

Start a queued report:

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/reports/queued

{
  "id": "1792677670112345",
  "job": "9f2c4e1a7b3d5f60a1c2e3f4a5b6c7d8",
  "status": "queued"
}

The worker terminal shows report 1792677670112345 is ready. When the worker is stopped, the job waits in the jobs table.

Count the primes:

curl http://localhost:3000/api/primes/100000

{"limit":100000,"primes":9592}

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Queue: drivers, retries, delays and failed jobs.
  • Scheduler: frequencies, time zones and hooks.
  • Isolate: what each isolate shares.
  • Custom errors: log the errors of a future.

docs.title: CORS for a browser front-end
docs.text:
Let a web app on another origin (http://localhost:5173 in development, https://my.app in production) call your API.

A browser blocks a call to an API on another origin. CORS headers tell the browser which origins may call.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app.
  • A front-end that runs on its own origin, like Vite, Next.js or Flutter web.

docs.title: 1. Write the config
docs.text:
A new app has lib/config/cors.dart with enabled: false. Replace the whole file with this one:

lib/config/cors.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

/// `enabled` is true by default, so every route sends the headers.
CORSConfig cors = CORSConfig(
  /// One origin, or a list of origins. Set CORS_ORIGIN to the real
  /// front-end URL in production.
  origin: env.corsOrigin,

  methods: <String>['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE'],

  /// the request headers the front-end sends
  headers: <String>['Content-Type', 'Authorization'],

  /// the response headers the front-end may read
  exposeHeaders: <String>['Content-Disposition'],

  /// true only when the front-end sends cookies. Not needed for a
  /// `Authorization: Bearer` token.
  credentials: false,

  /// the browser keeps the preflight answer for 10 minutes
  maxAge: 600,
);

AppConfig in lib/config/app.dart already uses it with cors: cors.

docs.title: 2. Set the origin per environment
docs.text:
Read the front-end URL from a new key, CORS_ORIGIN. Add a getter for it to the AppEnv class:

lib/config/env.dart
  /// the front-end URL that may call the API
  String get corsOrigin => 'http://localhost:5173';

Run dart run build_runner build. Then set the value in .env:

.env
CORS_ORIGIN=http://localhost:5173

In staging and production, set CORS_ORIGIN as an environment variable, like https://my.app. The origin is the scheme, host and port only, with no / at the end.

docs.title: 3. Choose credentials
docs.text:
The right origin and credentials depend on how the front-end logs in:

Your front-end sends origin credentials a token in Authorization: Bearer (see JWT authentication) your front-end URL false cookies (fetch(url, {credentials: 'include'})) your front-end URL, never * true nothing, a public API '*' false

For two or more front-ends, set origin to a list, like ['https://a.com', 'https://b.com'].

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Before a POST with JSON, the browser sends an OPTIONS request, the preflight. Dox answers it by itself:

curl -i -X OPTIONS http://localhost:3000/api/users \
  -H 'Origin: http://localhost:5173' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: Authorization'

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
access-control-allow-origin: http://localhost:5173
access-control-allow-methods: GET,POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE
access-control-allow-headers: Content-Type,Authorization
access-control-expose-headers: Content-Disposition
access-control-allow-credentials: false
access-control-max-age: 600

A normal request gets the origin header too:

curl -i http://localhost:3000/api/ping -H 'Origin: http://localhost:5173' \
    | grep -i access-control-allow-origin

access-control-allow-origin: http://localhost:5173

In the browser, open the front-end and call the API with fetch. The console shows no CORS error.

docs.title: When it still fails
docs.text: The console says The fix No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header CORS_ORIGIN does not match the page origin exactly. Check http or https, and the port. The value of ... header is 'a.com,b.com' origin is one text with commas. Use a List<String> instead. Request header field x-foo is not allowed Add the header to headers. credentials mode is 'include' with * Set origin to the front-end URL and credentials: true.

docs.title: Turning CORS off for some routes
docs.text:
A call from another server, like a Stripe webhook, does not use CORS. Turn CORS off for such routes:

Route.disabledCors(() {
  Route.post('/webhooks/stripe', (WebhookController c) => c.handle);
});

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• CORS: every option.
  • JWT authentication: log in with a token.

docs.title: Custom errors
docs.text:
Give your app its own exception classes, send every error in one JSON shape, and log the unexpected ones.

A client is easier to write when every error has the same shape.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A Dox app.

docs.title: How Dox handles an error
docs.text:
This is what Dox does when a controller or a middleware throws:

Error Status What Dox does an IHttpException, like NotFoundHttpException its code sends {"code": ..., "message": ...} a validation error (bad DTO input) 422 sends the field errors: {"field": "message"} any other exception or error 500 sends {"code":"server_error","message":"Server Error"}, or the error text when APP_ENV is development or local. Calls report

report is a method of the exception handler. The responseHandler of AppConfig sees every response last, so this guide sets the error shape there.

docs.title: 1. Write your own exceptions
docs.text:
For a quick error, use abort(403) or abort(409, 'The email is taken'). See HTTP exceptions.

For an error you throw in many places, extend IHttpException. Set code (the HTTP status), errorCode (a short text for the client) and message:

lib/app/exceptions/app_exception.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// 409. Thrown when the row already exists or was changed by someone else.
class ConflictException extends IHttpException {
  ConflictException({String message = 'Conflict'}) {
    super.code = HttpStatus.conflict;
    super.errorCode = 'conflict';
    super.message = message;
  }
}

Throw them anywhere in a controller, a middleware or a service:

lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/exceptions/app_exception.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class UserController {
  /// GET /api/users/{id}
  Future<User> show(int id) async {
    User? user = await User().find(id);
    if (user == null) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException(message: 'User $id not found');
    }
    return user;
  }

  /// DELETE /api/users/{id}
  Future<Map<String, bool>> destroy(int id) async {
    if (id == 1) {
      throw ForbiddenHttpException(
          message: 'The first user can not be deleted');
    }
    User user = await show(id);

    /// 0 rows: the user was deleted after show() found it
    if (await user.delete() == 0) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException(message: 'User $id not found');
    }
    return <String, bool>{'deleted': true};
  }
}

docs.title: 2. One JSON shape for every error
docs.text:
For an error, the content of the response is the exception. Turn it into your shape in the response handler:

lib/app/http/response_handler.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// Gives every error the same JSON shape:
/// `{"error": {"code": "not_found", "message": "..."}}`.
/// A validation error (422) also has `"errors": {field: message}`.
class ResponseHandler extends ResponseHandlerInterface {
  @override
  DoxResponse handle(DoxResponse res) {
    dynamic content = res.getContent();

    if (content is ValidationException) {
      return res.statusCode(content.code).content(<String, dynamic>{
        'error': <String, dynamic>{
          'code': content.errorCode,
          'message': 'The input is not valid',
        },
        'errors': content.message,
      });
    }

    if (content is IHttpException) {
      return res.statusCode(content.code).content(<String, dynamic>{
        'error': <String, dynamic>{
          'code': content.errorCode,
          'message': content.message.toString(),
        },
      });
    }

    // any other exception: hide the details from the client
    if (content is Exception || content is Error) {
      return res.statusCode(HttpStatus.internalServerError).content(
        <String, dynamic>{
          'error': <String, String>{
            'code': 'server_error',
            'message': 'Something went wrong',
          },
        },
      );
    }

    return res;
  }
}

The last if gives a 500 your shape in every environment. Without it, development and local send the error text, which can show a SQL query or a file path.

docs.title: 3. Log unexpected errors
docs.text:
report runs for every 500, and for errors outside a request, like a timer. Log the error there:

lib/app/error_handler.dart
import 'dart:convert';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// Dox calls [report] for every unexpected error (a `500`, or an error
/// outside a request). It does not run for `IHttpException` errors
/// like `404` or `422`, because those are expected.
/// One JSON line per error. Send it to Sentry or Datadog from here.
class AppExceptionHandler extends ExceptionHandler {
  const AppExceptionHandler();

  @override
  void report(Object error, StackTrace stackTrace) {
    print(
      jsonEncode(<String, String>{
        'timestamp': DateTime.now().toIso8601String(),
        'status': 'error',
        'message': error.toString(),
        'error': <String, String>{'stack': stackTrace.toString()},
      }),
    );
  }
}

docs.title: 4. Register both
docs.text:
Add both handlers to AppConfig:

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:my_app/app/error_handler.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/response_handler.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  responseHandler: ResponseHandler(),
  exceptionHandler: const AppExceptionHandler(),
  // ...
);

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Add a route that throws, only for this check:

Route.get('/boom', (DoxRequest req) => throw StateError('boom'));
Request Status Body GET /api/users/999 404 {"error":{"code":"not_found","message":"User 999 not found"}} GET /api/users/abc 404 {"error":{"code":"not_found","message":"Not Found"}} DELETE /api/users/1 403 {"error":{"code":"forbidden","message":"The first user can not be deleted"}} POST /api/auth/register with {} 422 {"error":{"code":"validation_failed","message":"The input is not valid"},"errors":{"name":"The name is required", ...}} GET /api/boom 500 {"error":{"code":"server_error","message":"Something went wrong"}}

After GET /api/boom, the server prints one line:

{"timestamp":"2026-10-22T14:01:12.000Z","status":"error","message":"Bad state: boom","error":{"stack":"#0  ApiRouter.register.<anonymous closure> (package:my_app/routes/api.dart:41:44) ..."},"source":"error"}

Remove the /boom route when you are done.

A URL with no route gets the same shape: {"error":{"code":"not_found","message":"GET /nothing not found"}}.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Error handling: report and render.
  • Response: errors: the built-in exceptions.
  • Response: change every response: the response handler.
  • Validation: the error response: the 422 body.
  • Isolate: when an isolate crashes: errors outside a request.

docs.title: Deploy to Google Cloud Run
docs.text:
Run the blog API on Cloud Run from the Dockerfile of your project, with Postgres on Cloud SQL and secrets in Secret Manager.

Cloud Run runs and scales the containers, and gives you an HTTPS URL.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Google Cloud project with billing, and the gcloud CLI (gcloud auth login, gcloud config set project PROJECT_ID).
  • The blog API from the tutorial, or any Dox app, with the Dockerfile of a new Dox app. See Docker.
  • A Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance with a database and a user. See step 3.

docs.title: Choosing the port
docs.text: Cloud Run gives the port in the PORT env variable: 8080 by default, or the --port value. Dox listens on PORT when APP_PORT is not set. So do not set APP_PORT, or set it to the --port value.

docs.title: 1. Turn on the APIs
docs.text:
Turn on the APIs one time:

gcloud services enable run.googleapis.com cloudbuild.googleapis.com \
  artifactregistry.googleapis.com secretmanager.googleapis.com \
  sqladmin.googleapis.com

docs.title: 2. Save the secrets in Secret Manager
docs.text:
Anyone who can see the service can read its plain env variables. So save APP_KEY and the database password in Secret Manager:

openssl rand -hex 16 | tr -d '\n' \
    | gcloud secrets create blog-app-key --data-file=-
printf '%s' '<the database password>' \
    | gcloud secrets create blog-db-password --data-file=-

Let the Cloud Run service account read them. By default this is the Compute Engine service account, PROJECT_NUMBER-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com:

for s in blog-app-key blog-db-password; do
  gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding "$s" \
    --member="serviceAccount:PROJECT_NUMBER-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com" \
    --role="roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor"
done

docs.title: 3. Reach Cloud SQL
docs.text:
Cloud Run can reach Cloud SQL by a Unix socket or by a private IP. This guide uses the socket, because it needs no VPC:

  1. Find the connection name of the instance: gcloud sql instances describe INSTANCE --format='value(connectionName)'. It looks like PROJECT_ID:europe-west1:INSTANCE.
  2. Deploy with --add-cloudsql-instances <connection name> (step 4). Cloud Run then makes the socket in /cloudsql/<connection name>.
  3. Give the service account the roles/cloudsql.client role.
  4. Set DB_HOST=/cloudsql/<connection name>. A host that starts with / is a Unix socket.

The same with one URL: DATABASE_URL=postgres://blog:<password>@/blog?host=/cloudsql/<connection name>.

For Cloud SQL for MySQL, use the same DB_HOST with DB_CONNECTION=mysql, and no DB_PORT. Or use one URL: DATABASE_URL=mysql://blog:<password>@/blog?socket=/cloudsql/<connection name>.

For a private IP, deploy with Direct VPC egress (--network default --subnet default --vpc-egress private-ranges-only), and use the private IP as DB_HOST.

Do not use SQLite on Cloud Run. The file system of an instance is in memory, so the data is lost when the instance stops.

docs.title: 4. Deploy from source
docs.text:
--source . uploads the folder, and Cloud Build builds the image with your Dockerfile:

gcloud run deploy blog \
  --source . \
  --region europe-west1 \
  --port 3000 \
  --allow-unauthenticated \
  --cpu 1 --memory 512Mi \
  --min-instances 1 \
  --add-cloudsql-instances PROJECT_ID:europe-west1:INSTANCE \
  --set-env-vars APP_ENV=production,APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE=1,DB_CONNECTION=postgres,DB_HOST=/cloudsql/PROJECT_ID:europe-west1:INSTANCE,DB_PORT=5432,DB_NAME=blog,DB_USERNAME=blog \
  --set-secrets APP_KEY=blog-app-key:1,DB_PASSWORD=blog-db-password:1

The flags do this:

Flag Why --port 3000 the port Cloud Run sends requests to. It also sets PORT=3000. See Choosing the port --min-instances 1 keeps one instance warm, so the first request does not wait for a cold start. An idle instance still costs money --add-cloudsql-instances makes the Cloud SQL Unix socket in /cloudsql/... --set-env-vars config that is not secret --set-secrets ENV_NAME=SECRET:VERSION. Pin a version number, not latest APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE=1 one isolate per CPU. Set it to the --cpu value

To build the image yourself, push it to Artifact Registry and deploy it with --image. Add the other flags from above:

docker build --platform linux/amd64 \
    -t europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT_ID/blog/api:1 .
docker push europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT_ID/blog/api:1
gcloud run deploy blog \
    --image europe-west1-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT_ID/blog/api:1 \
    --region europe-west1 --port 3000 ...

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
gcloud run deploy prints the service URL at the end. Call it:

curl https://blog-xxxxxxxx-ew.a.run.app/api/ping

pong

Read the logs. The live tail needs the log-streaming component:

gcloud run services logs read blog --region europe-west1 --limit 20
gcloud beta run services logs tail blog --region europe-west1

The first log lines after the first start:

Migrating: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrated: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrating: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
{"timestamp":"...","status":"info","message":"Server started at http://[::]:3000 with 1 isolate (native)","logger":{"name":"dox"},"source":"server"}

If the deploy fails with "the container did not listen on the port", check APP_PORT and --port.

docs.title: HTTPS and the client IP
docs.text:
Cloud Run handles HTTPS and sends plain HTTP to the container. Set trustedProxies, so req.ip() and req.scheme() show the real client. Only the Cloud Run front end can reach the container port, so ['*'] is safe here:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  trustedProxies: <String>['*'],
);

docs.title: Updating the app
docs.text:
To send a new version, deploy again. Cloud Run keeps the flags of the last revision:

gcloud run deploy blog --source . --region europe-west1
  • The new revision runs new migrations, and takes the traffic when it listens on the port.
  • If many instances start at the same time, each one runs the migrations. So keep migrations safe to run twice, or run one instance during a deploy with a migration.
  • For a new secret version, run gcloud secrets versions add. Then deploy with --update-secrets APP_KEY=blog-app-key:2.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Deployment: the bundle and HTTPS.
  • Environments: all the env keys and APP_KEY.
  • Docker: the Dockerfile and Docker Compose.
  • Cloud Run docs: the container contract.
  • Cloud SQL for Cloud Run: connect to the database.

docs.title: Deploy to Fly.io
docs.text:
Run the blog API on Fly.io from the Dockerfile of your project, with SQLite on a volume or with Postgres.

Fly.io builds the image from your Dockerfile and runs it with the config in fly.toml.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Fly.io account and the fly CLI (fly auth login).
  • The blog API from the tutorial, or any Dox app, with the Dockerfile of a new Dox app. See Docker.

docs.title: 1. Make the app on Fly.io
docs.text:
In the project folder, make the app but do not deploy it yet:

fly launch --no-deploy

fly launch asks for an app name and a region, and writes fly.toml.

docs.title: 2. Write fly.toml
docs.text:
Replace fly.toml with this file. Change app and primary_region to your values:

fly.toml
app = "blog-api"
primary_region = "ams"
# Dox waits up to 8 seconds for open requests on stop. Fly waits 5 by default.
kill_timeout = 10

[build]
  dockerfile = "Dockerfile"

# config that is not secret. Secrets come from `fly secrets set`.
[env]
  APP_ENV = "production"
  APP_PORT = "3000"
  DB_CONNECTION = "sqlite"
  DB_NAME = "/data/blog.sqlite"

[http_service]
  internal_port = 3000
  force_https = true
  # one machine, always on: the SQLite file is on its volume
  auto_stop_machines = "off"
  auto_start_machines = true
  min_machines_running = 1

  [[http_service.checks]]
    grace_period = "10s"
    interval = "30s"
    method = "GET"
    timeout = "5s"
    path = "/api/ping"

# the volume with the SQLite file
[mounts]
  source = "blog_data"
  destination = "/data"

[[vm]]
  memory = "256mb"
  cpu_kind = "shared"
  cpus = 1
  • Keep internal_port the same as APP_PORT.
  • Values in [env] must be strings, so write "3000", not 3000.
  • Each fly deploy sets the machine to the values of [[vm]].
  • Keep kill_timeout above shutdownTimeout of AppConfig. See Graceful shutdown.

docs.title: 3. Set the secrets
docs.text:
fly.toml goes into git, so set secrets like APP_KEY with fly secrets:

fly secrets set APP_KEY=<output of dox key:generate>

A secret is an environment variable on every machine of the app. It wins over an [env] key with the same name.

docs.title: SQLite on a volume
docs.text:
For a small app, use SQLite. Make the volume that [mounts] asks for, in the same region:

fly volumes create blog_data --region ams --size 1

A volume is attached to one machine only. So with SQLite, run exactly one machine.

docs.title: Postgres
docs.text:
For more than one machine, use Postgres. Make a Managed Postgres cluster with fly mpg create, and attach it to the app:

fly mpg attach <cluster-id> --app blog-api

This sets the secret DATABASE_URL. It wins over the DB_* keys.

Then delete DB_CONNECTION and DB_NAME from [env], and delete the [mounts] section. If the database asks for TLS, add ?sslmode=require to the URL with fly secrets set DATABASE_URL=....

docs.title: 5. Deploy
docs.text:
Build the image and start the machine. The app runs the migrations at start:

fly deploy

Make sure that there is one machine:

fly scale show

If the count is more than 1 and you use SQLite, run fly scale count 1.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Call the API:

curl https://blog-api.fly.dev/api/ping

pong

Look at the machines and the logs:

fly status    # the machines and their state
fly logs      # the app logs, live

The first log lines after the first start:

Migrating: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrated: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrating: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
{"timestamp":"...","status":"info","message":"Server started at http://[::]:3000 with 1 isolate (native)","logger":{"name":"dox"},"source":"server"}

docs.title: HTTPS and the client IP
docs.text:
Fly.io handles HTTPS and sends plain HTTP to port 3000. Set trustedProxies, so req.ip() and req.scheme() show the real client. Only the Fly.io proxy can reach the app port, so ['*'] is safe here:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  trustedProxies: <String>['*'],
);

docs.title: Scaling the app
docs.text:
Dox starts one isolate per CPU of the container:

You want Do this more speed on one machine raise cpus and memory in [[vm]], then fly deploy more machines use Postgres, then fly scale count 2. With SQLite, stay at one machine a fixed number of isolates set APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE in [env]

Machines do not share Socket.IO rooms or the memory cache.

docs.title: Updating the app
docs.text:
To send a new version, deploy again:

fly deploy

fly secrets set restarts the machines with the new value. With --stage, the next deploy uses the value. With one machine there is a short gap while it restarts.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Deployment: the bundle and HTTPS.
  • Environments: all the env keys and APP_KEY.
  • Docker: the Dockerfile and Docker Compose.
  • Fly.io docs: fly.toml, secrets, volumes and Managed Postgres.

docs.title: Deploy to a Linux server
docs.text:
Run the blog API on your own Linux server (a VPS), with systemd to keep it running and Caddy in front for HTTPS.

systemd starts the app again after a crash. Caddy gets the TLS certificate and sends the requests to the app:

  1. Browser or app
  2. Caddythe TLS certificate
  3. The appsystemd runs /opt/blog/bin/server

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Linux server (Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04 or newer) with SSH and sudo.
  • A domain name. Its A (and AAAA) record points to the server.
  • Docker on your machine, to build a Linux binary.
  • The blog API from the tutorial, or any Dox app.

docs.title: 1. Build the bundle for Linux
docs.text:
dox build makes a binary for the system it runs on. So build it in the dart:stable image, which is Debian:

docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/app -w /app dart:stable sh -c \
  'dart pub get && dart pub global activate dox &&
    /root/.pub-cache/bin/dox build'

The result is in build/bundle/:

build/bundle/
  bin/server                         the AOT binary
  lib/dox_http_native-linux-*.so     the native HTTP server
  lib/dox_postgres_native-linux-*.so the native Postgres driver
  lib/dox_mysql_native-linux-*.so    the native MySQL driver
  lib/libsqlite3.so                  SQLite
  db/                                the migrations
  .env.example

Keep bin/ and lib/ together, because the binary loads the libraries from ../lib.

Match the CPU of the server

Docker builds for the CPU of your machine. On a Mac with Apple silicon that is arm64, but most VPS plans are x86_64. For them, add --platform linux/amd64 after docker run. Check the server with uname -m.

The container writes Linux paths into your .dart_tool/. So run dart pub get on your machine again before you use dox serve.

docs.title: 2. Make a user and the folders
docs.text:
Do not run the app as root. On the server, make a user dox that can not log in:

sudo useradd --system --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin dox
sudo mkdir -p /opt/blog
sudo install -d -o dox -g dox /opt/blog/storage

The app uses these paths:

Path What it holds Owner /opt/blog the bundle (bin/, lib/, db/) root /opt/blog/storage files the app writes (uploads, file cache) dox /var/lib/blog the SQLite file. systemd makes it (see step 5) dox /etc/blog.env config and secrets root, mode 600

docs.title: 3. Copy the bundle to the server
docs.text:
Copy the bundle to a temp folder, then into /opt/blog:

rsync -a --delete --exclude storage/ \
    build/bundle/ you@server:/tmp/blog-bundle/
ssh you@server \
    'sudo rsync -a --delete --exclude storage/ /tmp/blog-bundle/ /opt/blog/'

docs.title: 4. Write the env file
docs.text:
Put the config and the secrets in /etc/blog.env:

/etc/blog.env
APP_NAME=blog
APP_ENV=production
APP_PORT=3000
APP_KEY=<output of dox key:generate>

DB_CONNECTION=sqlite
DB_NAME=/var/lib/blog/blog.sqlite

Only root may read the file:

sudo chown root:root /etc/blog.env
sudo chmod 600 /etc/blog.env

For Postgres, set DB_CONNECTION=postgres and add DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_USERNAME, DB_PASSWORD and DB_NAME. Or set one DATABASE_URL, like postgres://app:secret@localhost:5432/blog. It wins over the DB_* keys.

Do not put a .env file in /opt/blog. Keep all values in one place.

docs.title: 5. Write the systemd unit
docs.text:
The systemd unit starts the app at boot and starts it again after a crash:

/etc/systemd/system/blog.service
[Unit]
Description=Blog API (Dox)
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=dox
Group=dox
# the binary reads db/ and .env from this folder
WorkingDirectory=/opt/blog
EnvironmentFile=/etc/blog.env
ExecStart=/opt/blog/bin/server
# start again after a crash, and after `kill`
Restart=always
RestartSec=2
# makes /var/lib/blog, owned by the user dox
StateDirectory=blog
# small safety settings
NoNewPrivileges=true
PrivateTmp=true
ProtectSystem=full

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Start the app:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now blog
systemctl status blog

The app runs the migrations at start, before it takes requests. To change the number of isolates, set APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE in /etc/blog.env.

docs.title: 6. Close the app port
docs.text:
Only Caddy may talk to the app. Add this line to /etc/blog.env, so Dox listens on the local address only:

/etc/blog.env
APP_HOST=127.0.0.1

Also turn on a firewall, so that only SSH, HTTP and HTTPS are open:

sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw allow OpenSSH
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp
sudo ufw enable

docs.title: 7. Put Caddy in front
docs.text:
Install Caddy from its install page. Then write /etc/caddy/Caddyfile:

/etc/caddy/Caddyfile
api.example.com {
    encode zstd gzip

    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:3000 {
        # while the app restarts, wait up to 10s for it instead of failing
        lb_try_duration 10s
        lb_try_interval 250ms
    }
}

Check the file and load it:

sudo caddy validate --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile
sudo systemctl reload caddy

Caddy gets a TLS certificate for api.example.com by itself. Ports 80 and 443 must be open.

docs.title: 8. Trust Caddy in the app
docs.text:
Dox ignores the X-Forwarded-* headers of a proxy that is not in trustedProxies. List the local addresses:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  trustedProxies: <String>['127.0.0.1', '::1'],
);

Now req.ip() is the real client IP and req.scheme() is https. Build and copy again after this change (steps 1 and 3).

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Call the API over HTTPS:

curl https://api.example.com/api/ping

pong

Read the logs. In production the app writes one JSON line per log:

journalctl -u blog -f                     # follow new lines
journalctl -u blog --since "1 hour ago"   # the last hour
journalctl -u blog -b                     # since the last boot

The first lines after the first start look like this:

Migrating: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrated: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrating: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
{"timestamp":"...","status":"info","message":"Server started at http://127.0.0.1:3000 with 2 isolate (native)","logger":{"name":"dox"},"source":"server"}

(native) means the native HTTP server loaded.

From your machine, make sure that the app port is closed:

curl -m 5 http://api.example.com:3000/api/ping   # must time out

docs.title: Updating the app
docs.text:
1. Build a new bundle (step 1).

  2. Copy it to the server (step 3). Keep the old one first, so you can go back:

    ssh you@server \
    'sudo rm -rf /opt/blog.prev && sudo cp -a /opt/blog /opt/blog.prev'
rsync -a --delete --exclude storage/ \
    build/bundle/ you@server:/tmp/blog-bundle/
ssh you@server \
    'sudo rsync -a --delete --exclude storage/ /tmp/blog-bundle/ /opt/blog/'

  3. Restart the app. It runs new migrations at start.

    ssh you@server 'sudo systemctl restart blog'

  4. Read the logs (journalctl -u blog -n 20) and run the check.

To go back, copy /opt/blog.prev to /opt/blog and restart. A migration that already ran stays.

A restart takes about one second, and Caddy waits for the app. For an update with no downtime, run two copies on two ports and list both in Caddy. See Deployment: many processes.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Deployment: dox build, nginx and many processes.
  • Environments: config per environment and APP_KEY.
  • Docker: the app and Postgres in Docker Compose.
  • Native server: the native HTTP server.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Build a small production image with dox build, and run it with Postgres in Docker Compose, with a health check.

The image holds only the compiled app, so it is small and starts fast.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app with a database.
  • Docker with Compose.

docs.title: 1. Add a health route
docs.text:
Docker asks this route if the app works. It answers 503 when the database does not answer. Put it in register() of WebRouter:

lib/routes/web.dart
Route.health(
  '/health',
  checks: <String, HealthCheckFunction>{
    'database': () => QueryBuilder.query('select 1'),
  },
);

docs.title: 2. Add the health check binary
docs.text:
The final image has no shell and no curl, so the health check is a small Dart binary:

bin/health.dart
import 'dart:io';

/// Docker health check. The final image has no shell and no curl,
/// so this small binary asks the app itself. Exit 0 = healthy.
Future<void> main() async {
  String port = Platform.environment['APP_PORT'] ?? '3000';
  HttpClient client = HttpClient()
    ..connectionTimeout = const Duration(seconds: 3);
  try {
    HttpClientRequest request = await client.getUrl(
      Uri.parse('http://127.0.0.1:$port/health'),
    );
    HttpClientResponse response = await request.close();
    exit(response.statusCode == 200 ? 0 : 1);
  } catch (_) {
    exit(1);
  }
}

docs.title: 3. Write the Dockerfile
docs.text:
The first stage builds the AOT bundle. The second stage holds only the Dart runtime and the bundle, about 17 MB for the blog API:

Dockerfile
# Stage 1: build the AOT bundle with the Dart SDK and the dox CLI.
FROM dart:stable AS build

WORKDIR /app

# Resolve dependencies first, so Docker caches this layer.
COPY pubspec.* ./
RUN dart pub get

COPY . .
RUN dart pub get --offline

# `dox build` runs build_runner, then `dart build cli`.
# The bundle is in build/bundle: bin/server, lib/, db/, .env.example
# (and bin/queue, bin/schedule when the app has them)
RUN dart pub global activate dox \
  && /root/.pub-cache/bin/dox build

# The health check binary. Plain dart:io, so `dart compile exe` is fine.
RUN dart compile exe bin/health.dart -o build/bundle/bin/health

# Lay out the final file tree. /tmp must be writable: uploads bigger
# than 1 MB are streamed to a temp file.
RUN mkdir -p /out/app/storage /out/app/public /out/tmp \
  && chmod 1777 /out/tmp \
  && cp -r build/bundle/. /out/app/ \
  && cp -r public/. /out/app/public/

# Stage 2: the Dart AOT runtime and the bundle only. No SDK, no source.
FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /runtime/ /
COPY --from=build /out/ /
WORKDIR /app

# Config comes from env variables. The image has no .env file.
EXPOSE 3000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=15s --timeout=5s --start-period=10s --retries=3 \
  CMD ["/app/bin/health"]
CMD ["/app/bin/server"]

Delete the public lines if your app has no public folder.

The image has no copy of libgcc_s.so.1. The native libraries do not need it from dox_http_native 3.2.4, dox_postgres_native 3.2.2 and dox_mysql_native 3.2.2. With an older version, Dox stops at start with dox_http_native did not load. Run dart pub upgrade to get the new versions.

When the container starts, the start log must end with (native):

[server] Server started at http://[::]:3000 with 8 isolate (native)

dox build, not dart compile exe

dox_orm bundles SQLite with a build hook. dart compile exe does not run build hooks and stops with an error. Build the server with dox build.

Keep the build context small with a .dockerignore:

.dockerignore
.dart_tool/
.git/
.github/
.idea/
build/
storage/
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
Dockerfile
docker-compose.yml
pubspec_overrides.yaml

docs.title: 4. Write the compose file
docs.text:
Docker Compose runs the app and Postgres together. The lines under environment win over .env:

docker-compose.yml
services:
  app:
    build: .
    # secrets and config come from .env, never from the image
    env_file: .env
    environment:
      APP_ENV: production
      APP_PORT: 3000
      DB_CONNECTION: postgres
      DB_HOST: postgres
      DB_PORT: 5432
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    volumes:
      # uploads survive a new image
      - uploads:/app/storage
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
    restart: unless-stopped

  postgres:
    image: postgres:18
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: ${DB_USERNAME:-postgres}
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD:?set DB_PASSWORD in .env}
      POSTGRES_DB: ${DB_NAME:-dox}
    volumes:
      - postgres:/var/lib/postgresql
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "pg_isready", "-q", "-U", "${DB_USERNAME:-postgres}"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  postgres:
  uploads:

depends_on starts the app after Postgres answers, because the app runs the migrations at start.

docs.title: 5. Write the .env
docs.text:
Put the secrets in .env. It never goes into the image or into git:

.env
APP_NAME=my_app
APP_ENV=production
APP_KEY=<output of dox key:generate>
APP_PORT=3000

DB_CONNECTION=postgres
DB_NAME=my_app
DB_USERNAME=postgres
DB_PASSWORD=<a real password>

A new app skips the Postgres driver in pubspec.yaml. Remove the dox_postgres_native skip lines. See Skip unused drivers.

docs.title: 6. Build and run
docs.text:
Build the image and start both services:

docker compose up -d --build

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Both services are healthy:

docker compose ps

NAME             STATUS
my_app-app-1       Up 30 seconds (healthy)
my_app-postgres-1  Up 35 seconds (healthy)

Ask the health route:

curl http://localhost:3000/health

{"status":"ok","checks":{"database":"ok"}}

Now stop Postgres with docker compose stop postgres. After about 45 seconds, docker compose ps shows the app as unhealthy.

docs.title: HTTPS
docs.text: Put Caddy or nginx in front of the app, and set trustedProxies in AppConfig. See Deployment: HTTPS.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Deployment: dox build, the bundle and systemd.
  • Health check: more checks.
  • Environments: dev, staging and production config.
  • Migration: run on server start: the migrations at start.

docs.title: Environments
docs.text:
Run the same app in development, staging and production with different config, and keep secrets out of git and out of the image.

Each place needs other values, like another database or front-end URL. Dox reads them from the environment, not from the code.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app.
  • build_runner for the typed env class (a new app has it).

docs.title: How Dox reads config
docs.text:
Dox looks for each key in two places:

  1. A real environment variable (from the shell, Docker or systemd). This one wins.
  2. The .env file in the folder where the app starts.

So use a .env file on your machine, and real environment variables on a server.

docs.title: 1. The typed env class
docs.text:
The AppEnv class in lib/config/env.dart lists every key, with its type and its default. This guides app adds corsOrigin and appUrl:

lib/config/env.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'env.g.dart';

/// The env of the app, typed. Made by `dox env:generate`.
/// -------------------------------
/// Each getter reads one key: `appName` reads `APP_NAME`.
/// A getter body is the default. A nullable getter is optional.
/// Other getters are required: the app stops at startup when one is
/// missing.
/// Run `dart run build_runner build` after you change this class.
@DoxEnv()
abstract class AppEnv {
  /// reads and checks every key once
  static AppEnv load([EnvReader? reader]) {
    return _$AppEnv.load(reader);
  }

  String get appName => 'dox';

  /// development, staging or production. Not set: production.
  String get appEnv => 'production';

  int get appPort => 3000;

  /// required: used to sign tokens and encrypt cookies
  String get appKey;

  /// isolates (threads) of the HTTP server.
  /// Null: one per CPU the process may use.
  int? get appTotalIsolate;

  String get logLevel => 'info';

  /// memory, file or redis
  String get cacheStore => 'file';

  /// local, s3 or memory
  String get storageDisk => 'local';

  /// sqlite, postgres or mysql
  String get dbConnection => 'sqlite';

  /// the database name. For SQLite: the file path.
  String get dbName => 'db/dox.sqlite';

  String get dbHost => 'localhost';

  /// null: 5432 for Postgres, 3306 for MySQL
  int? get dbPort;

  String get dbUsername => 'postgres';

  String get dbPassword => '';

  /// the front-end URL that may call the API
  String get corsOrigin => 'http://localhost:5173';

  /// the public URL of this app, used in file links
  String get appUrl => 'http://localhost:3000';
}

/// The env of the app. Read and checked once, on first use.
final AppEnv env = AppEnv.load();

Each getter reads its name in upper snake case, so dbPort reads DB_PORT:

  • A getter with a body has a default: int get appPort => 3000;.
  • A nullable getter with no body is optional: int? get dbPort; is null when the key is not set.
  • Any other getter with no body is required: String get appKey;.

If a required key is missing, the app stops at start and lists all the problems.

docs.title: 2. Add a key
docs.text:
For a new value, add a getter to AppEnv, like this mail host:

  /// the SMTP server for mails
  String get mailHost => 'localhost';

Then run build_runner again:

dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs

Now env.mailHost reads MAIL_HOST. Add the key to .env.example too.

docs.title: 3. Use it in the config files
docs.text:
The config files read the typed getters. For a setting that changes per environment, use APP_ENV, like prettyPrint and debug here. Development is an APP_ENV of development, local, test or testing. Any other value is production:

lib/config/logger.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

LoggerConfig logger = LoggerConfig(
  name: env.appName,
  enabled: true,
  level: env.logLevel,
  // colors on your machine, one JSON line per log in staging and
  // production.
  // Env.appEnv, not appConfig.isDevelopment: appConfig is built from
  // this logger, so reading appConfig here would loop.
  prettyPrint: Env.appEnv == 'development',
);

The database prints every query in development only:

lib/config/database.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: env.dbConnection,
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.postgres,
      host: env.dbHost,
      port: env.dbPort ?? 5432,
      user: env.dbUsername,
      password: env.dbPassword,
      database: env.dbName,
      // print every query on your machine only
      debug: appConfig.isDevelopment,
    ),
    'sqlite': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.sqlite,
      database: env.dbName,
      debug: appConfig.isDevelopment,
    ),
  },
);

docs.title: 4. Write the env files
docs.text:
Commit .env.example with every key and a safe value. Never commit .env, because it holds your real secrets:

.env.example
APP_NAME=my_app
APP_ENV=development
APP_PORT=3000
# run `dox key:generate`
APP_KEY=
APP_URL=http://localhost:3000

DB_CONNECTION=postgres
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
DB_NAME=my_app
DB_USERNAME=postgres
DB_PASSWORD=postgres

CORS_ORIGIN=http://localhost:5173
LOG_LEVEL=debug

To start on a new machine, copy the example and make a key:

cp .env.example .env
dox key:generate   # writes a new APP_KEY into .env

Keep every .env file out of git, except the example:

.gitignore
.env
.env.*
!.env.example

The values live in a different place in each environment:

Environment Where the values live APP_ENV your machine .env development staging real env variables (compose environment:, a secrets manager) staging production real env variables production

On a server you can also keep a .env file next to the binary, with chmod 600. See Deployment.

docs.title: 5. APP_KEY
docs.text:
APP_KEY is your most important secret. It encrypts cookies and signs JWT tokens and local signed URLs.

  • Make one key per environment with dox key:generate. Never share the production key with staging.
  • The key must be exactly 32 characters.
  • In production a bad key stops the app at start. A bad key is empty, not 32 characters, or a public sample key.
  • A new key stops every cookie, token and signed URL, so every user is logged out.

docs.title: 6. Check the env before a deploy
docs.text:
dox env:check prints every missing or bad key. On a problem it exits with code 1, so CI stops:

dox env:check

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Start the app with a key missing:

APP_KEY= dart run bin/server.dart

Unhandled exception:
EnvException: the env is not valid
  - APP_KEY is missing

Now start it as staging on another port. The real variables win over .env:

APP_ENV=staging APP_PORT=4000 dart run bin/server.dart

The app listens on port 4000. env.appEnv is staging, and appConfig.isDevelopment is false.

docs.title: Things that differ per environment
docs.text:
Most apps change these settings between environments:

Setting Development Staging and production prettyPrint of the logger true false (one JSON line per log) debug of the database true false totalIsolate 1 or 2 is enough one per core (the default) CORS_ORIGIN http://localhost:5173 the real front-end URL the server dox serve (JIT) the dox build binary (AOT)

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Environment variables: all the types and rules of the env class.
  • Docker: set the env in a container.
  • Deployment: run the app on a server.

docs.title: File upload
docs.text:
Accept an image from a form, check its size and type, save it to a disk, and return its URL.

An uploaded file can be too big, or of a different type than its name says. So this guide checks the file in a DTO first, and then saves it.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A Dox app (dox create my_app). A new app has the dox_storage package, lib/config/storage.dart and lib/providers/storage_provider.dart.

docs.title: 1. Set up the disk
docs.text:
Give the local disk a url. Storage().url() uses it to make the public URL of a file:

lib/config/storage.dart
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

StorageConfig storageConfig = StorageConfig(
  defaultDisk: env.storageDisk,
  disks: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    /// uploads go to the `storage` folder.
    /// `url` is the public address of `Storage.route('files', ...)`.
    'local': <String, dynamic>{
      'driver': 'local',
      'root': 'storage',
      'url': '${env.appUrl}/files',
    },
  },
);

Add a getter for the new APP_URL key to the AppEnv class:

lib/config/env.dart
  /// the public URL of this app, used in file links
  String get appUrl => 'http://localhost:3000';

Run dart run build_runner build. Then add APP_URL=http://localhost:3000 to your .env.

The provider of a new app sets up the disks. Keep it as it is:

lib/providers/storage_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/storage.dart';

class AppStorageProvider extends StorageProvider {
  AppStorageProvider() : super(storageConfig);
}

docs.title: 2. Write the DTO
docs.text:
The DTO checks the file before the controller runs. A failed check answers 422:

lib/app/dtos/upload_image/upload_image.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'upload_image.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class UploadImage {
  /// jpg, jpeg, png, gif, webp or bmp. Dox reads the first bytes of the
  /// file to find the real type. The file name is not trusted.
  @Image()
  @MaxSize('5MB')
  final RequestFile image;

  const UploadImage({required this.image});

  static const DtoSchema<UploadImage> schema = $UploadImageDto;
}

For other file types, use @Mimes(<String>['pdf', 'docx']) in place of @Image().

docs.title: 3. Write the controller
docs.text:
Save the file with putFile, and return its path and URL. putFile gives the file a new UUID name:

lib/app/http/controllers/upload.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/upload_image/upload_image.dto.dart';

@Inject()
class UploadController {
  /// POST /api/upload (multipart/form-data, field `image`)
  Future<Map<String, String>> store(UploadImage body) async {
    // saves the file as /images/<uuid>.<ext> on the default disk
    String path = await Storage().putFile('images', body.image);
    String url = await Storage().url(path);
    return <String, String>{'path': path, 'url': url};
  }
}

Save the file before you return

Dox deletes the uploaded temp file when it sends the response. So call putFile, store or moveTo in the controller, not later.

docs.title: 4. Add the routes
docs.text:
One route takes the upload. Storage.route serves the saved files at /files/{key*}:

lib/routes/api.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/upload.controller.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.post('/upload', (UploadController c) => c.store);
  }
}
lib/routes/web.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';

class WebRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    // GET /files/{key*}, any file of the default disk
    Storage.route('files', signed: false);
  }
}

signed: false makes every file public. For private files, leave it out and use Storage().signedUrl(path) in place of Storage().url(path).

docs.title: 5. Register the DTOs
docs.text:
Add the dtos list that build_runner writes. Skip this step if your app.dart already has dtos: dtos:

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:my_app/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  dtos: dtos,
  // ...
);

docs.title: 6. Build and run
docs.text:
Build the code and start the server:

dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dox serve

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Upload a PNG:

curl -F image=@photo.png http://localhost:3000/api/upload

{
  "path": "/images/074aa0d0-ce21-11f1-938a-57265e28c4a3.png",
  "url": "http://localhost:3000/files/images/074aa0d0-ce21-11f1-938a-57265e28c4a3.png"
}

Open the URL in the browser. The image shows.

Now upload a text file. You get 422:

curl -F image=@notes.txt http://localhost:3000/api/upload

{"image":"The image must be an image"}

With no file, you also get 422, with {"image":"The image is required"}.

docs.title: Bigger files
docs.text: A multipart body can be 100 MB by default. To change the limit, set maxMultipartSize in AppConfig. Set the same limit in your proxy too, like client_max_body_size in nginx.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Request: form data: read a RequestFile.
  • Validation rules: files: all the file rules.
  • File storage: S3 and signed URLs.

docs.title: JWT authentication
docs.text:
Let users register and log in, give them a JWT token, protect routes with it, and read the user in a controller.

A JWT token is good for an API that a mobile app or a single page app calls. The client sends the token with every request, so the server needs no session.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app (dox create my_app). A new app has a database (SQLite), a User model and a users table with name, email and password columns.
  • The dox_auth package. Add it:
dart pub add dox_auth

docs.title: 1. Hide the password in the model
docs.text:
Anyone with the token can read the user in it. So put the password in hidden. The model of a new app already does this:

lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel(table: 'users', softDelete: true)
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get hidden => <String>['password'];

  @Column()
  String? name;

  @Column()
  String? email;

  @Column()
  String? password;
}

docs.title: 2. Set up the auth provider
docs.text:
The provider tells Dox how to make and check tokens, and how to find the user. Dox finds the provider by itself:

lib/providers/auth_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

class AppAuthProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Auth.initialize(
      AuthConfig(
        defaultGuard: 'api',
        guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
          'api': AuthGuard(
            driver: JwtAuthDriver(
              // APP_KEY signs the tokens. A new key logs every user out.
              secret: SecretKey(env.appKey),
              // a token stops working after this time
              expiresIn: const Duration(days: 7),
            ),
            provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
          ),
        },
      ),
    );
  }
}

The secret must have at least 32 bytes, like a key from dox key:generate. A shorter secret stops the app in production.

docs.title: 3. Write the DTOs
docs.text:
Write one DTO for register and one for login. @Unique comes from dox_orm, so hide the Schema class of dox_orm in the import:

lib/app/dtos/register_user/register_user.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart' hide Schema;

part 'register_user.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class RegisterUser {
  @Length(min: 2, max: 50)
  @Trim()
  final String name;

  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  @Unique('users', column: 'email')
  final String email;

  @MinLength(8)
  final String password;

  const RegisterUser({
    required this.name,
    required this.email,
    required this.password,
  });

  static const DtoSchema<RegisterUser> schema = $RegisterUserDto;
}
lib/app/dtos/login_user/login_user.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'login_user.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class LoginUser {
  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  final String email;

  final String password;

  const LoginUser({required this.email, required this.password});

  static const DtoSchema<LoginUser> schema = $LoginUserDto;
}

docs.title: 4. Write the controller
docs.text:
The controller makes the user, logs in, and returns the user of a token:

lib/app/http/controllers/auth.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/login_user/login_user.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/register_user/register_user.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class AuthController {
  /// POST /api/auth/register
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> register(RegisterUser body) async {
    User user = User()
      ..name = body.name
      ..email = body.email
      ..password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
    await user.save();

    String? token = Auth().login(user);
    return <String, dynamic>{'token': token, 'user': user};
  }

  /// POST /api/auth/login
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> login(LoginUser body) async {
    Auth auth = Auth();
    String? token = await auth.attempt(<String, dynamic>{
      'email': body.email,
      'password': body.password,
    });
    if (token == null) {
      throw UnAuthorizedException(message: 'Wrong email or password');
    }
    return <String, dynamic>{'token': token, 'user': auth.user<User>()};
  }

  /// GET /api/auth/me (behind AuthMiddleware)
  User? me(DoxRequest req) {
    return req.auth?.user<User>();
  }

  /// POST /api/auth/logout (behind AuthMiddleware)
  /// By default a JWT is not cancelled on the server. The client deletes
  /// the token, and it still works until `expiresIn` passes. To cancel it,
  /// turn on revocation and call `Auth().revokeToken(req)`.
  Map<String, String> logout(DoxRequest req) {
    return <String, String>{'message': 'Delete the token on the client'};
  }
}

auth.attempt finds the user by email and checks the password hash. It returns null if the email or the password is wrong.

docs.title: 5. Add the routes
docs.text:
Put every protected route inside AuthMiddleware. It reads the Authorization: Bearer <token> header. A missing or bad token gets 401:

lib/routes/api.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/auth.controller.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.post('/auth/register', (AuthController c) => c.register);
    Route.post('/auth/login', (AuthController c) => c.login);

    Route.middleware(<dynamic>[AuthMiddleware()], () {
      Route.get('/auth/me', (AuthController c) => c.me);
      Route.post('/auth/logout', (AuthController c) => c.logout);
      // put every protected route here
    });
  }
}

docs.title: 6. Register the DTOs
docs.text:
Add the dtos list that build_runner writes. Skip this step if your app.dart already has dtos: dtos:

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:my_app/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  dtos: dtos,
  // ...
);

docs.title: 7. Build and run
docs.text:
Build the code and start the server:

dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dox serve

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Register a user. You get a token and the user:

curl -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Ann","email":"ann@example.com","password":"secret123"}' \
  http://localhost:3000/api/auth/register

{
  "token": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...",
  "user": {
    "id": 1,
    "name": "Ann",
    "email": "ann@example.com",
    "created_at": "...",
    "updated_at": "..."
  }
}

A login with a wrong password gets 401:

{"error":{"code":"unauthorized","message":"Wrong email or password"}}

Now log in and use the token:

TOKEN=$(curl -s -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"ann@example.com","password":"secret123"}' \
  http://localhost:3000/api/auth/login | jq -r .token)

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://localhost:3000/api/auth/me

{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Ann",
  "email": "ann@example.com",
  "created_at": "...",
  "updated_at": "..."
}

Without the header, you get 401 with "Authentication failed".

The {"error": ...} shape comes from the handler in Custom errors. Without it, the body is {"code":"unauthorized","message":"Wrong email or password"}.

docs.title: Logout and expiry
docs.text:
By default the server can not cancel one token. You can do this:

You want Do this Log out on this device The client deletes the token. That is all logout does. Limit the damage of a stolen token Keep expiresIn short, for example Duration(hours: 12). Log every user out at once Change APP_KEY. Every old token stops working. Block one user Delete the user. AuthMiddleware loads the user on each request, so a deleted user gets 401.

To cancel one token, or all tokens of a user, turn on revocation. Or use access tokens.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Authentication: all the options of the guards and drivers.
  • Hashing: make and check password hashes.
  • Middleware: run code before a route.

docs.title: Pagination
docs.text:
Make a list route that takes page and per_page from the query string and returns one page of rows.

A table can have many thousands of rows, so the client asks for one page at a time.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A Dox app (dox create my_app). A new app has a database (SQLite), a User model and a users table.

docs.title: 1. Write the query DTO
docs.text:
The DTO reads and checks page and per_page. With source: Source.query, it reads the query string, not the body:

lib/app/dtos/list_users/list_users.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'list_users.dto.g.dart';

/// GET /api/users?page=2&per_page=10
@Dto(source: Source.query)
class ListUsers {
  @Min(1)
  final int page;

  @Range(1, 100)
  final int perPage; // query key: per_page

  const ListUsers({this.page = 1, this.perPage = 20});

  static const DtoSchema<ListUsers> schema = $ListUsersDto;
}

Both fields have a default, so the client can leave them out. The field perPage reads the key per_page.

docs.title: 2. Write the controller
docs.text:
paginate() returns a Pagination. Return it as it is, and Dox sends its toJson():

lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/list_users/list_users.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class UserController {
  /// GET /api/users?page=1&per_page=20
  Future<Pagination<User>> index(ListUsers query) async {
    return User()
        .orderBy('id', 'desc')
        .paginate(currentPage: query.page, perPage: query.perPage);
  }
}

Always add an orderBy. Without it, a row can show on two pages, or on none. To filter the rows, add a where before paginate.

docs.title: 3. Add the route
docs.text:
Add the list route to the API router:

lib/routes/api.dart
Route.get('/users', (UserController c) => c.index);

docs.title: 4. Register the DTOs
docs.text:
Add the dtos list that build_runner writes. Skip this step if your app.dart already has dtos: dtos:

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:my_app/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  dtos: dtos,
  // ...
);

docs.title: 5. Build and run
docs.text:
Build the code and start the server:

dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dox serve

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Ask for page 2, with 2 rows per page. With 3 users in the table, you get one user:

curl 'http://localhost:3000/api/users?page=2&per_page=2'

{
  "total": 3,
  "per_page": 2,
  "last_page": 2,
  "current_page": 2,
  "data": [
    {
      "id": 1,
      "name": "User 1",
      "email": "user1@example.com",
      "created_at": "2026-10-22T14:01:07.843207Z",
      "updated_at": "2026-10-22T14:01:07.843207Z"
    }
  ]
}

The keys of the response are:

Key Meaning total rows that match the query, on all pages per_page rows per page last_page the number of the last page current_page the page you asked for data the rows of this page, from toJson() of the model

A page after the last one gives an empty list in data.

Bad input gets 422:

curl 'http://localhost:3000/api/users?page=0&per_page=500'

{
  "page": "The page must be greater than or equal 1",
  "per_page": "The per_page must be between 1 and 100"
}

docs.title: Change the shape of a row
docs.text:
To send only some fields, pass the rows to a serializer. Make one with dox make:serializer User. page.data gives the typed rows:

Future<Map<String, dynamic>> index(ListUsers query) async {
  Pagination<User> page = await User()
      .orderBy('id', 'desc')
      .paginate(currentPage: query.page, perPage: query.perPage);
  return <String, dynamic>{
    ...page.toJson(),
    'data': UserSerializer(page.data).toJson(),
  };
}

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Query builder: paginate: all the paginate options.
  • DTOs: body and query string: read the query string.
  • Serializer: change the shape of a model.

docs.title: Share code with Flutter
docs.text:
Put a @Dto class in a shared Dart package, so the Dox server and the Flutter app check input with the same rules and error messages.

The app checks the form, so the user sees an error at once. The server checks the same input again, because it can not trust the client. The generated DTO code is pure Dart, so it runs in Flutter and on the web.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app (dox create server). Here it is in the server folder.
  • A Flutter app (flutter create app). Here it is in the app folder.

docs.title: The layout
docs.text:
The three parts live next to each other in one folder:

my_blog/
  packages/
    blog_shared/     # the DTOs. Pure Dart.
  server/            # the Dox app
  app/               # the Flutter app

The app and the server use the same DTO:
