packages/blog_sharedSaveBlog and SaveBlog.schema
  1. app: Flutterchecks the form
  1. server: Doxchecks the request

docs.title: 1. The shared package
docs.text:
Make a plain Dart package for the DTOs:

packages/blog_shared/pubspec.yaml
name: blog_shared
description: DTOs shared by the Dox server and the Flutter app.
version: 0.1.0
publish_to: none

environment:
  sdk: ^3.13.0

Add the packages:

cd packages/blog_shared
dart pub add dox_validation
dart pub add dev:dox_builder dev:build_runner

Now write the DTO. Import dox_validation, not dox_core, because dox_core does not run in Flutter:

packages/blog_shared/lib/src/save_blog.dart
import 'package:dox_validation/dox_validation.dart';

part 'save_blog.g.dart';

/// A new blog post. The server and the app check it with the same rules.
@Dto()
class SaveBlog {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 3, max: 255)
  final String title;

  @Trim()
  @MinLength(10)
  final String description;

  const SaveBlog({required this.title, required this.description});

  static const DtoSchema<SaveBlog> schema = $SaveBlogDto;
}

Export the DTOs. Also export dox_validation, so the app gets ParseResult and ValidationException from the same import:

packages/blog_shared/lib/blog_shared.dart
export 'package:dox_validation/dox_validation.dart';

export 'src/save_blog.dart';

Generate the code:

cd packages/blog_shared
dart pub get
dart run build_runner build

This writes lib/src/save_blog.g.dart and lib/generated/dtos.g.dart, the list of every DTO in the package. Commit both files, so the Flutter app does not need to run the generator.

@Unique and @Exists come from dox_orm, which the app can not import. Check them on the server only.

docs.title: 2. The Dox server
docs.text:
Add the shared package to the dependencies of the server:

server/pubspec.yaml
dependencies:
  # ... the packages of the new app stay
  blog_shared:
    path: ../packages/blog_shared

Run dart pub get.

Add the DTO list of the shared package to the dtos list of AppConfig:

server/lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:blog_shared/generated/dtos.g.dart' as shared;
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:server/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  dtos: <DtoSchema<Object>>[...dtos, ...shared.dtos],
);

The controller asks for SaveBlog like any other DTO. Bad input gets 422:

server/lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart
import 'package:blog_shared/blog_shared.dart' show SaveBlog;
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

@Inject()
class BlogController {
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> store(SaveBlog body) async {
    // body.title is already trimmed and checked.
    return <String, dynamic>{'title': body.title, 'saved': true};
  }
}

Use show SaveBlog in server code, because dox_core and blog_shared both export a ValidationException class.

Add the route:

server/lib/routes/api.dart
Route.post('/blogs', (BlogController c) => c.store);

A bad request gets the errors as {"key": "message"}:

POST /api/blogs  {"title": "ab", "description": "short"}
422 {"title":"The title must be between 3 and 255 characters",
     "description":"The description must be at least 10 characters"}

docs.title: 3. The Flutter app
docs.text:
Add the shared package to the app:

app/pubspec.yaml
name: app
publish_to: none

environment:
  sdk: ^3.13.0

dependencies:
  flutter:
    sdk: flutter
  http: ^1.6.0
  blog_shared:
    path: ../packages/blog_shared

The widget checks the form with SaveBlog.schema.safeParse(), and sends only good input. result.errors has the same shape as the 422 body of the server:

app/lib/new_blog_form.dart
import 'dart:convert';

import 'package:blog_shared/blog_shared.dart';
import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;

class NewBlogForm extends StatefulWidget {
  const NewBlogForm({super.key});

  @override
  State<NewBlogForm> createState() {
    return _NewBlogFormState();
  }
}

class _NewBlogFormState extends State<NewBlogForm> {
  final TextEditingController _title = TextEditingController();
  final TextEditingController _description = TextEditingController();
  Map<String, String> _errors = <String, String>{};

  Future<void> _submit() async {
    ParseResult<SaveBlog> result =
        SaveBlog.schema.safeParse(<String, dynamic>{
      'title': _title.text,
      'description': _description.text,
    });
    if (!result.success) {
      setState(() {
        _errors = result.errors;
      });
      return;
    }

    http.Response response = await http.post(
      Uri.parse('https://api.example.com/api/blogs'),
      headers: <String, String>{'Content-Type': 'application/json'},
      body: jsonEncode(SaveBlog.schema.toMap(result.value!)),
    );
    setState(() {
      _errors = response.statusCode == 422
          ? Map<String, String>.from(jsonDecode(response.body) as Map)
          : <String, String>{};
    });
  }

  @override
  void dispose() {
    _title.dispose();
    _description.dispose();
    super.dispose();
  }

  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return Column(
      children: <Widget>[
        TextField(
          controller: _title,
          decoration: InputDecoration(
              labelText: 'Title', errorText: _errors['title']),
        ),
        TextField(
          controller: _description,
          decoration: InputDecoration(
              labelText: 'Description',
              errorText: _errors['description']),
        ),
        ElevatedButton(onPressed: _submit, child: const Text('Save')),
      ],
    );
  }
}

docs.title: Other schema methods
docs.text:
The schema has more methods than safeParse:

  • parse throws a ValidationException when the input is bad.
  • toMap gives the JSON map to send.
  • toJsonSchema gives the JSON Schema of the DTO.

If the DTO has an async validate() method, use safeParseAsync or parseAsync.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Validation: all the rules.
  • dox_validation: all the schema methods.

docs.title: Static files and SPA
docs.text:
Serve a folder of files, or a single page app (React, Vue, Flutter web), from the Dox app, with the right cache headers.

With the front-end in the same app as your API, you have one server to run and no CORS setup.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Dox app.
  • A public folder with the built front-end (index.html, assets/...).
  • For the storage disk and the controller below: the dox_storage package, with its provider. See File storage.

docs.title: Serve a folder: one line
docs.text:
Route.staticFiles serves the files of a folder. Add it in register() of WebRouter:

lib/routes/web.dart
Route.staticFiles('/', 'public');

Now /app.js sends public/app.js. A route wins over a file with the same path. For a Cache-Control header, add maxAge. See Routing: serve static files.

For a single page app, add a fallback route that sends index.html.

docs.title: Or serve a storage disk
docs.text:
Storage.route serves every file of a disk. First add a public disk for the folder:

lib/config/storage.dart
StorageConfig storageConfig = StorageConfig(
  defaultDisk: env.storageDisk,
  disks: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    'local': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'local', 'root': 'storage'},

    /// the front-end files
    'public': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'local', 'root': 'public'},
  },
);

Then add the route in register() of WebRouter:

lib/routes/web.dart
// GET /static/{key*}
Storage.route('static', disk: 'public', signed: false);

Now /static/app.js sends public/app.js. This route sends no Cache-Control header.

docs.title: Serve an SPA
docs.text:
A single page app (SPA) needs two things:

  • index.html for every URL the SPA router handles, with no cache.
  • The built assets with a long cache. Build tools put a hash in the file name (app.3f9c2b.js), so a new build has new names.

docs.title: 1. Write the controller
docs.text:
Write one method for the assets and one for index.html:

lib/app/http/controllers/static.controller.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';

@Inject()
class StaticController {
  /// GET /assets/{path*}
  /// Built files have a hash in the name, so the browser may keep them
  /// for one year. The `public` disk rejects `..` in the path.
  Future<DoxResponse> asset(String path) async {
    StreamFile file = await Storage().disk('public').stream(path);
    return response(file).cache(const Duration(days: 365));
  }

  /// GET / and GET /{path*}
  /// Every other URL gets index.html, so the router of the SPA can
  /// handle it. Never cache it, so a new deploy shows at once.
  /// An unknown API URL stays a 404, it does not get the page.
  DoxResponse index(DoxRequest req) {
    if (req.uri.path.startsWith('/api/')) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException();
    }
    return response(File('public/index.html')).cache(Duration.zero);
  }
}

cache(duration) sets Cache-Control: max-age=<seconds>.

docs.title: 2. Add the routes
docs.text:
The catch-all route matches every URL, so it must come last. Put the API router before the web router in AppConfig:

lib/routes/web.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/static.controller.dart';

class WebRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    // the SPA: assets with a long cache, every other URL gets index.html
    Route.get('/assets/{path*}', (StaticController c) => c.asset);
    Route.get('/', (StaticController c) => c.index);
    Route.get('/{path*}', (StaticController c) => c.index);
  }
}

Set the order of the routers:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  /// the SPA catch-all route is in WebRouter, so it must come last.
  /// Listed routers come first, in this order.
  routers: <Router>[ApiRouter(), WebRouter()],
  // ...
);

Keep the route for /, because /{path*} does not match the start page.

docs.title: 3. Put the build in public
docs.text:
Build the front-end and copy the files to public:

# React (Vite)
npm run build && cp -r dist/. public/

# Flutter web
flutter build web && cp -r build/web/. public/

Flutter web puts the files next to index.html, not in assets/. So for Flutter, change the asset route to match.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
The start page comes with no cache:

curl -i http://localhost:3000/

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
cache-control: max-age=0
content-type: text/html

Any other page also gets index.html, and an asset gets a cache of one year:

curl -i http://localhost:3000/settings/profile   # same answer: index.html
curl -i http://localhost:3000/assets/app.js

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
cache-control: max-age=31536000
content-type: text/javascript

/assets/nope.js, /assets/..%2Fpubspec.yaml and /api/nothing answer 404.

docs.title: In production
docs.text: Put a proxy in front of Dox, and let it do gzip. For a big site, serve public from the proxy or a CDN.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Routing: serve storage files: all the options of Storage.route.
  • Response: files and big responses: send a file.
  • File storage: disks and drivers.

docs.title: Testing with a database
docs.text:
Run model tests against a real database: SQLite for fast local tests, or a test Postgres for the real thing.

A real database finds bugs that a mock can not find, like a wrong column name. The migrations run one time, and every test starts with empty tables.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: • A Dox app (dox create my_app). A new app has the User model, a users migration in db/migration and the test package.

docs.title: 1. Check the migration
docs.text:
The test makes its tables from your migrations. A new app has this one, with another date in the file name:

db/migration/2026_10_22_000000_create_users_table.dart
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

class CreateUsersTable extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.create('users', (Table table) {
      table.id();
      table.string('name');
      table.string('email').unique();
      table.string('password');
      table.timestamps();
      table.softDeletes();
    });
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.dropIfExists('users');
  }
}

The test imports the list of all migrations from db/migration/migrations.dart. dox make:migration updates this list.

docs.title: 2. Write the test (SQLite)
docs.text:
Start with SQLite, because it needs no server. The test has its own database config:

test/user_test.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

/// One SQLite file for this test file. No server, no Postgres.
const String dbFile = 'storage/test.sqlite';

DatabaseConfig testDatabase = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: 'sqlite',
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'sqlite': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.sqlite,
      database: dbFile,
      debug: false,
    ),
  },
);

Future<void> deleteDbFile() async {
  for (String suffix in <String>['', '-wal', '-shm']) {
    File file = File('$dbFile$suffix');
    if (await file.exists()) await file.delete();
  }
}

void main() {
  setUpAll(() async {
    await deleteDbFile();
    await Migrator(
      migrations: migrations,
      config: testDatabase.getConnectionConfig(),
    ).migrate();
    SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(testDatabase);
  });

  // every test starts with empty tables
  setUp(refreshDatabase);

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await deleteDbFile();
  });

  test('saves and finds a user', () async {
    User user = User()
      ..name = 'Ann'
      ..email = 'ann@example.com'
      ..password = Hash.make('secret123');
    await user.save();

    User? found = await User().where('email', 'ann@example.com').getFirst();
    expect(found?.id, user.id);
    expect(found?.name, 'Ann');
    expect(Hash.verify('secret123', found!.password!), isTrue);
  });

  test('the tables are empty again', () async {
    expect(await User().count(), 0);
  });
}

refreshDatabase() empties every table except the migrations table, and starts the ids at 1 again.

Put storage/test.sqlite in .gitignore. Use a file, not :memory:, because the migrator and the ORM each open their own connection.

docs.title: 3. Run it
docs.text:
Run the test file:

dart test test/user_test.dart

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
The migrations run, and then the tests pass:

00:00 +0: (setUpAll)
Migrating: 2026_10_22_000000_create_users_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_000000_create_users_table
Migrating: 2026_10_23_000000_create_queue_tables
Migrated: 2026_10_23_000000_create_queue_tables
00:00 +1: saves and finds a user
00:00 +2: the tables are empty again
00:00 +2: All tests passed!

docs.title: The same test on Postgres
docs.text:
If your app runs on Postgres in production, test on Postgres too. Use a separate database for tests, because the tests delete all rows.

Start a test database with Docker:

docker run -d --name my_app_test -p 5433:5432 \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres -e POSTGRES_DB=my_app_test postgres:18

Change the config at the top of the test:

DatabaseConfig testDatabase = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: 'postgres',
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.postgres,
      host: 'localhost',
      port: 5433,
      user: 'postgres',
      password: 'postgres',
      database: 'my_app_test',
      debug: false,
    ),
  },
);

Delete deleteDbFile() and its two calls. The rest of the test stays the same.

docs.title: Many test files
docs.text:
Test files run at the same time, so two files that use the same table can break each other. Give each file its own SQLite file, or run the files one by one:

dart test --concurrency=1

docs.title: Test a route with the database
docs.text:
This test uses the /api/users route of the Pagination guide. DoxTestClient starts the app in the test, with the config in lib/config/database.dart:

test/api_test.dart
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    await Migrator(
      migrations: migrations,
      config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
    ).migrate();
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });

  setUp(refreshDatabase);

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('GET /api/users has no rows', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.get('/api/users');
    res.expectStatus(200);
    expect(res.json['data'], isEmpty);
  });
}

Pick the test database with env variables:

DB_CONNECTION=sqlite DB_NAME=storage/test.sqlite \
    dart test test/api_test.dart

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Testing: test HTTP routes: all the client methods.
  • Migration: write migrations.
  • Database: SQLite: the SQLite settings.

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text:
GraphQL makes an API for your app from your models. You add annotations to a model, run the builder, and the API is ready.

A GraphQL API has one URL. The client writes the fields that it wants, and it gets JSON with only those fields. To learn GraphQL, read graphql.org/learn.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Run the setup command in your app:

dox add graphql

The command adds the packages, lib/config/graphql.dart and lib/providers/graphql_provider.dart. It does not overwrite a file. For an app with no models, see Without the ORM.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
All settings are fields of GraphQLConfig in lib/config/graphql.dart. Set only the settings that you want to change:

lib/config/graphql.dart
GraphQLConfig graphqlConfig = GraphQLConfig(
  schema: graphqlSchema,
  path: '/api/graphql',
);
Setting Default What it does path /graphql The URL of the API. middleware none Route middleware, like AuthMiddleware(). graphiql on in development The GraphiQL page. introspection on in development Lets tools like GraphiQL read the list of your types and fields. showInternalErrors on in development Sends the real text of an error to the client. rules none More validation rules, run after the rules of the GraphQL spec. maxDepth 64 How deep a query can nest fields. maxQueryLength 1000000 The most characters in the text of one query. maxFields 20000 The most fields one query can ask for. maxNodes 100000 The most values one request can load. maxRootFields 50 The most top-level fields in one request. Each alias counts. maxRelationRows 50000 The most rows that one list relation can load for all parent rows together. maxErrors 100 The most errors in one result. After it, the fields that start give null.

"On in development" means on when APP_ENV is development. A request that is larger than a max setting gets an error.

docs.title: Add a model to the API
docs.text:
Put @GraphQL() on a model. Then add one annotation for each operation that a client can use:

lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
@DoxModel()
@GraphQL()
@GraphQLAll()
@GraphQLFind()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  @Column()
  int? userId;

  @BelongsTo(User)
  User? user;
}

@GraphQLAll() adds the posts query, and @GraphQLFind() adds the post query. An operation with no annotation does not exist.

The id, the columns and the relations of the model are fields that a client can ask for. Post has a relation to User, so put @GraphQL() on User also.

Run the builder, and start the app again. Do these two steps after each change to an annotation:

dart run build_runner build

docs.title: Run a query
docs.text:
A query is a request that reads data. In development, open http://localhost:3000/graphql in a browser. This URL shows GraphiQL, a page where you write and run queries:

{
  posts(limit: 10) {
    title
    user { name }
  }
}

The result has the same shape as the query:

{ "data": { "posts": [{ "title": "Hello GraphQL", "user": { "name": "Ada" } }] } }

Dox loads the users of all ten posts with one database query.

Your client sends the same query as a POST request to /graphql. The JSON body is {"query": "..."}. A query can also come as a GET request, with query in the URL. A mutation needs POST.

docs.title: All operations
docs.text:
Each annotation adds one query or one mutation. A mutation is a request that changes data.

Annotation GraphQL field Function @GraphQLAll() posts(limit, offset) Reads a list. @GraphQLPaginate() posts(first, page) Reads a page of a list, with the total number of rows. @GraphQLFind() post(id) Reads one row. @GraphQLCreate(dto:) createPost(input) Adds a row. @GraphQLUpdate(dto:) updatePost(id, input) Changes a row. @GraphQLDelete() deletePost(id) Removes a row.

Create and update use a DTO, so the input gets the same validation as your HTTP routes. For each annotation, see Model annotations.

docs.title: Write your own query
docs.text:
Write your own query when the annotations are not sufficient, for example for a search. Put @GraphQLQuery() on a method of a class in lib/:

lib/app/graphql/post.resolver.dart
class PostResolver {
  @GraphQLQuery()
  Future<List<Post>> latestPosts({int limit = 10}) {
    return Post().orderBy('id', 'desc').limit(limit).get();
  }
}

The method name is the query name, and the parameters are the values that a client can send:

{ latestPosts(limit: 3) { title } }

For more, see Your own resolvers.

docs.title: Protect the API
docs.text:
By default, all clients can use all operations. Set guard: true on an operation that a guest must not use. Give an ability with can:, and Dox asks the policy of the model before the operation runs:

lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
@DoxModel()
@GraphQL(filter: Ability.view)
@GraphQLAll(can: Ability.viewAny)
@GraphQLFind(can: Ability.view)
@GraphQLCreate(
    dto: PostInput, can: Ability.create, guard: true, owner: 'userId')
@GraphQLUpdate(dto: PostInput, can: Ability.update, guard: true)
@GraphQLDelete(can: Ability.delete, guard: true)
class Post extends PostGenerator {}
  • guard: true makes the operation need a login.
  • can: asks the policy if the user can do the operation.
  • filter: hides the rows that the user cannot read.
  • owner: 'userId' sets the owner of a new row to the logged-in user.

A guest that Dox refuses gets the error UNAUTHENTICATED. A user that Dox refuses gets the error FORBIDDEN. The other fields of the request still give their data.

To set this up, see Authentication and Authorization.

docs.title: Production defaults and limits
docs.text:
In production, GraphiQL and introspection are off, and error details stay on the server. You do not set anything for this.

Limits stop a very large query before it causes much work on your server. For example, a query can nest 64 levels, and a list gives a maximum of 100 rows. Set lower limits when your API is open to the public:

lib/config/graphql.dart
GraphQLConfig graphqlConfig = GraphQLConfig(
  schema: graphqlSchema,
  maxDepth: 10,
  maxNodes: 10000,
);

For all settings, see Configuration.

docs.title: Model annotations
docs.text:
Each annotation can have these options:

Option Function name: A different name for the type or the field. description: The text that GraphiQL shows. guard: true A client must log in. See Authentication. can: The policy must allow the user. @GraphQL does not have this option. See Authorization.

docs.title: @GraphQL
docs.text:
Use it to make the model a type of the API. All other model annotations need it.

@GraphQL()

A model with only @GraphQL() has no queries and no mutations. A client gets it only through a relation, for example post.user.

Dox does not show the fields in the hidden list of the model, so a password stays on the server. To hide a different field, put @GraphQLIgnore() above its @Column().

A field can be a String, int, double, bool, DateTime, an enum, a @GraphQL class, or a List of them. A different type stops the build, so put @GraphQLIgnore() on a field that the API does not need.

To make a getter a field, put @GraphQLField() on it. It has name:, description:, deprecationReason: and guard: true:

@GraphQLField()
String get fullName => '$firstName $lastName';

@GraphQL also has filter:. See Hide rows.

docs.title: @GraphQLAll
docs.text:
Use it when a client must read a list with limit and offset:

@GraphQLAll()

{ posts(limit: 10, offset: 20) { title } }

The default limit is 20. A limit of more than 100 gives an error.

docs.title: @GraphQLPaginate
docs.text:
Use it when a client shows pages and needs the total number of rows. The client sends first, which is the number of rows on a page, and page:

@GraphQLPaginate()

{
  posts(first: 10, page: 2) {
    data { title }
    paginatorInfo { total currentPage lastPage hasMorePages }
  }
}

{
  "data": {
    "posts": {
      "data": [{ "title": "Hello GraphQL" }],
      "paginatorInfo": { "total": 11, "currentPage": 2, "lastPage": 2, "hasMorePages": false }
    }
  }
}

The default first is 20, and the default page is 1. A first of more than 100 gives an error.

data has the rows of the page. paginatorInfo has these fields:

Field Value total The number of rows on all pages. count The number of rows on this page. perPage The value of first. currentPage The number of this page. lastPage The number of the last page. hasMorePages true if there is a page after this page. firstItem The number of the first row of this page. The first row of page 1 is 1. null on an empty page. lastItem The number of the last row of this page. null on an empty page.

If the model also has @GraphQLAll(), the list is posts and the paged list is postsPaginate. To set a different name, use name::

@GraphQLPaginate(name: 'postPages')

docs.title: @GraphQLFind
docs.text:
Use it when a client must read one row by its id:

@GraphQLFind()

{ post(id: 1) { title } }

The result is null if no row has that id.

docs.title: @GraphQLCreate
docs.text:
Use it to let a client add a row. First, write a DTO with the fields that the client can set:

lib/app/dtos/post_input/post_input.dto.dart
@Dto()
class PostInput {
  PostInput({required this.title});

  @MinLength(3, message: 'The title is too short')
  final String title;
}

Then give the DTO to the annotation:

@GraphQLCreate(dto: PostInput)

mutation {
  createPost(input: { title: "My second post" }) { id title }
}

A client can set only the fields of the DTO. Thus, a client cannot set a different column, for example userId.

Dox applies the rules of the DTO before it saves the row. If the input is not correct, Dox saves nothing. The client gets the error VALIDATION_FAILED, with the message for each field in extensions.fields.

docs.title: Set the owner of a new row
docs.text:
Use owner: when each row belongs to the user that made it. Dox sets that column to the id of the logged-in user:

@GraphQLCreate(dto: PostInput, owner: 'userId')

With owner:, the client must log in to create a row. The owner column must not be a field of the DTO. An update never changes the owner column.

docs.title: @GraphQLUpdate
docs.text:
Use it to let a client change a row. It can use the same DTO as @GraphQLCreate:

@GraphQLUpdate(dto: PostInput, can: Ability.update, guard: true)

mutation { updatePost(id: 1, input: { title: "A better title" }) { title } }

updatePost changes only the fields that the client sends, and Dox applies only the rules of those fields. The result is null if no row has that id.

Warning

Without can:, each client that can call updatePost or deletePost can change or delete each row. Add can: to @GraphQLUpdate and @GraphQLDelete. The builder shows a warning if one of them has no can: and no guard:.

docs.title: @GraphQLDelete
docs.text:
Use it to let a client remove a row. It needs no DTO:

@GraphQLDelete(can: Ability.delete, guard: true)

mutation { deletePost(id: 1) }

The result is true, or false if no row has that id.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Use guard: true when a client must log in. If your app does not have a login, set it up first with dox add auth.

Add AuthMiddleware() to the config. Dox uses it to read the user:

lib/config/graphql.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_graphql/dox_graphql.dart';
import 'package:my_app/generated/schema.g.dart';

GraphQLConfig graphqlConfig = GraphQLConfig(
  schema: graphqlSchema,
  middleware: <Object>[AuthMiddleware()],
);

The middleware does not stop a request. All fields stay public until you add guard: true. The client sends its token in the Authorization: Bearer <token> header, as usual.

If you use a subclass of AuthMiddleware, override asOptional() to return your subclass. Else your changes do not run.

docs.title: Make a query or mutation need a login
docs.text:
Set guard: true on each operation that a guest must not use:

lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
@DoxModel()
@GraphQL()
@GraphQLAll()
@GraphQLFind()
@GraphQLCreate(dto: PostInput, guard: true)
@GraphQLUpdate(dto: PostInput, guard: true)
@GraphQLDelete(guard: true)
class Post extends PostGenerator {}

Here, a guest can read posts, but only a logged-in user can change them.

If a guest asks for a guarded field, the guest gets the error UNAUTHENTICATED for that field. The other fields in the same request still give their data.

guard: true needs AuthMiddleware() in the config. Without it, the app stops at start and shows the name of the type or field.

docs.title: Protect a model everywhere
docs.text:
Write @GraphQL(guard: true) on a model that a guest must never see, for example User:

lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart
@DoxModel()
@GraphQL(guard: true)
@GraphQLFind()
class User extends UserGenerator {}

Then each field that gives a user needs a login. This includes its queries, its mutations, each relation such as post.user, and your own resolvers.

docs.title: Read the logged-in user
docs.text:
Add a DoxGraphQLContext parameter to a resolver method. The client does not send this value. Dox puts the current request in it:

lib/app/graphql/user.resolver.dart
@GraphQLQuery()
Future<User?> me(DoxGraphQLContext context) {
  return context.user<User>();
}

context.user<User>() gives null for a guest. The context also has these members:

  • context.auth() gives the IAuth of the login, or null.
  • context.make<T>() gives a service from the container.
  • context.request is the DoxRequest.
  • context.loader gives a DataLoader of the request, see Without the ORM.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text: guard: true is only a login check. Use a policy when the answer is different for each user or each row.

docs.title: Write a policy
docs.text:
A policy is a class with one method for each rule. The abilities map gives a name to each method. This name is the ability. Ability has the usual names: viewAny, view, create, update and delete.

lib/app/policies/post_policy.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class PostPolicy extends Policy<User, Post> {
  bool update(User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id;

  @override
  Map<String, Function> get abilities => <String, Function>{
    Ability.update: update,
  };
}

Each ability section below adds one method to this policy. Add each new method to abilities also.

docs.title: Register the policy
docs.text:
Register the policy in the setup() of a provider. dox add graphql made the GraphQL provider, so you can use it. Keep the super.setup() call:

lib/providers/graphql_provider.dart
class AppGraphQLProvider extends GraphQLProvider {
  AppGraphQLProvider() : super(graphqlConfig);

  @override
  void setup() {
    Gate.policy<Post>(PostPolicy());
    super.setup();
  }
}

The config must have AuthMiddleware(). Without it, Dox cannot read the user, and each client is a guest.

When the app starts, Dox makes sure that the policy has each ability of can: and filter:. If one is missing, the app stops with an error that shows the available abilities:

@GraphQLDelete(can: 'delete') on Post: PostPolicy has no ability 'delete'. Available: update.

docs.title: Use it on a model
docs.text:
Give an ability to an operation with can:. Dox asks the policy before the operation runs. An operation with no can: does not ask the policy.

lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
@DoxModel()
@GraphQL(filter: Ability.view)
@GraphQLAll(can: Ability.viewAny)
@GraphQLPaginate(can: Ability.viewAny)
@GraphQLFind(can: Ability.view)
@GraphQLCreate(
    dto: PostInput, can: Ability.create, guard: true, owner: 'userId')
@GraphQLUpdate(dto: PostInput, can: Ability.update, guard: true)
@GraphQLDelete(can: Ability.delete, guard: true)
class Post extends PostGenerator {}

Some policy methods get a row, and some do not:

Annotation The policy method gets Use @GraphQLAll(can:), @GraphQLPaginate(can:) The user. Ability.viewAny @GraphQLCreate(can:) The user. Ability.create @GraphQLFind(can:) The user and the row. Ability.view @GraphQLUpdate(can:) The user and the row. Ability.update @GraphQLDelete(can:) The user and the row. Ability.delete @GraphQL(filter:) The user and each row. Ability.view

Do not use an ability that needs a row, like Ability.view, on @GraphQLAll, @GraphQLPaginate or @GraphQLCreate.

When the policy refuses a user, the field is null. The other fields keep their data:

{ "data": { "posts": null, "me": { "name": "Ada" } } }

The errors list of the result has one error for posts. Its code is FORBIDDEN, in extensions.code.

For an id that does not exist, Dox asks the policy about an empty row, so a refused user gets FORBIDDEN for each id. If your policy method allows an empty row, a client can find which ids exist.

docs.title: viewAny
docs.text:
Use viewAny when some users must not get lists of the model:

@GraphQLAll(can: Ability.viewAny)

bool viewAny(User user) => user.banned != true;

docs.title: view
docs.text:
Use view when a user can read some rows and not others. Here, a user can read a published post and their own posts:

@GraphQLFind(can: Ability.view)

bool view(User user, Post post) {
  return post.status == 'published' || post.userId == user.id;
}

A refused user gets FORBIDDEN from post(id).

docs.title: Hide rows
docs.text:
Use filter: on @GraphQL when a client must get only the rows that the user can read:

@GraphQL(filter: Ability.view)

Dox hides each row that the ability refuses, and gives no error. This applies to each field that gives the model:

  • A list, a paged list, or a list relation such as user.posts does not include the row. Thus, a list can have fewer rows than limit.
  • post(id) or a single relation such as comment.post gives null.
  • Your own queries, mutations and fields that return the model do the same.

Warning

filter: does not decide who can change a row. updatePost and deletePost ask only their can:. Give them a can:.

To get null and no error from post(id), use filter: and no can: on @GraphQLFind.

  • In a paged list, data and count do not include the hidden rows, but total and lastPage include them.
  • createPost always gives the new row. updatePost saves a hidden row, but its result is null.
  • A field can give a filtered model as Post, Post?, List<Post> or List<Post>?. A different shape stops the build.

docs.title: create
docs.text:
Use create when only some users can add a row. The method gets only the user, because no row exists yet:

@GraphQLCreate(dto: PostInput, can: Ability.create)

bool create(User user) => user.verified == true;

Dox asks the policy first. It applies the rules of the DTO only for a user that the policy allows. For a refused user, Dox saves nothing.

docs.title: update
docs.text:
Use update to decide who can change a row:

@GraphQLUpdate(dto: PostInput, can: Ability.update)

bool update(User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id;

For a refused user, Dox writes nothing.

docs.title: delete
docs.text:
Use delete to decide who can remove a row:

@GraphQLDelete(can: Ability.delete)

bool delete(User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id;

For a refused user, the row stays in the database.

docs.title: Add your own ability
docs.text:
Use your own ability when the five names of Ability are not sufficient. Write the name as a constant on the policy:

lib/app/policies/post_policy.dart
class PostPolicy extends Policy<User, Post> {
  static const String publish = 'publish';

  bool canPublish(User user, Post post) => user.editor == true;

  @override
  Map<String, Function> get abilities => <String, Function>{
    publish: canPublish,
  };
}

@GraphQLUpdate(dto: PostInput, can: PostPolicy.publish)

docs.title: Let guests in
docs.text:
A guest is a client that is not logged in. With Policy<User, Post>, Dox refuses each guest with the error UNAUTHENTICATED.

Use Policy<User?, Post> when a guest can read some rows. Then a guest gets to your methods, and user is null:

class PostPolicy extends Policy<User?, Post> {
  bool view(User? user, Post post) {
    if (post.status == 'published') return true;
    return user != null && post.userId == user.id;
  }

  @override
  Map<String, Function> get abilities =>
      <String, Function>{Ability.view: view};
}

Now a guest can read the published posts, and a user can also read their own drafts. To refuse guests on one operation of this model, add guard: true to that operation.

docs.title: Your own resolvers
docs.text:
A resolver is a method that gives the result of a query or a mutation. Write one when the model annotations are not sufficient. The builder finds each class in lib/ that has a resolver method.

lib/app/graphql/post.resolver.dart
import 'package:dox_graphql/dox_graphql.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/services/post.service.dart';

class PostResolver {
  PostResolver(this.postService);

  final PostService postService;

  @GraphQLQuery()
  Future<List<Post>> trendingPosts({int limit = 10}) {
    return postService.trending(limit);
  }
}

Dox gets the data of the query from the method:

  • The method name is the query name: trendingPosts.
  • The parameters are the values that a client can send. A parameter with a default value is optional.
  • The return type is the type that the client gets.
  • Dox gets the constructor parameters from the container.

A resolver annotation has name:, description: and guard: true, the same as a model annotation. It also has deprecationReason:, which marks the field as deprecated.

docs.title: Write your own mutation
docs.text:
Write your own mutation when one saved row is not sufficient. Put @GraphQLMutation() on a resolver method, and use a DTO for the input:

lib/app/graphql/post.resolver.dart
@GraphQLMutation()
Future<Post> importPost(PostInput input) {
  return postService.import(input);
}

Dox applies the rules of the DTO before your method runs.

docs.title: Send an error to the client
docs.text:
To send your own message, throw a GraphQLError:

throw GraphQLError('This post is not published yet',
    extensions: <String, Object?>{'code': 'NOT_PUBLISHED'});

extensions is optional. For all other errors, the client sees "Internal server error" in production. Dox sends the real error to the ExceptionHandler of your app.

docs.title: Check a policy in a resolver
docs.text:
can: works only on the model annotations. To refuse a user in your own resolver, call Gate yourself:

lib/app/graphql/post.resolver.dart
@GraphQLQuery()
Future<Post?> latestPost(DoxGraphQLContext context) async {
  Post? post = await postService.latest();
  User? user = await context.user<User>();
  if (post != null && await Gate.denies(user, Ability.view, post)) {
    throw GraphQLAuth.forbidden();
  }
  return post;
}

GraphQLAuth.forbidden() gives the same FORBIDDEN error as can:. filter: also hides rows in the result of your own resolvers.

docs.title: Without the ORM
docs.text:
If your app does not use models, install with dox add graphql --no-orm. Put @GraphQL() on a plain Dart class. Its public fields are the fields that a client can ask for. You write all the queries yourself:

lib/app/graphql/product.resolver.dart
@GraphQL()
class Product {
  Product({required this.id, required this.name, required this.shopId});

  final int id;
  final String name;

  @GraphQLIgnore()
  final int shopId;
}

class ProductResolver {
  ProductResolver(this.productRepository, this.shopRepository);

  final ProductRepository productRepository;
  final ShopRepository shopRepository;

  @GraphQLQuery()
  Future<List<Product>> products({int limit = 20}) {
    return productRepository.latest(limit);
  }

  @GraphQLResolveField()
  Future<Shop?> shop(Product product, DoxGraphQLContext context) {
    DataLoader<int, Shop> shops = context.loader<int, Shop>(
      'shops',
      () => DataLoader<int, Shop>(shopRepository.findByIds),
    );
    return shops.load(product.shopId);
  }
}

@GraphQLResolveField() adds a field to the class of its first parameter. Thus, Product gets a shop field, and Shop also needs @GraphQL().

The DataLoader collects the shop ids of the full request. Thus, fifty products cause one shop query, not fifty queries. findByIds takes a List<int> and returns a Future<List<Shop?>>, in the same order as the ids.

A DataLoader also has these methods:

  • loadMany(ids) loads a list of keys in the same batch.
  • prime(id, value) puts a value in the loader, if the key is not there. Use it when you already have the row.
  • clear(id) and clearAll() remove values, for example after a change.

When some keys can fail on their own, use DataLoader.withResults. The batch function gives one LoadValue(value) or LoadError(error) for each key:

DataLoader<int, Shop> shops = DataLoader<int, Shop>.withResults(
    (List<int> ids) async => <LoadResult<Shop>>[
          for (int id in ids) LoadValue<Shop>(await findShop(id)),
        ]);

DataLoader.of(loader) takes a class that implements BatchLoader.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
The same GraphQL API in Dox and in Go, on Postgres. The Dox app uses the ORM with @GraphQLAll and @GraphQLFind. The Go apps use gqlgen, one with pgx and one with GORM, and a dataloader for the relation.

2 cores: 20 rows, each with its related rows

{ worlds(limit: 20) { id randomNumber notes { id body } } }, 256 connections. Requests per second, higher is better.

req/s p99 RAM DoxORM 5,990fastest 84 ms 223 MB Gogqlgen + pgx 3,9181.5× slower 79 ms 132 MB Gogqlgen + GORM 3,6831.6× slower 221 ms 105 MB

Dox · Go 1.26 · gqlgen 0.17 · Postgres 18 · 2 cores · 256 connections · wrk

All three queries at 256 connections, requests per second:

Server One row by id 20 rows 20 rows with a relation peak MB Dox (ORM) 88,330 7,837 5,990 223 Go (gqlgen + pgx) 27,870 7,618 3,918 132 Go (gqlgen + GORM) 24,675 7,436 3,683 105
  • On one row by id, Dox is 3.2 times as fast as Go with pgx.
  • On a list of 20 rows, all three are about the same. Postgres is the limit here.
  • On a list with a relation, Dox is 1.5 times as fast.
  • Dox uses more memory at the peak. After the load, its memory goes down again.

How it was run: the same rig as the benchmark of the server. The server gets 2 CPUs, the database gets 2 CPUs and wrk gets the other 4. Each server has 8 database connections. Each query runs for 15 seconds, three times. The numbers are the median.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Authorization: write the policies for can: and filter:.
  • DTOs: the input of create and update.
  • Authentication: log users in.

docs.title: MCP server
docs.text:
dox_mcp lets AI clients like Claude, ChatGPT and IDE agents call tools in your app, with the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

A tool is an action the AI can call, like "add an expense". You write the tool in Dart and serve it from a normal Dox route. The server follows the MCP standard 2026-07-28: each request stands alone and gets a plain JSON reply, so every isolate and every server can answer any request. Older clients work on the same route. The server has tools only, no MCP resources, prompts or streams.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Run:

dox add mcp

It adds the package and writes lib/config/mcp.dart with an McpServer, and a sample tool in lib/app/mcp/echo.tool.dart. It never overwrites a file. To set it up by hand, run dart pub add dox_mcp and write those two files yourself.

APP_KEY must be set in .env, because the server signs data with it.

docs.title: Server options
docs.text: Option Default What it does name required the name of the server, for the client version required the version of your server, for the client tools required the tools. Two tools with the same name throw an ArgumentError title none a name for people instructions none text for the model about how to use the server allowedOrigins none see Checking the origin onToolError none see Errors in your code sessions SignedMcpSessions() sessions of older clients, see Sessions requestStateTtl 5 minutes how long the answers of a question work requestStateKey from APP_KEY the key that signs the answers

docs.title: Making a tool
docs.text:
A tool extends McpTool. It has a name, a description for the model, an input schema and a call method that does the work:

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_mcp/dox_mcp.dart';

class AddExpense extends McpTool {
  @override
  String get name => 'add_expense';

  @override
  String get description => 'Record an expense. Amount is in dollars.';

  @override
  ObjectSchema get input => v.object(<String, Schema<Object?>>{
    'amount': v.num().positive().describe('Amount, like 12.50.'),
    'note': v.string().max(500).optional(),
  });

  @override
  Future<McpToolResult> call(
    Map<String, dynamic> args,
    McpContext context,
  ) async {
    // ... save it
    return McpToolResult.text('Recorded ${args['amount']}.');
  }
}

The input is a validation schema. The client sees it as JSON Schema, and Dox checks every call before call runs. A tool can also have a title for people, and annotations like {'readOnlyHint': true}.

docs.title: Small tools
docs.text:
A small tool can be a function. Use McpTool.of:

McpTool.of(
  name: 'echo',
  description: 'Say the text back.',
  input: v.object(<String, Schema<Object?>>{'text': v.string()}),
  handler: (Map<String, dynamic> args, McpContext context) {
    return McpToolResult.text(args['text'] as String);
  },
);

docs.title: Tools that take a DTO
docs.text:
Extend McpDtoTool<T> to use a @Dto class as the input. handle gets the typed object, and @Describe explains a field to the model:

@Dto()
class NewCategory {
  @Describe('The category name, like Food.')
  @Length(min: 1, max: 50)
  final String name;

  @Describe('A color, like #1a2b3c.')
  @HexColor()
  final String color;

  const NewCategory({required this.name, required this.color});

  static const DtoSchema<NewCategory> schema = $NewCategoryDto;
}

class CreateCategory extends McpDtoTool<NewCategory> {
  @override
  String get name => 'create_category';

  @override
  String get description => 'Add a category.';

  @override
  DtoSchema<NewCategory> get dto => NewCategory.schema;

  @override
  Future<McpToolResult> handle(
      NewCategory input, McpContext context) async {
    // ... save it
    return McpToolResult.text('Added ${input.name}.');
  }
}

Dox checks the arguments like a DTO in a controller, also with async rules like @Unique and @Exists.

docs.title: Tool results
docs.text: A tool returns an McpToolResult.

docs.title: Text
docs.text:
McpToolResult.text sends one text:

return McpToolResult.text('Recorded 12.50.');

docs.title: JSON
docs.text:
McpToolResult.json sends a value as JSON text. A map is also sent as structured content:

return McpToolResult.json(<String, dynamic>{'id': 7, 'amount': 12.5});

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
For other content, give a list of McpContent items:

return McpToolResult(<McpContent>[
  McpContent.text('The chart of this month:'),
  McpContent.image(base64Png, 'image/png'),
]);

docs.title: Errors the model can fix
docs.text:
Return McpToolResult.error when the model can try again, like after a bad id. The model sees the text:

return McpToolResult.error('No expense has id 7.');

Bad arguments work the same way, with no code. The model gets one line with each problem:

Input validation error: Invalid arguments for tool create_category: name: The name is required; color: The color must be a hex color like #1a2b3c

docs.title: Errors in your code
docs.text:
If a tool throws, the client gets only Tool failed, because the real error can hold SQL or host names. The real error is shown only when APP_ENV is development or local. Set onToolError to log it:

McpServer(
  name: 'my-app',
  version: '1.0.0',
  tools: <McpTool>[AddExpense()],
  onToolError: (String tool, Object error, StackTrace stack) {
    Logger.danger('MCP tool $tool failed: $error');
  },
);

docs.title: Adding the route
docs.text:
Make one McpServer with your tools, and call handle from a route:

final McpServer mcp = McpServer(
  name: 'my-app',
  version: '1.0.0',
  tools: <McpTool>[AddExpense(), CreateCategory()],
  allowedOrigins: <String>['https://my.app'],
);

Route.match(<String>['GET', 'POST', 'DELETE'], '/mcp', (DoxRequest req) {
  return mcp.handle(req);
});

This route is open to everyone. That is fine only for a public server with no users.

docs.title: Checking who calls
docs.text:
The MCP route has no auth. Find the user before handle, then give auth (the user) and scope (a text that names the user):

Route.match(<String>['GET', 'POST', 'DELETE'], '/mcp',
    (DoxRequest req) async {
  User? user = await findUser(req.header('authorization'));
  if (user == null) return response('Invalid token').statusCode(401);
  return mcp.handle(req, auth: user, scope: 'user:${user.id}');
});

In a tool, read the user back:

User user = context.authAs<User>();

Warning

An app with users must always give scope. The server binds the data it signs to the scope. Without it, one user can send data that was signed for another user.

Proxies write a token in the URL to their logs, so send tokens in a header. To let clients sign in by themselves, use OAuth.

docs.title: What the client can do
docs.text:
context.clientCapabilities tells what the client supports:

McpClientCapabilities? client = context.clientCapabilities;
if (client != null && client.elicitationForm) {
  // the client can show a form to the user
}

It has elicitation, elicitationForm, elicitationUrl, sampling, roots and extensions. For other paths, has checks one, like client.has(<String>['sampling', 'tools']). It is null for older clients.

docs.title: Which client it is
docs.text:
context.clientInfo gives the name and version of the client, or null:

String name = context.clientInfo?.name ?? 'unknown';

Warning

The client says this about itself. Never use it for security.

docs.title: Asking the user
docs.text:
A tool can stop and ask the user a question, like "Delete this expense?". The client shows it, then calls the tool again with the answer. Make the question one time, in a static final field. The same object asks the question and reads the answer:

class DeleteExpense extends McpTool {
  static final McpInput<bool> confirmDelete = McpInput.confirm(
    'Delete this expense?',
  );

  // name, description, input ...

  @override
  Future<McpToolResult> call(
    Map<String, dynamic> args,
    McpContext context,
  ) async {
    McpAnswer<bool>? answer = context.answer(confirmDelete);
    if (answer == null) {
      return McpToolResult.inputRequired(
          <McpInput<Object?>>[confirmDelete]);
    }
    return switch (answer) {
      McpAccepted<bool>(value: true) => _delete(args),
      McpAccepted<bool>() ||
      McpDeclined<bool>() ||
      McpCancelled<bool>() => McpToolResult.text('Cancelled'),
    };
  }
}

The tool runs two times: first it asks, then context.answer gives the answer. It works the same in McpDtoTool.handle. The answers are signed, work only for the same user, tool and arguments, and expire after requestStateTtl.

Warning

The answers can be sent again until they expire. A tool that must run only one time, like a payment, must check that itself.

A question the client can not show gets an error that names the missing capability. An older client can not answer a question.

docs.title: Reading the answer
docs.text:
context.answer gives null when there is no answer yet, or the answer can not be read (like a form that fails the DTO rules). Then return McpToolResult.inputRequired. Else the answer is one of three classes:

  • McpAccepted<T>: the user answered. value holds the answer.
  • McpDeclined<T>: the user said no.
  • McpCancelled<T>: the user closed the question.

docs.title: Yes or no
docs.text:
McpInput.confirm asks a yes or no question. The answer is a bool:

static final McpInput<bool> confirmDelete = McpInput.confirm(
  'Delete this expense?',
);

docs.title: Text
docs.text:
McpInput.text asks for one line of text. The answer is a string:

static final McpInput<String> askNote = McpInput.text('Add a note:');

docs.title: Number
docs.text:
McpInput.number asks for a number. The answer is a num:

static final McpInput<num> askAmount = McpInput.number('How much was it?');

docs.title: Choice
docs.text:
McpInput.choice lets the user pick one value of an enum:

enum Color { red, green, blue }

static final McpInput<Color> askColor = McpInput.choice(
  'Pick a color:',
  Color.values,
);

docs.title: Form
docs.text:
McpInput.form asks for many fields at once, from a @Dto class. The answer is the DTO object, checked by its rules:

static final McpInput<NewExpense> askExpense = McpInput.form(
  'New expense',
  NewExpense.schema,
);

A form has flat fields only: text, numbers, booleans, enums and lists of enum values. The DTO can not have a nested object or async rules like @Unique.

Warning

Never ask for a password or a key in a form. Use a URL for that.

docs.title: URL
docs.text:
McpInput.url sends the user to a page, like a sign-in to another service. Use it for data that must not go through the client:

static final McpInput<void> connectBank = McpInput.url(
  'Connect your bank account.',
  'https://my.app/bank/connect',
);

McpAccepted means only that the user agreed to open the page, so check the result in your database. Never put a secret in the URL.

docs.title: Many questions
docs.text:
To ask many things at once, give a longer list. Read each answer with its own input. Two inputs with the same message throw an ArgumentError:

McpAnswer<String>? note = context.answer(askNote);
McpAnswer<num>? amount = context.answer(askAmount);
if (note == null || amount == null) {
  return McpToolResult.inputRequired(
      <McpInput<Object?>>[askNote, askAmount]);
}

A tool can also ask one question per round. Answers of earlier rounds are kept.

docs.title: Custom inputs
docs.text:
For a kind of input that dox_mcp does not have, extend McpCustomInput<T>. Give the method, the capability the client needs, the request as toJson, and parse to read the result:

class ListRoots extends McpCustomInput<List<String>> {
  @override
  String get method => 'roots/list';

  @override
  List<String> get capability => <String>['roots'];

  @override
  Map<String, Object?> toJson() {
    return <String, Object?>{};
  }

  @override
  List<String> parse(Map<String, Object?> result) {
    return <String>[
      for (Object? root in result['roots']! as List<Object?>)
        (root! as Map<String, Object?>)['uri']! as String,
    ];
  }
}

Use it like any other input, with context.answer and McpToolResult.inputRequired.

docs.title: Signing in with OAuth
docs.text:
With McpOAuth, you give the client only the address, like https://my.app/mcp. The client finds the rest and signs the user in, with OAuth 2.1 and PKCE. Your app makes the tokens and shows the consent page.

Option Default What it does issuer required the address of your app, like https://my.app tokens required your McpOAuthTokens codes the default cache store the cache store for the one-time codes mcpPath /mcp the path of the MCP route authorizePage <issuer>/oauth/authorize the address of the consent page codeTtl 1 minute how long a code works resourceName none a name for the server in the discovery file allowedClientHosts none see How clients sign in maxClientFetches 8 see How clients sign in maxClientFetchesPerHost 2 see How clients sign in clientCacheMaxAge 5 minutes the longest time a client document is kept in memory clientFetcher McpOAuthHttpFetcher() loads client documents. Tests give fake documents

docs.title: Tokens
docs.text:
Implement McpOAuthTokens. issue makes a token after the user said yes, and can throw an McpOAuthException, like access_denied. verify gives what a token stands for, like the user, or null. Keep only a hash of the token:

class McpTokens extends McpOAuthTokens {
  @override
  Future<String> issue(McpOAuthGrant grant) async {
    String token = newRandomToken(); // your own long random text
    // ... save Hash.sha256(token) for the user grant.subject
    return token;
  }

  @override
  Future<Object?> verify(String token) async {
    // ... find the user of this token, or return null
    return null;
  }
}

Warning

Keep MCP tokens apart from your other tokens, like in their own table. verify must accept only a token that issue made, so an API token does not work on the MCP route.

There is no refresh token. To revoke a client, delete its token.

docs.title: Routes
docs.text:
Make an McpOAuth and call routes in a router with no prefix, because clients look for /.well-known/... at the root of the host. Then check the token on the MCP route:

final McpOAuth oauth = McpOAuth(
  issuer: 'https://my.app',
  tokens: McpTokens(),
  codes: Cache().store('redis'),
);

class McpRouter extends Router {
  @override
  void register() {
    oauth.routes();
    Route.match(<String>['GET', 'POST', 'DELETE'], '/mcp', handleMcp);
  }
}

Future<DoxResponse> handleMcp(DoxRequest req) async {
  User? user = await oauth.authenticate(req) as User?;
  if (user == null) return oauth.unauthorized();
  return mcp.handle(req, auth: user, scope: 'user:${user.id}');
}

authenticate reads the Authorization: Bearer header and calls your verify. unauthorized answers 401 and tells the client where to sign in. All isolates must share the codes cache store, so use file on one server, or redis on many. The OAuth routes answer any origin and read no cookie.

Add a rate limit to the OAuth routes and the MCP route, because anyone can call /oauth/token, and each new client_id address makes the server load a file:

Route.middleware(<dynamic>[RateLimit(max: 30)], oauth.routes);

docs.title: The consent page
docs.text:
The client sends the browser to <issuer>/oauth/authorize. This page is yours: the person signs in there the usual way, then says yes or no. The page gets client_id, redirect_uri, state, code_challenge, code_challenge_method and resource in the query.

verifyClient gives the client for the page. It throws when the client or the redirect address is wrong:

McpOAuthClient client = await oauth.verifyClient(clientId, redirectUri);
// show client.name next to client.host, and the host of redirectUri

client.host is the host of the client address, like claude.ai. It is null for an older client that registered. findClient gives the client with no redirect check. The older checkClient and deny are not async: when the client document is not loaded yet, they start the load and throw invalid_client. Use verifyClient and denyClient in new code.

On yes, call approve. It gives the address to send the browser to:

String url = await oauth.approve(
  subject: '${user.id}',
  clientId: clientId,
  redirectUri: redirectUri,
  codeChallenge: codeChallenge,
  codeChallengeMethod: codeChallengeMethod,
  state: state,
  resource: resource,
);
return redirect(url);

On no, call denyClient:

String url = await oauth.denyClient(
  clientId: clientId,
  redirectUri: redirectUri,
  state: state,
);

The consent page decides who gets access, so keep these rules:

  • Put the yes route behind your login and CSRF protection. Without it, another site can make a signed-in person say yes.
  • Show the host of the redirect address, and the host of the client_id when it is an https address. The client chooses its own name, so the host is the part a person can trust.
  • HTML-escape the client name before you print it.

A redirect address must be https, or http on localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1].

docs.title: How clients sign in
docs.text:
A client names itself with a client metadata document. Its client_id is an https address of a JSON file with the name of the client and its redirect addresses. dox_mcp loads the file and checks it, so it stores nothing. Older clients can also register at POST /oauth/register.

The server loads only small files from public hosts, and follows no redirects. It keeps a document for its Cache-Control: max-age, at most clientCacheMaxAge. If the host does not answer, it uses the last document for up to 1 hour. A failed load is not tried again for 1 minute. These options limit the loads:

McpOAuth(
  issuer: 'https://my.app',
  tokens: McpTokens(),
  allowedClientHosts: <String>{'claude.ai'},
  maxClientFetches: 4,
);
  • allowedClientHosts: load client documents from these hosts only. By default, any public host works. It does not block clients that register.
  • maxClientFetches: how many documents one isolate loads at the same time. When all are busy, a new client is refused at once.
  • maxClientFetchesPerHost: how many of these loads can go to one host.
  • McpOAuthHttpFetcher(maxFetchesPerAddress:): how many loads can go to one IP address. The default is 2.

docs.title: Checking the origin
docs.text:
A web page on another site can try to call your MCP server from the browser of a user. Set allowedOrigins to your own sites to stop it, also for a server on localhost or a private network:

McpServer(
  name: 'my-app',
  version: '1.0.0',
  tools: <McpTool>[AddExpense()],
  allowedOrigins: <String>['https://my.app'],
);

A request with another Origin header gets 403. A request with no Origin is not from a browser, so it can always connect. When allowedOrigins is not set, the server writes a warning one time at start.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
Older clients (MCP 2025-11-25 and before) start with initialize and use a session. That is why the route takes GET, POST and DELETE. SignedMcpSessions signs each session id with a key from APP_KEY, so it stores nothing. A new APP_KEY stops all sessions, and clients start new ones.

To make DELETE end a session, give a cache store that all isolates share:

McpServer(
  name: 'my-app',
  version: '1.0.0',
  tools: <McpTool>[AddExpense()],
  sessions: SignedMcpSessions(ended: Cache().store('redis')),
);

For another kind of session, implement McpSessions. A batch from an older client can have at most 50 messages.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Authentication: users, tokens and login in a Dox app.
  • Validation: the schemas of tool arguments.
  • AI agents: help an AI agent write Dox code.

docs.title: OpenAPI
docs.text:
Dox makes OpenAPI 3.1 docs for your API from your routes, controllers and request classes.

You get three URLs: /docs, a Scalar page with every route and "Try it" buttons, /openapi.json and /openapi.yaml. The docs come from the routes, the @Dto request classes and the controller methods, so you write little by hand.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
A new app already serves /docs in development, but each route shows only its path and method. Do these steps to get the full docs:

  1. Write the config, with the generated openApiRegistry:

    lib/config/openapi.dart
    import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/generated/openapi.g.dart';

OpenApiConfig openApi = OpenApiConfig(
  info: Info(title: 'Blog API', version: '1.0.0'),
  registry: openApiRegistry,
);

    The import shows an error until the builder runs in step 3.

  2. Add it to AppConfig:

    lib/config/app.dart
    import 'package:my_app/config/openapi.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  openApi: openApi,
  // ...
);

  3. Run the builder. It writes lib/generated/openapi.g.dart. Run it again after you change routes, controllers, request classes or models, or use dox build_runner:watch:

    dart run build_runner build      # or: dox build_runner:build

  4. Start the app with APP_ENV=development in .env, and open http://localhost:3000/docs.

The docs are on only when APP_ENV is development or local. With no APP_ENV, the app is in production, and /docs gives 404.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Option Default What it does enabled none true or false turns the docs on or off. With none, they are on only when APP_ENV is development or local info Info(title: 'Dox API', version: '1.0.0') title and version of the API servers [] base URLs, like [Server('https://api.my.app')] registry empty openApiRegistry from lib/generated/openapi.g.dart securitySchemes, securityByMiddleware {} see Login schemes ui DocsUi.scalar the docs page: DocsUi.scalar or DocsUi.swagger scalar ScalarOptions() see Changing the docs page pageTitle info.title title of the /docs page include [] (all routes) only these paths go in the docs, like ['/api/*'] exclude [] these paths are left out, like ['/api/internal/*']

openApi.isEnabled tells you if the live docs are on.

docs.title: Describe a route
docs.text: A normal controller already gets docs, see What Dox fills in for you. For better text, put annotations from dox_core on the controller method. Each annotation also has a lower case name, like @summary('Log in'), except @Response.

docs.title: Adding a summary and tags
docs.text:
@Summary is the short title, @Description is the longer text, and @Tags puts the route in a group. @Tags also works on the class:

class BlogController {
  @Summary('Get one blog')
  @Description('Deleted blogs are not found.')
  @Tags(<String>['Blogs'])
  Future<Blog?> show(DoxRequest req, String id) async {
    return Blog().find(id);
  }
}

For GET /blogs/{id} with AuthMiddleware on the route, you get:

get:
  tags: [Blogs]
  summary: Get one blog
  description: Deleted blogs are not found.
  operationId: BlogController.show
  parameters:
    - {name: id, in: path, required: true, schema: {type: string}}
  responses:
    "200":
      content:
        application/json:
          schema: {$ref: "#/components/schemas/Blog"}
    "401": {description: Not logged in}
    "404": {description: Not found}
    "500": {description: Server error}
  security:
    - bearerAuth: []

For a class that is not in a Route.get(...) call, set its tag with @DoxController(tag: 'Users').

docs.title: Using doc comments
docs.text:
A /// comment on a method also sets the summary (the first line) and the description (the rest). An annotation wins over the comment:

/// Get one blog
///
/// Deleted blogs are not found.
Future<Blog?> show(DoxRequest req, String id) async {
  return Blog().find(id);
}

docs.title: Adding responses
docs.text:
@Response describes one answer. Add one for each status code:

@Summary('Log in')
@Request(LoginUser)
@Response(200, LoginResult)
@Response(401, null, description: 'Wrong email or password')
Future<dynamic> login(DoxRequest req) async { ... }

The type can be a model, List<User>, a @Dto, a Serializer or a basic type like String. With a 2xx @Response, the return type of the method is not used.

docs.title: Hiding a route
docs.text:
@ApiIgnore() leaves a method, or a full class, out of the docs. To leave out routes by path, use include and exclude in the config:

@ApiIgnore()
Future<void> internal(DoxRequest req) async { ... }

docs.title: Marking a route as deprecated
docs.text:
Use @ApiDeprecated() or the Dart @Deprecated:

@ApiDeprecated()
Future<List<Blog>> oldIndex() async { ... }

docs.title: Describing the request
docs.text:
The builder finds the request class of a method in this order:

  1. @Body(T), @Query(T) or @Request(T) on the method.
  2. An argument whose type is a @Dto class, like store(CreateBlog body).
  3. A req.validate<T>() call in the method, where T is a @Dto class.

For POST, PUT and PATCH, the request is the JSON body. For other methods, each field is a query param. @Body, @Query and @Dto(source: Source.query) set the place. The route body option wins over all of them.

@Dto()
class CreateBlog {
  @Length(min: 3, max: 200)
  final String title;

  /// Text of the blog.
  final String? description;   // nullable: optional

  final int views;             // default: optional, `default: 0`

  final Status status;         // enum: only `draft` or `published`

  final List<Tag> tags;        // a list of another @Dto class

  const CreateBlog({required this.title, this.description, this.views = 0,
      required this.status, required this.tags});
}

The keys are the keys the DTO reads: snake_case, or @Name('key'). @Dto(keyCase: KeyCase.field) keeps the field names. Each rule adds its JSON Schema keys, see the rules reference.

docs.title: Describing the response
docs.text:
The return type of the method gives the 200 answer. Future<T> counts as T.

Return type Schema a model (@DoxModel) $ref to the model. Keys in hidden are left out List<Model> an array of the model a @Dto class $ref to the class a Serializer<Model> the map that convert() returns, else the model Pagination total, per_page, last_page, current_page, data String, int, bool, Map, List the basic JSON type dynamic the types of the return values. A map literal gives its keys DoxResponse, void no schema

A model schema has the primary key, the @Column fields, created_at, updated_at, the relations (only when they are loaded) and the @Computed getters. It goes in components/schemas:

Blog:
  type: object
  properties:
    id: {type: integer}
    title: {type: [string, "null"]}
    user: {anyOf: [{$ref: "#/components/schemas/User"}, {type: "null"}]}
    created_at: {type: [string, "null"], format: date-time}

docs.title: Login schemes
docs.text:
"Try it" must know how a route is protected to send a token. Put @Security on a middleware class, and every route with this middleware gets the scheme:

/// `Authorization: Bearer <api key>`. Not a JWT.
@Security.bearer(format: 'API key')
class ApiKeyAuthMiddleware implements IDoxMiddleware { ... }

@Security.bearer() gives type: http, scheme: bearer, and format becomes bearerFormat. For a key in a header, use @Security.apiKey. The default header is X-API-Key:

@Security.apiKey(header: 'X-API-Key')
class HeaderKeyMiddleware implements IDoxMiddleware { ... }

Run dart run build_runner build after you add it. The scheme name is the class name without Middleware, with a small first letter: ApiKeyAuthMiddleware gives apiKeyAuth. Give scheme: 'myName' for another name.

A middleware with no @Security whose class name ends with AuthMiddleware gets bearerAuth.

docs.title: Setting schemes in the config
docs.text:
For a key in the query or a cookie, set the scheme in the config. The config wins over @Security:

OpenApiConfig(
  registry: openApiRegistry,
  securitySchemes: <String, SecurityScheme>{
    'apiKey': SecurityScheme.apiKey(name: 'key', location: 'query'),
  },
  securityByMiddleware: <String, List<Map<String, List<String>>>>{
    'ApiKeyMiddleware': <Map<String, List<String>>>[
      <String, List<String>>{'apiKey': <String>[]},
    ],
  },
);

SecurityScheme.bearer(bearerFormat: 'JWT') makes a bearer scheme, and SecurityScheme.raw(map) takes a raw OpenAPI map.

docs.title: What Dox fills in for you
docs.text:
A controller with no annotations gets docs. Annotations only change the result.

Part of the docs Where it comes from path, method the route table path param types the controller arguments after the first one, in order. int id gives integer tags the class name without Controller (BlogController gives Blog) operationId Class.method, like BlogController.show summary, description the annotations, else the /// comment request see Describing the request 200 answer the return type, see Describing the response 401 and a login scheme see Login schemes 401 and 403 the Can middleware, or a req.authorize(...) call in the method 403 the GuestMiddleware or ValidateSignature middleware, or a Gate.authorize(...) call in the method 404 the path has a {param} 422 the route has a request class, or the method calls req.validate<T>() or req.validateSchema(...) 500 every route
  • A @Response with the same status wins over an automatic answer. GuestMiddleware(redirectTo: ...) shows 403, but the app sends a redirect, so add a @Response(403, ...).
  • An optional param gives two paths: /blog/{id?} gives /blog/{id} and /blog. The short path gets no 404.
  • Dox matches a route to its docs by method name, HTTP method and the end of the path. When two controllers have a method with the same name, name the class in the route, like (LinkController c) => c.index.

docs.title: Changing the docs page
docs.text:
Change the look of the Scalar page with scalar:

OpenApiConfig(
  registry: openApiRegistry,
  pageTitle: 'Blog API docs',
  scalar: ScalarOptions(theme: ScalarTheme.purple, darkMode: true),
);
Option Default What it does theme ScalarTheme.default_ color theme, like moon, purple, deepSpace, saturn, kepler or mars darkMode false start in dark mode showDownloadButton true show the button that downloads the document proxyUrl none send "Try it" requests through this proxy. Without it, requests go from the browser to your API

To use Swagger UI, set ui:

OpenApiConfig(registry: openApiRegistry, ui: DocsUi.swagger);

docs.title: Turn the docs on in production
docs.text:
Set enabled: true to show the docs in production. enabled: false turns them off everywhere:

lib/config/openapi.dart
OpenApiConfig openApi = OpenApiConfig(
  enabled: true,
  info: Info(title: 'Blog API', version: '1.0.0'),
  registry: openApiRegistry,
);

Warning

/docs has no login, so anyone can see every route of your API. Do this only for a public API.

docs.title: Write the files
docs.text:
To get the document as files, for example for a client generator, run dox openapi:generate:

dox openapi:generate              # storage/openapi/openapi.json and .yaml
dox openapi:generate docs/api     # another folder

It runs bin/openapi.dart of your app. A new app does not have this file, so make it. writeOpenApi runs your providers and registers the routes:

bin/openapi.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);
  await Dox().writeOpenApi(args.isEmpty ? 'storage/openapi' : args.first);
  exit(0);
}

docs.title: Production setup
docs.text:
You can also make the document at build time, put the files in the image, and serve them. The URLs stay the same. You need lib/config/openapi.dart (see Setup) and bin/openapi.dart (see Write the files).

  1. Make both files, if you do not have them.

  2. Add a controller that serves the files. If your pubspec.yaml has no dox_openapi, run dart pub add dox_openapi:

    lib/app/http/controllers/docs.controller.dart
    import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_openapi/dox_openapi.dart'
    show OpenApiConstants, OpenApiServer;
import 'package:my_app/config/openapi.dart';

@Inject()
class DocsController {
  /// The same Scalar page as the live docs. It loads `/openapi.json`.
  final String _page = OpenApiServer(
    OpenApi(info: openApi.info),
    pageTitle: openApi.pageTitle,
    ui: openApi.ui,
    scalar: openApi.scalar,
  ).docsPage().body;

  DoxResponse page() {
    return response(_page).contentType(
        ContentType.parse(OpenApiConstants.htmlContentType));
  }

  DoxResponse json() {
    return _file('openapi.json', OpenApiConstants.jsonContentType);
  }

  DoxResponse yaml() {
    return _file('openapi.yaml', OpenApiConstants.yamlContentType);
  }

  DoxResponse _file(String name, String contentType) {
    File file = File('docs/openapi/$name');
    if (!file.existsSync()) throw NotFoundHttpException();
    return response(file.readAsStringSync())
        .contentType(ContentType.parse(contentType));
  }
}

  3. Add the routes only when the live docs are off, so they do not clash in development. Import openApi and the controller in this file:

    lib/routes/web.dart
    @override
void register() {
  if (!openApi.isEnabled) {
    Route.get('/docs', (DocsController c) => c.page);
    Route.get('/openapi.json', (DocsController c) => c.json);
    Route.get('/openapi.yaml', (DocsController c) => c.yaml);
  }
  // ...
}

  4. Make the files in the Docker build. In the build stage, right after RUN /root/.pub-cache/bin/dox build, add:

    Dockerfile
    RUN APP_KEY=only-for-the-build-not-a-key \
    /root/.pub-cache/bin/dox openapi:generate docs/openapi

    Then, in the RUN step that lays out /out, add /out/app/docs to mkdir -p and copy the files after the cp -r build/bundle/. /out/app/ line:

    Dockerfile
    RUN mkdir -p /out/app/storage /out/app/docs /out/tmp \
  && chmod 1777 /out/tmp \
  && cp -r build/bundle/. /out/app/ \
  && cp -r docs/openapi /out/app/docs/openapi \
  # ... the lines that follow stay as they are

    bin/openapi.dart loads your app config, so it needs an APP_KEY. The dummy key is only for this step. If a provider connects to a database in setup(), the build step must reach that database.

  5. Start the image with APP_ENV=production and open /docs.

To test it on your machine, run dox openapi:generate docs/openapi, then start the app with APP_ENV=production.

Warning

These routes have no login, so anyone can see every route of your API. To protect them, put a middleware on the three routes.

docs.title: Without Dox
docs.text:
dox_openapi also works on its own. Describe each route with ApiDoc:

import 'package:dox_openapi/dox_openapi.dart';

ApiDoc docs = ApiDoc();
Map<String, dynamic> user = docs.schema('User', userSchema); // a $ref

docs.route('GET', '/users/{id}',
    summary: 'Get one user',
    tags: <String>['users'],
    params: <String, Object>{'id': <String, dynamic>{'type': 'integer'}},
    responses: <int, ResponseDoc>{
      200: ResponseDoc(schema: user, description: 'The user'),
      404: const ResponseDoc(description: 'Not found'),
    });

OpenApi api = OpenApi(
    info: const Info(title: 'My API', version: '1.0.0'), docs: docs);

A schema can be a JSON Schema map, a dox_validation schema, or any object with toJsonSchema(). Paths can use {id} or :id. route also takes query, body, security, deprecated and operationId. OpenApi also takes servers, securitySchemes and security.

docs.title: Reading the docs back
docs.text: docs.ref('User') gives a $ref to a schema you added. docs.has('GET', '/users/{id}') tells you if a route has docs. docs.add(routeDoc) adds or replaces a RouteDoc.

docs.title: Getting the document
docs.text:
api.toJson();                              // Map
api.toJsonString();                        // pretty JSON
api.toYaml();                              // YAML
await api.writeFiles('storage/openapi');   // openapi.json + openapi.yaml

docs.title: Serving the docs from your own server
docs.text:
OpenApiServer gives the page and the document for a path. docsPage(), json() and yaml() give each one directly:

OpenApiServer server = OpenApiServer(api); // or ui: DocsUi.swagger
OpenApiResponse? page = server.handle('/docs'); // or '/openapi.json'
if (page != null) {
  // send page.body with the header Content-Type: page.contentType
}

docs.title: Text response keys
docs.text:
