  • Production checklist: what to check before you deploy.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
dox_auth lets users register, log in and log out, and it protects routes so only logged in users can use them.

It gives a password login against your user table, three ways to keep a user logged in (access tokens, JWT and sessions), AuthMiddleware to protect routes, and req.auth to get the user. Password reset, email checks, "remember me" and two-step login are for your app to build, for example with the two-step login recipe. Rules about who may do what are on the Authorization page.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: These steps start from a new app made with dox create my_app. It has a SQLite database, a User model and a users table with name, email and password columns.

docs.title: Choosing a guard
docs.text:
A guard is a named way to log in, like api or web. It has a driver (how the login is kept) and a provider (which model holds the users):

Your app Use An API for a mobile app, a front end on another domain, or scripts Access tokens. You can revoke each token, give it abilities and renew it. An API where other services check the token with a key JWT. The token is signed, so there is no token table. Web pages served by this app (forms, Inertia) Session. The browser sends the session cookie. Web pages and an API in one app More than one guard.

If you are not sure, use access tokens for an API.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
Run the command, then the migration it writes:

dox add auth
dox migrate

The command adds the dox_auth package, the auth config, the provider that loads the config, and the token table migration. It needs the ORM and a User model. It never overwrites a file. Without the command, run dart pub add dox_auth and write the config and provider below yourself. You always write the DTOs yourself.

docs.title: The user model
docs.text:
Put the password in hidden, so toJson() leaves it out. The model of a new app already does this:

lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel(table: 'users', softDelete: true)
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get fillable => <String>['name', 'email', 'password'];

  @override
  List<String> get hidden => <String>['password'];

  @Column()
  String? name;

  @Column()
  String? email;

  @Column()
  String? password;
}

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The config lists the guards. This config has one guard, api, with access tokens:

lib/config/auth.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

AuthConfig authConfig = AuthConfig(
  defaultGuard: 'api',
  guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
    'api': AuthGuard(
      driver: AccessTokenAuthDriver(expiresIn: const Duration(days: 30)),
      provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
    ),
  },
);

Auth() and AuthMiddleware() use the defaultGuard.

Option Default What it does AuthConfig(defaultGuard:) required the guard to use when no guard is given AuthConfig(guards:) {} the guards, by name AuthConfig(flags:) all off opt-in behavior. See Auth flags AuthGuard(driver:) required AccessTokenAuthDriver, JwtAuthDriver, SessionAuthDriver, or your own AuthDriver AuthGuard(provider:) required the AuthProvider AuthProvider(model:) required a function that makes a new model, like () => User() AuthProvider(identifierFields:) ['email'] the fields attempt searches by AuthProvider(passwordField:) 'password' the column with the bcrypt hash

The options of each driver are in its section: access tokens, JWT and session.

docs.title: Loading the config
docs.text:
A DoxProvider gives the config to dox_auth when the app starts. Dox finds it by itself. It is not the AuthProvider of the config:

lib/providers/auth_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/auth.dart';

class AppAuthProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Auth.initialize(authConfig);
  }
}

docs.title: Validating the input
docs.text:
Check the register and login body with DTOs. Bad input gets 422, and the controller does not run:

lib/app/dtos/auth/auth.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart' hide Schema;

part 'auth.dto.g.dart';

/// The body of a register request.
@Dto()
class RegisterUser {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 1, max: 255)
  final String name;

  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  @Unique('users', column: 'email')
  final String email;

  /// bcrypt reads at most 72 bytes
  @Length(min: 8, max: 72)
  final String password;

  const RegisterUser({
    required this.name,
    required this.email,
    required this.password,
  });

  static const DtoSchema<RegisterUser> schema = $RegisterUserDto;
}

/// The body of a login request.
@Dto()
class LoginUser {
  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  final String email;

  final String password;

  const LoginUser({required this.email, required this.password});

  static const DtoSchema<LoginUser> schema = $LoginUserDto;
}

Then run the code generator. It writes the DTO code and adds AppAuthProvider to lib/generated/container.g.dart:

dart run build_runner build

docs.title: Access tokens
docs.text:
An access token is an API token that you can revoke at any time. It looks like oat_12.<secret>, where 12 is the row id. The table keeps only a SHA-256 hash, so you see the plain token only once.

The setup above already added the api guard with AccessTokenAuthDriver. Its options:

Option Default What it does table 'auth_access_tokens' the table of the tokens connection the default connection the dox_orm connection name. Make the table on this connection expiresIn none how long a new token works hashRounds 10 the bcrypt cost of your stored hashes, for attempt type the guard name a token works only on a guard with the same type. If you rename a guard, set the old name here stringIds false true for users with text ids uuidIds false true for users with uuid ids throwOnError false true throws a database error in a token check, in place of 401. See When the database fails

docs.title: Creating the token table
docs.text:
dox add auth already wrote the migration. To write it yourself, run:

dox auth:tokens-table --users-table=users
dox migrate

--users-table=users adds a foreign key with cascade delete, so a deleted user loses its tokens.

Option of AccessTokenTables.up Flag Default What it does table none (edit the migration) 'auth_access_tokens' the table name. Use the same name as the driver table uuidIds --uuid false tokenable_id is a uuid column stringIds --string-ids false tokenable_id is text. Do not use it with --uuid usersTable --users-table=users none a foreign key from tokenable_id to usersKey of this table, with cascade delete usersKey --users-key=uid 'id' the key column of usersTable

AccessTokenTables.down(schema, table: 'auth_access_tokens') drops the table.

Warning

Without --users-table, call revokeAllAccessTokens(user) when you delete a user. Else old tokens can match a new user with the same id.

tokenable_type is the table name of the user model, so a rename of the users table stops old tokens.

docs.title: Issuing tokens
docs.text:
The controller makes a token on register and on login:

lib/app/http/controllers/auth.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/auth/auth.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class AuthController {
  /// POST /api/auth/register: make an account and give a token.
  Future<DoxResponse> register(RegisterUser body) async {
    User user = User()
      ..name = body.name
      ..email = body.email
      ..password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
    await user.save();

    AccessToken token = await Auth().createAccessToken(user, name: 'login');
    return response(<String, dynamic>{
      'token': token.value,
      'user': user,
    }).statusCode(201);
  }

  /// POST /api/auth/login: check the email and password, give a token.
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> login(DoxRequest req, LoginUser body) async {
    Auth auth = Auth(ip: req.ip());
    String? token = await auth.attempt(<String, dynamic>{
      'email': body.email,
      'password': body.password,
    });
    if (token == null) {
      throw UnAuthorizedException(message: 'Wrong email or password');
    }
    return <String, dynamic>{'token': token, 'user': auth.user<User>()};
  }

  /// GET /api/auth/me: the logged-in user.
  User? me(DoxRequest req) {
    return req.auth?.user<User>();
  }

  /// POST /api/auth/logout: the token of this request stops working.
  Future<Map<String, bool>> logout(DoxRequest req) async {
    await (req.auth as Auth).revokeToken(req);
    return <String, bool>{'logged_out': true};
  }
}

attempt finds the user by email and checks the password. It gives a new token with all abilities, or null. Auth(ip: req.ip()) gives the client ip to the login throttle.

docs.title: Protecting the API routes
docs.text:
Add AuthMiddleware() to a route. A request with no good token gets 401. Also put a rate limit on register and login, to slow down password guesses:

lib/routes/api.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/api.controller.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/auth.controller.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/ping', (ApiController c) => c.pong);

    // for guests
    Route.post('/auth/register', <dynamic>[
      RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'register'),
      (AuthController c) => c.register,
    ]);
    Route.post('/auth/login', <dynamic>[
      RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'login'),
      (AuthController c) => c.login,
    ]);

    // for logged-in users
    Route.get('/auth/me', <dynamic>[
      AuthMiddleware(),
      (AuthController c) => c.me,
    ]);
    Route.post('/auth/logout', <dynamic>[
      AuthMiddleware(),
      (AuthController c) => c.logout,
    ]);
  }
}

Run dart run build_runner build again, then start the app with dox s.

docs.title: Sending the token
docs.text:
The client sends the token in the Authorization header:

# log in, and keep the token in TOKEN
curl -X POST localhost:3000/api/auth/login \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"ada@example.com","password":"secret-pass"}'
# 200 {"token":"oat_2.OTAG...","user":{"id":1,...}}
TOKEN='oat_2.OTAG...'

curl localhost:3000/api/auth/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# 200 {"id":1,"name":"Ada","email":"ada@example.com",...}

curl localhost:3000/api/auth/me
# 401 {"code":"unauthorized","message":"Authentication failed"}

docs.title: Token abilities
docs.text:
An ability is a name like posts:read on a token. Give the abilities when you make the token. The default is *, which means all abilities:

AccessToken token = await auth.createAccessToken(
  auth.user<User>()!,
  name: 'script',
  abilities: <String>['posts:read'],
  expiresIn: const Duration(days: 90),
);

Check an ability with tokenCan. It is true when the token has the ability or *, and always false for a session or JWT login:

if (!(req.auth as Auth).tokenCan('posts:read')) {
  throw ForbiddenHttpException();
}

Warning

AuthMiddleware only checks that the token is good. Check the ability on each route that needs one. Guard the routes that make or renew tokens with an ability like tokens:manage, so a leaked script token can not make new tokens.

To replace all abilities of a token, use setAccessTokenAbilities:

await auth.setAccessTokenAbilities(token, <String>['posts:read']);

docs.title: Listing and revoking tokens
docs.text:
A revoked token is deleted from the table, so it stops at once:

await Auth().accessTokens(user);          // all tokens, newest first
await Auth().revokeAccessToken(user, id); // false when no such token
await Auth().revokeAllAccessTokens(user); // all tokens, gives how many
await Auth().revokeToken(req);            // the token of this request

Expired tokens stay in the table. Delete them from a scheduled task:

int deleted = await Auth().pruneExpiredAccessTokens();

docs.title: The token object
docs.text:
An AccessToken has these fields. token.toJson() has no hash and no plain token, so you can send a token list to the client:

Field What it is id the row id value the plain token. Set only by createAccessToken and rotateAccessToken name, type the name and the type tokenableType the table name of the user model tokenableId the user id: an integer, or a string with stringIds or uuidIds abilities the list of abilities lastUsedAt, expiresAt, createdAt, updatedAt times, in UTC user the user. Null in accessTokens(user) can(ability), cannot(ability) checks one ability (* passes every check) toJson() the token without the hash and the plain value

currentAccessToken on the Auth of a request gives the token of that request.

docs.title: Rotating tokens
docs.text:
rotateAccessToken renews a token before it expires. The new token has the same user, name and abilities, and the old token stops at once:

/// POST /api/auth/refresh: a new token in place of the token of this
/// request. The old token stops working at once.
Future<Map<String, dynamic>> refresh(DoxRequest req) async {
  Auth auth = req.auth as Auth;
  if (!auth.tokenCan('tokens:manage')) {
    throw ForbiddenHttpException();
  }
  AccessToken next = await auth.rotateAccessToken(auth.currentAccessToken!);
  return <String, dynamic>{
    'token': next.value,
    'expires_at': next.expiresAt?.toIso8601String(),
  };
}

A token can be rotated only once. A second rotate, or a rotate of a revoked or expired token, throws an UnAuthorizedException (401). Give name or expiresIn to change them on the new token.

If a client sends requests in parallel, give a short grace, so the old token works a few seconds more. A stolen old token also works in that time:

rotateAccessToken(token, grace: const Duration(seconds: 10))

Each rotate gives a full new life, so a client that rotates again and again stays logged in. To set a limit, keep the first login time yourself.

docs.title: A token table without rotated_at
docs.text:
An old token table without the rotated_at column works for all but rotate. Stop dox s, run dox make:migration add_rotated_at_to_auth_access_tokens, put this in the new file, then run dox migrate:

// ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

class AddRotatedAtToAuthAccessTokens extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.table('auth_access_tokens', (Table t) {
      t.dateTimeTz('rotated_at').nullable();
    });
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.table('auth_access_tokens', (Table t) {
      t.dropColumn('rotated_at');
    });
  }
}

docs.title: JWT tokens
docs.text: A JWT is a signed token. The server keeps no list of tokens, so a token works until it expires, unless you turn on revocation. The user is loaded from the database on each request, by the id in the token. For a walkthrough, see the JWT auth guide.

docs.title: Configuring the JWT guard
docs.text:
Use JwtAuthDriver. secret signs the tokens and must be at least 32 bytes, so APP_KEY works:

lib/config/auth.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

AuthConfig authConfig = AuthConfig(
  defaultGuard: 'api',
  guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
    'api': AuthGuard(
      driver: JwtAuthDriver(
        secret: SecretKey(env.appKey),
        expiresIn: const Duration(days: 7),
        // the token holds only the user id
        minimalPayload: true,
        // lets logout stop a token before it expires
        revocation: true,
      ),
      provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
    ),
  },
);
Option Default What it does secret required the key that signs tokens, at least 32 bytes algorithm JWTAlgorithm.HS256 the signing algorithm. A token with another algorithm is rejected expiresIn Duration(hours: 1) how long a token is valid issuer none the iss claim. When set, the check also reads it hashRounds 10 the bcrypt cost of your stored hashes userCacheTtl off keep the user of a token in memory for this time. See Caching the user previousSecrets none old secrets to check tokens after a key change. With none and secret set to APP_KEY, Dox uses AppConfig.previousKeys. [] turns it off minimalPayload false put only the user id (the sub claim) in new tokens revocation false turn on token revocation revocationStore the default store the cache store for revoked tokens

A token keeps the guard name in its aud claim, so it works only on its own guard.

docs.title: Issuing JWT tokens
docs.text:
The controller and routes are the same as for access tokens, with two changes. On register, Auth().login(user) gives a token with no password check:

String? token = Auth().login(user);

On logout, revoke the token. This needs revocation: true:

await Auth().revokeToken(req);

attempt checks the password and gives a JWT. To read the token of a request yourself, use JwtAuthDriver.bearerToken(req).

docs.title: Small tokens
docs.text: Anyone can read the payload of a JWT, because it is signed, not secret. By default the token holds the user (toJson() without the hidden fields). Set minimalPayload: true, so the token holds only the user id, and load the user with req.auth?.user<User>().

docs.title: Revoking tokens
docs.text:
Turn on revocation to let logout stop a token at once. The driver keeps revoked tokens in a cache store:

JwtAuthDriver(
  secret: SecretKey(env.appKey),
  revocation: true,
  revocationStore: 'auth',
)

revokeToken logs out one token. revokeAllTokens logs a user out on all devices, for example after a password change or a ban. Tokens made after the call still work:

await Auth().revokeToken(req);     // the bearer token of this request
await Auth().revokeAllTokens(id);  // all tokens of this user

With revocation off, these methods throw a StateError. When the store can not be read, the token is checked without it, and Dox prints a warning one time.

Warning

Give auth its own cache store, like redis with its own prefix, and never flush it. A flush brings revoked tokens back until they expire.

docs.title: Caching the user
docs.text:
userCacheTtl keeps the user in memory for that time, so a request makes no query. Each isolate has its own cache. After a ban or a change to the user, drop it from the cache with forgetUser. This needs revocation:

JwtAuthDriver(
  secret: SecretKey(env.appKey),
  revocation: true,
  userCacheTtl: const Duration(minutes: 1),
);

await Auth().forgetUser(user.id);

docs.title: Changing the secret
docs.text:
New tokens are signed with secret, and old tokens are also checked with the old secrets. If the secret is APP_KEY, follow Rotating the key. For a separate JWT secret, give the old one to the driver:

JwtAuthDriver(
  secret: SecretKey(env.jwtSecret),
  previousSecrets: <JWTKey>[SecretKey(env.jwtOldSecret)],
)

Remove the old secret when expiresIn has passed. To log out everyone, change the secret and keep no old secrets.

Warning

Never keep a leaked secret. A person who has it can make tokens.

Another service that checks the tokens needs the HMAC key, driver.signingKey. Dox makes it from secret with the label dox:jwt.

docs.title: Session login for web pages
docs.text: For web pages, keep the login in the session. The browser sends the session cookie. This needs SessionMiddleware and CsrfMiddleware. See Session and CSRF protection.

docs.title: Configuring the session guard
docs.text:
Use SessionAuthDriver. Its only option is hashRounds, the bcrypt cost of your stored hashes (default 10):

lib/config/auth.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

AuthConfig authConfig = AuthConfig(
  defaultGuard: 'web',
  guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
    'web': AuthGuard(
      driver: SessionAuthDriver(),
      provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
    ),
  },
);

The session keeps only the user id, so a deleted user is logged out on the next request.

Warning

With the default cookie session driver, an old copy of the cookie works until the session lifetime ends. If logout must end old cookies, use the cache session driver.

docs.title: Logging in
docs.text:
attemptSession checks the password and keeps the user id in the session. loginSession logs a user in with no password check. logout removes the login and all session data. Login and logout also give the session a new id and a new CSRF token.

This controller answers JSON, for a front end with axios or Inertia:

lib/app/http/controllers/session.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/auth/auth.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class SessionController {
  /// POST /register: make an account and log in.
  Future<DoxResponse> register(DoxRequest req, RegisterUser body) async {
    User user = User()
      ..name = body.name
      ..email = body.email
      ..password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
    await user.save();

    Auth().loginSession(req, user);
    return response(user).statusCode(201);
  }

  /// POST /login: check the email and password, keep the login.
  Future<User?> login(DoxRequest req, LoginUser body) async {
    Auth auth = Auth();
    bool ok = await auth.attemptSession(req, <String, dynamic>{
      'email': body.email,
      'password': body.password,
    });
    if (!ok) {
      throw UnAuthorizedException(message: 'Wrong email or password');
    }
    return auth.user<User>();
  }

  /// GET /me: the logged-in user.
  User? me(DoxRequest req) {
    return req.auth?.user<User>();
  }

  /// POST /logout: remove the login and all session data.
  Map<String, bool> logout(DoxRequest req) {
    Auth().logout(req);
    return <String, bool>{'logged_out': true};
  }
}

For an HTML form, answer with a redirect. The method then returns Future<DoxResponse>. See CSRF protection for the form token:

if (!ok) {
  req.session.flashErrors(<String, dynamic>{
    'email': 'Wrong email or password',
  });
  return back(req);
}
return redirect('/dashboard');

docs.title: Adding the routes
docs.text:
Put the session and CSRF middleware on the web router only, so the API routes have no session:

lib/routes/web.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/session.controller.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/web.controller.dart';

class WebRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[
    const SessionMiddleware(),
    const CsrfMiddleware(),
  ];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/ping', (WebController c) => c.pong);

    Route.post('/register', <dynamic>[
      RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'register'),
      (SessionController c) => c.register,
    ]);
    Route.post('/login', <dynamic>[
      RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'login'),
      (SessionController c) => c.login,
    ]);
    Route.get('/me', <dynamic>[
      AuthMiddleware(),
      (SessionController c) => c.me,
    ]);
    Route.post('/logout', <dynamic>[
      AuthMiddleware(),
      (SessionController c) => c.logout,
    ]);
  }
}

docs.title: Redirecting guests
docs.text:
Send a guest to the login page in place of 401 with redirectTo:

AuthMiddleware(redirectTo: '/login')

With the jsonNoRedirect flag, a JSON client gets 401 and no redirect.

docs.title: Ending sessions when the password changes
docs.text:
By default a session stays logged in after a password change, so a stolen session still works. Turn on the endSessionsOnPasswordChange flag. A password change then ends all sessions of the user on their next request through AuthMiddleware:

lib/config/auth.dart
AuthConfig authConfig = AuthConfig(
  defaultGuard: 'web',
  guards: guards,
  flags: const AuthFlags(endSessionsOnPasswordChange: true),
);

This also ends the current session. To keep it when your app changes the password, call updateSessionPasswordHash after save(). Give a fully loaded user, because a user with no password column ends the session:

user.password = await Hash.makeAsync(newPassword);
await user.save();
Auth().updateSessionPasswordHash(req, user);

A session made while the flag was off gets its check on its first request. To end all old sessions at once, change APP_KEY with no previousKeys, or clear the cache session store.

docs.title: Logging out other devices
docs.text:
logoutOtherDevices ends all other sessions of the user and keeps this one. It checks the password from a form, and needs a session guard and the flag above:

/// POST /logout-others: end the sessions on other devices.
Future<Map<String, bool>> logoutOthers(
    DoxRequest req, ConfirmPassword body) async {
  await (req.auth as Auth).logoutOtherDevices(req, body.password);
  return <String, bool>{'done': true};
}

ConfirmPassword is a DTO with one password field. A wrong password throws an UnAuthorizedException (401, code wrong_password). Put a rate limit on the route, like on a login.

docs.title: More than one guard
docs.text:
One app can have many kinds of login, like a session for web pages, tokens for the API, and admins in their own table. Each guard has its own driver and user model:

lib/config/auth.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/admin/admin.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

AuthConfig authConfig = AuthConfig(
  defaultGuard: 'web',
  guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
    'web': AuthGuard(
      driver: SessionAuthDriver(),
      provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
    ),
    'api': AuthGuard(
      driver: AccessTokenAuthDriver(),
      provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
    ),
    'admin': AuthGuard(
      driver: AccessTokenAuthDriver(table: 'admin_access_tokens'),
      provider: AuthProvider(model: () => Admin()),
    ),
  },
);

Pick a guard by name with guard:

String? token = await Auth(guard: 'admin').attempt(credentials);

Route.get('/admin', <dynamic>[
  AuthMiddleware(guard: 'admin'),
  (AdminController c) => c.index,
]);

To accept many guards on a route, use guards. The first guard with a good login sets req.auth:

Route.get('/me', <dynamic>[
  AuthMiddleware(guards: <String>['web', 'api']),
  (UserController c) => c.me,
]);

A token of one guard does not work on another guard. Give each user model its own token table, with table on the driver and in the migration: AccessTokenTables.up(schema, table: 'admin_access_tokens').

docs.title: Optional login
docs.text:
AuthMiddleware(optional: true) sets req.auth when the login is good, and lets guests through with req.auth as null:

Route.get('/posts', <dynamic>[
  AuthMiddleware(optional: true),
  (PostController c) => c.index,
]);

A database error in a token check then goes on as a guest and is reported. With the session driver, it gives 500.

docs.title: Pages for guests only
docs.text:
GuestMiddleware sends a logged-in user to redirectTo. With no redirectTo, the answer is 403. Give guard to check another guard:

Route.get('/login', <dynamic>[
  GuestMiddleware(redirectTo: '/dashboard'),
  (PageController c) => c.login,
]);

docs.title: Getting the logged in user
docs.text:
After AuthMiddleware, req.auth holds the login. It is null for a guest:

User? user = req.auth?.user<User>();
dynamic id = req.auth?.id();                  // the primary key
bool loggedIn = req.auth?.isLoggedIn() ?? false;
Map<String, dynamic>? json = req.auth?.toJson(); // no hidden fields

id() works also when the key is in hidden. On Auth, check() is the same as isLoggedIn(), and guest() is the opposite. For tokenCan, currentAccessToken and revokeToken, cast it: req.auth as Auth.

docs.title: Setting the user yourself
docs.text:
In your own middleware, set the user with setUser. Then req.auth gives this user:

Auth(guard: 'api').setUser(req, user);

docs.title: Login throttle
docs.text:
Limit failed logins, to stop password guesses on one account. The throttle is off by default. Turn it on in your auth provider, because it is static and each isolate must set it:

lib/providers/auth_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/auth.dart';

class AppAuthProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Auth.initialize(authConfig);
    Auth.throttle = LoginThrottle();
  }
}
Option Default What it does maxAttempts 5 failed logins allowed per login field and ip decay Duration(minutes: 1) how long the count is kept, from the first failed login store the default store the cache store for the counts

After maxAttempts failed logins for the same email and ip, the next try throws LoginThrottledException (429) until decay has passed. Its retryAfter gives the time to wait. A good login clears the count.

Warning

Always give the ip with Auth(ip: req.ip()). Without an ip, the count is per account only, so anyone can lock an account. attemptSession takes the ip from the request.

With many isolates or servers, use a shared store, like LoginThrottle(store: 'redis'). The throttle does not stop many tries sent at the same time, so also keep a RateLimit on the login route.

docs.title: Password hashing
docs.text:
Passwords use bcrypt with cost 10. If you raise it, set the cost for new hashes and on the driver, so a login for an unknown email takes as long as a wrong password:

Hash.rounds = 12;
JwtAuthDriver(secret: SecretKey(env.appKey), hashRounds: 12);
SessionAuthDriver(hashRounds: 12);
AccessTokenAuthDriver(hashRounds: 12);

Old hashes keep their cost and still work. Hash them again on the next good login:

if (Auth.needsRehash(user.password!)) {
  user.password = await Hash.makeAsync(password);
  await user.save();
  // with a session login and the endSessionsOnPasswordChange flag:
  // Auth().updateSessionPasswordHash(req, user);
}

Auth.needsRehash(hash, rounds: 12) checks against another cost. Auth.hashCost(hash) gives the cost of a hash, or null. bcrypt reads at most 72 bytes, so limit the length in the DTO. See Hashing.

docs.title: Logging in with another field
docs.text:
attempt searches the user by identifierFields and checks the column in passwordField. Change them for a username login, or a hash in another column:

AuthProvider(
  model: () => User(),
  identifierFields: <String>['username'],
  passwordField: 'password_hash',
)

docs.title: Checking a password only
docs.text:
once checks the password like attempt, but makes no token and does not touch the session. It gives true or false:

bool ok = await Auth(ip: req.ip()).once(credentials);

docs.title: Users with uuid or text ids
docs.text:
Access tokens keep the user id in tokenable_id, a big integer by default. Use the same choice in the migration and on the driver:

  • uuid ids: dox auth:tokens-table --uuid and AccessTokenAuthDriver(uuidIds: true).
  • text ids: dox auth:tokens-table --string-ids and AccessTokenAuthDriver(stringIds: true).

Session and JWT guards need nothing for this.

docs.title: Two-step login (2FA)
docs.text:
A two-step login asks for a password, then for a code. Your app makes and checks the code. dox_auth helps with tokens:

  1. Step one checks the password with once(), and gives a short token with only the 2fa:pending ability.
  2. Step two checks the code, rotates the token, and gives the new token all abilities with setAccessTokenAbilities.
  3. Each route that needs the second step uses a middleware that refuses 2fa:pending tokens.

The controller with both steps:

lib/app/http/controllers/two_factor.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/auth/auth.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/two_factor_code/two_factor_code.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class TwoFactorController {
  /// POST /api/auth/login, step one: check the password. The token
  /// works 10 minutes, and only for step two.
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> login(DoxRequest req, LoginUser body) async {
    Auth auth = Auth(ip: req.ip());
    bool ok = await auth.once(<String, dynamic>{
      'email': body.email,
      'password': body.password,
    });
    if (!ok) {
      throw UnAuthorizedException(message: 'Wrong email or password');
    }
    AccessToken token = await auth.createAccessToken(
      auth.user<User>()!,
      name: 'login',
      abilities: <String>['2fa:pending'],
      expiresIn: const Duration(minutes: 10),
    );
    // send the code to the user here, for example by mail
    return <String, dynamic>{'token': token.value, 'two_factor': true};
  }

  /// POST /api/auth/two-factor, step two: check the code. Give a new
  /// token for a full login. The step-one token ends.
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> verify(
      DoxRequest req, TwoFactorCode body) async {
    Auth auth = req.auth as Auth;
    AccessToken token = auth.currentAccessToken!;
    if (!token.abilities.contains('2fa:pending')) {
      throw ForbiddenHttpException();
    }
    if (!_codeIsGood(auth.user<User>()!, body.code)) {
      throw UnAuthorizedException(message: 'Wrong code');
    }
    // a new token with the expiresIn of the driver. It has 2fa:pending.
    AccessToken full = await auth.rotateAccessToken(token);
    // all abilities, like a normal login
    await auth.setAccessTokenAbilities(full, <String>['*']);
    return <String, dynamic>{'token': full.value};
  }

  /// Check the code with your own two-step code. Make each code expire,
  /// and limit the wrong tries per user.
  bool _codeIsGood(User user, String code) {
    throw UnimplementedError('check the two-step code');
  }
}

verify checks abilities.contains('2fa:pending'), not tokenCan, because tokenCan is also true for *. Rotate first, then set the abilities, so no token has * when a step fails.

The middleware for the routes of a logged-in user. Put it after AuthMiddleware():

lib/app/http/middleware/two_factor.middleware.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// Lets a request through only when its token did the second step.
/// Put it after AuthMiddleware.
dynamic requireTwoFactor(DoxRequest req) {
  Auth? auth = req.auth as Auth?;
  if (auth == null || auth.currentAccessToken == null) {
    throw UnAuthorizedException();
  }
  if (auth.currentAccessToken!.abilities.contains('2fa:pending')) {
    throw ForbiddenHttpException();
  }
  return req;
}

Use TwoFactorController.login as the login route, and add the step-two route with a rate limit:

Route.post('/auth/login', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'login'),
  (TwoFactorController c) => c.login,
]);
Route.post('/auth/two-factor', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'two-factor'),
  AuthMiddleware(),
  (TwoFactorController c) => c.verify,
]);

Warning

A route without requireTwoFactor still takes a step-one token. Register must give no token, and every other place that gives a token must also do both steps.

docs.title: Checking a login with no request
docs.text:
Code with no request, like a Socket.IO login, can check a token or a session. Both give null when the login is not good:

User? user = await Auth(guard: 'api').userFromToken(token);
User? user = await Auth(guard: 'web').userFromSession(session);

userFromToken works for JWT and access token guards. Give the token without the Bearer prefix. For userFromSession, load the session with SessionMiddleware().fromCookie(value). See Session.

docs.title: Writing your own guard
docs.text:
To log users in your own way, like with an API key in a header, extend AuthDriver and return the user from verifyToken. This driver finds the user by a SHA-256 hash of the key, with the crypto package:

lib/app/auth/api_key_auth_driver.dart
import 'dart:convert';

import 'package:crypto/crypto.dart';
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

/// `Authorization: Bearer <api key>` gives the user with this key.
class ApiKeyAuthDriver extends AuthDriver {
  @override
  Future<Model<dynamic>?> verifyToken(IDoxRequest req, String guard) async {
    String header = req.header('Authorization') ?? '';
    if (!header.startsWith('Bearer ')) return null;
    String key = header.substring(7).trim();
    String hash = sha256.convert(utf8.encode(key)).toString();
    Model<dynamic> model = AuthEngine().guard(guard).provider.model();
    return await model.where('api_key_hash', hash).getFirst();
  }

  /// no password login for this guard
  @override
  Future<Model<dynamic>?> attempt(
      Map<String, dynamic> credentials, String guard) async => null;

  /// no token to make: the key is the token
  @override
  String? createToken(Map<String, dynamic>? userPayload, String guard) =>
      null;
}

Add it as a guard, and use the guard on the route:

'key': AuthGuard(
  driver: ApiKeyAuthDriver(),
  provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
),

Route.get('/me', <dynamic>[
  AuthMiddleware(guard: 'key'),
  (DoxRequest req) => req.auth?.user<User>(),
]);

Make each key long and random, like openssl rand -hex 32. Then SHA-256 is safe. Do not use bcrypt here, because you can not search by a bcrypt hash.

For a password login in your driver, AuthDriver.checkCredentials(credentials, guard, rounds) gives the user when the password matches. AuthDriver.reportError(error, stackTrace) sends an error to the exception handler of the app.

docs.title: When the database fails
docs.text:
When the database fails in an access token check, the request gets 401 and the error is reported. Many clients take 401 as "logged out". Turn on throwOnError to throw the error:

AccessTokenAuthDriver(
  expiresIn: const Duration(days: 30),
  throwOnError: true,
)

The error then goes to your exception handler, which answers 500. To answer 503, so the client tries again, catch the database errors in render:

lib/app/exception_handler.dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:sqlite3/sqlite3.dart' show SqliteException;

class AppExceptionHandler extends ExceptionHandler {
  const AppExceptionHandler();

  @override
  dynamic render(Object error, HttpRequest req) {
    // a database error: ask the client to try again
    if (error is SqliteException ||
        error is PgException ||
        error is MysqlException) {
      return HttpStatusException(503,
          headers: <String, String>{'retry-after': '5'});
    }
    return super.render(error, req);
  }
}

SqliteException comes from the sqlite3 package (dart pub add sqlite3). Set the handler with exceptionHandler: const AppExceptionHandler() in AppConfig.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
DoxTestClient runs your app in the test, and withToken sends Authorization: Bearer <token>. This test works for access tokens and JWT. It uses the database of .env, so it runs the migrations first:

test/auth_test.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    Dox().initialize(appConfig);
    await Migrator(
      migrations: migrations,
      config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
    ).migrate();
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('register, then use the token', () async {
    String email = 'test-${DateTime.now().microsecondsSinceEpoch}@a.com';
    TestResponse register = await client.post(
      '/api/auth/register',
      body: <String, dynamic>{
        'name': 'Test',
        'email': email,
        'password': 'secret-pass',
      },
    );
    register.expectStatus(201);
    String token = register.json['token'] as String;

    TestResponse me = await client.withToken(token).get('/api/auth/me');
    me.expectStatus(200);
    expect(me.json['email'], email);
    expect(me.json.containsKey('password'), isFalse);
  });

  test('no token gives 401', () async {
    (await client.get('/api/auth/me')).expectStatus(401);
  });
}

To act as a user with no HTTP login, make a token with await Auth().createAccessToken(user), then use client.withToken(token.value!). For a session app, use client.withSession(), which keeps cookies and sends the CSRF token. See Testing.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
The status codes: 401 means the user is not logged in. 403 means the user may not do this, like a missing ability or a failed policy. 419 is a session request with no CSRF token. 429 is too many failed logins.

Error Cause Fix LateInitializationError: Field 'config' has not been initialized. Auth.initialize did not run. AppAuthProvider is missing, or the generator did not run. Add AppAuthProvider, then run dart run build_runner build. 401 Authentication failed No Authorization header, a bad, expired or revoked token, a deleted user, or a token of another guard. Send Authorization: Bearer <token>. Log in again. 403 Forbidden The token does not have the ability. Use a token with the ability. See Token abilities. Invalid argument (guard): no auth guard with this name: "admin" A guard name that is not in guards. Fix the name, or add the guard. Bad state: The auth guard 'api' does not use SessionAuthDriver. ... logout, attemptSession or loginSession on a token guard. Use revokeToken(req) to log out a token. Bad state: The auth guard 'api' does not use AccessTokenAuthDriver. An access token method on a JWT or session guard. Use a guard with AccessTokenAuthDriver. Bad state: The auth guard 'web' does not use JwtAuthDriver. revokeAllTokens, forgetUser, userFromToken or revokeToken on a session guard. A session logs out with logout(req). Bad state: AccessTokenAuthDriver makes tokens with Auth().createAccessToken(user), not login(). Auth().login(user) on an access token guard. Use createAccessToken(user). Bad state: revokeToken needs token revocation. ... A revoke method on a JWT guard without revocation. Set revocation: true. See Revoking tokens. Bad state: The table 'auth_access_tokens' has no rotated_at column. ... rotateAccessToken on an old token table. Add the column. See A token table without rotated_at. 401 The access token was already rotated. A second rotate of the same token. Rotate the new token, not the old one. 401 The access token is expired. or is revoked or does not exist. Rotate of an expired or revoked token. Log in again. Invalid argument(s) (secret): The JWT secret is empty. ... JwtAuthDriver with an empty secret. Set APP_KEY with dox key:generate. Invalid argument(s) (secret): The JWT secret is <n> bytes. ... A secret shorter than 32 bytes. In development, local, test and testing it is only a warning. Run dox key:generate. Invalid argument(s) (password): The password is too long. ... A password longer than 72 bytes. Limit the length in the DTO. Invalid argument(s): Set guard or a non-empty guards list, not both. AuthMiddleware with both guard and guards, or guards: []. Set one of them. 429 Too many login attempts. ... The login throttle. Wait retryAfter. 419 CSRF token mismatch A session POST without the CSRF token. See CSRF protection. 403 Already logged in GuestMiddleware with no redirectTo, for a logged-in user. Set redirectTo, or log out first. 401 wrong_password logoutOtherDevices with a wrong password. Show an error on the form. Bad state: logoutOtherDevices() needs the endSessionsOnPasswordChange flag logoutOtherDevices with the flag off. Turn the flag on.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text:
dox_auth lets you decide what a logged in user may do, with gates and policies.

Authentication tells you who the user is. Authorization tells you what this user may do. A gate is one rule, written as a function. A policy is a class with all the rules of one model, like Post.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Gates and policies are kept per isolate. Add them in the setup() of a provider, because it runs in every isolate:

lib/providers/gate_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/policies/post_policy.dart';

class GateProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Gate.define('update-post',
        (User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id);
    Gate.policy<Post>(PostPolicy());
  }
}

Run dart run build_runner build to add the provider to lib/generated/container.g.dart.

docs.title: Writing gates
docs.text:
A gate gets the user and a subject, and gives true when the user may do it. A check with another user or subject type is denied:

Gate.define('update-post',
    (User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id);

For a gate with no subject, use _ for the second parameter:

Gate.define('create-post', (User user, _) => user.verified == true);

A gate can also be async:

Gate.define('publish-post', (User user, Post post) async {
  return await user.canPublishIn(post.categoryId);
});

docs.title: Checking a gate
docs.text:
Gate.allows gives true when the user may do it, and Gate.denies gives the opposite:

if (await Gate.allows(user, 'update-post', post)) {
  // the user may update the post
}

if (await Gate.denies(user, 'create-post')) {
  // the user may not create a post
}

Gate.authorize throws when the check fails, and the client gets 403:

await Gate.authorize(user, 'update-post', post);

Gate.any checks that at least one ability is allowed. Gate.all checks that all are allowed:

await Gate.any(user, <String>['update-post', 'delete-post'], post);
await Gate.all(user, <String>['update-post', 'delete-post'], post);

An ability with no gate and no policy is always denied.

docs.title: Giving a reason
docs.text:
Return a GateResponse in place of a bool. The reason of GateResponse.deny becomes the message of the 403 answer:

Gate.define('delete-post', (User user, Post post) {
  if (post.published == true) {
    return GateResponse.deny('You can not delete a published post.');
  }
  return post.userId == user.id;
});

Gate.inspect gives the full answer. authorize() on it throws 403 when it is denied:

GateResponse response = await Gate.inspect(user, 'delete-post', post);
print(response.allowed); // or response.denied
print(response.message);
response.authorize();

docs.title: Writing policies
docs.text:
Put the rules of one model in a policy. Write one method per ability, then list the methods in abilities. A method takes the user, and the model when the ability needs one:

lib/app/policies/post_policy.dart
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class PostPolicy extends Policy<User, Post> {
  bool create(User user) => user.verified == true;

  bool update(User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id;

  bool delete(User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id;

  @override
  Map<String, Function> get abilities => <String, Function>{
    'create': create,
    'update': update,
    'delete': delete,
  };
}

Register the policy for its model. A method with another signature than (User user) or (User user, Post post) fails here, when the app starts:

Gate.policy<Post>(PostPolicy());

Now a check with a Post subject uses the policy. For an ability with no model, like create, give the type Post:

await Gate.allows(user, 'update', post);
await Gate.allows(user, 'create', Post);
await Gate.authorize(user, 'delete', post);

When the policy has no method for an ability, Dox uses the gate with that name.

docs.title: Using the ability constants
docs.text:
The Ability constants let the compiler find a wrong ability name: Ability.viewAny, Ability.view, Ability.create, Ability.update and Ability.delete. Ability.update is the same as 'update':

Map<String, Function> get abilities => <String, Function>{
  Ability.update: update,
};

await Gate.allows(user, Ability.update, post);

docs.title: Finding rules
docs.text:
Check if a rule exists, for example in a package that makes code for models:

Gate.isDefined('update-post');         // a gate with this name
Gate.hasAbility<Post>('view');         // the Post policy has 'view'
Gate.policyOf<Post>()?.abilities.keys; // the Post policy, or null

docs.title: Authorizing in a controller
docs.text:
In a controller, use req.authorize, req.can and req.cannot. They use the user of req.auth, so put the route after AuthMiddleware:

Future<Post> update(DoxRequest req, Post post) async {
  await req.authorize('update', post);
  post.title = req.input('title');
  await post.save();
  return post;
}

req.authorize answers 401 for a guest and 403 for a user who may not do it. req.can gives a bool, for example for the front end:

Future<Map<String, dynamic>> show(DoxRequest req, Post post) async {
  return <String, dynamic>{
    'post': post,
    'can_edit': await req.can('update', post),
  };
}

docs.title: Authorizing on a route
docs.text:
The Can middleware checks an ability before the controller runs. Put it after AuthMiddleware:

// a gate with no subject
Route.get('/admin', <dynamic>[
  AuthMiddleware(),
  Can('view-admin'),
  adminController.index,
]);

For a policy method with no model, give the type with subject:

Route.post('/posts', <dynamic>[
  AuthMiddleware(),
  Can('create', subject: Post),
  postController.store,
]);

For a policy method with a model, use param. The subject is the value that Route.bind gives for that route param. When Route.bind finds nothing, the answer is 404:

Route.bind<Post>('post', (String id) => Post().find(id));
Route.put('/posts/{post}', <dynamic>[
  AuthMiddleware(),
  Can('update', param: 'post'),
  postController.update,
]);

A guest gets 401, and a logged in user who may not do it gets 403.

docs.title: Guest users
docs.text:
A gate or policy denies a guest. For a rule that also works for guests, make the user type nullable:

Gate.define('view-post', (User? user, Post post) {
  return post.published == true || post.userId == user?.id;
});

The same works in a policy:

class CommentPolicy extends Policy<User?, Comment> {
  bool view(User? user, Comment comment) => comment.visible == true;

  @override
  Map<String, Function> get abilities => <String, Function>{'view': view};
}

On a public route, use AuthMiddleware(optional: true). It loads the user when the login is good, and lets guests through. Without it, a logged in user is a guest too:

Route.get('/posts/{post}', <dynamic>[
  AuthMiddleware(optional: true),
  Can('view-post', param: 'post'),
  postController.show,
]);

docs.title: Before and after hooks
docs.text:
Gate.before runs before every check. Return true or false to decide at once, or null to do the normal check:

Gate.before((User user, String ability) =>
    user.isAdmin == true ? true : null);

A hook runs only for users of its type, so a User hook does not run for guests.

Gate.after sees the answer of every check, for example to log it. It can not change the answer:

Gate.after((User user, String ability, GateResponse response) {
  print('${user.id} $ability ${response.allowed}');
});

A policy can have its own before. It runs before the methods of that policy:

class PostPolicy extends Policy<User, Post> {
  @override
  bool? before(User user, String ability) =>
      user.isAdmin == true ? true : null;

  // ...
}

docs.title: Auth flags
docs.text:
Turn on opt-in behavior with flags in AuthConfig. All flags are off by default:

AuthConfig authConfig = AuthConfig(
  defaultGuard: 'web',
  guards: guards,
  flags: const AuthFlags(forbidGuest: true, jsonNoRedirect: true),
);
  • forbidGuest: req.authorize and Can give a guest 403 with the gate message, not 401. AuthMiddleware still gives a guest 401.
  • jsonNoRedirect: AuthMiddleware(redirectTo: '/login') gives a JSON client 401, not a redirect. A JSON client sends a JSON Accept header, a JSON body, or X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest. An Inertia request still gets the redirect.
  • endSessionsOnPasswordChange: a session login ends when the password of the user changes. It also turns on logoutOtherDevices. See Ending sessions when the password changes.

AuthFlags.all() turns on every flag:

AuthConfig(defaultGuard: 'web', guards: guards,
    flags: const AuthFlags.all());

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Gate.flush() removes all gates, policies and hooks. Call it in setUp when each test adds its own rules. Policy methods are normal Dart methods, so a test can also call them directly.

docs.text:

  • Middleware: run a check before a route.

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
CORS headers let a web page on another domain call your API.

A browser blocks a request from https://my.app to https://api.my.app, unless the API sends CORS headers. Dox adds these headers from CORSConfig.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
The config is in lib/config/cors.dart. A new app has it with enabled: false, so it sends no CORS headers. Set origin to the URL of your front end, and set enabled: true:

lib/config/cors.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

CORSConfig cors = CORSConfig(
  enabled: true,
  origin: 'https://my.app',
  methods: <String>['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE'],
  headers: <String>['Content-Type', 'Authorization'],
  exposeHeaders: <String>['Content-Disposition'],
  credentials: true,
  maxAge: 600,
);

Then give it to AppConfig:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  cors: cors,
  // ...
);

Dox answers the preflight OPTIONS request with 204 and the CORS headers of the route. You do not add an OPTIONS route.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Each option sets one response header. An option that is not set sends no header. So with no origin, the browser blocks pages on other domains.

Option Header Value enabled - true adds the headers to every route. Default: true origin Access-Control-Allow-Origin one origin, a list of origins, or '*' for all methods Access-Control-Allow-Methods a list or a text like 'GET,POST'. '*' allows all headers Access-Control-Allow-Headers a list or a text. '*' allows all exposeHeaders Access-Control-Expose-Headers the response headers the page can read credentials Access-Control-Allow-Credentials true lets the browser send cookies maxAge Access-Control-Max-Age the seconds the browser keeps the preflight answer

docs.title: Allowing more than one origin
docs.text:
Give origin a list. Do not put many origins in one text, because Dox sends a text as it is:

CORSConfig cors = CORSConfig(
  origin: <String>['https://my.app', 'https://admin.my.app'],
);

Dox sends back the request origin when it is in the list, with Vary: Origin. For other origins it sends no header, and the browser blocks the call.

docs.title: Sending cookies
docs.text:
If the front end sends cookies, set credentials: true and set origin to your real front end URLs. The browser blocks every call with cookies when the origin is '*'.

Warning

A page on an allowed origin can send requests with the cookies of your users. List only sites that you trust.

docs.title: CORS for some routes
docs.text:
enabled is the default for all routes. Change it for a group of routes:

lib/routes/api.dart
// CORS headers only on these routes (use with enabled: false)
Route.enabledCors(() {
  Route.get('/public/posts', (PostController c) => c.index);
});

// no CORS headers on these routes
Route.disabledCors(() {
  Route.post('/webhooks/stripe', (WebhookController c) => c.handle);
});

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• CORS for a browser front-end: the setup for a React, Vue or Flutter web app.
  • CSRF protection: protect forms that use cookies.

docs.title: CSRF protection
docs.text:
CsrfMiddleware stops other sites from sending forms to your app in the name of your logged in users.

In this attack, cross site request forgery (CSRF), another site makes the browser of your user send a form to your app. The browser sends the session cookie with it. To stop it, each session has a secret token, and a request that changes data must send the token back.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
The middleware needs a session, so put it right after SessionMiddleware:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    const SessionMiddleware(),
    const CsrfMiddleware(except: <String>['/api/*', '/webhooks/stripe']),
  ],
  // ...
);

Now every POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE request must send the token. A request with no token or a wrong token gets 419 with {"code": "csrf_token_mismatch", "message": "CSRF token mismatch"}.

Warning

Dox does not check GET, HEAD and OPTIONS requests. Never change data in a GET route.

docs.title: Sending the token
docs.text:
Dox reads the token from the _token field of the body, or from the X-CSRF-TOKEN or X-XSRF-TOKEN header. In your code the token is req.session.token.

Do not put the token in a URL, because URLs go into logs and the browser history. Dox does not read _token from the query string.

docs.title: HTML forms
docs.text:
Put the token in a hidden field. In views, @csrf writes this field:

<form method="POST" action="/posts">
  @csrf
  ...
</form>

@csrf must be alone on its line. In the middle of a line, use {{ csrfField() }}. For the token only, for example in a <meta> tag, use csrfToken().

docs.title: axios and Inertia
docs.text:
Dox also sets an XSRF-TOKEN cookie that page scripts can read. axios sends it in the X-XSRF-TOKEN header, so axios and Inertia need no code.

With fetch, read the cookie and send the header yourself:

const token = document.cookie
  .split('; ')
  .find((c) => c.startsWith('XSRF-TOKEN='))
  ?.split('=')[1];

fetch('/posts', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'X-XSRF-TOKEN': token, 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ title: 'Hi' }),
});

docs.title: Excluding paths
docs.text:
List the routes that can not send the token, like webhooks and token APIs, in except. A path that ends with * matches all paths that start with it:

const CsrfMiddleware(except: <String>['/api/*', '/webhooks/stripe']);

Warning

Exclude only paths that do not use the session login. A webhook must check its own signature.

docs.title: After login
docs.text:
req.session.regenerate() also makes a new token, and Dox sends the new XSRF-TOKEN cookie in the same response. After login, the client must use the new token.

regenerate(keepToken: true) keeps the token, so forms in other tabs keep working. Do not use it at login, because a token from before the login stays valid.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Session: the session that holds the token.
  • CORS: let other origins call your API.

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
Crypt and AESEncryptor encrypt and decrypt text with AES-256-GCM, so you can store or send data that nobody else can read or change.

Dox uses the same encryption for cookies and the cookie session driver, with your APP_KEY. To store passwords, do not encrypt them: hash them.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
The key is APP_KEY in .env. Make a new random key of 32 letters and digits with the CLI:

dox key:generate

Warning

Keep APP_KEY in .env or in the secrets of your host. Never put it in code or in git.

The app stops at startup when APP_KEY is empty, is not 32 bytes, or is a public sample key. In development, local, test and testing it only prints a warning.

docs.title: Encrypting values
docs.text:
Crypt uses the APP_KEY of the app. Use encryptString for text, and encrypt for any JSON value:

String secret = Crypt.encryptString('card-1234');

String data = Crypt.encrypt(<String, dynamic>{'id': 5});

The result is base64 text. The same value gives a different result each time.

docs.title: Decrypting values
docs.text:
Use decryptString or decrypt to get the value back:

String card = Crypt.decryptString(secret); // 'card-1234'

Map<String, dynamic> map = Crypt.decrypt(data);

A changed text, or a text made with another key, throws a DecryptException, and the client gets 400. The old keys in previousKeys also work, see Rotating the key.

The flag decryptServerError makes this error a reported 500. See Core flags.

docs.title: Using your own key
docs.text:
Use AESEncryptor to encrypt with a key that is not APP_KEY:

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

String encoded = AESEncryptor.encode('Hello world', secret);
String decoded = AESEncryptor.decode(encoded, secret); // 'Hello world'

decode throws a DecryptException when the text was changed or the key is wrong. To also try old keys, give previousSecrets: Dox().config.previousKeys.

docs.title: One key per purpose
docs.text:
Dox makes a 32-byte key from your key and a label (the purpose). Give each use its own purpose, so a value made for one use does not work for another. decode needs the same purpose:

AESEncryptor.encode(text, secret, purpose: 'app:invoice');

Dox uses these labels for its own keys:

Label Used for dox:cookie encrypted cookies, and the cookie session driver dox:jwt the HMAC key of JwtAuthDriver (with a SecretKey) dox:encrypt AESEncryptor when you give no purpose dox:signed-url signed URLs

To get the raw 32-byte key of a label, use KeyDerivation.derive(secret, label), or KeyDerivation.forAppKey(label) for APP_KEY.

docs.title: Associated data
docs.text:
encode and decode also take associatedData, like a cookie name. It is not in the output, but decode needs the same value:

String encoded = AESEncryptor.encode(text, secret, associatedData: 'theme');
AESEncryptor.decode(encoded, secret, associatedData: 'theme');

docs.title: Encrypted cookies
docs.text:
DoxCookie encrypts its value with APP_KEY by default, and req.cookie(key) decrypts it:

return response().cookie(DoxCookie('theme', 'dark'));  // encrypted

String? theme = req.cookie('theme');                    // decrypted

For a plain text cookie, set encrypt: false. Read the raw value with decrypt: false:

DoxCookie('theme', 'dark', encrypt: false);             // plain text

String? raw = req.cookie('theme', decrypt: false);      // as sent

req.cookie(key) gives null when the cookie was changed, was made with another key, or was made for another cookie name. To decrypt a raw cookie value yourself, use DoxCookie.decrypt(name, value).

docs.title: Rotating the key
docs.text:
Change APP_KEY from time to time, or when a person who knew it leaves the team. A new key alone logs out every user and stops JWT tokens signed with the old key. With previousKeys, users stay logged in:

  1. Copy the current APP_KEY to APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS.

  2. Run dox key:generate. It writes a new APP_KEY. Now .env has both:

    .env
    APP_KEY=<the new key from dox key:generate>
APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS=<the old APP_KEY>

  3. Read it in the env class, and give it to AppConfig:

    lib/config/env.dart
    List<String> get appPreviousKeys => <String>[]; // APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS=a,b
    lib/config/app.dart
    AppConfig(
  appKey: env.appKey,
  previousKeys: env.appPreviousKeys,
)

  4. Deploy. Every instance must get the new env at the same time.

  5. Wait until the old cookies expire: the session lifetime, and the maxAge of your own cookies.
  6. Remove the old key from APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS and deploy again.

APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS can hold many keys, with commas between them. Dox writes a cookie again with the new key the next time it sends it.

The old keys read encrypted cookies, the cookie session driver, the CSRF token, Crypt.decrypt, and JWT tokens signed with APP_KEY. A JWT secret that is not APP_KEY needs its own previousSecrets, see Authentication.

docs.title: When the key leaked
docs.text:
Warning

Do not put a leaked key in previousKeys. A person who has it can make cookies and JWT tokens that Dox accepts. Change APP_KEY with no previousKeys. This logs out every user.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Hashing: store passwords.
  • Signed URLs: links that nobody can change.
  • Session: the cookie session driver.

docs.title: Hashing
docs.text:
Hash turns a password into a bcrypt hash that you can store, and checks a password against it later.

A hash is one-way: you can not turn it back into the password. Hash is in package:dox_core/dox_core.dart. For a normal login you do not need it, because Auth().attempt() checks the password. See Authentication.

docs.title: Hashing passwords
docs.text:
Hash the password before you save it. makeAsync runs bcrypt in another isolate, so the server does not wait:

user.password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
await user.save();

The result, like $2a$10$..., holds the salt, so you store only this one string.

Warning

Never send the hash to the client. Put the column in the hidden list of the model.

docs.title: Verifying passwords
docs.text:
verifyAsync gives true when the password matches the hash. It gives false for a wrong password or a hash that is not bcrypt:

bool ok = await Hash.verifyAsync('secret', user.password!);

docs.title: Outside a request
docs.text:
Hash.make and Hash.verify do the same, but they block the isolate while bcrypt runs. Use them only outside request handlers. Hash.check is the same as Hash.verify:

String hash = Hash.make('secret');
bool ok = Hash.verify('secret', hash);

docs.title: Changing the cost
docs.text:
Hash.rounds is the bcrypt cost for new hashes, from 4 to 31. The default is 10, and each step up doubles the time. Do not go below 10:

Hash.rounds = 12;
String hash = Hash.make('secret', rounds: 12); // or per call

Old hashes keep their cost, so they still verify. Also set hashRounds on your auth driver to the same value. See Authentication.

docs.title: Long passwords
docs.text:
bcrypt reads at most 72 bytes. Hash.make and Hash.makeAsync throw an ArgumentError for a longer password, and Hash.verify gives false. Limit the length in your DTO:

@Length(min: 8, max: 72)
String password;

@Length counts characters, and a letter outside ASCII can use up to 4 bytes. So catch the error and answer 422, or use a smaller max.

docs.title: Comparing secrets
docs.text:
To check an API key or a token, use Hash.equals, not ==. It takes the same time for every value of the same length, so the time does not tell how much of the key was right:

bool ok = Hash.equals(req.header('X-Api-Key') ?? '',
    Env.get<String>('API_KEY'));

docs.title: Storing tokens
docs.text:
For a long random secret in the database, like an API key, store only Hash.sha256(token). Then find the row by the hash of what the client sends:

String stored = Hash.sha256(token);          // save this, never the token
Token? row = await Token().where('hash', Hash.sha256(given)).getFirst();

Warning

Never use Hash.sha256 for passwords. A password is short and easy to guess, so use bcrypt.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Encryption: hide data that you must read again.
  • Authentication: login with hashed passwords.

docs.title: Rate limiting
docs.text:
RateLimit is a middleware that stops a client that sends too many requests.

Use it on login, sign up and other routes that bots attack.

docs.title: Limiting a route
docs.text:
Add RateLimit to the route. The defaults are max: 60 and per: Duration(minutes: 1):

lib/routes/api.dart
Route.post('/auth/login', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, per: Duration(minutes: 1)),
  (AuthController c) => c.login,
]);

Each client ip can now send 5 login requests per minute. The 6th request gets 429:

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 42
X-RateLimit-Limit: 5
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0

{"code":"too_many_requests","message":"Too Many Requests"}

Retry-After is the number of seconds until the client can try again. Every answer has the X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining headers. A blocked request also counts, so a client that keeps sending stays blocked.

docs.title: Limiting every route
docs.text:
Put it in globalMiddleware:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    RateLimit(max: 120),
  ],
  // ...
);

docs.title: Counting by user
docs.text:
Each ip has its own count. To count by another value, give a key function that returns a string, like the user id after AuthMiddleware:

Route.get('/reports', <dynamic>[
  AuthMiddleware(),
  RateLimit(
    max: 100,
    key: (DoxRequest req) => '${req.auth?.user<User>()?.id ?? req.ip()}',
  ),
  (ReportController c) => c.index,
]);

Warning

Do not count by a raw header, like req.header('X-Api-Key'). A client can send a new value each time and get a new count. Count by a value that you checked.

docs.title: Two limits with the same settings
docs.text:
Two limits with the same max and per share one count for a client. To keep the counts separate, give each one a name:

Route.post('/auth/login', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'login'),
  (AuthController c) => c.login,
]);
Route.post('/auth/register', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'register'),
  (AuthController c) => c.register,
]);

docs.title: Behind a proxy
docs.text: Behind Caddy, nginx or a load balancer, all clients come from the proxy ip and share one count. Add the proxy to AppConfig.trustedProxies, so req.ip() is the real client ip. See App config.

docs.title: IPv6 clients
docs.text:
An IPv6 client often has a full /64 block, so it can send from a new address each time. Turn on rateLimitIpv6Prefix to count each IPv6 client by its /64 prefix:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  flags: CoreFlags(rateLimitIpv6Prefix: true),
  // ...
);

An IPv4 address stays as it is. Your own key function does not change. To use the same rule in it, call RateLimit.ipBucket(req.ip()).

docs.title: Where the counts live
docs.text:
When the default cache store is Redis, the counts are in Redis, and all servers share them. For Redis options, see Redis options.

With any other default store, each server keeps its counts in its main isolate. So with 3 servers, a client can send up to 3 times max. To use a store by name, give store:

RateLimit(max: 10, store: 'redis')

In a test, give a ready store with cacheStore.

docs.title: Sliding window
docs.text:
By default the count starts at 0 in each window. So a client can send max requests at the end of one minute and max more at the start of the next. To stop this burst, set sliding: true:

RateLimit(max: 5, per: Duration(minutes: 1), sliding: true)

The count is then the count of this window plus a part of the window before. It costs one more read per request.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Middleware: add middleware to routes.
  • Security headers: safe headers on every answer.
  • Production checklist: what to set before you go live.

docs.title: Security headers
docs.text:
SecurityHeaders is a middleware that adds safe HTTP headers to every answer.

The browser reads these headers and blocks some common attacks, like a frame of your page on another site.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Put it first in globalMiddleware, so an error from a later middleware (like 419 or 429) also gets the headers:

lib/config/app.dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    const SecurityHeaders(),
  ],
  // ...
);

Every answer now has these headers:

Header Default value What it does X-Content-Type-Options nosniff The browser does not guess the file type. X-Frame-Options DENY No site can show your page in a frame. Referrer-Policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin Other sites see only your domain, not the full URL. Permissions-Policy camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=() The page can not use the camera, the microphone or the location. Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy same-origin A page of another site that opens yours can not reach it. Strict-Transport-Security max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains The browser uses only https for one year. Sent only on https requests. X-XSS-Protection 0 Turns off the old XSS filter of browsers.

Content-Security-Policy is off by default, because a good policy depends on your pages.

A 404 for an unknown URL and a preflight OPTIONS answer get only the server headers X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and X-XSS-Protection: 0, because middleware runs only for routes.

docs.title: Changing a header
docs.text:
Give an option a new value to change its header, or null to remove it. Use extra for other headers:

const SecurityHeaders(
  frameOptions: 'SAMEORIGIN', // allow frames from your own site
  permissionsPolicy: null, // do not send this header
  contentSecurityPolicy: "frame-ancestors 'none'",
  extra: <String, String>{'Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy': 'same-origin'},
)
Option Header contentTypeOptions X-Content-Type-Options frameOptions X-Frame-Options referrerPolicy Referrer-Policy permissionsPolicy Permissions-Policy crossOriginOpenerPolicy Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy strictTransportSecurity Strict-Transport-Security contentSecurityPolicy Content-Security-Policy xssProtection X-XSS-Protection extra any other headers, name to value. A null value removes that header

docs.title: HSTS behind a proxy
docs.text:
Dox sends Strict-Transport-Security only when a trusted proxy sends X-Forwarded-Proto: https. Add your proxy to AppConfig.trustedProxies, or Dox never sends HSTS:

AppConfig(trustedProxies: <String>['127.0.0.1', '::1']);

See App config.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Middleware: add middleware to routes.
  • CORS: let other origins call your API.
  • Rate limiting: stop clients that send too many requests.

docs.title: Signed URLs
docs.text:
A signed URL has a signature in its query, so nobody can change the URL without your APP_KEY.

Use it for links in emails, like "unsubscribe" or "download your file", when the user is not logged in.

docs.title: Creating signed URLs
docs.text:
Give the route a name and add the ValidateSignature middleware:

lib/routes/web.dart
Route.get('/unsubscribe/{user}', <dynamic>[
  const ValidateSignature(),
  (UserController c) => c.unsubscribe,
]).name('unsubscribe');

Then make the URL with Route.signedUrl:

String url = Route.signedUrl(
  'unsubscribe',
  params: <String, Object>{'user': 5},
);
// https://example.com/unsubscribe/5?signature=3f9a...

A URL with no signature, a wrong signature, or a changed path or query gets 403. URLs made with a key in AppConfig.previousKeys still work.

docs.title: Adding a query
docs.text:
Give query to add query params. They are signed too. signature is a reserved name:

String url = Route.signedUrl(
  'unsubscribe',
  params: <String, Object>{'user': 5},
  query: <String, Object>{'list': 'news'},
);

docs.title: URLs that expire
docs.text:
Give expires to make a link that works only for a time. After that time it gets 403:

String url = Route.signedUrl(
  'download',
  params: <String, Object>{'file': 12},
  expires: Duration(hours: 1),
);

docs.title: Relative URLs
docs.text:
By default Dox puts APP_URL in front, and signs the scheme and host too. Give baseUrl to use another one. The scheme, host and port of the request must match it.

To sign only the path and the query, use absolute: false, and check it with ValidateSignature(absolute: false):

Route.get('/files/{id}', <dynamic>[
  const ValidateSignature(absolute: false),
  (FileController c) => c.show,
]).name('files.show');

String url = Route.signedUrl(
  'files.show',
  params: <String, Object>{'id': 3},
  absolute: false,
);
// /files/3?signature=...

Behind a proxy that ends TLS, add the proxy to AppConfig.trustedProxies, so Dox sees the https scheme.

docs.title: Checking in a controller
docs.text:
To answer a bad link in your own way, use ValidateSignature.hasValidSignature(req):

if (!ValidateSignature.hasValidSignature(req)) {
  return redirect('/link-expired');
}

For a relative URL, give absolute: false.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• File Storage: signed URLs for files.
  • Encryption: the app key that signs the URL.

docs.title: Controller
docs.text: A controller holds the code that answers a route, so your route files stay short.

docs.title: Basic controllers
docs.text:
Make a controller with the CLI. It writes lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart with an empty index method:

dox make:controller Blog

Fill in the method:

lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

@Inject()
class BlogController {
  String index(DoxRequest req) {
    return 'all blogs';
  }
}

Then point a route to it:

lib/routes/api.dart
Route.get('/blogs', (BlogController c) => c.index);

@Inject() puts the controller in the container, so its constructor can ask for services. Run dart run build_runner build after you add one. See Dependency injection.

docs.title: Static methods
docs.text:
A static method works when the controller needs nothing from the container:

class AppController {
  static String ping(DoxRequest req) {
    return 'pong';
  }
}

Route.get('/ping', AppController.ping);

docs.title: Plain functions
docs.text:
A plain function works too:

String listBlog(DoxRequest req) {
  return 'all blogs';
}

Route.get('/blogs', listBlog);

docs.title: Resource controllers
docs.text:
A resource controller has the 7 methods that Route.resource uses. Make one with -r:

dox make:controller Blog -r
lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart
/// Route: Route.resource('path', BlogController);
@Inject()
class BlogController {
  /// GET /resource
  Future<dynamic> index(DoxRequest req) async {}

  /// GET /resource/create
  Future<dynamic> create(DoxRequest req) async {}

  /// POST /resource
  Future<dynamic> store(DoxRequest req) async {}

  /// GET /resource/{id}
  Future<dynamic> show(DoxRequest req, int id) async {}

  /// GET /resource/{id}/edit
  Future<dynamic> edit(DoxRequest req, int id) async {}

  /// PUT|PATCH /resource/{id}
  Future<dynamic> update(DoxRequest req, int id) async {}

  /// DELETE /resource/{id}
  Future<dynamic> destroy(DoxRequest req, int id) async {}
}

Register it with one route. Route.resource skips the methods you delete:

lib/routes/api.dart
Route.resource('blogs', BlogController);

See Routing: resource routes.

docs.title: API resource controllers
docs.text:
Make a resource controller with no create and edit, for an API with no form pages:

dox make:controller Blog --api

docs.title: Resource controllers for a model
docs.text:
Fill the methods with code for one model:

dox make:controller Blog --model=Blog
lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart
@Inject()
class BlogController {
  Future<dynamic> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Blog().all();
  }

  Future<dynamic> store(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Blog().create(req.body);
  }

  Future<dynamic> show(DoxRequest req, Blog blog) async {
    return blog;
  }

  Future<dynamic> update(DoxRequest req, Blog blog) async {
    await blog.update(req.body);
    return blog;
  }

  Future<dynamic> destroy(DoxRequest req, Blog blog) async {
    await blog.delete();
  }

  // ... create and edit
}

Route model binding loads the model by the {id}, and no row answers 404. create() and update() take only the columns in the fillable list of the model, so add your columns there first.

You can use --api and --model together. dox make:model Blog -r makes the model and this controller in one step.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
A controller method asks for what it needs by type, and Dox fills each parameter:

Route.put('/teams/{teamId}/users/{id}', (UserController c) => c.update);

@Inject()
class UserController {
