Read the CSRF token of the session. It is made on first use:

String token = req.session.token;

See CSRF protection.

docs.title: Validation errors and old input
docs.text:
When a form post fails validation, Dox redirects back to the form. It flashes the errors and the old input. Password fields and files are never kept:

Route.get('/register', (DoxRequest req) {
  Map<String, dynamic> errors = req.session.errors; // empty when none
  String? email = req.session.old('email');
  // ...
});

A request that wants JSON gets a 422 JSON answer instead.

docs.title: Flash errors yourself
docs.text:
Flash errors and input, then go back to the page the request came from:

req.session.flashErrors(<String, String>{'email': 'The email is taken'},
    input: req.all());
return back(req);

docs.title: Session without a request
docs.text:
Code with no request, like a Socket.IO login, loads the session from the raw cookie value. Changes to it are not saved:

Session session = await SessionMiddleware().fromCookie(value);
session.get('auth_web');

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
client.withSession() gives a test client that keeps cookies like a browser. It also sends the CSRF token:

DoxTestClient browser = client.withSession();
await browser.get('/cart/add?id=1');
(await browser.get('/cart')).expectJson(isNotEmpty);

See Testing: keep a session.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Cache: the stores a session can use.
  • CSRF protection: protect forms that use the session.
  • Authentication: session login.

docs.title: Validation rules
docs.text:
This page lists every annotation you can put on a @Dto field, with its error code and default message.

To learn how DTOs work, read Validation first. How to read the tables:

  • Code is the error code. Use it in @Dto(messages: ...) and in a MessageResolver.
  • Message is the default English text. {field} is the last key of the path.
  • Every annotation also takes message:. It wins over every other message.
  • All limits include the limit itself, unless the table says "exclusive".
  • On a list field, a value rule checks each item. Only the list rules check the list itself.

docs.title: Type errors
docs.text:
You get these errors when a value does not fit the field type. They have no annotation.

Code When Message required a required field is missing, null, or "" The {field} is required string not a string The {field} must be a string integer not a whole number The {field} must be an integer numeric not a number (double, num) The {field} must be a number boolean not a bool The {field} must be a boolean date not an ISO 8601 date The {field} must be a date in not a name of the enum The selected {field} is invalid. Valid options are {values} array not a list The {field} must be an array object not an object (nested DTO, Map) The {field} must be an object file not a file The {field} must be a file unrecognized_keys unknown key, with @Dto(strict: true) The {field} field is not allowed

docs.title: Text
docs.text:
Use these rules on string fields and string list items:

Annotation Code Message JSON Schema @Length(min: 3, max: 50) length_between The {field} must be between {min} and {max} characters minLength, maxLength @Length(min: 6, max: 6) length The {field} must be exactly {length} characters minLength, maxLength @MinLength(3) min_length The {field} must be at least {min} characters minLength @MaxLength(50) max_length The {field} may not be greater than {max} characters maxLength @Email() email The {field} is not a valid email format: email @Url() url The {field} must be a url format: uri @Uuid() uuid The {field} is invalid uuid format: uuid @Ulid() ulid The {field} must be a valid ULID pattern @Ip() ip The {field} must be an ip address anyOf ipv4 / ipv6 @Regex(r'[a-z]+') regex The {field} format is invalid pattern @In(['a', 'b']) in The selected {field} is invalid. Valid options are {values} enum @NotIn(['root']) not_in The {field} field cannot be {value} not: {enum} @StartsWith('dox') start_with The {field} must start with {prefix} pattern @EndsWith('.dev') end_with The {field} must end with {suffix} pattern @Alpha() alpha The {field} must be an alphabetic pattern @AlphaNumeric() alpha_numeric The {field} must be only alphabetic and number pattern @AlphaDash() alpha_dash The {field} must be only alphabetic, number, dash and underscore pattern
  • @Length needs min:, max: or both. With one of them, it acts like @MinLength or @MaxLength.
  • Length counts characters (Unicode code points), so é counts as 1.
  • @Url() needs http or https and a host.
  • @Uuid() takes any version, in upper or lower case.
  • @Ulid() takes 26 Crockford base32 characters, in upper or lower case. The first one is 0 to 7.
  • @Regex must match the full value, so you do not need ^ and $. A bad regex stops the build.
  • The alpha rules use the ASCII letters a-z and A-Z. @AlphaDash() also allows the digits 0-9, - and _.
  • @In and @NotIn compare exactly, and case matters.

docs.title: More text rules
docs.text:
These are also for string fields:

Annotation Code Message JSON Schema @Json() json The {field} is not a valid json contentMediaType: application/json @Digits(6) digits The {field} must be {digits} digits pattern @DigitsBetween(4, 6) digits_between The {field} must be between {min} and {max} digits pattern @DateFormatted('Y-m-d') date_format The {field} must match the format {format} @HexColor(), @HexColor(short: true) hex_color The {field} must be a hex color like #1a2b3c pattern @Password(min: 8, ...) password The {field} must have {rules} minLength
  • @HexColor() takes # and 6 hex digits, in any case. With short: true it also takes 3 digits, like #abc.
  • @Digits and @DigitsBetween take only 0-9, with no sign and no dot. Use a string field, so leading zeros stay.
  • @DateFormatted uses these letters: day d, j, D (Mon), l (Monday), N, w, S (st), z; month m, n, M (Jan), F (January), t; year Y, y, L; time a, A, g, h, G, H, i, s, v, u; time zone e, T, P, p, O, Z, I; full U, c, r. Put \ before a letter to use it as text, like Y-m-d\TH:i. Any other letter stops the build. Other characters must be there as they are. j, n, g, G, z and U take no leading zero, so j/n/Y rejects 01/02/2024. The date must exist, so 2023-02-29 fails. Names need the case shown (Jan, not jan), and a day name must fit the date. The field stays a string. Use a DateTime field for ISO 8601 dates.
  • @Password options: min (default 8), letters, mixedCase (one upper and one lower case letter), numbers and symbols. The others are off by default. Letters, numbers and symbols are Unicode. {rules} lists the options you set, like "at least 8 characters and one number".

docs.title: Other fields
docs.text:
These rules read another key of the same object, like a password and its confirmation. Give the input key, like account_type, not the Dart name. A Dart name stops the build.

Annotation Code Message @Confirmed() confirmed The {field} confirmation does not match @Same('email') same The {field} must match {other} @RequiredIf('type', 'company') required_if The {field} is required when {other} is {values} @RequiredWith(['phone']) required_with The {field} is required when {others} is present @RequiredUnless('type', 'guest') required_unless The {field} is required unless {other} is {values} @RequiredWithout(['email']) required_without The {field} is required when {others} is not present @RequiredWithoutAll(['email', 'phone']) required_without_all The {field} is required when none of {others} are present @Different('old_password') different The {field} and {other} must be different @ProhibitedIf('type', 'guest') prohibited_if The {field} is prohibited when {other} is {values} @GreaterThanField('min_price') greater_than The {field} must be greater than {min} @GreaterThanOrEqualField('min_price') min The {field} must be greater than or equal {min} @LessThanField('max_price') less_than The {field} must be less than {max} @LessThanOrEqualField('max_price') max The {field} must be less than or equal {max}
  • @Confirmed() on password needs the key password_confirmation with the same value. The error is on password. Use @Confirmed(other: 'password_again') for another key. The DTO needs no field for the confirmation key.
  • @Confirmed, @Same and @Different compare the raw input of both keys, so @Trim does not change the compare. A missing other key passes @Different.
  • Text and numbers match by text, so 1234 matches "1234".
  • The required rules work on a nullable field, a Maybe field or a field with a default. On an always-required field the build stops.
  • @RequiredIf and @RequiredUnless also take a list of values, like @RequiredIf('type', ['company', 'shop']). An enum value matches its name: @RequiredIf('role', Role.admin) matches "admin".
  • @RequiredWith: the field is required when any of the keys has a value. @RequiredWithout: when any of the keys is missing. @RequiredWithoutAll: when all of them are missing.
  • @RequiredUnless: a missing other key counts as null, so the field is required then.
  • @ProhibitedIf: when the other key matches, the field must be missing or empty. 0 and false fail.
  • The field compare rules (@GreaterThanField and the others) are for number fields. A missing other key, or one that is not a number, fails. {min} and {max} in the message are the other key.
  • On a list field, @Different checks the full list. The field compare rules do not fit a list.
  • Missing means: not there, null, blank text, an empty list or an empty map.

docs.title: Present or missing
docs.text:
These rules check if a key is sent and has a value:

Annotation Code Message @Filled() filled The {field} must have a value @Present() present The {field} must be present @Prohibited() prohibited The {field} is prohibited @Accepted() accepted The {field} must be accepted @Declined() declined The {field} must be declined
  • @Filled(): a missing key passes. A sent key must have a value: not null, not blank text, not an empty list.
  • @Present(): the key must be sent. Its value can be null or empty.
  • @Prohibited(): the key must be missing, or blank text. Any other value fails, also null, [], {}, 0 and false.
  • @Filled, @Present and @Prohibited are for a nullable, Maybe or default field.
  • @Accepted() takes true, 1, "1", "true", "yes" and "on". @Declined() takes false, 0, "0", "false", "no" and "off". The text is case sensitive. Use them on a bool field with no default. In a JSON body a bool field takes only true and false, unless the DTO has @Dto(coerce: true).
@Accepted()
final bool terms;

@Present()
final String? note; // the key must be there, null is fine

docs.title: Skip a field
docs.text:
These rules skip a field for some input, like a VAT number that is only for a company:

Annotation Does @ExcludeIf('type', 'person') when type is person, the field is skipped @ExcludeUnless('type', 'company') unless type is company, the field is skipped
  • A skipped field gets its default, null or Maybe.missing(), as if it was not sent.
  • They match like @RequiredIf, also with a list of values.
  • @ExcludeIf: a missing other key does not skip. @ExcludeUnless: a missing other key counts as null, so the field is skipped.
  • They are for a nullable, Maybe or default field.
  • Fluent schemas have .excludeIf() and .excludeUnless(). See Skip a field.
final String type;

@ExcludeIf('type', 'person')
@MinLength(5)
final String? vatNumber; // not checked for a person

docs.title: Change text
docs.text:
These change the value before the rules run. They always run in this order: @Trim, then @Lowercase or @Uppercase, then the "empty string is missing" check.

Annotation Does @Trim() removes spaces at the start and the end @Lowercase() makes the text lower case @Uppercase() makes the text upper case @AllowEmpty() keeps "" as a value. Without it, "" counts as missing.

@Lowercase() and @Uppercase() together stop the build.

docs.title: Bad value to default
docs.text:
Annotation Does @OrDefault() a bad value gives the default of the field (or null, or Maybe.missing()), not an error.
  • It drops type errors and the errors of the normal rules of the field.
  • Errors from async rules and from validate() still give 422.
  • The field needs a default, a nullable type or a Maybe type.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
Use these rules on int, double and num fields and list items:

Annotation Code Message JSON Schema @Min(18) min The {field} must be greater than or equal {min} minimum @Max(100) max The {field} must be less than or equal {max} maximum @Range(1, 10) between The {field} must be between {min} and {max} minimum, maximum @Positive() greater_than The {field} must be greater than 0 exclusiveMinimum: 0 @GreaterThan(0.5) greater_than The {field} must be greater than {min} (exclusive) exclusiveMinimum @LessThan(100) less_than The {field} must be less than {max} (exclusive) exclusiveMaximum @In([1, 2, 3]) in The selected {field} is invalid. Valid options are {values} enum @NotIn([0]) not_in The {field} field cannot be {value} not: {enum}

@Min(1.5) on an int field stops the build.

docs.title: Lists
docs.text:
Use these rules on list fields. They check the list, not the items:

Annotation Code Message JSON Schema @MinItems(1) min_items The {field} must have at least {min} items minItems @MaxItems(5) max_items The {field} may not have more than {max} items maxItems @UniqueItems() unique_items The {field} must not have duplicate items uniqueItems: true

@UniqueItems() works for strings, numbers, bools, enums and dates. On a list of DTOs it stops the build.

docs.title: Dates
docs.text:
Use these rules on DateTime fields:

Annotation Code Message JSON Schema @After('2000-01-01') after The {field} must be a date after {date} format: date-time @Before('now') before The {field} must be a date before {date} format: date-time @AfterOrEqual('today') after_or_equal The {field} must be a date after or equal to {date} format: date-time @BeforeOrEqual('end_date') before_or_equal The {field} must be a date before or equal to {date} format: date-time
  • The value is one of these:
    • an ISO 8601 date, like '2000-01-01',
    • a word: 'now' (the time of the request), 'today', 'tomorrow' or 'yesterday'. These are in UTC, and 'today' is the start of the day,
    • the input key of another date field of the same DTO, like 'start_date'. When that field has no value, the check passes.
  • @After and @Before are exclusive. @AfterOrEqual and @BeforeOrEqual accept the same time.
final DateTime startDate;

@After('start_date')
@BeforeOrEqual('tomorrow')
final DateTime endDate;

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
Use these rules on RequestFile and List<RequestFile> fields:

Annotation Code Message JSON Schema @MaxSize('2MB') max_size The {field} may not be larger than {max} maxLength (bytes) @Mimes(['pdf', 'png']) mimes The {field} must be a file of type: {types} contentMediaType @Image() image The {field} must be an image contentMediaType: image/* @MinSize('10KB') min_size The {field} must be at least {min} minLength (bytes) @MimeTypes(['image/png', 'image/*']) mime_types The {field} must be a file of type: {types} contentMediaType @Dimensions(minWidth: 100, ratio: 3 / 2) dimensions The {field} has invalid image dimensions contentMediaType: image/*
  • Size units are B, KB, MB and GB. 1KB is 1024 bytes.
  • @Mimes takes file extensions. Dox finds the real type from the first bytes of the file. The file name extension must not name another type, or a type a browser runs (like html or svg). For zip types (like docx), the extension must match too. For types with no byte signature (like txt or csv), Dox uses the extension.
  • @Image() is @Mimes(['jpg', 'jpeg', 'png', 'gif', 'webp', 'bmp']), with no svg.
  • @MimeTypes takes MIME types and checks the real bytes like @Mimes. image/* means jpg, jpeg, png, gif, webp, bmp, tif, tiff, ico, heic, heif, avif and psd. Browsers can not show most of these, so for web images use @Image(). Write image/jpeg: image/jpg never matches.
  • @Dimensions limits: width, height (exact), minWidth, maxWidth, minHeight, maxHeight and ratio (width / height). It reads the header of PNG, GIF, WebP and JPEG files. Any other file fails. A ratio passes when it is off by less than one pixel.

With fluent schemas, use v.file(). Sizes there are in bytes:

v.file()
    .maxSize(2 * 1024 * 1024) // 2 MB
    .mimeTypes(<String>['image/jpeg', 'image/png'])
    .dimensions(minWidth: 100, maxWidth: 2000);

The fluent methods are maxSize, minSize, mimes, mimeTypes, dimensions, image and extensions.

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
These rules come from dox_orm. They run after all other checks pass:

Annotation Code Message @Unique(table, {column, ignoreParam, ignoreColumn, connection}) unique The {field} has already been taken @Exists(table, {column, connection}) exists The selected {field} is invalid
  • The default column of @Unique is the input key. The default column of @Exists is id.
  • They read the table, not the model, so soft-deleted rows count too.
  • ignoreParam: 'id' skips the row where ignoreColumn (default id) equals the path param {id}.

See Database rules. In a fluent schema, use v.string().unique('users', column: 'email') and v.int().exists('teams'). See Fluent schemas.

docs.title: Keys and DTO options
docs.text:
These options change how the full DTO reads its input:

Annotation Does @Name('emailAddress') the input key for this field. Default: the field name in snake case. @Dto() marks the class. @Dto(source: Source.query) where to read: Source.auto (default), Source.query, Source.body. @Dto(keyCase: KeyCase.field) keys: KeyCase.snake (default) or KeyCase.field (the Dart name as it is). @Dto(strict: true) unknown keys are errors. Default false: they are dropped. @Dto(emptyStringsToNull: true) "" is read as null, not as missing. Default false. @Dto(trim: true) trims every string field and text item, like @Trim() on each. Default false. @Dto(coerce: true) a JSON body can send text for numbers and bools, like a form. Default false. @Dto(messages: {...}) messages by code or key.code. A dotted path like address.city.required or tags.*.required works too. See Short rule names. @Dto(attributes: {...}) the names shown for {field}, by key. See Names for field. @Describe('...') on a field: the description of the field in the JSON Schema.

A nested DTO uses its own trim and coerce. A /// doc comment on a field also becomes its description. @Describe wins over it. The OpenAPI docs and MCP tools show it:

@Describe('Category ID (see list_categories).')
final int categoryId;

docs.title: Types in detail
docs.text:
This is how each field type reads input. The short table is in Field types.

  • JSON is strict. In a JSON body, "18" is not an integer, and you get the error integer. With @Dto(coerce: true), JSON is read like form text for numbers and bools, and a bool also takes 1 and 0.
  • Query and form data are text. Dox changes the text into the field type first.
  • int takes 18 or 18.0, never a fraction.
  • bool in text takes true, 1, yes, on and false, 0, no, off, in any case.
  • DateTime takes 2024-01-31 or 2024-01-31T10:00:00Z. A value with no time zone is read as UTC, and the result is always UTC. A timestamp number is not allowed.
  • An enum matches the Dart name exactly, so "Admin" does not match Role.admin.
  • Object? and dynamic take any value, with no check.
  • Map<String, dynamic> must be an object. Its values are not checked.
  • In query and form data, one value for a list field gives a list with one item. Bracket indexes are sorted and packed, so items[3] alone gives a list with one item.
  • In query and form data, a list can have at most 1000 items, and keys can nest at most 10 levels. More gives 422 with the key _root.

docs.title: Body types
docs.text:
The content type of the body decides how Dox reads it:

Body Result application/json (or any +json type) read with strict JSON types application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data read as text, then converted any other content type 415 Unsupported Media Type JSON that is not valid 400 Bad Request JSON that is not an object (like [1, 2]) 422 with the key _root

docs.title: The order of checks
docs.text:
Dox checks the input in four steps:

  1. Read the input and convert types. Change text (@Trim, @Lowercase, @Uppercase). Find missing required fields and run the rules that read other keys, except @Confirmed and @Same.
  2. The field rules, top to bottom. The first rule that fails stops the other rules of that field. A fluent schema runs all rules, unless you add .bail(). See Stop at the first error.
  3. The validate() method, nested DTOs first.
  4. Async rules (@Unique, @Exists, your AsyncRule), one at a time, in field order.

Each step runs only when the step before it had no errors, so the database never gets input that is already wrong. Inside one step, Dox collects the errors of all fields.

docs.title: What the generator checks
docs.text:
The build stops with a clear error when:

  • a field is not final, or is not a parameter of the unnamed constructor,
  • a field type is not supported (see Field types),
  • a rule does not fit the field type (like @Email() on an int),
  • a Maybe<T> field has no const Maybe.missing() default,
  • a required, present, prohibited or exclude rule, or @OrDefault(), is on a field that is always required,
  • a rule that reads another key names a Dart field (like accountType) instead of its input key (account_type),
  • a date rule has a text that is not a date, a word or another date field,
  • @DateFormatted has a letter it does not know,
  • @Regex has a bad pattern, or a size text is bad,
  • two @Dto classes in the app have the same name,
  • the class is generic, or extends another class (other than Object).

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Validation: messages, custom rules and checks across fields.
  • DTOs: make and use a DTO.
  • Validation package: fluent schemas.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Validation checks the request input with a typed DTO class, so your controller only gets good data.

Put rules on the fields of a DTO, then ask for it in your controller. When the input is wrong, Dox answers 422 with the errors:

lib/app/dtos/create_user/create_user.dto.dart
@Dto()
class CreateUser {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 3, max: 50)
  final String name;

  @Email()
  final String email;

  @MinLength(8)
  final String password;

  const CreateUser({
    required this.name,
    required this.email,
    required this.password,
  });

  static const DtoSchema<CreateUser> schema = $CreateUserDto;
}
lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart
Future<User> store(CreateUser body) async {
  // body is already checked
  User user = User()
    ..name = body.name
    ..email = body.email
    ..password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
  await user.save();
  return user;
}

To make and register a DTO, see DTOs.

docs.title: Required and optional fields
docs.text:
The Dart type decides if a field is required:

Field Key missing Value null final String name; error required error required final int? age; null null final Role role; with this.role = Role.user Role.user error required

Rules on an optional field run only when it has a value. The rules do not check a default value.

docs.title: Empty strings and spaces
docs.text:
An empty string counts as missing, so a required string rejects "". Add @AllowEmpty() to keep it:

@AllowEmpty()
final String note;

Spaces are kept, so " " passes, unless the field has @Trim(). To trim all text fields, set it on the DTO:

@Dto(trim: true) // trim every text field
class CreatePost { ... }

@Dto(emptyStringsToNull: true) makes "" null.

docs.title: Using the default for bad values
docs.text:
Turn a bad value into the default, with no error. The field needs a default, a nullable type or a Maybe type:

@OrDefault()
@NotIn(<int>[0])
final int page; // with this.page = 1, page=abc and page=0 give 1

docs.title: Missing or null (for PATCH)
docs.text:
A T? field gives null for a missing key and for null. Use Maybe<T> to know the difference:

@Length(max: 500)
final Maybe<String?> bio; // default: const Maybe.missing()

// in the controller
if (body.bio.isPresent) {
  user.bio = body.bio.value; // can be null: the client cleared it
}

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
Rules run from top to bottom, and the first rule that fails gives the error:

@Trim()
@Lowercase()
@Email()
@MaxLength(255)
final String email;

A rule on a list checks each item. Only the list rules check the list itself. Every rule, with its error code and message, is in Validation rules:

Kind Annotations Text @Length, @MinLength, @MaxLength, @Email, @Url, @Uuid, @Ulid, @Ip, @Regex, @In, @NotIn, @StartsWith, @EndsWith, @Alpha, @AlphaNumeric, @AlphaDash Change text @Trim, @Lowercase, @Uppercase, @AllowEmpty Numbers @Min, @Max, @Range, @Positive, @GreaterThan, @LessThan, @In, @NotIn Lists @MinItems, @MaxItems, @UniqueItems Dates @After, @Before, @AfterOrEqual, @BeforeOrEqual Other fields @Same, @Confirmed, @Different, @GreaterThanField, @GreaterThanOrEqualField, @LessThanField, @LessThanOrEqualField, @ProhibitedIf Present or missing @RequiredIf, @RequiredUnless, @RequiredWith, @RequiredWithout, @RequiredWithoutAll, @Filled, @Present, @Prohibited, @Accepted, @Declined Skip a field @ExcludeIf, @ExcludeUnless Files @MaxSize, @MinSize, @Mimes, @MimeTypes, @Image, @Dimensions Database @Unique, @Exists

docs.title: Checks across fields
docs.text:
Add a validate method to the DTO. Dox calls it after all field rules pass:

void validate(DtoErrors errors) {
  if (password != passwordConfirmation) {
    errors.add('password_confirmation', 'The passwords do not match');
  }
}

The key is the input key. Use _root for an error about the full body. errors.has(key) tells if a key already has an error. The method can be async.

docs.title: Database rules: @Unique and @Exists
docs.text:
Check the database, for example that an email is not taken. Import package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart in the DTO file:

@Unique('users', column: 'email')
final String email;

@Exists('teams') // column defaults to id
final int teamId;

For an update, skip the row of the route param:

// PUT /users/{id}
@Unique('users', column: 'email', ignoreParam: 'id')
final String email;

These rules run last. See Validation rules: database.

docs.title: The error response
docs.text:
Dox answers 422 with one message for each field. The key is the path to the value:

{
  "email": "The email is not a valid email",
  "tags.0": "The tags may not be greater than 20 characters",
  "items.1.quantity": "The quantity must be greater than 0"
}

On a form post with a session, Dox redirects back with the errors. The laravelErrors flag sends {"message": "...", "errors": {"field": ["..."]}}. See Core flags.

For another shape, read error.issues of the ValidationException in your ExceptionHandler. Each issue has dottedPath, code, message and params.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
Set your own error text. There are three places, and the first one wins.

On the rule:

@Email(message: 'Please check your email')
final String email;

On the DTO, by code or by key.code. Use * for list items, like 'tags.*.required':

@Dto(messages: <String, String>{
  'email.required': 'We need your email',
  'integer': 'The {field} must be a number',
})

For the full app, with a MessageResolver:

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  validationMessages: MessageResolver(
    messages: <String, String>{'required': 'Please fill in {field}'},
  ),
);

A message can use {field} (the last key), {value}, and rule values like {min} and {max}.

docs.title: Messages in other languages
docs.text:
Extend MessageResolver and override resolve. request.locale comes from Accept-Language:

class AppMessages extends MessageResolver {
  static const Map<String, Map<String, String>> _texts =
      <String, Map<String, String>>{
    'th': <String, String>{'required': 'กรุณากรอก {field}'},
  };

  @override
  String resolve(MessageRequest request) {
    String? template = _texts[request.locale]?[request.code];
    if (template == null) {
      return super.resolve(request);
    }
    return format(template, request.params);
  }
}

setMessages adds messages to a resolver at a later time.

docs.title: Names for {field}
docs.text:
Show a nice name in place of the key, on the DTO:

@Dto(attributes: <String, String>{'first_name': 'first name'})
class CreateUser { ... }
// The first name is required

Or for the full app, also for fluent schemas:

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  validationMessages: MessageResolver(
    attributes: <String, String>{'first_name': 'first name'},
  ),
);

The key in the error response stays the same. setAttributes adds names later, and a custom resolver can override attributeName(path).

docs.title: Short rule names in message keys
docs.text:
With the laravelMessageKeys flag, a message key can use a short name. So 'name.min' gives the message for the min_length error of name. Set it in the setup() of a provider, like the other flags:

Validator.flags = const ValidationFlags(laravelMessageKeys: true);

The full code wins over the short name. The error code in the response stays min_length:

Dox code Short name min_length min max_length max length size length_between between start_with starts_with end_with ends_with alpha_numeric alpha_num greater_than gt less_than lt min_items min max_items max unique_items distinct min_size min max_size max mime_types mimetypes datetime date

docs.title: Custom rules
docs.text:
Extend Rule<T>. T is the field type, or the item type for a list:

class Slug extends Rule<String> {
  const Slug({super.message});

  @override
  String get name => 'slug'; // the error code

  @override
  String get defaultMessage => 'The {field} must be a slug';

  @override
  bool check(String value, RuleContext context) {
    return _pattern.hasMatch(value);
  }

  static final RegExp _pattern = RegExp(r'^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$');
}

Then use it like any rule:

@Slug()
final String slug;
  • Override params to give values to the message, like {'min': 3}.
  • Override toJsonSchema to add JSON Schema keys, like {'format': 'slug'}.
  • context.lookup('other.key') reads another input value, and context.sibling('key') reads a field next to this one. Both give undefined for a missing value.
  • context.value, context.field and context.root give the value, the field name and the full input.

docs.title: Rules that read the database
docs.text:
Extend AsyncRule<T> and write checkAsync:

class FreeName extends AsyncRule<String> {
  const FreeName({super.message});

  @override
  String get name => 'free_name';

  @override
  String get defaultMessage => 'The {field} is taken';

  @override
  Future<bool> checkAsync(String value, RuleContext context) async {
    return await nameIsFree(value); // your database check
  }
}

For a list field, override failedItems to check all items in one query. It gives the indexes of the bad items.

docs.title: Dynamic input
docs.text:
For input you know only at runtime, like form fields from the database, use a fluent schema:

Map<String, dynamic> data = await req.validateSchema(v.object(fields));

See Fluent schemas.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Test the checks of a DTO with safeValidateMap. See DTOs: testing.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• DTOs: the typed class that holds the input.
  • Validation rules: every rule.
  • Validation package: opt-in flags, fluent schemas and use without Dox.

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
Views are HTML templates that Dox fills with your data and sends as the response.

The dox_view package has the template engine. Templates are .dox.html files in resources/views.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Add the package with the CLI. It adds the package, the provider, the resources/views folder and a sample view:

dox add view

docs.title: Set it up by hand
docs.text:
Add the package:

dart pub add dox_view

Add the provider in lib/, so every isolate sets up the engine:

lib/providers/view_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_view/dox_view.dart';

class AppViewProvider extends ViewProvider {
  AppViewProvider() : super(const ViewConfig());
}

To make a view file, run dox make:view emails/welcome. See dox make:view.

docs.title: Config
docs.text:
Set the options in ViewConfig:

Option Default What it does path resources/views the folder of the templates extension .dox.html the file extension cache on, but off when APP_ENV is development or local keep parsed templates in memory. With the cache off, a changed template shows on the next request. globals empty variables for every template. See Globals. directives empty your own tags, by name. See Your own tags. strictVariables false a variable that does not exist throws. See Strict options. stringZeroIsFalse false the text '0' is false in a condition bladeOutput false print true as 1, false as nothing and 10.0 as 10 bladeWarnings true warn about tag names of other template engines. See Unknown tag warnings.

To set up the engine with no provider, call View.configure(config).

docs.title: Rendering views
docs.text:
Render a template and send it as HTML. Leave out the .dox.html extension:

DoxResponse show(DoxRequest req) {
  return view(req, 'users/show', <String, dynamic>{
    'user': user,
    'posts': posts,
  });
}

This renders resources/views/users/show.dox.html:

<h1>{{ user.name }}</h1>

docs.title: Rendering to a string
docs.text:
Get the HTML as a string, for example for an email:

String html =
    View.render('emails/welcome', <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann'});

View.engine.exists('emails/welcome') tells if a template is there.

docs.title: Displaying data
docs.text:
{{ }} prints a value. It escapes HTML, so a user can not add a script tag to your page:

<p>Hello {{ user.name }}</p>

{{{ }}} prints a value with no escape. Use it only for HTML you trust:

<article>{{{ post.html }}}</article>

A null value and a variable that does not exist print nothing.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
A comment is not in the output:

{{-- only you see this --}}

To print {{ or a tag as text, put @ before it: @{{ name }} prints {{ name }}, and @@if prints @if.

docs.title: Stay safe
docs.text:
{{ }} escapes HTML, but that does not make every place in a page safe:

  • Always quote attributes. Write href="{{ url }}", not href={{ url }}.
  • Check URLs from users. href="{{ url }}" does not block a javascript: URL, so allow only http and https URLs.
  • Do not print user data inside a script or style tag with {{ }}. Use @json, or a quoted data- attribute.
<div id="app" data-user-name="{{ user.name }}"></div>
<script>
  const name = document.getElementById('app').dataset.userName;
</script>

docs.title: Expressions
docs.text:
Use these expressions inside {{ }} and tags:

What Example Values 'text', "text", 42, 1.5, true, false, null Lists and maps [1, 2], { name: 'Ann', 'full name': 'Ann Lee' } Fields user.name, user?.name, items[0], map['key'] Math +, -, *, /, %, ~/ Compare ==, !=, <, <=, >, >= (=== and !== work too) Logic &&, \|\|, !, a ?? b, a ? b : c Functions route('users.show', { id: 5 }), name.toUpperCase()

+ joins text. Fields work on maps, and on objects with a toJson() method, like Dox models. These methods work too:

  • Lists, maps and text: length, isEmpty, isNotEmpty.
  • Lists: first, last, contains(), join(), indexOf().
  • Text: toUpperCase(), toLowerCase(), trim(), contains(), startsWith(), endsWith(), split(), replaceAll(), substring(), indexOf().
  • Numbers: toStringAsFixed(), round(), floor(), ceil(), abs().

In a condition, these values are false: null, false, 0, an empty string, an empty list and an empty map.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
Show a part only in some cases. Close it with @end:

@if(user.isAdmin)
  <a href="/admin">Admin</a>
@elseif(user.isEditor)
  <a href="/posts">Posts</a>
@else
  <p>Welcome</p>
@end

@unless(x) is @if(!x). A tag alone on its line leaves no empty line in the output.

A tag right after a letter or a digit stays text, so me@mail.com is safe. Put a space before the tag, or use {{ on ? 'active' : '' }}.

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
Print a list. The @else part shows when the list is empty:

<ul>
  @each(user in users)
    <li>{{ user.name }}</li>
  @else
    <li>No users yet</li>
  @end
</ul>

Use two names to get the index, or the key of a map:

@each((user, index) in users)
  {{ index + 1 }}. {{ user.name }}
@end

@each((value, key) in settings)
  {{ key }}: {{ value }}
@end

docs.title: The loop variable
docs.text:
$loop tells you where the loop is:

@each(tag in tags)
  {{ tag }}{{ $loop.last ? '' : ', ' }}
@end
Field What it is $loop.index the round, from 0 $loop.iteration the round, from 1 $loop.first true in the first round $loop.last true in the last round $loop.count the number of items. $loop.length is the same. $loop.remaining the rounds left after this one $loop.even true in the 2nd, 4th, ... round $loop.odd true in the 1st, 3rd, ... round $loop.depth 1 for a loop, 2 for a loop inside a loop $loop.parent the $loop of the outer loop, or null

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Make a variable with @let, and change it with @assign:

@let(total = 0)
@each(item in cart)
  @assign(total = total + item.price)
@end
Total: {{ total }}

docs.title: Partials
docs.text:
Put another template in this one. It sees the same variables:

@include('partials/nav')

Pass a map to give it more variables, only for this include:

@include('partials/card', { title: 'Profile', user: post.author })

Include a template only when a condition is true. @includeIf and @includeWhen are the same:

@includeIf(user, 'partials/account')
@includeWhen(user.isAdmin, 'partials/admin', { level: 2 })

docs.title: More tags
docs.text:
Close a block tag with @end. @else works in all of them, but not in @once and @verbatim:

Tag What it does @isset(user.phone) ... @end shows when the value is not null @empty(items) ... @end shows when the value is false @auth ... @end shows when the user is logged in (req.auth) @guest ... @end shows when the user is not logged in @env('local') ... @end shows when APP_ENV is this value. A list works too: @env(['local', 'staging']). @production ... @end shows when APP_ENV is production @once ... @end shows only the first time in one render, for example a script in a component @verbatim ... @end prints the text as it is, for JavaScript frameworks that also use {{ }}. The text can not have @end. @extends('layouts/app') the layout of the page. See Layouts with sections. @section('name') ... @end fills a section. Short form: @section('title', 'Home'). @yield('name') prints a section. @yield('title', 'My app') has a default. @stack('scripts') prints every push of the stack. See Stacks. @push('scripts') ... @end adds to the end of a stack @prepend('scripts') ... @end adds to the start of a stack @csrf the hidden _token field. See Forms. @method('PUT') the hidden _method field @error('email') ... @end shows when the field has a validation error @json(value) the value as JSON. See JSON for JavaScript.

Put @auth, @guest, @production, @once and @verbatim alone on their line. In View.render there is no request, so @guest shows.

docs.title: Attributes from conditions
docs.text:
Print an HTML attribute when a condition is true:

<a @class(['link', { active: isActive, muted: !isActive }])>Home</a>
<input type="checkbox" name="news" @checked(user.news)>
<option value="en" @selected(lang == 'en')>English</option>
<button @disabled(saving)>Save</button>

@class takes text, a map of class name to a condition, or a list of these.

docs.title: Layouts and components
docs.text:
A component is a template with its own props and slots. Use one for the page layout:

resources/views/layouts/main.dox.html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>{{ title ?? 'My app' }}</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <header>{{ $slots.header }}</header>
    <main>{{ $slots.main }}</main>
  </body>
</html>

A page puts its content in the component:

resources/views/home.dox.html
@component('layouts/main', { title: 'Home' })
  @slot('header')
    <h1>Welcome</h1>
  @end

  <p>Hello {{ user.name }}</p>
@end
  • The second argument is the props. In the component they are variables, and also $props.title.
  • @slot('name') ... @end fills a named slot. All other content goes into $slots.main, which is also $slot.
  • A component does not see the variables of the page. It sees its props, the slots, $attributes, the globals and the form helpers.

@!component(...) is a component with no body and no @end.

docs.title: Components as tags
docs.text:
A template in resources/views/components/ is also a tag with its name. A . in the tag is a folder:

resources/views/components/button.dox.html
<button class="btn btn-{{ type ?? 'primary' }}">{{ $slots.main }}</button>

@button({ type: 'danger' })
  Delete
@end

@!form.input({ name: 'email' })   {{-- components/form/input.dox.html --}}

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
{{ $attributes }} prints the props as escaped HTML attributes, like id="save" title="Save". merge adds defaults. A prop wins, but class is joined:

<button {{ $attributes.merge({ class: 'btn', type: 'button' }) }}>
  {{ $slot }}
</button>

@button({ class: 'btn-big', type: 'submit' })
  Save
@end

This prints <button class="btn btn-big" type="submit">.

Leave out props that are only for the logic of the component with except. It can go before merge:

<button {{ $attributes.except(['variant']).merge({ class: 'btn' }) }}>

Only text, numbers and true are attributes, and true prints the name alone. $attributes keeps any attribute name, like onclick, so do not pass a map from the user as props.

docs.title: Layouts with sections
docs.text:
A page can name its layout with @extends. The page fills sections, and the layout prints them with @yield:

resources/views/layouts/app.dox.html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>@yield('title', 'My app')</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <main>@yield('content')</main>
  </body>
</html>
resources/views/home.dox.html
@extends('layouts/app')

@section('title', 'Home')

@section('content')
  <p>Hello {{ user.name }}</p>
@end
  • @extends must be the first thing in the template.
  • Only the sections reach the layout. Text outside a section is not printed.
  • A layout can extend another layout. When both fill the same section, the page wins.

Use @extends for the page layout. Use a component when you need props or more than one copy on a page.

docs.title: Stacks
docs.text:
A stack collects HTML from many templates and prints it in one place, like scripts in the head. The layout prints it:

<head>
  @stack('styles')
</head>
<body>
  @yield('content')
  @stack('scripts')
</body>

A page, an include or a component adds to it:

@push('scripts')
  <script src="/js/chart.js"></script>
@end

@prepend adds to the start. Put @once inside @push in a component, so the script is added one time only.

docs.title: Forms
docs.text:
With SessionMiddleware, view() adds these to every template, also to components and layouts:

Name What it is csrfField() the hidden _token field for CsrfMiddleware. @csrf prints the same. csrfToken() the CSRF token errors the flashed validation errors, like errors.email old('email') the input of the request before session('key') a value from the session request.path, request.method, request.query the current request (also with no session) 
<form method="POST" action="/register">
  @csrf
  <input name="email" value="{{ old('email') }}">
  @error('email')
    <p class="error">{{ message }}</p>
  @end
  <button>Register</button>
</form>

With no session, @csrf throws a ViewException.

docs.title: Validation errors
docs.text: @error('field') shows its body when the field has an error. Inside it, message is the error. A dotted name, like @error('user.email'), works for nested fields, and the name can be a variable.

docs.title: Method fields
docs.text:
For a PUT, PATCH or DELETE route, send a POST with @method. The MethodOverride middleware reads it:

<form method="POST" action="/posts/{{ post.id }}">
  @csrf
  @method('PUT')
  <input name="title" value="{{ post.title }}">
  <button>Save</button>
</form>

docs.title: Globals
docs.text:
A global is a variable or a function that every template can use. route() is there by default:

const ViewConfig(globals: <String, Object?>{'appName': 'My app'});

View.global('year', DateTime.now().year);
View.global('money', (num cents) => (cents / 100).toStringAsFixed(2));

<footer>{{ appName }} {{ year }}</footer>
<p>{{ money(order.total) }}</p>

Each isolate has its own engine, so add globals in your provider, after super.setup():

lib/providers/view_provider.dart
class AppViewProvider extends ViewProvider {
  AppViewProvider() : super(const ViewConfig());

  @override
  void setup() {
    super.setup();
    View.global('year', DateTime.now().year);
  }
}

A global that holds HTML must be a SafeString, so it is printed with no escape:

View.global('logo', const SafeString('<img src="/logo.svg" alt="Logo">'));

To escape text yourself in Dart, use escapeHtml(text).

docs.title: JSON for JavaScript
docs.text:
Print a value as JSON. The output is safe in a script block and in an attribute in single quotes:

<script>
  const user = @json(user);
</script>

<div data-tags='@json(tags)'></div>

Do not use it in an attribute in double quotes, because the JSON has " in it. A value that can not be JSON, like a DateTime, throws a ViewException.

json(value) does the same in an expression, and SafeString.json(value) does it in Dart:

@!chart({ points: json(points) })

docs.title: Your own tags
docs.text:
A directive is a tag that your app adds. Its render method gets the values between the brackets, and gives the text to print:

class DateTimeDirective implements ViewDirective {
  @override
  Object? render(List<Object?> args, Scope scope) {
    Object? value = args[0];
    DateTime time = value is DateTime ? value : DateTime.parse('$value');
    return '${time.day}/${time.month}/${time.year}';
  }
}

View.directive('datetime', DateTimeDirective());

<time>@datetime(post.createdAt)</time>

The text is escaped. Give a SafeString to print HTML. scope.lookup('name') reads a variable, and scope.has('name') tells if it is there. Add directives in your provider like globals, or in ViewConfig(directives: ...).

docs.title: Strict options
docs.text:
These three options are off by default. Turn them on in ViewConfig:

const ViewConfig(
  strictVariables: true,
  stringZeroIsFalse: true,
  bladeOutput: true,
);
  • strictVariables: a variable that does not exist throws a ViewException with the name, the template and the line. So a typo like {{ titel }} shows as an error.
  • stringZeroIsFalse: the text '0' is false in a condition. Other text, like '00', is still true.
  • bladeOutput: {{ }} prints true as 1, false as nothing, and 10.0 as 10.

With strictVariables, these ways to read a variable that may not exist never throw:

Code What it gives when user does not exist @isset(user) ... @end the body is not printed @empty(user) ... @end the body is printed {{ user ?? 'Guest' }} Guest {{ user?.name }} nothing

{{ user.name ?? 'Guest' }} still throws when user does not exist. Write {{ user?.name ?? 'Guest' }}.

docs.title: Unknown tag warnings
docs.text:
Some tag names of other template engines, like @foreach, are not Dox tags. Dox prints them as text, and writes one warning to stderr:

dox_view: warning: posts/index:12 "@foreach" is not a Dox tag. Use "@each(item in items) ... @end".
Other name Dox {!! html !!} {{{ html }}} @foreach, @forelse, @for @each(item in items) ... @else ... @end @endif, @endforeach, @endsection and the other @end... names, @stop @end @switch @if ... @elseif ... @else ... @end @php, @endphp @let(name = value) @show @end, then @yield('name') @parent not there. Use @stack and @push to add content.

ViewConfig(bladeWarnings: false) turns the warnings off.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A syntax error, or an error in an expression, throws a ViewException with the template name and the line:

ViewException: expected ")" but found the end (in "users/show", line 12)

docs.title: Prettier
docs.text:
Prettier does not know the @ tags. Add this line to .prettierignore:

*.dox.html

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Render templates from a map, with no files:

ViewEngine engine = ViewEngine(MemoryTemplateLoader(<String, String>{
  'hello': 'Hello {{ name }}',
}));

engine.render('hello', <String, Object?>{'name': 'Ann'}); // Hello Ann

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Inertia: pages with React, Vue or Svelte.
  • Mail: use a view as a mail template.

docs.title: Build a blog API
docs.text:
This tutorial takes you from an empty folder to a small blog API that runs as one native binary.

Each step has the full code and a curl command to check your work. The finished project is on GitHub: examples/blog-api. CI builds it and runs its tests on each push.

docs.title: What you will build
docs.text:
A JSON API for blog posts. Anyone can read posts. Only a logged in user can write them:

Method Path Who What it does GET /api/posts anyone list all posts GET /api/posts/{id} anyone one post, or 404 POST /api/posts logged in user make a post (201, or 422 on bad input) PUT /api/posts/{id} logged in user change a post POST /api/auth/register anyone make an account, get a token POST /api/auth/login anyone log in, get a token GET /api/auth/user logged in user the user of the token

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Dart 3.13 or newer. Check it with dart --version.
  • curl, to call the API.
  • Approximately 15 minutes.

You do not need Docker or a database server. The app uses SQLite, which keeps the database in one file in your project.

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
1. Create the project
  2. Model and migration
  3. Routes and controller
  4. Validation
  5. Authentication
  6. Test
  7. Build and deploy

docs.title: The finished project
docs.text:
This is the project at the end. A * marks the files that you make or change. The template has more files, but this tree shows only the files of this tutorial.

blog/
├── bin/
│   ├── migrate.dart              runs the dox migration:* commands
│   ├── server.dart               runs the migrations, starts the server
│   └── queue.dart, schedule.dart, seed.dart
├── db/migration/
│   ├── ..._create_posts_table.dart   *
│   ├── ..._create_users_table.dart
│   └── migrations.dart           the list of migrations (Dox writes it)
├── lib/
│   ├── app/http/controllers/
│   │   ├── auth.controller.dart  *
│   │   └── post.controller.dart  *
│   ├── app/dtos/
│   │   ├── login_user/login_user.dto.dart   *
│   │   ├── register_user/register_user.dto.dart *
│   │   └── save_post/save_post.dto.dart    *
│   ├── app/models/
│   │   ├── post/post.model.dart  *
│   │   └── user/user.model.dart
│   ├── config/
│   │   ├── app.dart              * adds the DTO list
│   │   ├── database.dart
│   │   └── env.dart              the .env keys, typed
│   ├── routes/api.dart           *
│   ├── providers/
│   │   ├── auth_provider.dart    *
│   │   └── orm_provider.dart
│   └── generated/
│       ├── container.g.dart      * generated
│       └── dtos.g.dart           * generated
├── test/http_test.dart           *
├── .env                          made by dox create
├── Dockerfile
└── pubspec.yaml                  * adds dox_auth

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: • Step 1: Create the project: make the project and start the server.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the project
docs.text: In this step you make a new Dox project, start the dev server and call the first route.

docs.title: 1. Make the project
docs.text:
Install the dox command line tool, then make a project with the name blog:

dart pub global activate dox
dox create blog
cd blog
dart pub get

The package name is blog, so each import in this tutorial starts with package:blog/.

docs.title: 2. Look at the database settings
docs.text:
You do not change anything here. dox create made a .env file with a new random app key, and the template uses SQLite:

.env
APP_PORT=3000
APP_KEY=<your new random key>

DB_CONNECTION=sqlite
DB_NAME=db/dox.sqlite

Dox makes the database file at the first start, but not its folder. If you set a path in a new folder, make the folder first. See Environment variables.

docs.title: 3. Start the server
docs.text:
Start the dev server:

dox s

It runs the code generator and the server. It hot reloads your code in lib/app/, and it restarts the server when you change routes or config.

The first start is slower, because it compiles the SQLite library and runs the migrations of the template. At the end you see this log line:

[server] Server started at http://[::]:3000 with 8 isolate (native)

The number of isolates is the number of CPU cores on your machine.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Call the ping route from a second terminal:

curl -i http://localhost:3000/api/ping

You see:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
...

pong

The route is in lib/routes/api.dart. Its router has the prefix api, so /ping is at /api/ping.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: • Step 2: Model and migration: make the posts table and its model.

docs.title: Step 2: Model and migration
docs.text: In this step you make the posts table with a migration, and a Post model to read and write it.

docs.title: 1. Make the model and the migration
docs.text:
Stop dox s first with Ctrl+C. The server runs new migrations when it starts, so it would run the migration before you add the columns.

Make the model and its migration:

dox make:model Post -m

This makes two files and updates one:

File What it is lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart the model (new) db/migration/<date>_create_posts_table.dart the migration (new) db/migration/migrations.dart the list of all Dart migrations. Dox writes it. Do not edit it.

docs.title: 2. Add the columns to the migration
docs.text:
Open the new file in db/migration and add a title and a body:

db/migration/2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table.dart
// ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

class CreatePostsTable extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.create('posts', (Table table) {
      table.id();
      table.string('title');
      table.text('body');
      table.timestamps();
    });
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.dropIfExists('posts');
  }
}

table.id() makes an auto increment primary key. table.timestamps() makes the created_at and updated_at columns, and the model fills them.

docs.title: 3. Add the fields to the model
docs.text:
Add one field for each new column:

lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'post.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel(table: 'posts')
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get hidden => <String>[];

  @Column()
  String? title;

  @Column()
  String? body;
}

Each field is nullable, because a new Post() has no values. The id and the timestamps come from PostGenerator.

docs.title: 4. See how migrations run
docs.text:
You do not change anything here. The template's bin/server.dart runs the migrations before the server starts:

bin/server.dart
import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() async {
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);

  await Migrator(
    migrations: migrations,
    config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
  ).migrate();

  await Dox().startServer();
}

This also works in the native binary of step 7.

docs.title: 5. Run the migration and the generator
docs.text:
Run the new migration:

dox migration:run

Migrating: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table

If dox s was still on, the table can exist without the new columns. Then run dox migration:rollback and dox migration:run again.

The model also needs its generated file. dox s makes it, so if the server is off, run the generator one time:

dart run build_runner build

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
See which migrations ran:

dox migration:status

You see:

Migration                                 Batch  Status
2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table   1      Ran
2026_10_25_000000000_create_queue_tables  1      Ran
2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table      2      Ran

The first two come with the template. The server ran them in step 1.

Start the server again with dox s.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: • Step 3: Routes and controller: add the post routes.

docs.title: Step 3: Routes and controller
docs.text: In this step you add a controller and the routes to list, create and show posts.

docs.title: 1. Make the controller
docs.text:
A controller holds the code that answers a request. Make one for posts:

dox make:controller Post -r

The -r flag makes a resource controller with seven methods. You need three now, so replace the file with this:

lib/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart
import 'package:blog/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

@Inject()
class PostController {
  /// GET /api/posts
  Future<List<Post>> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Post().all();
  }

  /// POST /api/posts
  Future<DoxResponse> store(DoxRequest req) async {
    Post post = Post()
      ..title = req.input('title')
      ..body = req.input('body');
    await post.save();
    return response(post).statusCode(201);
  }

  /// GET /api/posts/{id}
  Future<Post> show(int id) async {
    Post? post = await Post().find(id);
    if (post == null) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException();
    }
    return post;
  }
}

What the code does:

  • @Inject() puts the controller in the container. The code generator adds it to lib/generated/container.g.dart, and a new project uses that file.
  • A model or a list of models goes back as JSON.
  • statusCode sets the status code.
  • show(int id) gets the id from the URL. A path like /api/posts/abc gets 404, because abc is not an integer.
  • input reads the input with no check. You add checks in step 4.

docs.title: 2. Add the routes
docs.text:
Open lib/routes/api.dart and add Route.resource:

lib/routes/api.dart
import 'package:blog/app/http/controllers/api.controller.dart';
import 'package:blog/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/ping', (ApiController c) => c.pong);

    Route.resource('posts', PostController);
  }
}

It makes one route for each method of the controller:

Method Path Controller method GET /api/posts index POST /api/posts store GET /api/posts/{id} show

Dox finds each router class, so you do not register it.

docs.title: 3. Start the server
docs.text:
If the server is off, start it:

dox s

If it is on, it restarts when you save a file.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Make a post:

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Hello Dox","body":"My first post."}'

You get 201 and the new post:

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
...

{"id":1,"title":"Hello Dox","body":"My first post.","created_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z"}

List the posts:

curl http://localhost:3000/api/posts

[{"id":1,"title":"Hello Dox","body":"My first post.","created_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z"}]

Show one post:

curl http://localhost:3000/api/posts/1

{"id":1,"title":"Hello Dox","body":"My first post.","created_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z"}

Ask for a post that does not exist. You get 404:

curl -i http://localhost:3000/api/posts/99

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
...

{"code":"not_found","message":"Not Found"}

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: • Step 4: Validation: check the input of a post.

docs.title: Step 4: Validation
docs.text: In this step you check the input of create and update with a DTO class, so bad input gets a 422 answer.

docs.title: 1. Make the DTO
docs.text:
A DTO is a class for the input that you expect, with a rule on each field. Make one:

dox make:dto SavePost

Create and update use the same fields, so one class is sufficient. Replace the file with this:

lib/app/dtos/save_post/save_post.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'save_post.dto.g.dart';

/// Typed, checked input. Run `dox build_runner:build` after a change.
@Dto()
class SavePost {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 3, max: 100)
  final String title;

  @Trim()
  @MinLength(10)
  final String body;

  const SavePost({required this.title, required this.body});

  static const DtoSchema<SavePost> schema = $SavePostDto;
}

A field that is not nullable and has no default is required. The rules run from top to bottom, so after @Trim() an empty string counts as missing. See Validation for all rules.

docs.title: 2. Give the DTO list to the app
docs.text:
The code generator writes a list of all DTOs to lib/generated/dtos.g.dart. Add two lines to lib/config/app.dart:

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:blog/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  /// DTOs (generated list in lib/generated/dtos.g.dart)
  dtos: dtos,

  // ... the rest stays the same
);

docs.title: 3. Use the DTO in the controller
docs.text:
Ask for SavePost as a parameter of the controller method. Dox checks the body and gives you a typed object. This version also adds update:

lib/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart
import 'package:blog/app/dtos/save_post/save_post.dto.dart';
import 'package:blog/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

@Inject()
class PostController {
  /// GET /api/posts
  Future<List<Post>> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Post().all();
  }

  /// POST /api/posts
  Future<DoxResponse> store(SavePost body) async {
    Post post = Post()
      ..title = body.title
      ..body = body.body;
    await post.save();
    return response(post).statusCode(201);
  }

  /// GET /api/posts/{id}
  Future<Post> show(int id) async {
    return _find(id);
  }

  /// PUT /api/posts/{id}
  Future<Post> update(int id, SavePost body) async {
    Post post = await _find(id);
    post
      ..title = body.title
      ..body = body.body;
    await post.save();
    return post;
  }

  Future<Post> _find(int id) async {
    Post? post = await Post().find(id);
    if (post == null) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException();
    }
    return post;
  }
}

The routes stay the same. The resource route finds the new method and adds PUT and PATCH for /api/posts/{id}.

docs.title: 4. Run the generator
docs.text:
dox s runs the generator. If the server is off, run it one time:

dart run build_runner build

It writes save_post.dto.g.dart and lib/generated/dtos.g.dart.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Send a title and a body that are too short:

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Hi","body":"Short"}'

You get 422 with one message for each field:

HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Entity
content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
...

{"title":"The title must be between 3 and 100 characters","body":"The body must be at least 10 characters"}

Send an empty body:

curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'

{"title":"The title is required","body":"The body is required"}

Good input gives 201:

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Second post","body":"Validation works now."}'

HTTP/1.1 201 Created

Update the first post:

curl -X PUT http://localhost:3000/api/posts/1 \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Hello Dox (edited)","body":"My first post, edited."}'

{"id":1,"title":"Hello Dox (edited)","body":"My first post, edited.","created_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T13:59:13.539886Z"}

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: • Step 5: Authentication: protect the write routes.

docs.title: Step 5: Authentication
docs.text: In this step you add register and login with a JWT token, so only a logged in user can create or change posts.

docs.title: 1. Add the package
docs.text:
The dox_auth package does the login and the tokens. Add it:

dart pub add dox_auth

docs.title: 2. Look at the users table
docs.text:
The template has a user model and a users table. This is the User model:

lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel(table: 'users', softDelete: true)
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get hidden => <String>['password'];

  @Column()
  String? name;

  @Column()
  String? email;

  @Column()
  String? password;
}

The password is in hidden, so it is never in the JSON. This is important, because the token holds the user as JSON and anyone can read a JWT.

The server ran this migration at the first start in step 1:

db/migration/2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table.dart
class CreateUsersTable extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.create('users', (Table table) {
      table.id();
      table.string('name');
      table.string('email').unique();
      table.string('password');
      table.softDeletes();
      table.timestamps();
    });
  }
  // ...
}

softDeletes() makes the deleted_at column for the soft delete. The email is unique, so a second register with the same email fails.

docs.title: 3. Make the DTOs
docs.text:
Register and login have different input, so make two DTOs:

dox make:dto RegisterUser
dox make:dto LoginUser

Replace the register DTO with this:

lib/app/dtos/register_user/register_user.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart' hide Schema;

part 'register_user.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class RegisterUser {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 2, max: 50)
  final String name;

  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  @Unique('users', column: 'email')
  final String email;

  @MinLength(8)
  final String password;

  const RegisterUser({
    required this.name,
    required this.email,
    required this.password,
  });

  static const DtoSchema<RegisterUser> schema = $RegisterUserDto;
}

@Unique comes from dox_orm and reads the database, so it runs after the other rules. The ORM also has a class with the name Schema, so the import hides it.

Replace the login DTO with this:

lib/app/dtos/login_user/login_user.dto.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'login_user.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class LoginUser {
  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  final String email;

  final String password;

  const LoginUser({required this.email, required this.password});

  static const DtoSchema<LoginUser> schema = $LoginUserDto;
}

docs.title: 4. Set up the auth provider
docs.text:
A provider tells the auth package which model to use and how to sign tokens. It runs one time in each isolate at start. Make this file:

lib/providers/auth_provider.dart
import 'package:blog/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:blog/config/env.dart';
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// Auth provider
/// --------------------------
/// Sets up JWT login with the User model.
/// Tokens are signed with APP_KEY and last 7 days.
class AppAuthProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Auth.initialize(
      AuthConfig(
        defaultGuard: 'api',
        guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
          'api': AuthGuard(
            driver: JwtAuthDriver(
              secret: SecretKey(env.appKey),
              expiresIn: const Duration(days: 7),
            ),
            provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
          ),
        },
      ),
    );
  }
}

Dox finds the provider, and the code generator adds it to lib/generated/container.g.dart.

docs.title: 5. Write the auth controller
docs.text:
This controller has the register, login and "who am I" routes:

lib/app/http/controllers/auth.controller.dart
import 'package:blog/app/dtos/login_user/login_user.dto.dart';
import 'package:blog/app/dtos/register_user/register_user.dto.dart';
import 'package:blog/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

@Inject()
class AuthController {
  /// POST /api/auth/register
  Future<DoxResponse> register(RegisterUser body) async {
    User user = User()
      ..name = body.name
      ..email = body.email
      ..password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
    await user.save();

    String? token = Auth().login(user);
    return response(<String, dynamic>{
      'token': token,
      'user': user,
    }).statusCode(201);
  }

  /// POST /api/auth/login
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> login(LoginUser body) async {
    Auth auth = Auth();
    String? token = await auth.attempt(<String, dynamic>{
      'email': body.email,
      'password': body.password,
    });
    if (token == null) {
      throw UnAuthorizedException(message: 'Wrong email or password');
    }
    return <String, dynamic>{'token': token, 'user': auth.user<User>()};
  }

  /// GET /api/auth/user
  User? user(DoxRequest req) {
    return req.auth?.user<User>();
  }
}
  • Hash.makeAsync() makes a bcrypt hash of the password on another isolate. Never save a plain password.
  • attempt() finds the user by email and checks the password. It gives a token, or null.
  • login(user) gives a token with no password check. Register uses it for the new user.

docs.title: 6. Protect the write routes
docs.text:
Read routes stay public, and write routes need a login. Replace the resource route with single routes, and put the write routes in Route.middleware:

lib/routes/api.dart
import 'package:blog/app/http/controllers/api.controller.dart';
import 'package:blog/app/http/controllers/auth.controller.dart';
import 'package:blog/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart';
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/ping', (ApiController c) => c.pong);

    // Anyone can read posts.
    Route.get('/posts', (PostController c) => c.index);
    Route.get('/posts/{id}', (PostController c) => c.show);

    // Register and log in.
    Route.post('/auth/register', (AuthController c) => c.register);
    Route.post('/auth/login', (AuthController c) => c.login);

    // Only a logged in user can write posts.
    Route.middleware(<dynamic>[AuthMiddleware()], () {
      Route.get('/auth/user', (AuthController c) => c.user);
      Route.post('/posts', (PostController c) => c.store);
      Route.put('/posts/{id}', (PostController c) => c.update);
    });
  }
}

AuthMiddleware reads the bearer token in the Authorization header and loads the user. A missing or wrong token gets 401. For a public route that still knows the user, use AuthMiddleware(optional: true).

docs.title: 7. Run the generator
docs.text:
dox s runs the generator. If the server is off, run it one time:

dart run build_runner build

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Register a user. You get 201 with a token:

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/auth/register \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Ann","email":"ann@example.com","password":"secret123"}'

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
...

{"token":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...","user":{"id":1,"name":"Ann","email":"ann@example.com","created_at":"2026-10-22T14:01:07.827769Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T14:01:07.827769Z"}}

Register with the same email again. You get 422:

{"email":"The email has already been taken"}

Log in with a wrong password. You get 401:

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/auth/login \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"ann@example.com","password":"wrong"}'

HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
...

{"code":"unauthorized","message":"Wrong email or password"}

Log in with the right password, and keep the token in a shell variable:

TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/auth/login \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"ann@example.com","password":"secret123"}' \
  | sed -E 's/.*"token":"([^"]+)".*/\1/')
echo $TOKEN

Make a post with no token. You get 401:

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Third post","body":"Written with a token."}'

HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
...

{"code":"unauthorized","message":"Authentication failed"}

Send the same post with the token:

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Third post","body":"Written with a token."}'

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
...

{"id":3,"title":"Third post","body":"Written with a token.","created_at":"2026-10-22T14:01:08.094211Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T14:01:08.094211Z"}

Ask who you are:

curl http://localhost:3000/api/auth/user \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

{"id":1,"name":"Ann","email":"ann@example.com","created_at":"2026-10-22T14:01:07.827769Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T14:01:07.827769Z"}

The answer has no password, because it is hidden.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: • Step 6: Test: test the API in code.

docs.title: Step 6: Test
docs.text: In this step you write one HTTP test for the list route and run it.

docs.title: 1. Write the test
docs.text:
A test calls your routes like a real client. Replace the template's test/http_test.dart with this:

test/http_test.dart
import 'package:blog/config/app.dart';
import 'package:blog/config/database.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    await Migrator(
      migrations: migrations,
      config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
    ).migrate();
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('GET /api/posts gives a list', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.get('/api/posts');
    res.expectStatus(200).expectJson(isA<List<dynamic>>());
  });
}

DoxTestClient.start runs the app in the test on a free port. The test runs the migrations first, so it also works on an empty database.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Run the test:

dart test test/http_test.dart

You see:

00:01 +1: All tests passed!

The test reads .env, so it uses your dev database. To use another database, make a .env.testing file with DB_NAME=test.sqlite. The test reads it on top of .env.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: • Step 7: Build and deploy: make a native binary and a Docker image.

docs.title: Step 7: Build and deploy
docs.text:
In this step you compile the app to one native binary, run it, and run it in Docker.

Use a native binary in production

dox s and dart run use the JIT compiler. It uses approximately 25 times more memory and starts slower.

docs.title: 1. Build the binary
docs.text:
Build the app:

dox build

Built with build_runner/aot in 1s; wrote 0 outputs.
Running build hooks...Running link hooks...
Generated: /.../blog/build/bundle/bin/server
[Dox] Built build/bundle. Run it with: cd build/bundle && ./bin/server

It runs the code generator, then dart build cli. The build/bundle folder has all that the app needs:

Path What it is bin/server the binary, approximately 10 MB. It needs no Dart SDK. bin/queue the queue worker. Run it as its own process. bin/schedule the scheduler. Run it as its own process. lib/ native libraries from build hooks, like libsqlite3. Keep it next to bin/. db/ your migrations. Your local SQLite file is not copied. .env.example a copy of the example env file.

docs.title: 2. Run the binary
docs.text:
The binary reads .env from the folder where you start it, so copy your file there:

cd build/bundle
cp ../../.env .env
./bin/server

Migrating: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrated: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrating: 2026_10_25_000000000_create_queue_tables
Migrated: 2026_10_25_000000000_create_queue_tables
Migrating: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
... "message":"Server started at http://[::]:3000 with 8 isolate (native)" ...

The migrations run again, because the bundle has a new database file. The binary has the migration list in it.

On a server you can set real environment variables in place of .env. They win over .env.

docs.title: Check it
docs.text:
Call the binary from a second terminal:

curl http://localhost:3000/api/ping
curl http://localhost:3000/api/posts

pong
[]

The list is empty, because the database file is new. Stop the server with Ctrl+C.

docs.title: 3. Docker
docs.text:
The project has a Dockerfile. It builds the same bundle and copies it into an empty scratch image:

Dockerfile
FROM dart:stable AS build

# Resolve dependencies first, so this layer is cached.
WORKDIR /app
COPY pubspec.* ./
RUN dart pub get

COPY . .
RUN dart pub get --offline

# The dox CLI. `dox build` runs build_runner, then AOT-compiles
# bin/server.dart, bin/queue.dart and bin/schedule.dart with
# `dart build cli`. It puts all of them in build/bundle/bin, the native
# libraries in build/bundle/lib and the migrations in build/bundle/db.
# The queue worker and the scheduler run as their own processes:
# `/app/bin/queue work` and `/app/bin/schedule work`.
RUN dart pub global activate dox
RUN /root/.pub-cache/bin/dox build

# Lay out the final file tree:
# /app/bin/server, /app/bin/queue, /app/bin/schedule, /app/lib (native
# libraries), /app/db/migration, /app/storage and a writable /tmp
# (uploads bigger than 1 MB are streamed to a temp file).
RUN mkdir -p /out/app/storage /out/tmp \
  && chmod 1777 /out/tmp \
  && cp -r build/bundle/. /out/app/

# Minimal serving image: the AOT runtime files from the dart image
# (`/runtime/`) plus our bundle. No Dart SDK, no source code.
FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /runtime/ /
COPY --from=build /out/ /
WORKDIR /app

# Config comes from env variables. The image has no .env file,
# so secrets stay out of it.
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["/app/bin/server"]

Build and run the image. The image has no .env file, so give the config as environment variables. The app key must have exactly 32 characters, or the app does not start:

docker build -t blog .
docker run -p 3000:3000 \
  -e APP_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 16) \
  -e DB_CONNECTION=sqlite \
  -e DB_NAME=storage/blog.sqlite \
  blog

SQLite in Docker

The database file is in the container, so you lose it when you remove the container. Mount a volume for it: -v blog-data:/app/storage. For a busy app, use Postgres or MySQL. See Database.

  • Model: relationships and events.

  • Authentication: all options of the auth package.
  • OpenAPI: API docs from your routes and DTOs.
